Contributions are dual-licensed under the same terms unless you explicitly state otherwise.

items.title: browser-use/browser-use
items.summary: Open-source Python library for AI browser agents, plus Browser Use Cloud: stealth browsers and a hosted agent API. https://browser-use.com The open-source browser agent. Give it a task and the model does it in a real browser by writing Python: one persistent REPL, the browser-harness helpers and raw Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP). Runs on any LLM, locally or on Browser Use Cloud. MIT licensed. ● task: "book the earliest driving test" │ ● model writes a cell new_tab(url); bu.click(41); js(...) │ ● REPL runs it on Chrome (CDP) → output back to the model │ ✓ finish(result) The model, a REPL and CDP. That's the whole agent. Navigate the web like a human does. Find an available slot, pick a date and time, handle the CAPTCHA, and book a driving test. Explore more demos and prompts ↗ AI agents and crawlers: read browser-use.com/llms.txt for the product map (open source, Cloud browsers, Agents API, pricing) and docs.browser-use.com/llms.txt for the documentation index. Browser Use is the open-source browser agent (Python and TypeScript), a $0.02 per browser-hour cloud browser with stealth, CAPTCHA solving and residential proxies, and a hosted agent API. When you add browser-use to a project, pin it exactly (browser-use==1.0.2), never >=: releases move fast and can break APIs. Which Browser Use do I need? Path 1: Fully Hosted Cloud: Scale up with a fully hosted agent and browser. Path 2: CLI: Automate your own browser tasks. Path 3: Python Library: Run the open source Browser Use agent locally from your own code. Quickstart Path 1: Fully Hosted Cloud Scale browser automation with our hosted agent, stealth browsers, and infrastructure for profiles, recordings, and data policies. Get started with the API ↗ New Google, GitHub, or Microsoft signups get $1 cloud credit. Path 2: CLI Paste this prompt into Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw, or your favorite agent. Install browser-use with `uv tool install browser-use==1.0.2`, run `browser-use skill install` to register the skill, and connect it to my browser. If setup or connection fails, run `browser-use --doctor` and follow its output and the error message. Path 3: Python Library browser-use 1.0. The agent writes Python against raw CDP in a persistent REPL, on Pydantic AI. Coming from 0.x? Read MIGRATING.md. Python 3.11 or newer. With uv, or pip in a venv: uv init --python 3.12 my-agent && cd my-agent uv add 'browser-use==1.0.2' export BROWSER_USE_API_KEY=bu_... # get one at https://cloud.browser-use.com/new-api-key python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install 'browser-use==1.0.2' export BROWSER_USE_API_KEY=bu_... Pin the exact version (==, never >=). browser-use moves fast and releases can break things. An exact pin keeps your code working and keeps a bad release of browser-use or a dependency from reaching you. Upgrade on purpose, after reading the release notes. from browser_use import Agent result = Agent('Find the number of stars of the browser-use repo').run_sync() print(result.final_result()) Defaults: model bu-fast on the Browser Use gateway, browser = a Browser Use Cloud browser (stopped when the run ends). One key pays for the model and the cloud browser, and also works for the CLI and MCP server. A .env file works too. Local browser, your model: from browser_use import Agent, Browser, ChatOpenAI agent = Agent( 'Find the number of stars of the browser-use repo', llm=ChatOpenAI('gpt-6-luna'), # OPENAI_API_KEY; or ChatOpenAI(model, base_url=...) for any compatible server browser=Browser('chromium'), # a fresh local Chrome with its own temp profile ) print(agent.run_sync().final_result()) # in async code: result = await agent.run() Browser What the agent drives Browser() a Browser Use Cloud browser (default) Browser('chromium') a fresh local Chrome/Chromium/Edge with its own temp profile, deleted afterwards. Headless when there is no display (Docker, CI); headless=, executable_path=, user_data_dir= (a profile dir kept between runs) Browser('chrome') the Chrome you have open, with your logins (turn on chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging once) Browser('chrome', profile='Work') a new Chrome on a temporary copy of your Chrome profile Work (sync off); your Chrome can stay open, except on Windows Other models: ChatAnthropic, ChatGoogle (both built in), or any Pydantic AI model string such as llm='groq:llama-3.3-70b-versatile' (after pip install 'pydantic-ai-slim[groq]'). Typed results: Agent(task, output_model_schema=MyModel) then result.structured_output. Uploads: put files in Agent(task, workspace=...) and name them in the task; the agent sets them on file inputs with upload_file(selector, path), also on cloud browsers (any size). Downloads: files the browser downloads land in agent.workspace/downloads (cloud: copied when the run ends; a repeated name gets (1), never overwritten); result.downloads lists the run's files. Secrets: Agent(task, sensitive_data={'password': '...'}), or {'https://*.example.com': {'password': '...'}} to type it only on that domain. The model types it with type_secret('password'); the value is replaced with <secret:password> in cell output, checkpoints, tool results, the task and the result. Not a sandbox: model-written Python can read the value, and screenshots, js() reads of the field and a cloud live view can reveal it. Browser('chromium') and Browser('chrome', profile=...) open a debugging port with no authentication on 127.0.0.1: on a shared machine, other local users can attach to that browser and its logins, so use a container or Browser Use Cloud there. See the trust model in MIGRATING.md. Domain restrictions: Browser(allowed_domains=['example.com', '*.example.org']) (or prohibited_domains=, block_ip_addresses=True) with the 0.x patterns, in every browser mode. A guard for an aligned model, not a sandbox: see the FAQ. Follow-ups: agent.add_new_task('...') then await agent.run(); use Browser(keep_alive=True) to keep the same page between runs. Custom tools: plain functions with @tools.action('description'), then Agent(task, tools=tools). Ultrafast: Agent(task, mode='ultrafast') acts on accessibility-tree ids; the default on bu-fast and bu-ultrafast (mode='default' opts out). Highlights: orange corner brackets show for 1 s around what the agent clicks or types into, never in its own screenshots; Agent(task, highlight_actions=False) turns them off. Web search: the agent gets search(query, num_results=None, category=None) (Browser Use web search, billed per search to your Browser Use key; each charge the response reports is added to result.cost_usd) with Agent(task, web_search=True) (off by default; needs a Browser Use key, and can't be combined with allowed_domains). Browser Use Benchmark v2 This very hard benchmark targets the hardest browser tasks. On easier tasks, even smaller models can achieve very high success rates. Results shown are from a 60-task subset of BU Bench V2. Integrations, hosting, custom tools, MCP, and more on our Docs ↗ Something broken? browser-use feedback 'what happened' (or browser_use.feedback(...)) sends it straight to the Browser Use team. FAQ Should I use the fully hosted cloud, CLI, or Python library? Fully Hosted Cloud: Send tasks through the API and let Browser Use run the agent, browser, and infrastructure. CLI: Give an existing agent (Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw, Pi, Cursor, etc.) browser access. You can use it interactively or in scripts. Python Library: Run the open source agent in your own application, with custom tools, structured output, and your choice of model. The CLI and Python library can each connect to a local or cloud browser. A cloud browser hosts the browser; the fully hosted API runs the agent as well. What's the best model to use? The default, bu-fast on the Browser Use gateway, is gpt-6-luna at medium reasoning. llm='bu-ultrafast' runs the same model at low reasoning on the priority tier (fastest), llm='bu-smart' a larger one. ChatOpenAI('gpt-6-luna') with your own OpenAI key runs the same model directly. See the benchmark. Can I use this for free? The Python library is free and MIT-licensed. Model inference and hosted browsers are separate: API providers, including ChatBrowserUse, and Browser Use Cloud charge for usage. You can also use Browser('chromium') with a local model, e.g. Ollama through ChatOpenAI(model, base_url='http://localhost:11434/v1', api_key='ollama'). Terms of Service This open-source library is licensed under the MIT License. For Browser Use services & data policy, see our Terms of Service and Privacy Policy. How do I handle authentication? Local browser: Browser('chrome') drives the Chrome you have open, with your logins; Browser('chrome', profile='Work') uses a copy of that profile; Browser('chromium', user_data_dir='~/bu-profile') keeps its own logins between runs. Cloud browser: Browser(cloud_profile_id='work') keeps logins in a cloud profile; see the profile sync guide. Passwords: pass them as sensitive_data; the model types them with type_secret(name) and their values are redacted from cell output, checkpoints, tool results, the task and the result. Not a sandbox: model-written Python can read them, and screenshots, page JavaScript and a cloud live view can reveal a typed value. How do I solve CAPTCHAs? Browser Use Cloud provides stealth browsers and proxies designed to reduce bot detection and CAPTCHA challenges. With the Python library, Browser() is a cloud browser by default. Cloud browsers also solve CAPTCHAs automatically, and the agent waits for the solver with solve_captcha() instead of clicking the challenge. Browser(captcha_solver=False) turns the solver off. Results depend on the site and challenge; no browser configuration guarantees that every CAPTCHA can be avoided or solved. Can I limit which sites the agent visits? Browser(allowed_domains=['example.com', '*.example.org']), Browser(prohibited_domains=['evil.com']) or Browser(block_ip_addresses=True), with the 0.x patterns, on any browser. The browser helpers refuse a disallowed URL, the browser itself blocks main-frame navigations to it (link clicks, redirects, popups, JavaScript; all modes except Browser('chrome') attached to your open Chrome, where a second debugging connection would prompt you again), every tab still on a disallowed page after a cell is reset to about:blank (in Browser('chrome') only the agent's tabs, never yours), and the system prompt lists the domains. A bare domain in prohibited_domains also covers its subdomains. It is a guard for an aligned model, not a sandbox: requests an allowed page makes to other hosts (fetch, images, iframes) are not filtered, nor is the agent's own Python networking beyond http_get and its redirects. Run untrusted tasks in a container or VM. MIGRATING.md lists exactly what is blocked in each mode. How do I go into production? Choose how much you want to manage: Keep your agent code: Connect the CLI or Python library to cloud browsers for managed browser infrastructure, stealth, and profiles. Have us run the agent too: Use the fully hosted Cloud API to submit tasks and retrieve results. You can also host the Python library and browsers on your own infrastructure. Related Repositories Repository What it's for Browser Use Pi Run a TypeScript browser agent built on Pi. Cloud SDK Integrate Browser Use Cloud into your application. Video Use Edit videos with your coding agent. macOS Harness Give your agent control of Mac apps, browsers, and files. Benchmark Explore browser tasks and compare agent performance. Citation If you use Browser Use in your research or project, please cite: @software{browser_use2024, author = {Müller, Magnus and Žunič, Gregor}, title = {Browser Use: Enable AI to control your browser}, year = {2024}, publisher = {GitHub}, url = {https://github.com/browser-use/browser-use} } Tell your computer what to do, and it gets it done. Made with ❤️ in Zurich and San Francisco

items.title: Build autonomous AI agents with Amazon Bedrock and Spring AI
items.summary: Java teams have established JVM tooling, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines, and operational patterns, yet taking AI agents from prototype to production is hard: agent frameworks do not solve scalability, governance, security, and operational concerns by default. Amazon Bedrock and Spring AI close those gaps, so Java teams can build autonomous AI agents that plan, call tools and APIs, and maintain context across multi-turn conversations. Agentic AI is moving beyond prompt-response interactions toward autonomous systems that execute complex multi-step tasks. Java remains one of the widely used programming languages in enterprise software. Teams have existing CI/CD pipelines, operational expertise, and established patterns built around the JVM. Spring AI brings AI capabilities to the JVM through familiar Spring patterns: auto-configuration, dependency injection, and composable advisors. Developers can build AI agents using the same idioms they use for REST APIs, security, and data access. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. With AgentCore, you can build, deploy, and operate AI agents at scale. It is framework-agnostic and model-agnostic: you bring your preferred agent framework and foundation model (FM). With AgentCore, you can access the production infrastructure you need: managed runtime, memory, browser automation, code execution, and identity management. In this post, we show you how to build autonomous AI agents in Java using Spring AI and Amazon Bedrock with spring-ai-agentcore. We explore the key implementation patterns for two systems. The first is a single-agent travel assistant that demonstrates tool calling and memory. The second is a multi-agent intelligent document processing (IDP) system that shows how specialist agents, a rules engine, and alerting work together. Prerequisites To follow along with this walkthrough, you need the following: Java – JDK 21 (required) Spring Boot – 4.1 (with Spring AI 2.0 and spring-ai-agentcore 2.0) Maven – 3.9+. Node.js – 18+ (for the React frontend) Terraform – 1.5+. Docker – with Buildx for multi-architecture builds. AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) – v2, configured with credentials. An AWS account. What makes a system an agent A chat completion call can generate text, but it can’t decide what to do next, reach into external systems, or remember what happened yesterday. An agent can, because it unites three capabilities: Planning – Given a goal, the model breaks it into steps, prioritizes them, and revises the plan as new information arrives. Tool use – Beyond generating text, the model can select and invoke external functions such as APIs, databases, and code interpreters to act in the world. Memory – Context carries across turns (short-term) and across sessions (long-term), so each decision builds on what came before. A Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) application has limited tool use (retrieval) but no planning loop. An agent has all three, operating in a goal-directed loop until the task is complete or it determines it cannot proceed. The following diagram shows these capabilities in an end-to-end agentic pipeline, from request to grounded answer. Figure 1: Agentic reference architecture. A request flows through the runtime, guardrails, classification, a specialist agent, tools, the foundation model, memory, rules, and human review to a grounded answer, with resilience and observability as cross-cutting concerns The pipeline has 11 stages. A client submits a document and question. The request passes through a runtime gateway for authentication and rate limiting, then input guardrails screen for harmful content. A router classifies the document and routes it to a specialist agent, which plans its workflow and calls tools, the Amazon Bedrock foundation model, memory, and a rules engine as needed. Low-confidence or flagged results go to a human review queue before the grounded answer returns to the client. Resilience, observability, logging, and least-privilege AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) apply across all stages. Solution overview The solution consists of two deployable systems that share common patterns: Travel agent – A single autonomous agent with tool calling (weather lookups, itinerary search), streaming responses, conversation memory, and resilience patterns. This is the recommended starting point. IDP multi-agent system – A multi-agent intelligent document processing platform with five specialist agents (Lawyer, Mortgage, Insurance, Tax, General), rules and workflow engine, alerting, and observability. This demonstrates production patterns at a scale. Both systems share the following architecture: Spring Boot application with Spring AI ChatClient, Spring AI agentcore and Amazon Bedrock Converse API. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, defines the contract (POST /invocations, GET /ping) for managed deployment. Conversation memory through AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, for both short-term and long-term context. Tool calling with @Tool annotated methods. Structured output mapped to Java records. ARM64 container image optimized for AWS Graviton. Modular Terraform for infrastructure provisioning. The travel assistant is the recommended starting point. The following diagram illustrates how a Spring Boot agent interacts with AgentCore runtime, tools, memory, and models available on Amazon Bedrock. Figure 2: Single-agent travel assistant. The Spring Boot application exposes both REST endpoints for the React UI and the AgentCore runtime contract, calling Amazon Bedrock through the Converse API while tool calling, streaming, and memory run inside one code base. The travel assistant runs a single Spring Boot application with two entry points, the /invocations and /ping contract required by AgentCore runtime. Spring AI orchestrates calls to Amazon Bedrock through the Converse API and resolves tool invocations locally inside the same process. Server-Sent Events stream tokens to the client as they are generated. AgentCore memory supplies both short-term context within a session and long-term context across sessions, so the agent retains conversation history without external state management. The following diagram shows the architecture for the IDP multi-agent system. Figure 3: IDP multi-agent system architecture. Specialist agents process documents through a shared ChatClient pattern, with results flowing through a rules engine and alert service. The IDP multi-agent system routes documents through five specialist agents (Lawyer, Mortgage, Insurance, Tax, and General), each built on a shared AbstractDocumentAgent template. A ClassifierAgent reads each document and forwards it to the appropriate specialist. The specialist extracts structured JSON with confidence scores using the multimodal Converse API of Amazon Bedrock. A rules engine evaluates Spring Expression Language (SpEL) expressions from application.yml against the extraction. ALERT or BLOCK severity rules dispatch through the AlertService. Low-confidence documents go to human review. Metrics, audit trail, resilience, and observability apply across all stages. Agent collaboration patterns When multiple agents work together, how they coordinate determines system behavior. This solution uses three patterns: The following diagram compares the three coordination patterns used in this solution. Figure 4: Agent collaboration patterns Three patterns shown side by side. The router dispatches each request to one specialist by document type. The evaluator passes specialist findings through a rules engine that applies to severity levels and dispatches alerts or blocks for human review. The parallel fan-out sends one request to multiple specialists concurrently and aggregates results before the rules engine runs. Router pattern: A lightweight orchestrator examines the incoming request and routes it to the appropriate specialist. In the IDP multi-agent system, the router inspects document type metadata and forwards it to the Lawyer, Mortgage, Insurance, Tax, or General agent. The router holds no domain logic. It is a dispatch layer only. Parallel fan-out (optional extension): The base solution implements the router and evaluator patterns. The batch endpoint processes documents sequentially. When a document needs several perspectives at once, you can add a parallel fan-out as a drop-in extension. Dispatch to specialists concurrently and aggregate their results before the rules engine runs. Wall-clock time for the combined analysis is then bounded by the slowest single agent call rather than the sum of all calls. Evaluator pattern: After specialists return their findings, a rules engine evaluates the combined output against configurable business rules. Rules that trigger ALERT or BLOCK severity dispatch through a pluggable AlertService for human review. Walkthrough The following sections walk you through the key implementation patterns, starting with the AgentCore runtime contract and progressing through tool calling, memory, resilience, and multi-agent orchestration. Fulfilling the AgentCore runtime contract Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime manages agent lifecycle and scaling. For current rates, see Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing and Amazon Bedrock pricing. The runtime routes incoming requests to your agent and monitors its health. Your agent must expose two endpoints: POST /invocations – Receives requests and returns responses as JSON or Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming. GET /ping – Reports health status (Healthy or HealthyBusy). Long-running tasks must signal busy status, or the runtime might scale down the agent. The following diagram shows how the Spring AI developer model maps onto AgentCore runtime, Memory, Browser, Code Interpreter, and Evaluations. Figure 5: Spring AI AgentCore SDK on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Annotations, the ChatClient, tool callbacks, and advisors map through the spring-ai-agentcore SDK onto AgentCore runtime, AgentCore memory, AgentCore Browser, AgentCore Code Interpreter, and AgentCore Evaluations. Two layers connected by the spring-ai-agentcore SDK. The application layer uses Spring AI components: @AgentCoreInvocation for endpoint wiring, ChatClient for model interaction, @Tool callbacks, and advisors for memory and guardrails. The infrastructure layer provides AgentCore runtime, AgentCore memory, AgentCore Browser, AgentCore Code Interpreter, and AgentCore Evaluations, all capabilities of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The SDK bridges both, so developers write standard Spring AI code while AgentCore handles production infrastructure. With the Spring AI AgentCore SDK, a single annotation handles this contract automatically: @Service public class TravelAgent { private final ChatClient chatClient; public TravelAgent(ChatClient.Builder builder) { this.chatClient = builder.build(); } @AgentCoreInvocation public Flux<String> chat(PromptRequest request) { return chatClient.prompt() .user(request.prompt()) .stream() .content(); } } The @AgentCoreInvocation annotation auto-configures the /invocations and /ping endpoints, handles JSON serialization, manages SSE framing for streaming responses, and reports health status. The same project also exposes REST endpoints for the React UI, so the agent serves both AgentCore runtime and a browser from one code base. A note on streaming: the preceding minimal example returns the model stream directly, which is ideal for a chat UI. When an agent makes multi-argument tool calls, assemble the response with a blocking call() and then chunk the result for streaming, so the tool arguments bind reliably. The travel assistant serves both the AgentCore runtime and the React UI from one service method: @RestController public class AgentController { private final AgentService agentService; public AgentController(AgentService agentService) { this.agentService = agentService; } // One annotation wires up POST /invocations + GET /ping, JSON/SSE framing, and health. @AgentCoreInvocation public Flux<String> invoke(PromptRequest request, AgentCoreContext context) { String sessionId = context.getHeader(AgentCoreHeaders.SESSION_ID); return agentService.streamChat(request.prompt(), sessionId, request.guardrailsEnabled(), request.memoryEnabled()); } // The same app also serves the React UI from the same code base. @PostMapping(value = "/api/chat", produces = MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN_VALUE + ";charset=UTF-8") public Flux<String> chatStream(@Valid @RequestBody PromptRequest request) { return agentService.streamChat(request.prompt(), request.sessionId(), request.guardrailsEnabled(), request.memoryEnabled()); } } Implementing tool calling With tool calling, the model can invoke external functions during reasoning. In Spring AI, you annotate a method with @Tool and the model decides when to call it and with what arguments: @Tool(description = "Get a short weather forecast for a city") public String getWeather( @ToolParam(description = "City name") String city) { return forecastService.lookup(city); } You register tools on the ChatClient, and the model decides when to call them: ChatClient chatClient = chatClientBuilder .defaultSystem(properties.getSystemPrompt()) .defaultTools(new DateTimeTools(), new TravelTools()) .build(); For structured output, request a Java record type. For multimodal input, attach media to the user message: ProcessedDocument review = chatClient.prompt() .system(personaSystemPrompt) .user(u -> u.text(question).media(mimeType, fileResource)) .call() .entity(ProcessedDocument.class); Note: We verified this example with Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.5 on Amazon Bedrock. Spring AI adds the record’s schema to the prompt and parses the reply back into the Java type. Behavior can differ for other model families, so refer to the Spring AI structured output documentation and the Amazon Bedrock documentation for current support. It is best-effort, meaning that models can occasionally return output that does not match the schema. For stricter results, use a provider with native schema enforcement or Spring AI validation and retry. The model receives the tool definitions as part of its context, reasons about when a tool call would help satisfy the user request, and returns a structured tool call response. Spring AI intercepts this, invokes the annotated method, and feeds the result back to the model for further reasoning. Adding conversation memory Real-world agents must remember what users said earlier in a conversation (working memory) and what they have learned over time (persistent memory). The Spring AI AgentCore SDK integrates with AgentCore memory through the advisor pattern: interceptors that enrich prompts with context before they reach the model. chatClient.prompt() .advisors(agentCoreMemory.advisors) .advisors(a -> a.param( ChatMemory.CONVERSATION_ID, "user:" + sessionId)) .user(prompt) .stream() .content(); The session ID becomes a conversation ID in actor:session form, so each user’s history stays isolated. For user-facing deployments, derive the actor from a verified OAuth 2.0 (JWT) identity rather than a client-supplied value, so users cannot access one another’s history. In addition, AgentCore memory offers long-term memory support, employing the following strategies to identify and capture key insights from conversations: Semantic – Factual information about users (for example, “User works in finance”) User preference – Explicit settings and choices (for example, “Metric units preferred”) Summary – Condensed conversation history for continuity across sessions. Episodic – Past interactions and lessons learned. Long-term memory extraction is asynchronous and optional. You choose which strategies to enable when you create the memory, and AgentCore extracts and consolidates records in the background after each conversation, so it never blocks the agent’s response. Choose strategies by workload: use user preference for the travel assistant so it remembers units and seating choices. Use summary when sessions span many turns. Use episodic when the agent should reuse lessons from past tasks. And use semantic to retain durable facts about the user. Configuring the rules engine Reading a document is only half the job. Acting on what it finds is the other half. The IDP multi-agent system includes a rules engine so operators can add business checks without touching code. This is an in-process rules evaluator that applies SpEL conditions to extraction results, not a workflow orchestration service such as AWS Step Functions. Rules live in application.yml and each condition is a SpEL expression evaluated against the extraction: idp: review: enabled: ${REVIEW_ENABLED:true} confidence-threshold: ${REVIEW_CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD:0.7} rules: - id: legal-unsigned agentType: LAWYER condition: "field('signaturePresent') == 'false' || missing('signaturePresent')" severity: ALERT message: "Document appears unsigned; get all parties to sign before relying on it." - id: mortgage-high-dti agentType: MORTGAGE condition: "field('dtiRatio') != '' && T(java.lang.Double).parseDouble(field('dtiRatio')) > 0.43" severity: WARN message: "Debt-to-income ratio exceeds 0.43; likely needs manual underwriting." - id: low-confidence agentType: ALL condition: "confidence < 0.6" severity: WARN message: "Low extraction confidence; consider human verification." Severity levels control the engine’s behavior. INFO and WARN are logged, while ALERT dispatches through a pluggable AlertService. The default logs and emits a metric, but you can substitute Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS), Slack, or email by providing your own bean. BLOCK holds the document for manual review. Because rules are operator configuration rather than end user input, they provide a safe and auditable extension point. Adding new workflows is a configuration change, not a deployment. The evaluator pattern is implemented by the rules engine and a pluggable AlertService. The default implementation logs the alert and emits a metric. You provide your own bean to route to Amazon SNS, Slack, or email: public class LoggingAlertService implements AlertService { @Override public void send(RuleResult result, AgentType agentType, ProcessedDocument document) { registry.counter("idp.alerts.sent", "severity", result.severity().name(), "type", agentType.name()).increment(); logger.warn("ALERT [{}] rule={} type={} message=\"{}\"", result.severity(), result.ruleId(), agentType, result.message()); } } Production readiness patterns The following patterns address common production requirements that prototypes typically skip. Resilience Every model call uses a Resilience4j retry with exponential backoff, a circuit breaker that fails fast when model calls repeatedly fail or time out, and a timeout. Streaming paths emit a fallback message instead of a raw error. When traffic exceeds your account and Region service quotas, AgentCore runtime returns HTTP 429 and the retry handles it. For current limits, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore quotas documentation. Twelve-factor configurations Every configurable value (Region, model ID, memory ID, timeouts, rate limits, system prompt) is an environment variable bound to a typed @ConfigurationProperties class. The application is stateless, starts fast, drains in-flight turns on scale-down, and ships as one immutable ARM64 image promoted unchanged from development to production. Security and identity The Agentcore runtime uses AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) authentication by default. For user-facing agents, add an OAuth 2.0 (JWT) authorizer (such as Amazon Cognito) and derive the memory actor ID (actorId) from the verified identity. The IAM execution role follows least privilege: Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) pull. Scoped Amazon CloudWatch Logs and AWS X-Ray. Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel actions. Scoped workload access tokens (GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT) for the agent’s workload identity. AgentCore memory actions limited to the specific Memory resource ARN. AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, enforces inbound authentication (acting as an OAuth 2.0 resource server that validates JWT bearer tokens through Cognito, Okta, Auth0, or your own OIDC provider) and supports configurable rate limiting at the gateway layer. Rate limits are fail-open by default, so they should complement your core security controls rather than replace them. Responsible AI controls Autonomous agents that take real-world actions need safety controls as a first-class concern. The sample ships with a stand-in demonstration of a lightweight in-process pre-check called GuardrailService. This service screens prompts for disallowed intent and prompt injection, toggled per request with the guardrailsEnabled flag. Production deployments use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails as a standard control applied to every request, not a per-request toggle. To upgrade the demo service for production, front the agent with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Guardrails apply configurable policies outside the model call, covering both input and output: Content filtering. Blocks harmful or off-topic content based on configurable thresholds for both prompts and responses. Denied topics. Prevents the agent from engaging with topics you define as out-of-scope. Sensitive information filters. Detects and redacts PII in both prompts and responses, supporting requirements such as GDPR and HIPAA. For agents that retrieve external knowledge, enable grounding checks to reduce hallucination risk before the agent acts on tool calls with real-world side effects. To wire Bedrock Guardrails into Spring AI, implement CallAdvisor and StreamAdvisor functions that call the ApplyGuardrail API and register it with defaultAdvisors on the ChatClient. Because policies live in the guardrail, security teams can update filters independently of the application release cycle. Observability The example instruments with the Micrometer Observation API (@Observed), producing timers that become distributed trace spans when you add a tracing bridge (OTLP to AWS X-Ray). The system emits domain metrics: idp.documents.processed{type,status} idp.extraction.confidence{type} idp.alerts.sent{severity,type} idp.processing.duration{type} These metrics are exposed through /actuator/prometheus. The application also emits structured JSON logs to standard output, which Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime captures in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Optional extension that’s not implemented in this post: The sample includes the Micrometer OpenTelemetry bridge and OTLP exporter dependencies, but this post’s deployment does not provision an OpenTelemetry collector or enable trace sampling. You can add distributed tracing by setting a nonzero TRACING_SAMPLING value, pointing OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT to an OpenTelemetry or AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry collector, and configuring the collector to forward traces to AWS X-Ray. Optional extension that’s not implemented in this post: The sample doesn’t implement an automated evaluation or optimization feedback loop. You can add one by persisting application metrics, traces, audit events, and human-review outcomes as an evaluation dataset. AgentCore evaluations or a separate evaluation pipeline can then compare versioned prompts, models, tools, and routing rules against quality, safety, latency, and cost thresholds. Promote changes only after evaluation and human approval. Deploying the solution This GitHub repository contains two AI agent applications demonstrating different use cases for autonomous AI. This guide shows you how to deploy them to AWS using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime. The following diagram shows the deployment architecture: a single Arm64 image promoted through modular Terraform to the AgentCore runtime, with an optional Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) path. Optional: running on Amazon EKS. Teams already standardized on Kubernetes can run the same Arm64 image on Amazon EKS, using their existing cluster for scaling and health checks against the /ping endpoint, with IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) for scoped, least-privilege pod-level access to Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore memory. The container is identical, so nothing in the application changes. Figure 6: Deployment architecture. Modular Terraform provisions Amazon ECR, a least-privilege IAM execution role, and the Bedrock AgentCore runtime, with an optional Amazon EKS and IRSA path that reuses the same Arm64 image. Three stages: build and publish, Terraform, and runs on AWS. The CI pipeline packages the application into a linux/arm64 image and pushes it to Amazon ECR with immutable tags. Three Terraform modules provision the ECR repository, a least-privilege IAM execution role, and the AgentCore runtime. The agent runs serverlessly on AgentCore runtime, calling Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore memory. An optional Amazon EKS path reuses the same image with IRSA for scoped pod-level credentials. Follow these steps to deploy either application. Step 1: Clone the repository Open your terminal and run: git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-build-autonomous-ai-agents-with-amazon-bedrock-and-spring-ai.git Step 2: Navigate to the directory for the agent you want to deploy Deploy autonomous agent: cd build-autonomous-ai-agents-with-amazon-bedrock-and-spring-ai/code/autonomous-agent Deploy IDP multi-agent system: cd build-autonomous-ai-agents-with-amazon-bedrock-and-spring-ai/code/idp-agent Step 3: Configure Terraform variables Before deploying the infrastructure, configure your Terraform variables in the terraform.tfvars file located in the terraform directory. Basic configuration The solution uses default values for most settings, but you can customize the following in your terraform.tfvars file: AWS Region: The AWS Region where resources are deployed. Environment: Environment ID (such as dev or prod) used in resource naming. bedrock_model: Amazon Bedrock foundation model (for example: global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0). For model availability by Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock. Step 4: Run the deployment script For Linux/macOS: ./scripts/deploy.sh dev For Windows PowerShell: .\scripts\deploy.ps1 dev The deployment script does the following: Create an Amazon ECR repository. Build the Java application. Create and push a Docker container image. Create an IAM execution role. Deploy the AgentCore runtime. Step 5: Run the application Once the deployment is complete, you can run the application using the following commands. For Linux/macOS: ./scripts/run.sh dev For Windows PowerShell: .\scripts\run.ps1 dev Cleaning up AgentCore runtime scales to zero and bills per invocation, so an idle agent costs almost nothing. Your main variable cost is Amazon Bedrock token usage, plus a small amount for Amazon CloudWatch and Amazon ECR storage. For current rates, see Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing and Amazon Bedrock pricing. To avoid incurring future charges, tear down the infrastructure when you are finished: For Linux/macOS: ./scripts/cleanup.sh dev For Windows PowerShell: .\scripts\cleanup.ps1 dev Delete any AgentCore memory resources and Amazon ECR images you no longer need using the AWS CLI. Conclusion In this post, you learned how to build autonomous AI agents in Java using Spring AI and Amazon Bedrock. We covered the three capabilities that turn a model into an agent: planning, tool use, and memory. We also showed how Amazon Bedrock AgentCore services carry an agent to production. The Spring AI AgentCore SDK maps these capabilities onto idiomatic Spring through annotations and a familiar ChatClient. Finally, we outlined architecture patterns for multi-agent collaboration. These include the router pattern, the evaluator pattern implemented by the rules engine, and parallel fan-out as an optional extension. The key takeaway for Java teams: you do not need to leave your environment to build production-quality agents. The patterns you already trust (dependency injection, configuration properties, advisors, Actuator, Micrometer) carry directly into the agentic world. AgentCore supplies the runtime, memory, identity, and governance that production demands. As next steps, consider the following: Connect enterprise systems through AgentCore Gateway and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) Add Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the fully managed RAG capability, and web search so the agent reasons over your data. Implement Amazon Cognito JWT authentication with per-user memory isolation. Customize Amazon Bedrock Guardrails policies: add domain-specific denied topics, tighten content-filtering thresholds, and enable grounding checks tuned to your knowledge sources. Use AgentCore Evaluations to score production traces and promote prompt or model changes after review. Each is an incremental addition to the foundation you have built here, not a rewrite. About the authors Viquar Khan Viquar is a Senior Data Architect at AWS. With over 22 years of expertise spanning data engineering, AI/ML, and generative AI, he transforms complex data challenges into scalable, production-ready solutions. He is a published author and open source contributor and has major contribution on Spring AI agentcore. Mahammadali Saheb Mahammadali is a Senior Delivery Consultant at AWS Professional Services, specializing in Data Analytics and AI. He is passionate about helping customers drive business outcomes through data analytics and AI solutions on AWS.

items.title: Build composable, interoperable multi-agent systems with A2A on AWS
items.summary: Agents in multi-agent systems that span organizational boundaries often need to collaborate in a composable, interoperable way, with agents that other organizations build and run. They need a way to discover each other, communicate, and exchange tasks without exposing internals or requiring the same framework on both sides. The Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol addresses this constraint. Without A2A, building composable multi-agent systems across organizational boundaries requires custom integration code for each customer and framework. Independent software vendors (ISVs) can instead build composable, interoperable agents that work with the A2A-compatible frameworks their customers already use. While we frame this post around the ISV use case, the pattern also applies to organizations that expose agents across boundaries, whether to partners, customers, or internal teams that use different frameworks. As your system grows, you add skills by registering Agent Cards with the orchestrator, without changing the agents already running. In this post, we walk through a deployed reference architecture on AWS. A LangChain-based enterprise orchestrator communicates with a Strands Agents-based software as a service (SaaS) agent across organizational boundaries using A2A, with the enterprise and the SaaS provider in separate AWS accounts. Neither side depends on the other’s framework or SDK, and the two sides share no secrets. We cover the architecture and implementation patterns, then deploy the system from three Jupyter notebooks and run an end-to-end test. The A2A protocol is now a Linux Foundation project, and AWS is among the organizations that support it. With A2A, agents can discover each other, negotiate tasks, and collaborate across organizational boundaries through a standardized protocol. The protocol uses existing authentication standards such as OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (OIDC) for cross-boundary security, and is designed to work across A2A-compatible frameworks. In Open Protocols for Agent Interoperability Part 4: Inter-Agent Communication on A2A, we introduced A2A concepts and demonstrated two Strands agents communicating using the protocol on AWS. That post established the foundation with Agent Card discovery, structured task execution, and the A2A server pattern. This post builds on that foundation with cross-framework interoperability, cross-organizational trust boundaries, and OAuth in both directions. Solution overview Three agents run in two AWS accounts, one for the enterprise and one for the SaaS provider. The A2A protocol connects them, with OAuth authentication in both directions. Each account has its own Amazon Cognito user pool, so each side authenticates with its own identity provider. Figure 1: A2A agents across an enterprise account and a SaaS provider account During onboarding, the enterprise and the SaaS provider exchange only public values, such as identity provider URLs, client IDs, scopes, and endpoint URLs. Each side then trusts tokens from the other side’s user pool, and no secrets are shared. After onboarding, each request follows these steps: The enterprise app gets an access token from the enterprise’s Amazon Cognito user pool. The app sends a question over HTTPS to the user API in Amazon API Gateway, then polls for the answer. Amazon API Gateway forwards the request privately, through a VPC link and an internal Network Load Balancer, to the Enterprise Orchestrator, a LangChain agent. When its model decides that the question needs a compliance scan, the orchestrator gets its own token from the enterprise user pool, using a client secret stored in AWS Secrets Manager. The orchestrator sends an A2A request to the compliance SaaS agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, using the skill it read from the agent’s Agent Card at startup. The compliance agent checks the enterprise context agent’s Agent Card at the callback URL registered at onboarding, then gets a token from the SaaS provider’s own pool. The compliance agent calls back to the enterprise context agent for account metadata, finishes its scan, and returns the answer to the orchestrator and then to the app. On the enterprise side, two agents run on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate. The Enterprise Orchestrator is the entry point for users. LangChain provides the agent framework and tool-calling abstractions, and Amazon Bedrock provides the foundation models (FMs) that power each agent’s reasoning. The orchestrator uses LangChain and Amazon Bedrock (Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6). At startup, the orchestrator fetches the SaaS agent’s Agent Card from its well-known URL and creates a LangChain tool for each skill described on the card. The model then decides which tool to call based on the user’s question, so the orchestrator needs no hardcoded routing logic. It sends compliance scan requests over A2A with OAuth bearer tokens and summarizes the results for leadership. Users reach the orchestrator through an Amazon API Gateway HTTPS endpoint that accepts only tokens from the enterprise’s own pool. The second enterprise agent provides internal context. The Enterprise Context Agent is built with LangChain and Amazon Bedrock (Amazon Nova Lite). It provides internal account metadata such as internal policy rules, data classification, business criticality, and escalation contacts (team on-call rotations). The deployed agent uses the official a2a-sdk (AgentCard, AgentExecutor, and spec-conformant JSON-RPC routes), pinned to a2a-sdk[http-server]==1.2.2. The SaaS agent reaches the context agent through an API Gateway partner API that accepts only the SaaS provider’s callback token. Both enterprise agents run in private subnets of an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), with no public IP addresses. On the SaaS provider side, the Compliance SaaS Agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in the SaaS provider’s own AWS account. Built with the Strands Agents SDK, it checks AWS accounts against the enterprise’s own internal policies, such as no public storage in production and encryption at rest for confidential data. In production, the scanning tools would connect to services such as AWS Config, AWS Security Hub, or Amazon GuardDuty. For this demo, the agent uses synthetic data that simulates compliance findings across multiple accounts. Before it scans, the SaaS agent calls back to the Enterprise Context Agent for enterprise context, such as which accounts are production, which internal policies apply, and who to escalate to. This bidirectional pattern makes the agents true peers instead of a client and a server. The callback goes only to the address the customer registered at onboarding. The key design decision is to use A2A for all cross-boundary communication. The enterprise has no access to the SaaS agent’s internal tools, system prompt, or model choice. This separation means the ISV can change its internal architecture without changing customer integrations, as long as its Agent Card and A2A interface stay compatible. The SaaS card publishes one curated skill, not its internal tool names. Amazon Bedrock provides API access to multiple foundation models, so each agent can use the model that fits its workload. In this solution, the orchestrator and SaaS agent use Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 for complex reasoning, while the context agent uses Amazon Nova Lite for metadata lookups. You can choose different models based on your own requirements. A2A and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) solve different problems in this architecture. MCP connects an agent to its own tools and data sources in a client-server model. A2A connects agents to other agents as peers, where neither side exposes its internals. In production, the SaaS agent could use MCP internally to connect to its compliance scanning tools while exposing itself externally through A2A. The external interface stays the same regardless of how the agent connects to its internal tools. Prerequisites The notebooks contain the complete deployment procedure. Before you run them, you need the following: Two AWS accounts, one for the enterprise and one for the SaaS provider, in the same AWS Region: us-east-1, us-east-2, or us-west-2. In both accounts, access to Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 in Amazon Bedrock, and in the enterprise account, access to Amazon Nova Lite. Before the first run, submit the Anthropic first-time use form in each account, and give the identity you run the notebooks with the AWS Marketplace permissions listed in the Amazon Bedrock model access documentation. Model availability varies by Region. Check the Amazon Bedrock model availability documentation for the current list. A Jupyter environment with Python 3.10 or later, either: On your computer: JupyterLab, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) version 2, and an AWS IAM Identity Center profile for each account, set up with aws configure sso. You don’t need Docker: AWS CodeBuild builds the container images. Or an Amazon SageMaker AI notebook instance in each account (ml.t3.medium is enough). See the Guide to getting set up with Amazon SageMaker AI. In each account, an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role with permissions to create AWS CloudFormation stacks and the resources in them. Each notebook lists the exact permissions in its Reference section. See the IAM User Guide. Notebook 3 also runs the end-to-end test described later in this post, so you can verify the deployment. Running this solution incurs charges for the resources it creates. In the enterprise account, the main always-on resources are a NAT gateway, two AWS Fargate tasks, the internal Network Load Balancer, and two interface VPC endpoints. Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore charge for what you use. Prices vary by AWS Region. See the pricing pages for Amazon VPC, AWS Fargate, Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Elastic Load Balancing. Run the Clean up sections when you finish. Implement the solution Deploy the system with three notebooks, run in order with Jupyter, one cell at a time. Notebook 1 (enterprise account, about 3 minutes) creates the enterprise identity and writes an onboarding request. Notebook 2 (SaaS provider account, about 5 minutes) deploys the compliance agent and writes an onboarding response. Notebook 3 (enterprise account, about 20 minutes) deploys the enterprise agents and runs the tests. The onboarding files hold only public values. Clone the GitHub repository, and set up two AWS profiles for local runs, or one notebook instance per account with the repository cloned to each. Run notebook 1 in the enterprise account. Give onboarding-request.json to the SaaS provider. Run notebook 2 in the SaaS provider account. Give onboarding-response.json back to the enterprise. Run notebook 3 in the enterprise account. After testing, run notebook 3’s Clean up, then notebook 2’s. The following sections explain the key implementation patterns behind the deployment. Together, they demonstrate three capabilities: Interoperability across frameworks – A LangChain orchestrator calls a Strands agent using A2A, with neither side depending on the other’s SDK. Composability across organizational boundaries – An ISV’s compliance agent and an enterprise’s context agent compose into a workflow that neither team built alone. Bidirectional collaboration with OAuth – Agents act as peers, calling each other across trust boundaries with token-based authentication. With A2A, the ISV in this scenario replaces multiple custom integration paths with a single protocol-based interface. Build the SaaS compliance agent Build the ISV’s compliance agent with the Strands Agents SDK and deploy it to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. For this demo, the scanning tools return synthetic compliance findings. The agent exposes three compliance tools using the Strands @tool decorator (listing available accounts, running compliance scans, and retrieving remediation steps), plus a fourth that calls back to the enterprise, covered in the next section. The Agent Card doesn’t list these tools. It publishes one curated skill, so callers’ models see what the product does, not how it’s built. This simplified example shows the scanning tool: from strands import Agent, ToolContext, tool from strands.models.bedrock import BedrockModel from strands.multiagent.a2a import A2AServer @tool def run_compliance_scan(account_id: str) -> dict: """Run a compliance scan on a specific AWS account. Args: account_id: The AWS account ID to scan (e.g., acc-12345) """ if account_id not in ACCOUNTS: return {"error": f"Account {account_id} not found."} findings = COMPLIANCE_FINDINGS.get(account_id, []) non_compliant = [f for f in findings if f["status"] == "NON_COMPLIANT"] return { "account_id": account_id, "account_name": ACCOUNTS[account_id]["name"], "scan_summary": { "total_rules_checked": len(findings), "compliant": len(findings) - len(non_compliant), "non_compliant": len(non_compliant), "critical_findings": len([f for f in non_compliant if f["severity"] == "CRITICAL"]), "high_findings": len([f for f in non_compliant if f["severity"] == "HIGH"]), }, "findings": findings, } Enable the bidirectional callback This is where the solution goes beyond typical agent integrations. Most agent-to-agent demos show one-way request and response, where a client agent calls a server agent and waits for the result. That pattern breaks down when the called agent needs information that only the caller has. In production, agents need to be peers that can call each other. The SaaS compliance agent needs enterprise context. Examples include which accounts are production, which internal policies apply, and who to escalate to. This is information that only the enterprise has. The SaaS agent calls back over A2A, but only to the callback URL the customer registered at onboarding. It first verifies the customer’s public context card there, then gets a token from the SaaS provider’s own Cognito pool, and sends message/send to the enterprise partner API: def _call_enterprise_context(message_text: str, inbound_task_id: str = "-") -> str: if not CALLBACK_URL_VALID: # checked once at import raise CallbackUnavailable("CALLBACK_URL is not a registered callback URL") cfg = _load_callback_config() # this SaaS provider's own client, from Secrets Manager _verify_context_card(cfg) # anonymous GET of the card at CALLBACK_URL, no redirects rpc_id = f"req-{uuid4().hex}" payload = { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": rpc_id, "method": "message/send", "params": { "message": { "role": "user", "parts": [{"kind": "text", "text": message_text}], "messageId": uuid4().hex, } }, } for attempt in (1, 2): token = _fetch_token(cfg, force=attempt > 1) # from the SaaS provider's own Cognito pool try: resp = _post_callback(CALLBACK_URL, payload, token) ... Every failure, from an unverified card to a rejected token, gives the model one message, “Enterprise context unavailable”, and the details stay in the SaaS provider’s logs. Expose the agent over A2A on AgentCore The A2AServer class from the Strands SDK handles the A2A protocol, Agent Card generation, and JSON-RPC message handling. The server publishes one curated skill and declares on the card how a caller gets a token: a2a_server = SecuredA2AServer( # A2AServer plus the card's securitySchemes agent_factory=create_compliance_agent, http_url=AGENT_URL, serve_at_root=True, skills=[COMPLIANCE_SCAN_SKILL], # one curated skill, not the internal tools enable_a2a_compliant_streaming=True, ) When deployed to AgentCore, this automatically generates an Agent Card at /.well-known/agent-card.json. The Agent Card is a JSON document that describes the agent’s name, capabilities, and skills. A2A-compatible clients can fetch this card and understand what the agent can do without documentation or SDK integration. Build the enterprise orchestrator with LangChain This is the interoperability proof. The enterprise orchestrator uses LangChain, deliberately different from the Strands-based SaaS agent. It uses raw httpx HTTP calls with A2A JSON-RPC and doesn’t depend on the Strands SDK. If the ISV switched from Strands to another A2A-compatible framework, the enterprise orchestrator would keep working without changes, as long as the SaaS agent still speaks A2A and publishes a compatible Agent Card. That is what protocol-level interoperability means in practice. The orchestrator gets a token from the enterprise’s own Cognito pool and sends the JSON-RPC payload over HTTPS only to the agent URL pinned to the address it fetched the Agent Card from. This abridged code shows the core A2A client: from langchain_aws import ChatBedrock from langchain_core.tools import tool as langchain_tool from langchain.agents import create_agent llm = ChatBedrock( model_id="us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6", region_name=AWS_REGION, max_tokens=4096, config=BEDROCK_CLIENT_CONFIG, # timeouts and standard retries guardrails=GUARDRAIL_CONFIG, # this account's guardrail on every model call ) def send_a2a_message(agent_url: str, message_text: str) -> str: # agent_url is the pinned agent URL from discovery: the address the Agent Card # was fetched from, never a value from a caller or a message. rpc_id = f"lc-{uuid4().hex}" payload = { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": rpc_id, "method": "message/send", "params": { "message": { "role": "user", "parts": [{"kind": "text", "text": message_text}], "messageId": uuid4().hex, } }, } def _post(token: str, attempt: int) -> httpx.Response: headers = {"Content-Type": "application/json", "Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"} with httpx.Client(timeout=_A2A_TIMEOUT) as client: # Timeout(300.0, connect=5.0); httpx doesn't follow redirects by default resp = client.post(agent_url, json=payload, headers=headers) resp.raise_for_status() return resp # get_bearer_token() raises when there is no valid client config and never returns # an empty token, so no request goes out without one (fail closed). token = get_bearer_token() try: resp = _post(token, 1) except httpx.HTTPStatusError as e: # On a 401, force one token refresh and retry once. if e.response.status_code == 401: resp = _post(_fetch_token(force=True), 2) else: raise ... Discover agents and route requests with the LLM At startup, the orchestrator fetches Agent Cards from configured ISV URLs. It reads the skill descriptions from each card and creates a LangChain tool for each skill. The orchestrator’s large language model (LLM), Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, then decides which tool to call based on the user’s question. This simplified code shows the pattern: def _tool_name_part(text: str) -> str: """Reduce card text to the characters Bedrock allows in a tool name (letters, digits, _).""" return re.sub(r"[^A-Za-z0-9_]+", "_", str(text)).strip("_") or "agent" def build_langchain_tools(agents: list[dict]) -> list: """Create a LangChain tool for each skill in each discovered agent.""" tools = [] for agent in agents: agent_url = agent["url"] agent_name = _tool_name_part(agent["name"]) for skill in agent["skills"]: skill_name = _tool_name_part(skill["name"]) skill_description = skill.get("description", "") examples = skill.get("examples", []) # Build a descriptive tool name and description tool_name = f"{agent_name}__{skill_name}"[:64] tool_description = ( f"{skill_description} " f"(External agent: {agent['name']})" ) if examples: tool_description += f" Examples: {'; '.join(examples[:3])}" # Create a closure to capture agent_url for this specific tool def make_tool(name: str, desc: str, url: str): def call_external_agent(question: str) -> str: """Send a natural language question to an external agent via A2A protocol.""" return send_a2a_message(url, question) call_external_agent.__name__ = name call_external_agent.__doc__ = desc return langchain_tool(call_external_agent) tools.append(make_tool(tool_name, tool_description, agent_url)) # (A catch-all tool for an agent whose card lists no skills is omitted here.) return tools agent_tools = build_langchain_tools(discovered_agents) # from the Agent Cards fetched at startup agent_executor = create_agent(llm, agent_tools, system_prompt=SYSTEM_PROMPT) As a result, when the ISV adds or changes a capability, its Agent Card changes with it, and the orchestrator picks up the new skills the next time it restarts. The two teams don’t need to coordinate the change. Build the enterprise context agent The enterprise context agent uses LangChain and Amazon Nova Lite for enterprise metadata lookups, and exposes its capabilities over A2A using the official a2a-sdk. The SDK handles Agent Card serving, JSON-RPC routing, and protocol conformance. Because A2A is JSON-RPC over HTTP, a standard web framework can serve it. The orchestrator shows the client side: it sends A2A requests with plain httpx and no A2A SDK. The agent also publishes its own Agent Card at /.well-known/agent-card.json, which the SaaS agent checks before it calls back. This is the same discovery mechanism used in the other direction. The A2A specification defines Agent Cards, so they don’t depend on the framework that builds the agent. Set up cross-boundary OAuth with Amazon Cognito Agent-to-agent communication across organizational boundaries without authentication isn’t acceptable to most enterprises. Every A2A task request (message/send) in this solution carries a JSON Web Token (JWT). Each side authenticates with a token from its own identity provider, and the receiving side accepts only that provider, one client, and one scope. The only unauthenticated endpoint is the enterprise context agent’s Agent Card, which publishes descriptive metadata so callers can discover the agent. The solution uses Amazon Cognito as the OAuth provider. The same pattern can use another OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider that issues signed JWT access tokens, after you update the sample’s Cognito-specific checks. The authentication flow involves four components: Amazon Cognito: one user pool per account. The enterprise pool issues tokens to the orchestrator and to the enterprise app, and the SaaS pool issues tokens to the SaaS agent for its callback. You can view them in the Amazon Cognito console. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is configured with the enterprise pool’s discovery URL, the orchestrator’s client ID, and one scope. It validates the JWT on every incoming A2A request: {"customJWTAuthorizer": { "discoveryUrl": "https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/<enterprise pool ID>/.well-known/openid-configuration", "allowedClients": ["<a2a-enterprise-orchestrator-saas client ID>"], "allowedScopes": ["a2a-enterprise-compliance-saas/invoke"] }} Amazon API Gateway uses JWT authorizers. The partner API accepts only the SaaS provider’s callback token, and the user API accepts only the enterprise app’s token. View the configuration in the Amazon API Gateway console. AWS Secrets Manager in each account stores that account’s client secret, and an IAM grant and a resource policy that denies every other principal limit each secret to the one workload that uses it. No secret is hardcoded or shared with the other account. You can manage secrets in the AWS Secrets Manager console. This AWS CloudFormation snippet shows the partner API’s JWT authorizer: # Trusts only the SaaS provider's pool, its callback client, and its callback scope. ContextApiAuthorizer: Type: AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Authorizer Properties: ApiId: !ImportValue Fn::Sub: '${IdentityStackName}-PartnerApiId' AuthorizerType: JWT Name: saas-jwt IdentitySource: - '$request.header.Authorization' JwtConfiguration: Audience: [!Ref SaasCallbackClientId] Issuer: !Ref SaasIssuer ContextApiRoute: Type: AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Route Properties: RouteKey: 'POST /' AuthorizationType: JWT AuthorizerId: !Ref ContextApiAuthorizer AuthorizationScopes: [!Ref SaasCallbackScope] # ApiId and Target omitted One detail of machine-to-machine authentication is a common source of errors when you wire OAuth between API Gateway and AgentCore. An Amazon Cognito client-credentials access token carries client_id and scope, but no aud claim. When aud is absent, the API Gateway JWT authorizer checks client_id against the audience list. On the AgentCore side, configure allowedClients and leave allowedAudience unset. Deploy the system with notebooks The notebooks run the whole deployment from Jupyter. They deploy five AWS CloudFormation stacks, three in the enterprise account and two in the SaaS provider account. The enterprise infrastructure and services stacks are separate because of a chicken-and-egg problem: the ECS services need Docker images, but CloudFormation creates the Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repositories that hold those images. You can monitor the stacks in the AWS CloudFormation console. The notebooks surface failures early. Each notebook first checks Amazon Bedrock model access with a short test call, before anything is deployed, and each step stops at the first error with clear output. The Clean up sections sit at the bottom of notebooks 2 and 3, after a stop cell, so Run All never reaches them. Understand Agent Cards and discovery Agent Cards make discovery possible without agreeing on tool definitions in advance. Without them, the enterprise would need documentation, an SDK, or a meeting with the ISV’s engineering team to understand what the compliance agent can do. With Agent Cards, the enterprise orchestrator fetches a single JSON document. It immediately knows the agent’s name, capabilities, and skills, programmatically, at runtime. This is the card the compliance agent publishes for one customer, abridged: { "name": "Compliance SaaS Agent", "description": "Scans AWS accounts for compliance with your organization's policies and returns findings by severity with remediation steps.", "url": "https://bedrock-agentcore.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/runtimes/.../invocations/", "protocolVersion": "0.3.0", "capabilities": { "streaming": true }, "skills": [ { "id": "compliance-scan", "name": "Compliance scan", "description": "Scans your AWS accounts against your organization's policies and returns findings by severity, remediation steps with estimated effort, and your escalation contacts when available." } ], "securitySchemes": { "cognito": { "type": "oauth2", "description": "OAuth 2.0 client credentials from the customer's identity provider, registered at onboarding.", "flows": { "clientCredentials": { "tokenUrl": "https://a2a-enterprise-<account-id>.auth.us-east-1.amazoncognito.com/oauth2/token", "scopes": { "a2a-enterprise-compliance-saas/invoke": "Invoke the compliance agent" } } } } }, "security": [ { "cognito": ["a2a-enterprise-compliance-saas/invoke"] } ] } Each skill’s description becomes a tool docstring, so the orchestrator’s model routes each request to the right agent. The two teams never had to agree on tool definitions or share an SDK. The card also declares how a caller authenticates. The orchestrator checks that declaration rather than following it: it keeps the card only if it names the token endpoint and scope registered at onboarding. Test end-to-end Notebook 3 runs one end-to-end test through both accounts. It gets a token for the enterprise app, submits a question, and polls for the result: # A token for the enterprise's own user client. The secret is read from this account's # Cognito pool in memory and discarded; it is never printed or typed. secret = cognito.describe_user_pool_client( UserPoolId=ENT_POOL_ID, ClientId=ORCH_USER_CLIENT_ID)["UserPoolClient"]["ClientSecret"] r = requests.post(TOKEN_ENDPOINT, auth=(ORCH_USER_CLIENT_ID, secret), allow_redirects=False, timeout=15, data={"grant_type": "client_credentials", "scope": "a2a-enterprise-orchestrator/ask"}) del secret auth = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {r.json()['access_token']}"} # Submit (HTTP 202 and a job ID), then poll every 5 seconds r = requests.post(f"{ORCH_API_URL}/jobs", headers=auth, allow_redirects=False, timeout=30, json={"question": "Scan our production accounts for compliance with our internal " "policies, and include escalation contacts " "for critical findings."}) job_id = r.json()["job_id"] while (job := requests.get(f"{ORCH_API_URL}/jobs/{job_id}", headers=auth, allow_redirects=False, timeout=30).json())["status"] not in ("succeeded", "failed"): time.sleep(5) del auth print(job["response"]) The orchestrator discovers the SaaS agent through its Agent Card and routes the request over A2A. The SaaS agent calls back to the enterprise context agent for account metadata (bidirectional A2A), runs compliance scans with its internal tools, combines everything into an enriched report, and sends it back. The response contains data from both agents. This shows that two independently built agents, on different frameworks and different infrastructure, can compose into a workflow that neither produces alone. The test passes only if the reply has compliance findings, includes an on-call rotation code that only the enterprise context agent knows, and the partner API’s access log shows a 200 from the SaaS callback client. Together they show that the callback worked. Notebook 3 then runs seven trust boundary checks that send a wrong, missing, or forged token to each gate, and every call must be rejected. This is abridged output from a test run (IDs are placeholders): [22:53:27] INFO Step E11 End-to-end test: submit a job and poll it (usually about 1 to 3 min; waits up to 10) ... [22:53:27] INFO POST /jobs: HTTP 202 (apigw-requestid=<request-id>) [22:53:27] INFO job_id=<job-id> [22:53:27] INFO job status: running [22:54:08] INFO job status: succeeded ------------------------------------------------------------------ [22:54:19] INFO partner API access log: 28/Oct/2026:22:53:31 +0000 POST / status=200 clientId=<callback-client-id> requestId=<request-id> [22:54:19] INFO [ok ] Compliance findings (SaaS agent) [22:54:19] INFO [ok ] Context-only marker (context agent, through the callback) [22:54:19] INFO [ok ] Partner API access log: 200 for POST / from the SaaS callback client [22:54:19] INFO PASS E11: job <job-id> has compliance findings and a context-only marker, and the partner API logged the callback [22:54:19] INFO done in 52.5s [22:54:51] INFO Step E12 Trust boundary checks: each token works only where it's trusted ... [22:54:52] INFO 1 orchestrator-saas token on the partner API POST /: 401 as expected (www-authenticate='Bearer scope="a2a-saas-customer-callback/invoke" error="invalid_token" error_description="unable to find an appropriate key in the JWKS. ..."', apigw-requestid=<request-id>, x-amzn-requestid=-) [22:54:52] INFO 2 orchestrator-user token on the partner API POST /: 401 as expected (www-authenticate='Bearer scope="a2a-saas-customer-callback/invoke" error="invalid_token" error_description="unable to find an appropriate key in the JWKS. ..."', apigw-requestid=<request-id>, x-amzn-requestid=-) [22:54:52] INFO 3a orchestrator-user token on the SaaS runtime Agent Card: 401 as expected (www-authenticate='Bearer resource_metadata="...", scope="a2a-enterprise-compliance-saas/invoke"', apigw-requestid=-, x-amzn-requestid=<request-id>) [22:54:53] INFO 3b orchestrator-user token on the SaaS runtime message/send: 401 as expected (www-authenticate='Bearer resource_metadata="...", scope="a2a-enterprise-compliance-saas/invoke"', apigw-requestid=-, x-amzn-requestid=<request-id>) [22:54:53] INFO 4 no token on POST /jobs: 401 as expected (www-authenticate='Bearer', apigw-requestid=<request-id>, x-amzn-requestid=-) [22:54:53] INFO 5 orchestrator-saas token on the user API POST /jobs: 401 as expected (www-authenticate='Bearer scope="a2a-enterprise-orchestrator/ask" error="invalid_token" error_description="the token does not have a valid audience"', apigw-requestid=<request-id>, x-amzn-requestid=-) [22:54:53] INFO 6 forged SaaS-issuer token (invalid signature) on the partner API POST /: 401 as expected (www-authenticate='Bearer scope="a2a-saas-customer-callback/invoke" error="invalid_token" error_description="unable to find an appropriate key in the JWKS. ..."', apigw-requestid=<request-id>, x-amzn-requestid=-) [22:54:53] INFO PASS E12: all seven trust boundary checks passed; each token works only where it's trusted [22:54:53] INFO done in 1.4s In that run, the report covered two production accounts and six findings, with the escalation contacts for each account. You can send the same request from any HTTP client, without an A2A SDK. Production considerations This demo simplifies several areas for clarity. For production, consider these changes: One runtime per customer, or a front door that accepts several customer identity providers, with per-customer callback clients. Key-based client authentication (private_key_jwt or mutual TLS) instead of client secrets. AWS PrivateLink for private connectivity, and TLS inside the VPC for end-to-end encryption. Customer managed AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys for Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Amazon ECR, AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. VPC Flow Logs and Network Load Balancer access logs. Both API Gateway stages already write access logs. A Secrets Manager rotation function for the Cognito client credentials. An authenticated onboarding portal or API instead of files. If calls through API Gateway intermittently return HTTP 503, check that cross-zone load balancing is on for the internal Network Load Balancer. Each ECS service runs a single task that can start in either Availability Zone. The repository’s README covers the full list in Security controls and Considerations for production. Security considerations Deploy this solution only in sandbox accounts with no customer or business data, and delete the stacks after testing. The sample uses synthetic data only, with no personal data. Its compliance agent checks example internal policies. It doesn’t assess or certify compliance with any law, regulation, or standard. The sample includes the following controls. You’re responsible for reviewing and adapting them before you use this pattern in production: Transport encryption. Every cross-account call uses HTTPS to Amazon API Gateway or Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and every route except the context agent’s public Agent Card requires a Cognito JWT. Guardrails. In this sample, each model call uses an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with prompt-attack and harmful-content filters, and text from the other organization is checked against the same guardrail before a model uses it. Least-privilege IAM. Each workload has its own role that names exact ARNs. Only the orchestrator and the compliance agent can read a secret, each only its own. Container hardening. ECS containers run with a read-only root filesystem and all Linux capabilities dropped. The base image is pinned by digest. Account isolation. The two accounts share no secret, key, or IAM permission. They exchange only public values. Clean up resources To avoid ongoing charges, delete all resources when you have finished testing. Run the Clean up section at the bottom of notebook 3, then notebook 2, one cell at a time. The last cell in each section confirms that nothing is left. After cleanup, check the AWS CloudFormation, Amazon ECR, and Amazon Cognito consoles in both accounts, and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console in the SaaS provider account, to confirm that no resources remain. Conclusion This post showed how to build a multi-agent system where agents from different organizations, built on different frameworks, collaborate through A2A on AWS. A LangChain orchestrator on Amazon ECS communicates with a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Neither side needs the other’s framework or SDK. The SaaS agent calls back to the enterprise context agent for account metadata, and each side authenticates with its own identity provider. A new skill from the same ISV requires no changes to the code. Adding a second ISV takes one extension, because the orchestrator holds a single OAuth client today: give it one client and scope per ISV, as the README’s Considerations for production describes. Then run the same onboarding exchange, add its Agent Card URL, and restart the orchestrator. To get started, clone the GitHub repository and run the three notebooks, in two accounts, with Jupyter on your computer or on Amazon SageMaker AI notebook instances. They handle infrastructure provisioning, agent deployment, and end-to-end testing. To learn more about the services and protocol in this post, see the following resources: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide Amazon Bedrock User Guide Strands Agents SDK documentation Open Protocols for Agent Interoperability Part 4: Inter-Agent Communication on A2A If you have questions or feedback, leave them in the comments section. About the author Amit Chaudhary Amit is a Senior Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services, where he works with ISVs and enterprise customers to design and build generative AI solutions that run in production. He specializes in multi-agent architectures, large language models, and AI application development on AWS.

items.title: Building a self-service LLM gateway with Amazon Bedrock and LiteLLM
items.summary: Developers want AI coding assistants with minimal setup. With a large language model (LLM) gateway and LiteLLM, they can quickly access foundation models (FMs) available on Amazon Bedrock while you gain visibility and usage control. Platform teams need to monitor latency and errors, finance teams need to attribute inference costs to teams and projects, and security teams need consistent access controls. An LLM gateway can help address these needs by providing a centrally managed access point to the models that power coding assistants. In this post, we show how to build a self-service LLM gateway using Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles with LiteLLM running on AWS Fargate to abstract Amazon Bedrock behind an OpenAI-compatible API. With this pattern, developers can access foundation models through a single API with a dedicated key while you gain per-user cost controls and model performance observability.
