By the end, you will understand the pattern well enough to build your own version from the illustrative snippets and AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) constructs. This post uses Claude Sonnet and Claude Haiku models for example purposes. For a list of models and availability by AWS Region, see Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock. This LLM gateway pattern follows a straightforward request flow from the developer, through the LiteLLM layer, to Amazon Bedrock and the underlying FM. The following diagram illustrates the production topology behind that flow. For simplicity, we don’t cover the addition of Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, such as content filtering and grounding, but you would normally include appropriate responsible AI controls before deploying to production. A developer’s OpenAI-compatible client reaches the LLM gateway through Amazon Route 53, Amazon CloudFront, and an Application Load Balancer (ALB). It authenticates to LiteLLM on Fargate with a per-user API key. Behind that, the request draws on Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) (PostgreSQL) for virtual-key and spend state. It also interacts with Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey as a cache, and AWS Secrets Manager for secrets. LiteLLM then ultimately invokes Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles using a scoped AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) task role. Amazon CloudWatch captures requests per minute (RPM) and tokens per minute (TPM) metrics and the quota alarm. Figure 1: LLM gateway architecture (production topology) The architecture consists of these core components: LiteLLM on AWS Fargate: LiteLLM provides a proxy that exposes an OpenAI-compatible API. We run it on an AWS Fargate task with target-tracking Auto Scaling on CPU utilization. Developers point their tools at this endpoint and don’t interact with Amazon Bedrock directly. Self-service portal: LiteLLM includes a lightweight portal for admin and developer self-service. This web app can integrate with your corporate single sign-on (SSO). Using the portal, operations engineers set the spend policy while developers self-provision API keys within those parameters. Persistent and cache storage: LiteLLM uses Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey for non-persistent response caching. It also coordinates rate-limiting across AWS Fargate tasks. A separate Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL) database is the database of record for persistent state such as API key metadata and spend tracking. Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles: Each model (such as Claude Sonnet and Claude Haiku) gets its own inference profile, which you manage using the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). With this, you get per-model quota isolation and a clean abstraction layer between LiteLLM’s configuration and the model versioning of Amazon Bedrock. Langfuse: Open source LLM observability for prompt-level telemetry, latency tracking, and debugging. It complements the infrastructure-level metrics of Amazon CloudWatch with application-level insight. By using an OpenAI-compatible protocol, developers can configure their tools, such as Claude Code, Continue, and Cursor, with a single base URL and API key. Developers then operate at a level above the Amazon Bedrock backend and can swap models, add fallbacks, or migrate model providers without touching developer configurations. Prerequisites You will need an AWS account, Amazon Bedrock model access, and appropriate IAM permissions to deploy this project. You will also need LiteLLM. The LiteLLM AI Gateway component is open source and suitable for a small pilot with some limitations. LiteLLM documents the AI Gateway as free for up to five users with a license required beyond that. LiteLLM Enterprise is a scalable, production-minded licensed version that includes the open source gateway plus single sign-on, audit logs, delegated admin roles, and support. While the free tier supports virtual keys, the self-service key issuance described in this post requires the Enterprise version. End-to-end configuration: Left to right We walk through each configuration layer from the developer’s machine to the foundation model. Step 1: Developer IDE configuration (for example, Claude Code) Developers configure their coding assistant to point to the LLM gateway. This is the only configuration a developer needs to make to their tool: { "apiProvider": "openai-compatible", "apiBaseUrl": "https://llm-gateway.internal.example.com/v1", "apiKey": "sk-user-abc123", "model": "claude-sonnet-4-20250514" } With that configuration, each developer gets their own API key from the self-service portal and drops it into their tool configuration. Step 2: LiteLLM gateway configuration Deploy LiteLLM to a container service following the LiteLLM documentation. In this example we are using AWS Fargate. This will include the portal, which you can open at http://localhost:4000/ui during local testing. The LiteLLM gateway is where you will map and enforce model names to Amazon Bedrock inference profile ARNs with per-key spend limits: model_list: - model_name: claude-sonnet-4-20250514 litellm_params: model: bedrock/arn:aws:bedrock:us-east-1:111122223333:application-inference-profile/sonnet-profile-id aws_region_name: us-east-1 max_retries: 3 timeout: 900 # 15 min for extended thinking # REQUIRED for spend tracking: when `model` is a raw inference-profile ARN, # LiteLLM can't find it in its built-in cost map and defaults the cost to $0 # which means per-key `spend` stays 0 and budgets NEVER enforce. Set the # per-token costs explicitly. model_info: input_cost_per_token: 0.000003 # example cost output_cost_per_token: 0.000015 # example cost - model_name: claude-haiku-4-5 litellm_params: model: bedrock/arn:aws:bedrock:us-east-1:111122223333:application-inference-profile/haiku-profile-id aws_region_name: us-east-1 timeout: 120 model_info: input_cost_per_token: 0.000001 # example cost output_cost_per_token: 0.000005 # example cost litellm_settings: max_budget: 250 # example per key cost budget_duration: 7d # Rolling 7-day window max_parallel_requests: 10 set_verbose: false cache: true cache_params: type: redis # Valkey is protocol-compatible, so this stays "redis" host: elasticache-endpoint port: 6379 master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY database_url: os.environ/DATABASE_URL Set on the Fargate task from AWS Secrets Manager: LITELLM_MASTER_KEY=sk-platform-admin-... DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:password@rds-endpoint:5432/litellm Note: Don’t hardcode the master_key or database credentials in config.yaml. LiteLLM resolves os.environ/VAR_NAME references at load time, so set LITELLM_MASTER_KEY and DATABASE_URL as environment variables on the Fargate task, sourced from AWS Secrets Manager. Set the Langfuse credentials the same way in Step 5. When a developer calls claude-sonnet-4-20250514, for example, LiteLLM resolves it to the inference profile ARN. It then authenticates to Amazon Bedrock using the AWS Fargate task’s IAM role and streams the response back in OpenAI format. Step 3: Bedrock inference profiles (CDK) With Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles you can create named endpoints for specific models, so you get quota isolation and fine-grained IAM control. Choosing cross-Region inference (CRIS): Geographic or Global Amazon Bedrock CRIS avoids the overhead of implementing cross-Region request routing yourself. Other benefits include: Access to a broader pool of Regional capacity. Automatic routing of requests to a supported Region with available capacity. Broader model selection, because some models are available only through an inference profile. For this proxy pattern, we recommend Global cross-Region inference when the selected models support it and organizational policies permit inference processing across supported AWS commercial Regions worldwide. Geographic cross-Region inference keeps processing within a defined geography. For example, a US inference profile routes requests only to supported US Regions. Global cross-Region inference provides access to a broader pool of Regional capacity with potential pricing benefits compared with Geographic cross-Region inference. You can verify model availability, applicable service quotas, and model-specific pricing through current AWS documentation and AWS pricing pages. CDK construct import * as cdk from 'aws-cdk-lib'; import * as bedrock from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-bedrock'; import * as iam from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-iam'; // Create an Application Inference Profile pointing to the Global CRIS // system-defined inference profile (note the `global.` prefix in the ARN). const sonnetProfile = new bedrock.CfnApplicationInferenceProfile(this, 'SonnetProfile', { inferenceProfileName: 'claude-sonnet-gateway', modelSource: { copyFrom: `arn:aws:bedrock:us-east-1:${this.account}:inference-profile/global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-20250514-v1:0`, }, description: 'Claude Sonnet for developer coding assistants (Global CRIS)', }); // Grant LiteLLM's task role access to invoke the profile. // For Global CRIS, include the inference profile, the regional FM, and the global FM resources. litellmTaskRole.addToPolicy(new iam.PolicyStatement({ effect: iam.Effect.ALLOW, actions: ['bedrock:InvokeModel', 'bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream'], resources: [ sonnetProfile.attrInferenceProfileArn, 'arn:aws:bedrock:us-east-1::foundation-model/anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-20250514-v1:0', 'arn:aws:bedrock:*::foundation-model/anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-20250514-v1:0', ], })); Important: For Global CRIS, the copyFrom ARN must reference the system-defined inference profile prefixed with global., not the foundation-model ARN directly. Using a foundation-model ARN creates a single-Region profile without cross-Region routing. Additionally, the IAM policy must include the resource ARNs the invocation actually touches: the application inference profile and the underlying foundation model in any Region it might route to (Region-wildcarded). Scoping only to the application-inference-profile ARN returns not authorized to perform: bedrock:InvokeModel on resource: arn:aws:bedrock:us-east-1::foundation-model/... at invoke time. This is scoped least-privilege: it names the exact models in use, not bedrock:* or *. Step 4: Bedrock invokes the foundation model The inference profile handles model resolution and cross-Region routing transparently without additional configuration. When LiteLLM calls the inference profile ARN, Amazon Bedrock routes to available capacity across configured AWS Regions and returns the response. Step 5: Langfuse observability LiteLLM integrates with Langfuse through logging callbacks, providing visibility into model invocations without requiring changes to developer tool configurations. To enable the integration, merge the following entries into the existing litellm_settings block from the Step 2 configuration, preserving existing callback entries: litellm_settings: success_callback: ["langfuse"] failure_callback: ["langfuse"] # also log failed requests Configure the Langfuse public key, secret key, and deployment endpoint as environment variables on the Fargate task. Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager: LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY=pk-lf-... LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY=sk-lf-... LANGFUSE_HOST=https://us.cloud.langfuse.com # or your self-hosted URL The endpoint must match the selected Langfuse Cloud region or self-hosted deployment. Choose the hosting option based on data governance and operational requirements. Before enabling prompt and response logging, review the content captured by the integration and configure appropriate redaction, retention, and access controls. Langfuse traces can include prompts, responses, model parameters, token usage, and latency, depending on the integration and logging configuration. This information helps investigate unexpected model responses and complements the operational metrics collected in Amazon CloudWatch. Implementing cost controls Cost controls are an important dimension to a successful AI strategy. Without cost controls, heavy usage of extended thinking features can lead to unexpectedly high charges, which we observed in our early pilots. The spend limits configured in Step 2 (max_budget: 250, budget_duration: 7d) enforce a rolling 7-day window per API key, provided per-model model_info costs are set (refer to the Step 2 note). When a user reaches their limit, LiteLLM returns an HTTP 429 code with a clear message explaining that their budget has been exceeded. There’s no silent degradation or surprise bill. Developers and engineering teams can check current spend and reset timing through any of the following: Daily spend: Query GET /user/daily/activity with a start_date and end_date range to get per-day metrics: spend, prompt tokens, completion tokens, and API requests, broken down by model, provider, and API key. Per user spend: Query GET /user/info?user_id=… for a summary of a user’s total spend and the spend on each of their associated API keys. Portal dashboard: The Admin UI (at https://<proxy-host>/ui) includes a Usage tab where developers and admins can browse spend by model, user, and tag without hitting the API directly. These same endpoints are how your finance team gets per-user attribution without you building custom metering infrastructure. A scheduled job hitting /user/daily/activity or /global/spend/report is enough to feed a cost dashboard or chargeback report. Developer self-service portal The self-service portal also handles key lifecycle processes. Developers authenticate with your corporate SSO to generate a key bound to their identity, which they can later regenerate if the key is exposed or to match a rotation policy. Platform engineers configure the budget policy once for individual developers to autonomously operate within their constraints. Two things developers use the portal for directly: Key generation: On the Admin UI’s Virtual Keys page (https://<proxy-host>/ui), developers authenticated through SSO choose Generate Key to create their own key, bound to their identity. Rate limit visibility: Each /chat/completions response includes x-litellm-key-remaining-requests-{model} and x-litellm-key-remaining-tokens-{model} headers, so developers can see their remaining RPM and TPM headroom for that model directly in their tool’s response. This is distinct from the dollar-based spend tracking earlier in this post. Monitoring and observability For an LLM gateway, traditional metrics like latency percentiles can be misleading, especially with extended thinking models, where a single request can take several minutes. Instead, we focus on requests per minute (RPM) and tokens per minute (TPM) as primary signals. Here, Amazon CloudWatch can help you monitor and alarm for these signals with the following configuration. Amazon CloudWatch alarms for quota management new cloudwatch.Alarm(this, 'BedrockTPMAlarm', { metric: new cloudwatch.Metric({ namespace: 'LiteLLM/Gateway', metricName: 'TokensPerMinute', statistic: 'Sum', period: cdk.Duration.minutes(1), }), // Alert at ~60% of your account's TPM quota (check Service Quotas for your // actual limit, defaults vary by model and account). threshold: 600000, evaluationPeriods: 3, comparisonOperator: cloudwatch.ComparisonOperator.GREATER_THAN_THRESHOLD, alarmDescription: 'TPM approaching Bedrock quota - request increase proactively', }); Note that the alarm configuration alerts at 60–70 percent quota utilization rather than waiting for throttling. This provides lead time to scale Amazon Bedrock quotas before users experience degradation. Emitting the metric: LiteLLM has no built-in callback that publishes a metric named TokensPerMinute to a LiteLLM/Gateway namespace, so the alarm needs a source. A small custom-logger callback that calls CloudWatch PutMetricData on each request does the job. Register it through litellm_settings.success_callback (which is additive), not callbacks. The callbacks list replaces LiteLLM’s internal logger list, which includes the built-in spend-tracking logger, and will silently disable budget enforcement. Here’s a minimal version of that callback, using LiteLLM’s CustomLogger class: import boto3 from litellm.integrations.custom_logger import CustomLogger cloudwatch = boto3.client("cloudwatch") class TPMEmitter(CustomLogger): async def async_log_success_event(self, kwargs, response_obj, start_time, end_time): total_tokens = kwargs.get("standard_logging_object", {}).get("total_tokens", 0) cloudwatch.put_metric_data( Namespace="LiteLLM/Gateway", MetricData=[{ "MetricName": "TokensPerMinute", "Value": total_tokens, "Unit": "Count", }], ) # Register alongside success_callback, not in place of it: import litellm litellm.callbacks = [TPMEmitter()] For prompt-level debugging, we run Langfuse alongside CloudWatch. When a developer reports “the model gave a bad response,” you can use Langfuse to inspect the exact prompt, token counts, and model parameters. For compliance-sensitive environments, Amazon Bedrock’s native invocation logging to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) provides an immutable audit trail. Lessons learned at scale We deployed this pattern end-to-end on a fresh AWS account to confirm the sample snippets work. In our own deployment, we scaled this LLM gateway to several hundred developers and learned several lessons. Operational lessons The main findings from running at scale: Extended thinking changes everything about latency. Requests using Claude’s extended thinking can take several minutes or longer, depending on the thinking budget. If your load balancer has a 60-second idle timeout, those requests will fail silently. To address that, you can set load balancer idle timeouts to at least 900 seconds and configure LiteLLM’s request timeout accordingly (timeout: 900 in the Step 2 configuration earlier in this post). When throttled, back off and retry on the same model before initiating a fallback. Our initial instinct was to fall back from Sonnet to Haiku upon throttling. But this is suboptimal for coding assistants because changing models breaks the consistent behavior developers rely on. Instead, retry the same model with exponential backoff at the proxy level (max_retries: 3 in Step 2). When a request cannot be served after retries, surface the error clearly rather than returning an alternate model’s completions. Separate automation tool invocations from developer traffic. continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines and automated code review tools should call Amazon Bedrock directly with their own inference profiles and quotas. Mixing automation traffic with interactive developer traffic leads to unpredictable latency and hinders meaningful cost attribution. Start with Global CRIS from day one, if feasible. We initially used Geographic (US) CRIS but ultimately migrated our inference profiles when we reached Regional quota limits. For our use case, we didn’t have data residency constraints so we could use Global CRIS. Global CRIS routes requests across Regions to draw on a broader capacity pool, simplifying management at scale. Deployment considerations Two configuration mistakes are common and hard to notice until spend or connectivity breaks: Configuring per-model costs is mandatory for enforcing budgets. The model_info block on each model isn’t optional if you want to track per-user cost controls. When model points at an Amazon Bedrock inference-profile ARN, LiteLLM can’t look up the ARN in its built-in pricing table. It instead records $0 per token, so the max_budget and 429 throttle enforcement silently don’t trigger. Spend remains at $0 no matter how many tokens flow. Fix this by setting input_cost_per_token and output_cost_per_token (or input_cost_per_million_tokens). Database compared to cache: The database_url must be PostgreSQL. LiteLLM’s virtual keys (/key/generate), store_model_in_db, and spend tracking are Postgres-backed. A handful of smaller deployment details rounded out our checklist: Global CRIS IAM needs the foundation-model resources, not only the app-inference-profile ARN. Otherwise, invocation is denied at runtime. Give the Fargate task enough memory. LiteLLM’s gateway image runs out of memory and is killed at 512 MB (exit 137) before it can pass a health check. About 2 GB is a safe floor. Override the container entryPoint. The official image’s entrypoint is litellm. If you render a config at startup with a shell script, set entryPoint: ['/bin/sh','-c'] or your script is passed as arguments to litellm. IAM role and security-group descriptions must be ASCII. Em-dashes and -> arrows are rejected by IAM and Amazon EC2. Confirm model availability in your account and Region. Model IDs and CRIS profiles change. Verify with aws bedrock list-inference-profiles (for example, we used claude-haiku-4-5 because claude-haiku-3-5 was not available). Clean up This post walks through the pattern with illustrative snippets rather than a single deployable stack, there’s no one-command teardown. But the architecture relies on several resources that continue to bill while they run. These include the AWS Fargate service, Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL), Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey, and the Application Load Balancer, along with supporting Secrets Manager secrets, CloudWatch alarms, and Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles. When you finish testing, remove them to avoid ongoing charges. If you deployed the full solution using the Guidance for Multi-Provider Generative AI Gateway on AWS, follow that solution’s cleanup instructions to remove everything it created. For AWS CDK, run cdk destroy. For AWS CloudFormation, delete the stack. If you built the pattern yourself from the snippets in this post, remove each resource: AWS Fargate service and cluster: Delete the Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) service to stop and drain the tasks, then delete the cluster. Application Load Balancer: Delete the ALB along with its listeners and target groups. Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL): Delete the database instance. Take a final snapshot first only if you need to retain API key and spend data. Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey: Delete the replication group or cluster. It holds only cache data, so no snapshot is needed. Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles: Delete the profiles created in Step 3, either by removing the AWS CDK construct or by running aws bedrock delete-inference-profile. AWS Secrets Manager secrets: Schedule deletion of the proxy’s secrets, such as the master key and database credentials. Amazon CloudWatch alarms and log groups: Delete the TPM alarm and any LiteLLM log groups. Delete the AWS Fargate service and ALB before the Amazon RDS and ElastiCache endpoints they depend on, so running tasks don’t error against removed backends during teardown. Conclusion In this post, we detailed a pattern for an LLM gateway that abstracts the multi-model architecture of Amazon Bedrock to provide your teams with scalable and observable self-service access. Because Amazon Bedrock routes across models through a single interface without changing infrastructure, your developers get instant access to foundation models through familiar APIs. Cost governance, observability, and a single control plane go to your engineering and security teams while finance gets per-user attribution without you building a custom metering infrastructure. Start by working through the pattern and snippets in this post to understand how the pieces fit together. The AWS CDK snippets cover the Amazon Bedrock application inference profile, its IAM policy, and the CloudWatch alarm. The surrounding AWS Fargate service, Amazon RDS, Amazon ElastiCache, ALB, and AWS Secrets Manager resources follow standard AWS CDK patterns and aren’t shown. When you’re ready for a complete, deployable implementation, the Guidance for Multi-Provider Generative AI Gateway on AWS closely aligns with this pattern. You can find the guide on the AWS Solutions Library with the accompanying blog post and GitHub projects. While this post stepped through the same core pattern, it focused on Amazon Bedrock for developer coding assistants. The larger solution architecture adds multi-provider support, Amazon ECS or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Amazon CloudFront and AWS WAF options, and an admin UI. Explore the components of this architecture with additional documentation for Amazon Bedrock Inference Profiles, LiteLLM gateway, AWS Fargate, and Langfuse. Try this pattern in your organization. Start with a pilot team, validate the cost controls, and scale from there. About the authors Sitaraman Vijay Krishna Sitaraman Vijay Krishna is a Senior Technical Account Manager at AWS, where he works with customers on Generative AI, Agentic AI, and AI observability, including hands-on adoption of the AWS DevOps Agent. Outside work, he’s a lifelong sports fan who’s as happy on the field as watching from the stands. Saurav Bhattacharya Saurav Bhattacharya is a Senior Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services (AWS) with extensive experience within the telecom, broadband, and media domains. In his current role, he is focused on solving the challenges of the media and entertainment industry, accelerating technical sales and building solutions that scale to accelerate digital transformation for the customers. Eric Christensen Eric Christensen is a Technical Account Manager at Amazon Web Services (AWS) with deep experience in cloud financial management and cost optimization. He has published extensive code samples and multiple cost and health tracking dashboards to the AWS Solutions Library.

items.title: Bye Bye, Dial
items.summary: Today we're saying goodbye to the Dial and its four modes: low, medium, high, and ultra. A model selector takes its place: You can now pick the model and its effort for each thread. And you can now also switch both in the middle of a thread. The model selector now also shows you which of your subscriptions or API keys will be billed for each model, or whether it uses Amp credits. If you don't want to pick the model yourself, use the Staff Pick, which is the model we would choose. Yes, We Changed Our Mind In January we explained why Amp does not have a model selector. In July we then shipped the Dial so you could focus on how hard a task is instead of thinking about model names and version numbers. And it worked: when we changed the default model behind the Dial, nobody complained. But then we added the ability to Amp to bring your own subscriptions and keys, and Amp became free when you do. That changed what the selected model does. Not only is it what produces the tokens, but it also started to decide who gets billed. medium on the Dial could use your Claude plan, or your ChatGPT plan, or Amp credits, and it became very hard to tell who's paying for which model when. And that's not to speak of all the settings we had to add to the Dial to make it work in every combination. So we decided to stop hiding the model and now have a model selector. Now, when you pick it yourself, you know where the tokens come from and who's paying. And yet, it's still not just a model you pick. An agent is more than a model. You pick the model, and we build the harness around it: each model in the selector gets a system prompt and tools optimized for it, and both switch when you switch models in a thread. Switch Models in a Thread With the Dial, a thread kept the mode (and model) it started with. We did that because a model became confused when it continued a conversation that another model had started. But now models are good enough to recover from that. Now you can change the model mid-thread by opening the selector and making the change. After your next message the new model will be used and the transcript will show a record: "Switched to GPT-6.1 Sol · High". But some things haven't changed. A model switch still has a price. Prompt caches belong to one model, so the new model reads the whole thread uncached, and the first message after a switch costs more. Threads that run an agent from a plugin keep that agent. Staff Pick New threads start on Staff Pick by default. (Except if you had previously configured the Dial to have a default mode.) Staff Pick is the model we would pick ourselves, which is Claude Opus 5.5 today. We keep benchmarking models, and we'll change the pick when another model does better. In Settings → Model Selector, under New Threads Start On, you can also start new threads on the model you picked last, or on one fixed model you choose. What Happens to Your Dial Until today everyone used the Dial, so this applies to you. New threads start on Staff Pick, whichever mode you used last. Existing threads keep working. A thread you started in high continues on the model it ran. Dial settings don't carry over. If you changed the model behind a mode in Tune Modes, pick that model in the selector now. If you put your own agents on the Dial in Build Dial, you find them under Other Models. If you never changed those settings, these are the models your modes ran. The first three are at the top of the selector, and Claude Fable 5.2 is under Other Models: low: GLM-5.3-Flash medium: Claude Opus 5.5 high: GPT-6 Astra ultra: Claude Fable 5.2 Pin your models in Settings → Model Selector, or leave the selector on Staff Pick. Read the Model Selector docs for everything the selector and its settings do.

items.title: CodeRabbit Passes $100 million in ARR
items.summary: AI has disrupted the software development lifecycle. Teams now generate code at agentic speed, but the rest of the lifecycle still runs on processes built for human speed. As teams climb the maturity curve of AI adoption, they hit a different bottleneck at each stage: reviewing what the agents wrote, deciding which changes to merge first, understanding what a change actually does, and continuously monitoring the software for risk once it ships. To realize AI’s productivity gains, every step of the lifecycle has to become agentic. CodeRabbit was founded to do exactly that: remove every one of those bottlenecks. We started with code review, simply because it’s the first bottleneck teams hit. That starting point became an entirely new category of AI software validation tools. Today we’re sharing a milestone that shows how far the AI disruption has spread, and how quickly our category is growing: CodeRabbit has grown from $10 million to $100 million in annual recurring revenue in just over a year. More than 20,000 customers and 400,000 monthly active users now use CodeRabbit to review, triage, explain, and secure their codebases, with the average team shipping software at twice the rate it did before CodeRabbit. Engineering teams put more than 3 million pull requests through CodeRabbit every week. To date, CodeRabbit has surfaced more than 100 million issues, bugs, and vulnerabilities to be fixed before code reaches production. CodeRabbit’s path from $1 million to $100 million ARR, compared with other application software companies. ## Code generation got cheap. Judgment didn't. Coding agents have fundamentally changed the shape of pull requests. There are more of them: among a cohort of tracked users, weekly PRs [rose 128% year over year](https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/whats-the-roi-of-software-engineers). PRs are also larger and harder to read, and agent-written changes are often no longer human-readable at all. But engineers are still being asked to validate every PR and do so at the same speed that agents create them. Many teams are responding by skipping the reading. In a [June 2026 New Relic survey](https://newrelic.com/sites/default/files/2026-06/New-Relic-2026-AI-Code-Report-06-09-2026.pdf), 62% of tech leaders said their teams often ship AI-generated code to production without line-by-line review. Giving up quality for speed is a trade-off we refuse to accept. Engineering teams can only ship software as fast as they can trust it. If agents produce changes faster than people can judge them, judgment has to scale too. The engineers of the next decade won't spend their days writing code. They'll be architects, setting intent and standards and judging what ships. At agent scale, no human can judge every change line by line, so you need an AI layer that validates each PR against your standards as fast as agents produce them. And the AI layer can’t be the agent that wrote the code. Hunting for bugs and known bad patterns is now only a small part of validating a PR. When agents write most of your code, the harder questions are whether it is fit for purpose and fit for your company. Does it follow your standards? Is it architecturally sound? Is it duplicative or bloated? And are you feeding what you learn from each release back into what you expect of the agents? ## Trusting code your engineers didn’t write CodeRabbit is used by fast-growing AI-native companies and established, regulated institutions alike. Dialpad sells an AI-powered customer communications platform to more than 50,000 companies. Questrade Financial Group is a Canadian financial institution with more than $100 billion CAD in assets under administration. Both arrived at the same conclusion about trusting AI-written code. > We build AI for a living and our engineers build with it every day, so we know generating code was never the hard part. Trusting it is. We aren’t going to let the model that wrote the code decide whether it is fit to ship. CodeRabbit gives every change an independent review, tells us what it does and how risky it is, and keeps watching after it merges. Our engineers spend their time on the decisions that need a person, and we ship more with greater confidence. — Brian Peterson, co-founder and CTO, Dialpad > We hold every change to the same standard, however it was written. CodeRabbit gives us a consistent, independent review before anything ships, so our teams can use AI in the way that works best for them. — David Wieler, Chief AI Officer, Questrade Financial Group ## Security is part of code quality now The definition of quality expanded this year to include security. Attackers can now point agents at code they have never seen to find and exploit vulnerabilities cheaply and at massive scale. The answer is to turn the same kind of agents on your own code and find those vulnerabilities first. In October, we [joined the OpenAI Daybreak Defense Network](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261026814225/en/CodeRabbit-Commits-%241M-in-Free-Security-Scans-for-Any-Company-Joins-OpenAI-Daybreak-Defense-Network), which embeds frontier models directly in software security workflows, and brought OpenAI's GPT Cyber models into [CodeRabbit Secure](https://www.coderabbit.ai/security). We also committed $1 million to fund free Deep Scans for any organization or open-source project. In the program's first ten days, more than 2,700 organizations ran over 13,000 scans. Those scans surfaced more than 43,000 critical or high-severity findings, and one in three scanned repositories had at least one. Nearly 10,000 of those vulnerabilities have already been fixed. ## Independent review, wherever the agents are built The companies building frontier coding agents now offer CodeRabbit on their platforms. In May, CodeRabbit became available on [Anthropic’s Claude Marketplace](https://www.coderabbit.ai/blog/CodeRabbit-in-Claude-Marketplace), and in September we joined the [OpenAI Marketplace](https://www.coderabbit.ai/blog/coderabbit-openai-marketplace) as an anchor partner; both let customers apply existing spend commitments toward CodeRabbit on a single invoice. In October, we became an [authorized partner](https://www.coderabbit.ai/blog/coderabbit-spacex-super-intelligence-partner-network) in the SpaceX Super Intelligence Partner Network and launched in the Grok Build Plugin Marketplace. And this week, CodeRabbit arrived in the [Google Antigravity Plugin Marketplace](https://www.coderabbit.ai/blog/agentic-software-development-coderabbit-google-antigravity), where Antigravity writes the code, CodeRabbit reviews it, and Antigravity fixes the findings in the same agentic loop. Each puts CodeRabbit next to the agents those labs ship as the independent layer that validates what the agents produce. That layer has to stay independent of any single model, too. Our review pipeline is model-agnostic, and in January we added NVIDIA's [Nemotron](https://developer.nvidia.com/nemotron) family of open models to it alongside the frontier models already there. ## A milestone on a longer mission Revenue is a lagging indicator. What $100 million represents is progress on a larger mission of helping every engineering team in the world ship software as fast as they can imagine. The milestone is a reflection of the decision made by thousands of engineering teams this year to validate code as fast as they generate it, and to trust CodeRabbit to make that possible. If your team is ready to ship better software, faster, [try CodeRabbit](https://app.coderabbit.ai) on your next pull request. It takes two clicks to set up, and is free to get started.

items.title: Deploy frontier AI models on AWS Trainium with SGLang-Neuron
items.summary: Today, Amazon announced that SGLang-Neuron is publicly available and can be accessed through an AWS Deep Learning Container, released by RadixArk in collaboration with Annapurna Labs. With SGLang-Neuron, you can serve models and generate reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts with SGLang on AWS Trainium using the same SGLang interface you use today. Trainium is a portfolio of AWS AI chips that delivers strong economics for AI training and inference at scale. Now, running SGLang on Trainium follows the SGLang workflow you already know: you launch models through SGLang’s server interface and invoke the endpoint using the same generation APIs. Underneath that interface, SGLang-Neuron runs on native PyTorch. With its out-of-tree plugin design, Trainium support and SGLang core develop independently and iterate faster. How SGLang runs on Trainium SGLang-Neuron is an out-of-tree plugin that connects SGLang with AWS Trainium. Installing the plugin registers the neuron platform through SGLang’s plugin entry points, and setting SGLANG_PLATFORM=neuron selects it when the server starts. SGLang core continues to provide the API server, request lifecycle, RadixAttention, and prefix-cache bookkeeping. The plugin implements the Trainium-specific models, attention, mixture of experts (MoE), and the graph runner. Figure 1: SGLang-Neuron on AWS Trainium TorchNeuron registers Trainium as a native PyTorch device. SGLang-Neuron uses standard PyTorch operations for the model execution path and incorporates kernels written with the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) for performance. It compiles these operations and kernels into executable programs using torch.compile, which the graph runner prepares and executes during serving. SGLang-Neuron also supports PD disaggregation. In this configuration, a prefill server computes the prompt KV cache and transfers it to a decode server using NIXL over Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA). The decode server then generates the remaining tokens. Each server still uses SGLang’s scheduler and request lifecycle, while the plugin manages the Trainium execution and KV-cache transfer path. Serving models on AWS Trainium using SGLang-Neuron To follow this walkthrough, you use a Trainium3 Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance with a pytorch-inference-sglang-neuronx container. Here are the steps: Start the container. docker run --rm -it \ --privileged --ipc=host \ -v /path/to/work:/work \ public.ecr.aws/neuron/pytorch-inference-sglang-neuron:v0.1.0-neuron-py314-sdk-2.33.0-ubuntu26.04 \ /bin/bash Launch the SGLang model server inside the container. SGLANG_PLATFORM=neuron \ python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path openai/gpt-oss-120b \ --tp-size 8 \ --ep-size 8 \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \ --context-length 10240 \ --chunked-prefill-size 8192 \ --max-running-requests 64 \ --max-total-tokens 655360 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.8 \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 30000 Send a request to the model server. curl -s http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "model": "openai/gpt-oss-120b", "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "Explain why the sky appears blue."} ], "temperature": 0, "max_tokens": 128 }' For additional information, please see the SGLang-Neuron getting started guide for setup instructions, and explore the repository documentation for supported models, features, and validated configurations. Conclusion SGLang-Neuron brings SGLang’s familiar serving workflow to AWS Trainium through native PyTorch. You can get started by launching the SGLang-Neuron container and following the quickstart to serve a supported model. Try it with your workloads, contribute through the project repository, and share feedback to help shape future model and feature support. About the authors Alex Nails Alex is a Member of Technical Staff at RadixArk. He leads MultiHardware and is a core developer of SGLang. Yihao Wang Yihao is a Member of Technical Staff at RadixArk. He works on both multi-modal/diffusion models and multi-hardware. Lingyan Hao Lingyan is a Product Manager at RadixArk. She works on SGLang adoption and multi-hardware enablement. Srecharan Selvam Srecharan is a software engineer working on AI Inference technology at Annapurna Labs, Amazon. Zeyu Wang Zeyu is a software engineer working on AI Inference technology at Annapurna Labs, Amazon. Vinesh Ravuri Vinesh is a software engineer working on AI Inference technology at Annapurna Labs, Amazon. Yuchen Jiang Yuchen is a software engineer working on AI Inference technology at Annapurna Labs, Amazon. Pinak Panigrahi Pinak works on performance optimization of AI models on AWS Trainium at Annapurna Labs, Amazon. items.title: dream-num/univer
items.summary:
Build your own AI office with Univer Office SDK. Bring editing, calculation, collaboration, and file processing into your product for people and AI agents. Built on an extensible open-source core. https://univer.ai Build your own AI office with Univer Office SDK. Start with open-source Sheets and Docs, then connect your own application or agent. 🚀 Quick start · 📚 Documentation · ⚖️ Feature comparison · 🌐 Website · 🎮 Showcase · 🔧 API Reference · 📝 Blog English · Français · Deutsch · Español · 简体中文 · 繁體中文 · 日本語 · 한국어 Table of contents 💡 What is Univer? Open-source capabilities 🚀 Build on the open-source foundation Quick start: an open-source spreadsheet editor Connect your application to editable content 🏗️ Explore the open-source architecture Give custom features clear boundaries Compose cross-feature edits and undo/redo Connect applications and agents through Facade APIs and events 🧩 Extend your application with Univer Office SDK Scope and licensing 🌐 Application patterns and ecosystem Univer Workspace: an Office SDK reference application CLI, agent integrations, and developer skills 📚 Documentation and contributing Runtime compatibility 💬 Community 🔒 Security ❤️ Sponsors 📄 License 💡 What is Univer? Univer is an Office SDK for building Office applications inside your own product. It provides Office editing, calculation, collaboration, and file processing for people and existing agents, using your data and permissions. The product family covers spreadsheets, documents, presentations, relational tables, canvases, and PDFs. Univer Office SDK has three parts: Web SDK is the foundation: content models, editing, rendering, formula calculation, and Facade APIs (application-facing APIs). Compose its plugins into an embedded editor or your own Office application, and reuse the content models, commands, and calculation for Headless processing without an interactive editor. Server SDK adds backend services for real-time collaboration, edit history, and Office file import and export. AI SDK connects Office capabilities to existing agents and workflows, with content tools, execution, and review integrations. This repository provides the Web SDK's core architecture and engine implementations under Apache-2.0: content models and snapshot formats, plugin and dependency management, the command system, formula and rendering engines, Facade APIs, UI foundation, and Sheets and Docs editing capabilities. Commercial Web SDK plugins, Server SDK, and commercial AI SDK extensions are distributed and licensed separately. Agents can use the same open-source APIs; your application supplies the model and tool orchestration. The quotation example demonstrates editing, calculation, and saving without an AI SDK dependency. Open-source capabilities Area Selected capabilities Sheets · Editing and layout Cell styles, merged cells, in-cell rich text, freeze panes, floating images, and undo/redo. Sheets · Data and calculation Formulas, defined names, filtering, sorting, data validation, conditional formatting, hyperlinks, comments, and find and replace. Docs Rich-text editing, paragraph formatting, lists, hyperlinks, comments, and drawing integration. Features are composed through plugins and presets; the quick start uses only the Sheets Core preset. Images use the corresponding drawing plugins. See the feature comparison for detailed open-source and commercial coverage. The demos below showcase the wider Univer Office SDK, including commercial capabilities. They show more than the default open-source setup; see open source and commercial extensions for scope. 🚀 Build on the open-source foundation Your goal Use the open-source foundation Start here Embed Sheets or Docs Add an editable Office surface to your application or agent product, and connect your data through Facade APIs. Quick start Process content without an editor Reuse content plugins, models, commands, and calculation in Node.js for editing, snapshots, and automated tasks. Headless guide Develop custom features or editors Reuse the engines, UI components, plugin boundaries, dependency injection, and command/undo systems. Follow existing features to extend Sheets and Docs or develop your own editors. Open-source architecture Coordinate edits and undo/redo across features. Inserting a row inside a filter range changes both the base content and the filter range; undo needs to restore both. Each feature supplies its own changes and undo data, and the command composes their execution and history. The architecture walkthrough explains how to extend these editing workflows. Quick start: an open-source spreadsheet editor In a browser application using a bundler such as Vite: pnpm add @univerjs/presets @univerjs/preset-sheets-core Create the container before initializing Univer:
import { UniverSheetsCorePreset } from '@univerjs/preset-sheets-core' import UniverPresetSheetsCoreEnUS from '@univerjs/preset-sheets-core/locales/en-US' import { createUniver, LocaleType, mergeLocales } from '@univerjs/presets' import '@univerjs/preset-sheets-core/lib/index.css' const { univerAPI } = createUniver({ locale: LocaleType.EN_US, locales: { [LocaleType.EN_US]: mergeLocales(UniverPresetSheetsCoreEnUS), }, presets: [ UniverSheetsCorePreset({ container: 'app', }), ], }) univerAPI.createWorkbook({}) Your page now contains a spreadsheet editor. Use the returned univerAPI to work with its content. This example uses open-source packages and needs no commercial Univer license or Server SDK. For component frameworks, retain the univer instance returned by createUniver and call univer.dispose() when the component unmounts. See the lifecycle guide. Presets compose plugins and register their Facade APIs. For manual control, see the Plugin Mode example below. The installation guide covers both modes, peer dependencies, and framework integrations. Keep coordinated @univerjs/* packages on the same version. Commercial packages must use the matching release line; independently released packages such as icons follow their declared compatibility. See the API Stability Policy. Connect your application to editable content Facade APIs are the application-facing interface to workbooks, worksheets, and ranges. Continue from the quick start to populate a quotation, update a quantity from application code, and read the recalculated total: // Wait for formula controllers before editing a newly created workbook. await new Promise((resolve) => { if (univerAPI.getCurrentLifecycleStage() >= univerAPI.Enum.LifecycleStages.Steady) { resolve() return } const listener = univerAPI.addEvent(univerAPI.Event.LifeCycleChanged, ({ stage }) => { if (stage === univerAPI.Enum.LifecycleStages.Steady) { listener.dispose() resolve() } }) }) const workbook = univerAPI.getActiveWorkbook()! const sheet = workbook.getActiveSheet() sheet.getRange('A1:D4').setValues([ ['Item', 'Quantity', 'Unit price', 'Amount'], ['Seats', 2, 25, '=B2*C2'], ['Support', 1, 100, '=B3*C3'], ['Total', '', '', '=SUM(D2:D3)'], ]) // An application control or agent can make the same edit. sheet.getRange('B2').setValue(4) univerAPI.getFormula().onCalculationResultApplied().then(() => { console.log(sheet.getRange('D4').getValue()) // 200 localStorage.setItem('quotation', JSON.stringify(workbook.save())) }).catch(console.error) The editor and your application operate on the same workbook; formula changes are recalculated automatically. workbook.save() returns a JSON snapshot containing the workbook and its registered plugin data. Your application owns persistence; this example uses browser storage. On a later page load, after initialization, restore the snapshot instead of creating a blank workbook: const saved = localStorage.getItem('quotation') if (saved) { univerAPI.createWorkbook(JSON.parse(saved)) } This workflow uses only open-source packages. Snapshot persistence is separate from XLSX import and export, which uses the separately distributed file-conversion capabilities. Use public Facade APIs for application integration; the source links below explain internal implementation and extension points. See the API Stability Policy before depending on an extension point. Advanced: compose plugins manually (Plugin Mode) Use Plugin Mode when you need precise control over plugin selection, dependencies, or loading. The preset above handles this composition for you. This alternative initialization uses the same app container and the Sheets Core preset's browser plugin stack without a Worker. Use it instead of the preset initialization, then run the same quotation example with the returned univerAPI. pnpm add @univerjs/core @univerjs/design @univerjs/docs @univerjs/docs-ui \ @univerjs/engine-formula @univerjs/engine-render @univerjs/network \ @univerjs/sheets @univerjs/sheets-ui @univerjs/sheets-formula \ @univerjs/sheets-formula-ui @univerjs/sheets-numfmt \ @univerjs/sheets-numfmt-ui @univerjs/ui import { LocaleType, mergeLocales, Univer } from '@univerjs/core' import { FUniver } from '@univerjs/core/facade' import DesignEnUS from '@univerjs/design/locale/en-US' import { UniverDocsPlugin } from '@univerjs/docs' import { UniverDocsUIPlugin } from '@univerjs/docs-ui' import DocsUIEnUS from '@univerjs/docs-ui/locale/en-US' import { UniverFormulaEnginePlugin } from '@univerjs/engine-formula' import FormulaEnUS from '@univerjs/engine-formula/locale/en-US' import { UniverRenderEnginePlugin } from '@univerjs/engine-render' import { UniverNetworkPlugin } from '@univerjs/network' import { UniverSheetsPlugin } from '@univerjs/sheets' import SheetsEnUS from '@univerjs/sheets/locale/en-US' import { UniverSheetsFormulaPlugin } from '@univerjs/sheets-formula' import SheetsFormulaEnUS from '@univerjs/sheets-formula/locale/en-US' import { UniverSheetsFormulaUIPlugin } from '@univerjs/sheets-formula-ui' import SheetsFormulaUIEnUS SheetsNumfmtUIEnUS from '@univerjs/sheets-numfmt-ui/locale/en-US' import { UniverSheetsUIPlugin } from '@univerjs/sheets-ui' import SheetsUIEnUS from '@univerjs/sheets-ui/locale/en-US' import { When adding a feature, include its corresponding Facade extensions, locale bundles, and UI styles. Dispose univer when its container is unmounted. 🏗️ Explore the open-source architecture Give custom features clear boundaries Univer organizes content logic and UI interaction in separate plugins. Feature plugins manage rules and content changes; UI plugins provide the interface and user interactions. For example, sheets-filter manages filter ranges and rules, while sheets-filter-ui provides panels, menus, and shortcuts. %%{init: {'htmlLabels': false, 'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'Arial, PingFang SC, Microsoft YaHei, sans-serif', 'fontSize': '17px', 'lineColor': '#64748b'}, 'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': false, 'curve': 'linear', 'nodeSpacing': 28, 'rankSpacing': 45, 'padding': 16, 'wrappingWidth': 270}}}%% %% A layered overview, not a complete dependency graph. %% Group arrows indicate reuse of the layer below; internal arrows show selected dependencies. flowchart TD subgraph FEATURES["Feature Plugins"] direction LR FUI["Filter
UI Plugin"] VUI["Data Validation
UI Plugin"] FILTER["Filter Plugin"] VALIDATION["Data Validation Plugin"] FUI --> FILTER VUI --> VALIDATION end subgraph PRODUCTS["Product Plugins"] direction LR SUI["Sheets UI Plugin"] SHEETS["Sheets Plugin"] SUI --> SHEETS end subgraph FOUNDATION["Core Framework & Plugins"] direction LR UI["UI Plugin"] FORMULA["Formula Engine Plugin"] RENDER["Render Engine Plugin"] CORE["Core"] UI --> RENDER RENDER --> CORE FORMULA --> CORE end FEATURES --> PRODUCTS PRODUCTS --> FOUNDATION classDef logic fill:#eff6ff,color:#17365f,stroke:#93b4df,stroke-width:1.5px classDef ui fill:#f0fdf4,color:#17543a,stroke:#91c8a7,stroke-width:1.5px classDef shared fill:#f6f7f9,color:#334155,stroke:#bac3ce,stroke-width:1.5px classDef feature fill:#172d50,color:#ffffff,stroke:#172d50 class FUI,VUI ui class FILTER,VALIDATION logic class SUI,SHEETS logic class UI,FORMULA,RENDER,CORE shared style FEATURES fill:#f7fcf9,stroke:#b5d8c1,color:#17543a style PRODUCTS fill:#f5f9ff,stroke:#b6cbea,color:#17365f style FOUNDATION fill:#fafbfc,stroke:#cbd2dc,color:#334155 Figure 1: three plugin layers. Feature plugins build on product plugins, which reuse the core framework and plugins. Group arrows show dependencies on the layer below; Core provides content models, commands, dependency injection, and lifecycle management. Some plugins and dependencies are omitted. New features keep their rules in their own plugins and cooperate through public services, commands, and defined extension points. UI plugins build on shared UI services and components. Dependencies are explicit at two levels: Between plugins: DependentOn declares runtime plugin dependencies. The plugin service orders them, and lifecycle stages separate dependency registration, content initialization, and UI initialization. Inside plugins: dependency injection connects controllers and services through declared dependencies. Supported overrides let an application replace an implementation, adapt a platform service, or supply a test double. Instance-scoped injectors keep application state separate between Univer instances. Disposable registration also gives commands, listeners, components, and icons a cleanup path when their owner is disposed. The filter plugin and its UI plugin show these boundaries in working code. Inside a feature: Model, Controller, Service, and the UI foundation For filtering, sheets-filter owns content logic and sheets-filter-ui owns UI interaction. Each module has a focused responsibility. %%{init: {'htmlLabels': false, 'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'Arial, PingFang SC, Microsoft YaHei, sans-serif', 'fontSize': '17px', 'lineColor': '#64748b'}, 'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': false, 'curve': 'linear', 'nodeSpacing': 28, 'rankSpacing': 45, 'padding': 16, 'wrappingWidth': 270}}}%% %% Every arrow means contains. This is code organization, not execution order. flowchart LR FEATURE["Filter Feature"] LOGIC["Filter Plugin"] UI["Filter UI Plugin"] MODEL["Model"] SERVICE["Service"] CONTROLLER["Controller"] COMMAND["Command / Mutation"] FACADE["Facade API"] VIEW["View"] UICTRL["UI Controller"] UISERVICE["UI Service"] FEATURE --> LOGIC FEATURE --> UI LOGIC --> MODEL LOGIC --> SERVICE LOGIC --> CONTROLLER LOGIC --> COMMAND LOGIC --> FACADE UI --> VIEW UI --> UICTRL UI --> UISERVICE classDef logic fill:#eff6ff,color:#17365f,stroke:#93b4df,stroke-width:1.5px classDef ui fill:#f0fdf4,color:#17543a,stroke:#91c8a7,stroke-width:1.5px classDef shared fill:#f6f7f9,color:#334155,stroke:#bac3ce,stroke-width:1.5px classDef feature fill:#172d50,color:#ffffff,stroke:#172d50 class FEATURE feature class LOGIC,MODEL,SERVICE,CONTROLLER,COMMAND,FACADE logic class UI,VIEW,UICTRL,UISERVICE ui Figure 2: code organization. Arrows mean “contains.” Both plugins can contain Controllers and Services: logic Controllers coordinate content changes and related features; UI Controllers connect menus, shortcuts, and interactions, with UI Services managing panel state. These responsibilities give new features a consistent structure to implement and test. The UI foundation follows the same division. @univerjs/design supplies shared components and styles, @univerjs/ui provides workbench services such as menus, shortcuts, panels, and component registration, and @univerjs/icons supplies icons. A feature registers its components and icons, contributes menus, and attaches its rendering through these extension points. Teams can add a panel or toolbar feature while reusing the application's UI infrastructure. See the UI overview and the filter plugin's component and icon registration. Compose cross-feature edits and undo/redo For example, when rows are inserted inside a filter range, the filter plugin supplies the corresponding range change and its undo data. The row command composes the base edit and participating feature changes, executes them, and records their undo/redo information together. The row insertion feature can use the shared extension mechanism while the filter plugin owns its range-update rules. The command system distinguishes three kinds of action: Command orchestrates a business action and the changes it requires. Mutation changes content saved in a snapshot, with serializable parameters. Operation changes transient state, such as an open panel or the scroll position. A shared structure for undo/redo. For an undoable edit, the feature implementation supplies the forward mutations and corresponding inverse mutations, and the Command records them through IUndoRedoService. When one action affects several features, the Command can combine their changes and undo data in a single undo/redo record, so the user can undo and redo the complete action. See extending commands. Features still need to cooperate. Interceptors and reference-range handlers give that cooperation a defined place. At supported extension points, plugins contribute checks or related mutations; interceptor priorities control ordering where the API defines it. Example: commands, callbacks, feature coordination, and undo/redo %%{init: {'htmlLabels': false, 'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'Arial, PingFang SC, Microsoft YaHei, sans-serif', 'fontSize': '17px', 'lineColor': '#64748b'}, 'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': false, 'curve': 'linear', 'nodeSpacing': 28, 'rankSpacing': 45, 'padding': 16, 'wrappingWidth': 270}}}%% %% Simplified insert-row example. A command composes mutations and records undo after success. %% Events may also fire for nested command executions; not every callback is drawn. flowchart TD BEFORE["Before execution
Inspect or cancel"] CMD["Insert-row Command"] BASE["Row mutations"] EXT["Feature extension points
Filter range changes"] MODEL["Execute combined mutations"] UNDO["Record undo and redo"] AFTER["After execution
Notify listeners"] BEFORE --> CMD CMD --> BASE CMD --> EXT BASE --> MODEL EXT --> MODEL MODEL --> UNDO UNDO --> AFTER classDef entry fill:#f6f7f9,color:#334155,stroke:#bac3ce,stroke-width:1.5px classDef core fill:#eff6ff,color:#17365f,stroke:#93b4df,stroke-width:1.5px classDef extension fill:#f0fdf4,color:#17543a,stroke:#91c8a7,stroke-width:1.5px class BEFORE,AFTER entry class CMD,BASE,MODEL,UNDO core class EXT extension This diagram simplifies an insert-row workflow. Nested command executions have their own callbacks; it does not show every event or the separate Operation path. See the row command, filter controller, and interceptor service. These boundaries support a practical testing strategy: test models and services independently, replace external dependencies through DI, and add regression cases for combined actions and undo/redo. The filter controller tests exercise row and column changes and their effect on filtering. Connect applications and agents through Facade APIs and events The repository includes the content models, formula engine, and Canvas rendering and layout engine behind the editors. They are shared building blocks: spreadsheet rich text, for example, reuses document layout and rendering. Custom features can build on these engines instead of implementing a separate content stack. Read about the formula engine architecture and rendering engine architecture. Browser editors, Node.js Headless tasks, and appropriately composed Workers can reuse the corresponding content plugins, models, commands, and calculation. See Headless Univer and the isomorphic architecture. ICommandService exposes execution callbacks so plugins can observe commands before and after execution. Facade APIs wrap the underlying capabilities in application objects such as FWorkbook, FWorksheet, and FRange. Each plugin contributes its own Facade extensions, typed events through univerAPI.Event, and enums through univerAPI.Enum. Application code can discover event names and constants from one entry point instead of importing private services or repeating strings. For example, BeforeCommandExecute can inspect and cancel an execution; CommandExecuted reports executions to listeners. Listeners return disposables, and cancellation applies where the event supports it. Facade extensions stay with their feature packages, so a content API does not have to pull in unrelated UI APIs. See the Facade design, command callbacks and event bridge, and Enum entry point. The repository provides working feature implementations and patterns for extending them. Read the filter implementation walkthrough for a complete example, or the API Stability Policy before depending on an extension point. 🧩 Extend your application with Univer Office SDK When you want more ready-to-integrate capabilities, compose the corresponding Univer Office SDK modules: additional content types, advanced editing plugins, collaboration, file conversion, and agent tooling. They extend the same content models, plugin architecture, command system, and Facade design introduced above, so you can build on your existing integration. Part How it extends the foundation Open-source Web SDK core · this repository Open-source models, engines, plugins, UI foundation, and Sheets and Docs capabilities, with corresponding Headless content operations. Use them in commercial applications under Apache-2.0. Commercial Web SDK plugins Follow the core's Plugin, dependency injection, Command/Mutation, and Facade extension patterns. Add charts, shapes, pivot tables, SmartArt, and other features for the corresponding content types. Server SDK Extends the same content models and mutation conventions with real-time collaboration, revision history, and Office file conversion. Integrates with your application's identity, permissions, and storage. AI SDK extensions Reuse Web SDK Headless and Facade capabilities to provide composable Node.js APIs and CLI building blocks for agents to inspect, edit, and check content, with collaboration and Worktree review integrations. Scope and licensing This repository: Apache-2.0 packages that can be used in commercial applications under that license, including the open-source Headless content capabilities. Commercial extensions: Commercial Web SDK plugins, Server SDK, and AI SDK capabilities beyond the open-source foundation are distributed and licensed separately. Freemium evaluation includes watermarks and feature limits. Reference applications: Open-source applications such as Univer Workspace have their own source licenses. Their SDK dependencies retain their respective licenses. See the feature comparison, including its Open source only filter, for detailed coverage and plans and licensing for commercial options. How shared content models connect editing, collaboration, and files These capabilities operate on serializable Unit snapshots, including Sheets' IWorkbookData, Docs' IDocumentData, Slides' ISlideData, and canvases' IBoardData (called Boards in the API). These types come from core and the respective product packages; current Slides and Boards capabilities are separately distributed commercial products. The shared Unit conventions let browser editors, backend services, and agents work with the same content. Commands orchestrate edits; Mutations describe content changes. Collaboration packages those mutations into changesets, applies operational transformation (OT) to concurrent changes, and manages confirmed revisions and snapshots. History can reconstruct a revision from a snapshot and subsequent changesets. Read the collaboration design and Collaboration SDK overview. Exchange maps Office file structures to and from Univer content snapshots. For OOXML formats such as XLSX, DOCX, and PPTX, it parses the file into the corresponding Sheet, Doc, or Slide data and generates the file representation on export. The converted content can enter the same editing, calculation, collaboration, and agent workflows. See Office file import and export. How AI SDK gives agents the same content capabilities AI SDK builds on the Web SDK's Headless content models, commands, calculation, and Facade APIs. It exposes structured TypeScript APIs and optional Commander presets that applications can compose into their own Office CLI or agent tools. Understand, discover, and edit. Inspection returns structured content. API Reference helps the agent find Facade symbols and signatures shipped with its SDK. Facade execution distinguishes read and write modes, captures mutations, and works with explicit synchronization and commit results. See content operations. Check the rendered result. A browser Render Runtime reuses Web SDK rendering for screenshots. Slide layout lint adds structured findings for issues such as off-page or overlapping text, giving the agent evidence for another editing pass. See visual inspection. Edit drafts for human review. With the corresponding collaboration and Web capabilities, agents can edit and verify an isolated Worktree draft over several rounds, then hand it to a person to review, merge, or reopen. The workflow uses the same snapshots, mutations, and revision conventions. See Worktree. For repeated calls, optional Worker pools and a daemon reuse loaded content instances and reduce repeated initialization. Your application owns the root CLI, targets, authorization, and output. Explore the AI SDK package catalog to select the required capabilities. 🌐 Application patterns and ecosystem Univer Workspace: an Office SDK reference application For a complete application reference, start with Univer Workspace. It shows how to compose Univer Office SDK editors, collaboration, file capabilities, existing agents, and human review into a self-hostable workspace. Follow its integration patterns when building your own Office application or agent workspace. Agents and editable Office content Keep conversations, spreadsheet editing, and Office content in one workspace. Try Workspace · Workspace source and setup Web App × Sheet · Experimental Bind controls to cells: the app writes to the sheet, and sheet changes update the app. Try the sheet-powered app demo Workspace is open source; its SDK dependencies follow their respective licenses. See the Workspace overview for connected apps and review workflows. Watch an SDK integration demo CLI, agent integrations, and developer skills The same SDK capabilities can also be composed into the agents and tools you already use: Project What it provides Univer CLI A local command-line workspace for creating, editing, inspecting, and delivering Office content. Univer Office for DeepSeek Harness Linked content, result verification, versioned changes, and isolated Worktree collaboration. Univer Office for WorkBuddy Local Office integration, MCP previews, and draft review. Developer preview. Univer Office for OpenClaw Tools for creating, reviewing, and delivering Office content. Univer SDK Skills Instructions that help coding agents integrate the SDK, develop plugins, and implement backend workflows. Each repository documents its setup and SDK dependencies. Explore the ecosystem for agent entry points, or the documentation to build your own integration. 📚 Documentation and contributing Thanks to all contributors who build and improve Univer. Contributions to engines, plugins, tests, documentation, and examples are welcome. 🧩 Web SDK · 🖥️ Server SDK · 🤖 AI SDK · 🔧 API reference · 🎮 Live showcase Edge Firefox Chrome Safari Electron >=88 >=90 >=88 >=14.1 >=12 Univer is compiled with a Chrome 88 target and aims to work with the versions listed above. Runtime compatibility Polyfills: Univer relies on Intl.Segmenter. Add a polyfill such as @formatjs/intl-segmenter if your target browser or runtime does not provide it. Build tools: We recommend Vite, esbuild, or Webpack 5. If your build tool does not support the exports field in package.json (common in Webpack 4), you may need extra path mapping. React: Univer's view layer is built on React 18, supports React 18 and 19, and provides minimal compatibility support for React 16.9+ and 17. Node.js runtime: Headless Univer supports Node.js >=18.17.0. Developing this monorepo requires Node.js >=22.18. Developing in this repository Repository layout . ├── packages/ Core packages, engines, document types, UI plugins, and feature plugins ├── examples/ All-in-one Vite workbench used for local browser development ├── common/ Shared internal tooling, storybook, and utilities ├── tests/ Additional integration test projects └── docs/ Architecture notes, images, and repository-local documentation Package-level READMEs live beside each package under packages/. Local development Requirements: Node.js >=22.18 pnpm: use the version declared by packageManager in package.json. git clone https://github.com/dream-num/univer.git cd univer pnpm install pnpm dev Useful commands: Command Purpose pnpm dev Start the Sheets and Docs development workbench. pnpm build Build workspace packages, excluding internal common packages. pnpm test Run unit tests through Turbo. pnpm typecheck Run TypeScript checks through Turbo. pnpm lint Run ESLint. pnpm storybook:dev Start Storybook for UI component development. Read CONTRIBUTING.md before opening a pull request. Architecture and contributor references Repository packages, presets, and examples. Building Isomorphic Univer. Contributing to Facade API. API Stability Policy. Naming Convention and Fixing Memory Leaks. Architecture TLDRs and OLE attachment notes. 💬 Community Ask questions in GitHub Discussions, join Discord, and follow X or YouTube. Please read the Code of Conduct. 🔒 Security If you believe you have found a security issue, please follow the Security Policy. ❤️ Sponsors Univer is supported by the community and sponsors. You can support the project through Open Collective. 📄 License Copyright (c) 2021-present DreamNum Co., Ltd. The open-source packages in this repository are licensed under Apache-2.0.
