items.title: Four Amazon Bedrock inference choices that affect cost
items.summary: Your Amazon Bedrock inference bill can keep climbing after you tune prompts and application logic. Request-level choices can still change how many tokens the service processes and the rate applied to them. Cache duration, service tier, reasoning effort, and maxTokens can affect cost without changing your model or prompt. Each choice depends on the model and workload. This post shows how we tested each choice and how to verify its effect from response metadata, logs, and billing data. To try these settings yourself, start with the Amazon Bedrock Samples notebooks Mixed TTL Caching and Tenant Isolation with Prompt Caching. For maxTokens and reasoning effort, see the 01-low-effort folder of the sample-code-for-genai-cost-management-workshop GitHub repo. Each sample sets its own model ID, so change it, and the inference parameters, to match the model you call. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Models at a glance. For broader decisions such as model selection, batch inference, routing, and distillation, see Effective cost optimization strategies for Amazon Bedrock. Where inference cost comes from Every Amazon Bedrock response carries usage metadata. Input and output tokens bill at the rate for the model and tier that served the request. Cache reads and writes use separate token counters, and reasoning tokens count as output tokens. Prompt cache duration Repeated system instructions, tool definitions, or reference context can be processed again when the cache expires before the next request. The Prompt caching for faster model inference guide lists 5-minute and 1-hour time-to-live (TTL) values for supported Anthropic models. It also lists a 30-minute minimum TTL for supported GPT-5.6 models. Support and API fields depend on the model, so check the current support matrix before selecting a duration. For supported models, Amazon Bedrock also offers implicit prompt caching, which attempts to reuse eligible prompt prefixes without cache controls in your request. Because implicit caching is best effort and doesn’t guarantee a cache hit, the duration choices in this section apply to explicit caching. This Converse API signature requests a 1-hour entry on models that support it: { "cachePoint": { "type": "default", "ttl": "1h" } } For supported Anthropic models, InvokeModel places the same ttl value in cache_control. A longer duration is not automatically cheaper. The Amazon Bedrock Pricing page lists separate rates for 5-minute writes, 1-hour writes, and cache reads. For Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5 and Anthropic Claude Opus 5 on Amazon Bedrock, a 5-minute write costs 1.25 times the input rate. A 1-hour write costs 2 times, and a cache read costs 0.1 times. These rates set the break-even, assuming each request reuses the exact prefix and each cache read refreshes the TTL. A 5-minute cache pays back on the first reuse within 5 minutes. When requests for the same prefix arrive more than 5 minutes apart, it rewrites at 1.25 times on every request. The 1-hour cache is then cheaper from the second request within the hour. Cache rates and checkpoint minimums differ by model. Check the Amazon Bedrock Pricing page and the prompt caching guide for the model you call. Rerun the comparison for your model, then confirm it with cache read and write tokens after rollout. Keep stable content before dynamic content, meet the model’s checkpoint minimum, and use on-demand inference because prompt caching doesn’t work with batch inference. Changing a cached prefix, including a system instruction or tool definition, causes a miss and a new write. Checkpoints are evaluated in the order tools, system, then messages, so a change in an earlier section also invalidates the later ones. Version prompts that change often so each version gets its own cache entry. We ran six calls on Claude Sonnet 5 with a 1-hour checkpoint, changing the system prompt once and the tool definition once. Each change produced zero cache reads and a new write. AWS describes cache entries as scoped to your account and Region, not to your tenants. In a multi-tenant application, prepend a tenant-specific SHA-256 hash to the cacheable prefix. The Optimizing cost and latency with Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for Anthropic models post describes this pattern. Enforce tenant authorization before you build the prompt. The hash partitions entries inside one account. If a regulated workload needs a hard data boundary, keep each tenant in a separate AWS account. Keep the 5-minute default for frequent reuse. Move from it to a longer supported duration when the same prefix recurs at least twice an hour with gaps longer than 5 minutes. To beat no caching at all, the 1-hour cache needs three requests an hour. Service tiers for latency-tolerant workloads Background jobs, evaluation harnesses, nightly summarization, and backfills don’t always need the latency profile used by interactive requests. For models that support Flex, select it with this request signature: { "serviceTier": { "type": "flex" } } Use default, not standard, to request the Standard tier. You can also omit serviceTier: { "serviceTier": { "type": "default" } } Tier support is model-specific, so record support by exact model version. The Amazon Nova 2 Lite and OpenAI gpt-oss-120b model cards list Flex as supported. The cards for Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5 and Anthropic Claude Opus 5 on Amazon Bedrock list it as not supported. A Flex request to an unsupported model fails with a ValidationException instead of silently running on Standard. Our request to Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5 returned that error. If your policy allows Standard as a fallback, catch the unsupported-tier error and retry once with default. Don’t retry every ValidationException, because malformed requests raise it too. Cap application-level retries. The bounded retry strategy of the AWS SDK handles throttling and transient errors. Set your own deadline for Flex requests. A supported response reports the resolved tier, which you can also verify with Amazon CloudWatch ResolvedServiceTier. See Service tiers for optimizing performance and cost and the Amazon Bedrock Pricing page for the exact model you call. We tested Flex on Amazon Nova 2 Lite with 200 default requests and 200 flex requests, sent in interleaved pairs. Both tiers processed the same number of input and output tokens. All 400 requests resolved to the requested tier, and the median latency difference was too small to separate from noise. At the time of writing, the published Flex rate for Nova 2 Lite in us-west-2 is half the Standard rate, and our bill reflected that. Check the Amazon Bedrock Pricing page for current rates. Keep latency-sensitive traffic on default. Adaptive thinking effort Reasoning tokens bill as output tokens. Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Opus 5 use adaptive thinking at high effort by default, even when a request omits the thinking field. An application moved from Claude Sonnet 4.6 without changes starts billing thinking tokens, and maxTokens now caps thinking plus response text. Claude Haiku 5.5 defaults to medium. All three models support low, medium, high, xhigh, and max. Lower the effort for a task with this request signature: { "thinking": { "type": "adaptive" }, "output_config": { "effort": "low" } } Keep effort in output_config, not inside thinking. Check Adaptive thinking whenever you change models. We tested a tool-calling agent on Claude Opus 5. Its three tasks follow the design in Build long-horizon agents with Grok 4.7 on Amazon Bedrock, and each has one correct answer. We ran each task eight times at every effort level. The table shows median output tokens: Effort Correct runs Median output tokens Change from low (95% interval) low 24 of 24 936 baseline medium 24 of 24 1,484 +59% (50% to 78%) high (default) 24 of 24 2,521 +169% (112% to 190%) xhigh 24 of 24 2,964 +217% (170% to 260%) max 24 of 24 3,762 +302% (180% to 402%) Accuracy at lower effort depends on the model and the task. Measure on tasks shaped like yours. On the Amazon Bedrock Samples Invoke Bedrock model for code generation workload, median output tokens were 676 at low and 743 at high, a difference within run-to-run variation. The programs we graded passed at each effort level. Use per-request output-token counts, CloudWatch AWS/Bedrock OutputTokenCount, invocation logs, and a task pass rate to evaluate the choice. Start below high for routine, well-bounded tasks. Keep high where your quality tests show that the task needs it. A token reduction that breaks the task is not a saving. Output token limits maxTokens is an application output ceiling. It limits the output that a bad prompt, regression, or loop can produce before the request stops. The quota rule is documented in How tokens are counted in Amazon Bedrock. Amazon Bedrock deducts your input tokens plus maxTokens when a request starts, so an oversized value reduces concurrency. An output ceiling isn’t a safety control. Use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails as a standard responsible AI control in production generative AI workloads. Guardrails can filter content, detect prompt attacks, and check grounding on supported inputs and responses. See Detect and filter harmful content by using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Set maxTokens per task type after observing a representative output-token distribution: { "inferenceConfig": { "maxTokens": 155 } } See Inference using Converse API for the request parameters. In our test on Claude Sonnet 5, five normal outputs peaked at 103 tokens, so we set an illustrative fence of 155 tokens with headroom. We then sent the same deliberately verbose prompt with adaptive thinking disabled, once under a 2,048-token ceiling and once under the 155-token fence. The first request generated 2,048 output tokens and the second generated 155, so the fence avoided 1,893 output tokens. Both stopped at max_tokens, so both responses were truncated. The fence limits spend but does not make an unsuitable prompt useful, and in a multi-turn or agentic chain a truncated turn can break the steps after it. For production calibration, compare the 95th and 99th percentiles (P95 and P99) for each task type and add headroom to the selected percentile. With adaptive thinking on, maxTokens also caps thinking tokens, so calibrate with thinking enabled. P95 limits exposure more aggressively but accepts more truncation risk. P99 preserves more valid long-tail responses at a higher ceiling. Monitor max_tokens stops and investigate the request before raising the task’s limit. Putting it together Use the same test loop for each setting: confirm model support, change one request choice, measure tokens or cost, and track quality or completion. If you route across models, keep a capability record for each model version, Region, and API: supported cache duration, service tiers, reasoning levels, and output ceiling. Validate each request against that record before you send it, then check the response for the resolved tier and cache counters. Setting Default or permissive state Result Risk to accept Cache duration Model-specific TTL From published Sonnet 5 and Opus 5 rates, a 1-hour cache wins from the second request per hour when gaps exceed 5 minutes A 1-hour write costs 2 times input, so low reuse loses money. Partition tenant prefixes Service tier default At the time of writing, Nova 2 Lite Flex was published at half the Standard rate, and our bill matched Longer processing. Set your own deadline and a fallback Reasoning effort high on the tested adaptive model Low to high: +169% median output tokens on the agent test, no reliable difference on code generation Quality can drop near the task’s capability boundary. Track pass rate with tokens maxTokens Permissive 2,048-token cap An illustrative 155-token fence avoided 1,893 output tokens in one test Truncation can cascade through multi-turn or agentic chains. Check stopReason before raising the limit Signals to watch Setting Symptom Verify with First response Cache duration Repeated context does not produce the expected latency or cost benefit Application latency and cost telemetry Check prefix stability, reuse interval, and model support before changing TTL Service tier The requested tier is unsupported or the serving tier differs from expectation Response serviceTier and CloudWatch ResolvedServiceTier Use a supported tier or return latency-sensitive traffic to default Reasoning effort Output tokens rise while quality holds Per-request response telemetry, CloudWatch OutputTokenCount, invocation logs, and task pass rate Lower effort for that task class and rerun its quality test maxTokens stopReason is max_tokens Response stop reason and task-scoped output-token distribution Inspect the prompt and task fence before raising the limit Derive P95 and P99 for each task type from task-tagged application telemetry or invocation logs. Conclusion All four choices live in the inference request. Recheck support when you change models, then change one setting at a time and measure the result in your application. Use these resources to evaluate the choices for your workload: Amazon Bedrock console: console.aws.amazon.com/bedrock. Prompt caching: Prompt caching for faster model inference. Service tiers: Service tiers for optimizing performance and cost. Adaptive thinking: Adaptive thinking. Responsible AI controls: Detect and filter harmful content by using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Related reading: Effective cost optimization strategies for Amazon Bedrock. Related samples and posts: Invoke Bedrock model for code generation and Build long-horizon agents with Grok 4.7 on Amazon Bedrock. About the authors Sai Pavan Kasani Sai is a Technical Account Manager at AWS. As a technical advisor and customer advocate, he helps customers move generative AI proofs of concept into production, with a focus on agentic AI workloads, inference optimization, and cost efficiency at scale. Outside of work, Sai enjoys exploring new coffee shops and spending time with family. Aswath Ram Srinivasan Aswath is a Senior Worldwide Specialist Solutions Architect for Generative AI at Amazon Web Services, focused on helping customers build generative AI applications with Amazon Bedrock. He works with enterprise teams to design inference architectures that balance performance, cost, and operational simplicity.

items.title: From prototype to production: Engineering agents with Agent DLC
items.summary: Over the past year, AI agents have moved from exploration into engineering. Enterprise teams are shipping large language model (LLM) systems that call tools, orchestrate APIs, and answer questions over internal knowledge. A successful demo can show what an agent is capable of. Before release, the team needs to answer a further question: “Is this agent ready for production?” The person responsible for that decision needs evidence that the agent meets the agreed requirements. To make that decision consistently, teams need a repeatable, affordable way to assess the agent’s current behavior and whether the latest change has improved it. In traditional software development, teams answer these questions with unit tests, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD), and passing builds. Those mechanisms are necessary but not sufficient for agents, for three reasons, each requiring additional checks. This post explains these three properties and presents a measured case where an aggregate metric hides a coverage problem. It then introduces the Agent Development Lifecycle (Agent DLC): one lifecycle, two loops, and a single explicit standard for judging every change. A note on terminology: Throughout this post, gold standard means one specific artifact: the bundle of verifiable criteria, their thresholds, and the approved examples they are checked against. Business owners approve this standard as the basis for acceptance decisions. 1. Three properties of agents that require additional engineering practices Conventional software testing and CI/CD still apply to agents, but three properties require additional checks. First, agents are non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different outputs and execution paths. Second, changes to prompts, tool descriptions, retrieval settings, or memory configuration can alter behavior in ways that a text review alone can’t reveal. Third, model endpoints, knowledge bases, and external APIs can change independently of the repository and affect agent behavior. Table 1 summarizes the engineering practices needed to address each property. Table 1. What each property invalidates, and what it requires instead. Property The conventional answer Why it falls short What Agent DLC requires Non-determinism One assertion per case in CI Measures a single sample of a distribution. Passes and fails for reasons unrelated to your change Run each example k times. Judge on pass rate and failure distribution Prompts are source code Review the diff, approve the change Behavior can’t be read off the text of a prompt Every prompt, tool, retrieval, and memory change is versioned with an evaluation attached, and the lineage is kept Dependencies move on their own Pin versions, validate on upgrade Doesn’t fire because nothing in your repository changed Re-run the standard on a schedule and alert on deviations from the baseline 2. A measured example: High retrieval precision can hide missing information The following example shows how the choice of metrics affects diagnosis. We built a reference implementation to exercise the method end to end: an internal policy assistant answering HR policy questions over a document knowledge base. We chose a narrow, well-scoped domain to make the evaluation and diagnosis straightforward to follow. The following results were measured on this reference implementation. It isn’t a customer outcome and it isn’t a benchmark result. The accompanying AWS Samples repository includes infrastructure deployment, the HR agent, custom evaluators, and scripts for baseline evaluation and prompt-change re-evaluation (09-run-eval.sh and 10-optimize-prompt.sh). It also includes optional checks for judge repeatability, model comparison, cost, and latency. The scripts reproduce the workflow. Scores can vary across runs and repository versions. Three golden questions, five measures each: Groundedness: Decompose the answer into claims and check each against the retrieved sources. Chunk-level source precision: Is each retrieved chunk, as a whole, necessary for this question? Fact-level source precision: Decompose each chunk into individual facts and check whether each fact is necessary. Retrieval coverage: For each sub-question, does any retrieved chunk answer it? Response precision: Of the claims in the answer, how many are necessary? Table 2. First evaluation round. Measured on the reference implementation. Not a customer outcome. Question Groundedness Chunk-level precision Fact-level precision Retrieval coverage Verdict Performance review 0.83 1.00 0.59 1.00 Pass Benefits enrollment 0.90 1.00 0.53 1.00 Pass Sick-leave certificate 0.39 1.00 0.09 0.00 Fail Chunk-level precision is 1.00 for all three questions. A release gate based only on this metric would accept all three answers. Fact-level precision tells a different story: 0.59, 0.53, 0.09. For the third question, roughly nine out of ten facts in the retrieved material are irrelevant to what was asked. Chunk-level precision only asks whether a passage is on topic. It doesn’t measure how much of the passage is relevant. Then we changed exactly one thing: the system prompt. We added three constraints: ground strictly in retrieved content, ignore irrelevant retrieved content, and keep answers focused. The agent, the knowledge base, the evaluators, and the questions were untouched, so the before-and-after differs by one variable. Table 3. After a prompt-only change. One change, two opposite outcomes. Performance review, before Performance review, after Sick leave, before Sick leave, after Groundedness 0.83 0.87 0.39 (fail) 0.31 (still fail) Fact-level precision 0.59 0.85 0.09 0.04 Response precision 0.58 0.73 0.33 — The first question improved substantially. The third got worse. The evaluation suggested where to investigate before we made the change. Look at the third row of Table 2 again: chunk-level precision 1.00, fact-level precision 0.09, retrieval coverage 0.00. Together, these scores suggested a knowledge-coverage problem: the retrieved material was nominally on topic but didn’t answer the question. Telling the model to “ground strictly in retrieved content” couldn’t supply the missing information. We checked that diagnosis against the source documents used in the experiment. The corpus lacked a dedicated sick-leave policy document, although the leave-management policy contained brief references to sick leave. The next step was to address policy coverage and then check retrieval, rather than keep changing the prompt. In this case, the source material lacks the information needed to answer the question, so prompt changes alone can’t resolve the failure. In this example, evaluation helped identify what needed investigation before further changes. Another result shows why groundedness needs to be checked alongside other criteria. The benefits-enrollment answer passed with groundedness 0.90, and it contained this sentence: “I also noticed from your profile that your preferred contact method is Social Media.” No such profile exists. The policy document lists contact preference as an option inside a process step. The public, crowd-sourced, noisy FAQ corpus contains a pair answering that question with “social media”. The model combined a policy option with an unrelated FAQ answer and presented it as a fact about the user. The high groundedness score didn’t catch this false personal claim. Passing a quality threshold doesn’t establish that responsibility constraints have been met. These scores can vary between runs, and a borderline Pass can become a Fail. Interpret score differences alongside repeated runs and the underlying evidence. Section 5 discusses how to check evaluator reliability. This small reference-implementation example illustrates how evaluation can guide diagnosis. It doesn’t establish a general improvement rate or validate a production release. 3. Agent DLC: One lifecycle, two loops Agent DLC connects six activities around one explicit gold standard: Define, Build, Evaluate, Release, Observe, and Feed Back. Evaluation-driven development has been described in earlier work, including Xia et al.’s Evaluation-Driven Development of LLM Agents: A Process Model and Reference Architecture. Agent DLC applies this approach to delivery through six activities with explicit acceptance conditions, release authority, and evidence requirements. The acceptance-first approach also appears in Fotor’s published AWS customer case study. The team defined scalability, cost, isolation, and architectural flexibility criteria before migrating to AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, then validated changes against operating data. The case reports workflow overhead falling from minutes to seconds, excluding model inference, and support for thousands of concurrent active sessions. It documents Agent DLC-guided architecture delivery. Quality evaluation is identified as the next step. Define translates business objectives into criteria, thresholds, and approved examples. Build designs the prompts, tools, context, memory, and runtime mechanisms that must satisfy them. Evaluate produces the evidence that says whether a candidate version does. When it does, the version goes to a controlled release. Observe watches it in production. Feed Back returns what production teaches to Define. Figure 1: The six activities of Agent DLC each relate to the gold standard at the center. Define produces it, Build follows it, and Evaluate uses it. Release checks against it, Observe reuses it, and Feed Back iterates it. The five dimensions of the standard are listed beneath Figure 1 shows how each activity uses or updates the standard, making its role in development and release explicit. Inside that outer loop runs a faster inner loop: score → inspect the path → change one thing → re-evaluate. It operates on one candidate version and answers two questions: where to change, and whether the change helped. The two loops do different jobs, and the difference matters. The inner loop improves the agent against a fixed standard. The outer loop lets the standard change. Finding during development that the agent recommends products without checking inventory is an inner-loop problem. Suppose production users ask the agent to look things up on behalf of a family member, but no criterion covers this case. This requires the outer loop: define the authorization boundary and add examples. Then use the inner loop to meet the updated standard. Confusing the two can lead teams to try to fix a missing criterion with a prompt change. Teams might also widen the standard during an improvement cycle, leaving them unable to tell which change moved the score. Both loops build reusable assets: business criteria, approved examples, evaluators, and the record of how past failures were handled. These assets outlive the model and the framework. When you change models, evaluate the replacement against the same criteria and examples. The next four sections explain how to define good so it can be checked (section 4) and improve the agent against that standard (section 5). They then cover updating the standard through production feedback (section 6) and designing the architecture to provide evaluation evidence (section 7). 4. Define good: Five dimensions, three tiers Start with a business outcome defined by its owner. For a recommendation agent, this might be: “Recommend suitable products to returning customers while protecting their information.” Translate that requirement into verifiable criteria across five dimensions. Table 4. Consider all five dimensions when defining criteria. Dimension Key question Areas of focus Domain understanding Does it actually understand your business? Terminology, aliases, multi-hop relationships, internal enterprise knowledge Quality Is it correct, complete, and consistent throughout? Correctness, completeness, consistency, support for citations Responsibility Are permissions, boundaries, compliance, and auditability addressed? Unauthorized access, information disclosure, compliance hard constraints, traceability Cost What does each run cost, and does it stay economical at scale? Token consumption, evaluator cost, redundant steps Performance Is it fast, stable, and able to carry the load? Latency, throughput, stability, availability For each criterion, specify how it’s verified and who approves it. “It must be accurate” is a goal. “Every factual claim must be traceable to a retrieved source” is verifiable. Business experts should approve examples that make the expected behavior concrete. Table 5. Criteria fall into three tiers. The tier, not the dimension, decides whether a criterion blocks a release. Tier Blocks release? How it’s expressed Example Hard constraint Yes Boolean, evaluated per run Disclosing another customer’s information Release gate Until it’s met Pass-rate threshold over k runs At least 95% of cited clauses traceable to a source Monitoring only No Tracked and reviewed, promoted later Tone appropriateness, until its evaluator is calibrated Assign each criterion its own tier and, where applicable, threshold. Never let a high score elsewhere offset a hard-constraint violation. In the recommendation example, recommendation quality is a release gate under Quality, while protecting another customer’s information is a hard constraint under Responsibility. One business requirement produces criteria in different dimensions and tiers. Assess each against its own acceptance condition. These criteria also determine what evidence the system must expose. The next section uses that evidence to improve the agent and decide whether to release it. Section 7 explains how evidence requirements shape the architecture. 5. The inner loop: Evaluate, diagnose, and improve Score. Match the evaluator to the criterion. Use code for unambiguous rules, runtime telemetry for cost and latency, and load tests and operating data for capacity and availability. Use model-based judges for criteria requiring judgment, calibrated against human-reviewed examples. Include authorization and cross-user isolation tests alongside checks for prohibited fields when evaluating information protection. Run each example k times to assess variable behavior. For model-based judges, repeat evaluations to measure scoring variability and compare their judgments with human-reviewed examples. Small score gains need supporting evidence before they count as improvements. Inspect the path. Locate a failure at three levels: session, trajectory, and step. If a recommendation exposes a phone number, follow the affected session to response composition and inspect where profile fields entered the draft. The cause might be upstream of the visible symptom, as section 2 showed. Change one thing, then re-evaluate. Correct the identified cause and repeat evaluation against the unchanged standard under the same conditions. Verify that disclosure stopped and recommendation quality still meets its gate. Assess release readiness separately for each task type, or intent. Release only those that meet their criteria, with any fallback for an unreleased intent also meeting the agreed release conditions. Table 6. Release decisions by dimension, tier, and intent. State of the grid Decision Any hard constraint failed Don’t release. All hard constraints pass, but one or more release gates missed Don’t release the affected intent unless a limited rollout was approved in advance with explicit safeguards and stop criteria. Otherwise, route it to a human. All hard constraints pass, and all release gates met Full release. A limited rollout needs acceptance conditions, safeguards, and stop criteria agreed before evaluation. It can’t override a hard constraint or lower a threshold after a failed result. Before release, include blocked and refused requests in the evaluation, checking whether each was handled as expected. Record the criteria, thresholds, evaluator versions, and release decision so the team can trace why a version was approved. Passing these checks supports release within the tested scope. Production monitoring then checks whether the agent continues to meet the standard as usage and dependencies change. 6. The outer loop: Keep the data flowing Record execution traces from the first test request so failures can be diagnosed in development and production. Sample and evaluate production interactions to identify failures, then review them with the business owner to confirm the expected behavior. Add cases covered by existing criteria to the regression set. When a case reveals a missing requirement, update the standard and use the inner loop to meet it. Run evaluations regularly to catch behavior changes caused by external dependencies. When the standard changes, compare results under both versions to distinguish agent regression from broader test coverage. Link each result to its standard, test set, evaluator, and agent version. 7. Design the architecture to support evaluation The evaluation and feedback loops need evidence that the architecture must provide. Work backward from each criterion to the system behavior and records needed to verify it. For example, to distinguish a tool-selection error from an execution failure, define the tool’s purpose, accepted inputs, outputs, and error conditions. Expose the actual inputs, results, and errors in traces so evaluators can locate the failure. Acceptance criteria therefore shape both evaluation and architecture. With those foundations in place, start with one business task and establish a baseline. 8. Getting started on AWS Choose one clearly scoped business task and aim to establish an initial evaluation baseline within a week. Days 1–2. Have the business owner and engineers agree on acceptance criteria, tiers, and thresholds. Prepare 20–30 golden examples covering common requests and important edge cases, with expected behavior approved by the business owner. Days 3–5. Implement the evaluators described in section 5 and run the golden set repeatedly. Publish the baseline, including failures and the evidence needed to investigate them. Week 2. Change one thing and re-evaluate under the same conditions. Record the release decision and its supporting evidence. After reviewing the baseline, integrate evaluation into the release process and run it regularly to detect drift. Assign an owner to review production failures and feed confirmed cases back into the standard. On AWS, use models available through Amazon Bedrock to build the agent. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, assesses agent behavior with built-in evaluators and supports custom evaluators for business-specific criteria. AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, provides execution visibility, complemented by Amazon CloudWatch for runtime monitoring and diagnostics. AgentCore runtime, Gateway, Identity, and Memory support execution, tool integration, identity management, and memory management. About the authors Yuan Wei Yuan is an Applied Scientist at the AWS GCR Service Specialist Org with years of experience in algorithm development. Yuan has extensive hands-on experience developing and deploying solutions across large language models (LLMs), multimodal models, time series forecasting, and AI-generated content (AIGC). Tianqin Cai Tianqin is an Applied Scientist at the AWS GCR Service Specialist Org. His research focuses on generative AI, natural language processing, and multimodal pre-training. He has extensive experience in algorithm development and real-world applications across advertising and recommendation systems, search ranking, foundation model pre-training, and multimodal AI. Jiade Wu Jiade is a Solutions Architect Manager at Amazon Web Services (AWS), where he leads the Partner Solutions Architecture team in Greater China. His work focuses on taking AI agents from prototype to production, including evaluation-driven development and agent lifecycle methodology. He is also an open-source contributor, with projects on aws-samples covering agent infrastructure and serverless architectures on AWS.

items.title: garrytan/gbrain
items.summary: Garry's Opinionated OpenClaw/Hermes Agent Brain Give the agent you already use a memory you control. GBrain stores explicit facts with their sources, supports corrections and withdrawal, and makes the same memory available across your agents. Start with keyless memory and keyword retrieval; add semantic search, synthesis, and background enrichment when you need them. GBrain is MIT-licensed and free to self-host; gbrain.io is optional paid hosting. Tip Need hosted? First time running an agent? Try gbrain.io, hosted GBrain, for the easiest experience: one brain for you and your team, connected to ChatGPT, Claude and Cursor, with nothing to install or keep online. Stuck? Email support@gbrain.io and a person will set it up with you, free. Keep skills beside knowledge. New local brains include memory skills in their content root. Agents can join an authorized catalog; only approved editors can publish. Managed coding-agent installs add an owned native router; restart and real-use verification are separate steps. Staged migration preserves sharing choices and personal edits. See shared brain skills. Choose your setup Add GBrain to my existing agent — recommended. Keep your agent's identity and save memory inside its environment. No new personal-agent identity or private repository is required. Start with the guide for Grok Bot, Muse, or Codex / Claude Code. Other harnesses. Use the brain on my own computer from everywhere. One command publishes it over MCP on your Tailscale tailnet and keeps it running: gbrain mcp expose (add --funnel for cloud agents such as Grok Bot, Muse and ChatGPT). Follow use your brain from anywhere over MCP. Say to your agent: "use my brain over mcp" — "put my brain on tailscale". Connect my existing hosted brain. Follow hosted harness access to choose native OAuth or a private machine connection. For dashboard login, clients, and permissions, use MCP administration with the server's separate owner credential. Delegation is an explicit choice. Grok Bot and Grok Build are different products. Muse's personal agent and Muse Code are different products too. Muse already has native editable memory; GBrain adds an explicit, portable record with provenance and shared access. See each guide's dated evidence and remaining verification steps. I'm Garry Tan, President and CEO of Y Combinator. I built GBrain to run my own AI agents. It's the production brain behind my OpenClaw and Hermes deployments: 155,795 pages, 24,589 people, 5,340 companies, 66 cron jobs running autonomously. My agent ingests meetings, emails, tweets, voice calls, and original ideas while I sleep. It enriches every person and company it encounters. It fixes its own citations and consolidates memory overnight. I wake up smarter than when I went to bed — and so will you. It works as a company brain too. Authenticated remote clients are constrained by source and operation grants plus visibility filters. Local files and shared database credentials are a different trust boundary: sources alone do not isolate those callers. The authorization tests exercise specific access paths, not a universal no-leak guarantee. Read the sharing boundaries and company-brain tutorial before setting up shared access. Alongside keyword and semantic retrieval, GBrain offers two optional ways to use your stored knowledge: A synthesis layer that gives you the actual answer. Synthesized, well-cited prose across people, companies, deals, and ideas. Not "here are 10 chunks that mention your query"; an actual answer with citations and an explicit note on what the brain doesn't know yet. The gap analysis is the part that changes how you use the brain. A typed knowledge graph. Trusted local page writes extract supported references without LLM calls when auto-linking is enabled. Remote put_page edges arrive later, via sweeps, maintenance or add_link. Ask "who works at acme-example?": walks are breadth-first, milliseconds on dense clusters (how). On BrainBench relationship questions, relationship retrieval lifts production R@5 from 0.6626 to 0.7241 (benchmark); 0.9791 is the graph-oracle-parse upper bound, not a product score. The point of building a 150K-page brain is to use it as a strategic moat. To never lose context. To query what's in your own head without re-reading it. The brain layer is what makes the moat usable. The 24/7 dream cycle is what keeps it sharp. Both run on your hardware, your DB, your keys. It's easier to ship a daemon that runs 24/7 to ingest, enrich, and consolidate than it is to keep an agent in chat working hard. GBrain is that daemon, generalized. Install in 30 minutes. Your agent does the work. As my personal agent gets smarter, so does yours. Start keyless. Your harness subscription and any separately configured model API usage are different costs. The optional personal-agent bootstrap takes about 15 minutes; always-on enrichment needs its own compute and API configuration. Durable preferences and facts can be shared across agents; transient task and harness configuration state stay local. Configured cloud embedding, reranking, extraction, and synthesis providers can receive text, and the harness model sees recalled memory even in keyless mode. Markdown export is not a full database backup. Read memory boundaries. LLMs: fetch llms.txt for the documentation map, or llms-full.txt for the same map with core docs inlined in one fetch. Agents: start with AGENTS.md (or CLAUDE.md if you're Claude Code). What this looks like Say you have a meeting with Alice tomorrow. You want to walk in remembering what she works on, when you last talked, and what's still open between you. Here's what you'd type, and what you'd get back. You ask: "What do I need to know before my meeting with Alice tomorrow?" Most personal-knowledge tools give you back a list of pages. Something like: 1. people/alice — Alice runs engineering at Acme... 2. meetings/2026-03-15-alice-q1 — Q1 product review with Alice... 3. meetings/2026-01-08-acme-kickoff — Kickoff meeting with Acme team... 4. customers/acme — Acme is a series-B fintech we work with... 5. notes/2026-04-22 — Quick chat with Alice about pricing... Five pages you now have to open and read yourself to actually prepare. The tool found the right material, but it didn't do the work. GBrain gives you back the answer, with sources: Alice runs engineering at Acme (a series-B fintech). You last spoke on April 22 in a quick pricing chat. Three things are still open from that conversation: 1. She owes you the security review for the new tier (deadline was May 1; no update since). 2. You committed to pricing for a 500-seat tier (you sent it April 25; no response yet). 3. She mentioned they're hiring a CISO; you said you'd intro someone from your network. Heads up: nothing's been added to the brain about Alice or Acme since April 22, six weeks ago. She may have replied through email or Slack DM, channels the brain doesn't see. Worth asking her to catch up before assuming any of this is still current. Every claim has a source page behind it. The "heads up" at the end tells you what the brain doesn't know yet, so you can ask Alice about it directly instead of being surprised. The brain just did your meeting prep. This is the difference between a search engine and a brain. Search finds the pages. The brain reads them for you and writes the answer. Install Tip Fastest: hosted GBrain at gbrain.io, for any harness. One command launches a GBrain hosted on gbrain.io; Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT, Cursor and every other AI you use connect to it, with nothing to keep online. curl -sSL https://gbrainio.terminalwire.sh | bash gbrainio terminal connect # in a new terminal gbrainio workspace new # pick a plan in the browser curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash # skip if Bun 1.4.4+ is installed export PATH="$HOME/.bun/bin:$PATH" bun install -g github:garrytan/gbrain#stable # the gbrain CLI only; no local brain # Claude Code (an existing gbrain entry is kept): (claude mcp get gbrain >/dev/null 2>&1 || claude mcp add --transport http --scope user gbrain https://gbrain.io/mcp) && gbrain setup claude-code --instructions-only # Codex (an existing gbrain entry is kept): (codex mcp get gbrain >/dev/null 2>&1 || codex mcp add gbrain --url https://gbrain.io/mcp) && gbrain setup codex --instructions-only gbrain setup <harness> --instructions-only tells the agent the brain is there; agents seldom call an MCP server nobody told them about. It writes the brain-first block into ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md or Codex's AGENTS.md (a non-empty AGENTS.override.md instead when Codex has one) with a per-turn rule hook, and leaves the MCP entry alone; the same command with --no-instructions added takes them out. The installer is a shell script for macOS and Linux; read it before you run it. Here's how to self-host it GBrain is MIT-licensed and free to self-host. It needs Bun 1.4.4 or newer; existing worker installs read the authorization and queue upgrade guide before restarting on this version. Warning GBrain is NOT distributed on npm. The npm gbrain package is unrelated and can shadow the real binary, so never run npm install -g gbrain or bun add -g gbrain. Install only via bun install -g github:garrytan/gbrain#stable (the soaked stable channel; #latest-stable is the alpha line with every release) or git clone --branch stable + bun install && bun link. Installed by mistake? gbrain doctor gives the fix. Schema not migrated (#218)? Run gbrain apply-migrations --yes --no-autopilot-install; if it exits 1, run gbrain doctor --json, not another --yes (wedged: relay its fix). bun install -g github:garrytan/gbrain#stable gbrain setup claude-code # or: gbrain setup codex gbrain init --pglite --no-embedding # any other harness, or no agent gbrain setup shows what it will write first (--dry-run previews, --remove undoes), creates a keyless brain only if none exists, wires MCP, hooks and a brain-first block in the agent's instruction file (--no-instructions skips it), and smoke-tests them (setup guide). For any other coding agent, paste: Add GBrain memory to this existing agent. Read and follow: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/garrytan/gbrain/master/INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md Keep my current identity and instructions, start keyless, and show me the search-mode choice. Verify a remember/recall round trip with real GBrain calls. Postgres, thin clients, API keys and upgrades: docs/INSTALL.md. Agents: INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md. Memory-only walkthrough: give your coding agent a memory. CLI standalone (no agent) gbrain init --pglite --no-embedding # keyless; no server, no Docker gbrain import ~/notes/ --no-embed # index your markdown gbrain search "a phrase from a note" --json gbrain doctor # verify health Optional: a new personal agent To have GBrain create a new persistent personal agent with identity files and its own private GitHub repo, open Codex (CLI or ChatGPT desktop) or Claude Code in a new, empty folder and paste: Read and follow every step of: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/garrytan/gbrain/stable/BOOTSTRAP_FOR_AGENTS.md Goal: set yourself up as my persistent personal agent in this folder, with gbrain as your memory. Interview me before writing any identity file — never invent answers. Ask before anything destructive. You are not done until `gbrain bootstrap verify` exits 0. The repo is not a complete backup; see the bootstrap guide. For the always-on version (24/7 ingestion and the overnight dream cycle on a server with 8GB+ RAM and its own API usage), run GBrain under OpenClaw or Hermes and point it at INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md; the personal-brain tutorial walks it end to end. Connect GBrain to your AI client (MCP) Local stdio client: gbrain setup claude-code or gbrain setup codex registers gbrain serve (lists the memory verbs; --surface full lists every tool) behind gbrain's launcher, so a session opened in a cloned repository never loads that repository's bunfig.toml or .env, and adds the brain-first instructions: agents seldom call a brain nobody told them about. Cursor, Windsurf and other stdio clients take "$(command -v gbrain)" serve --surface starter --advertise verbs. Plugins with curated skills: Codex codex plugin marketplace add garrytan/gbrain@codex-plugin + codex plugin add gbrain@gbrain; Claude Code /plugin marketplace add garrytan/gbrain + /plugin install gbrain@gbrain. This brain from anywhere: gbrain mcp expose publishes it on your Tailscale tailnet as a user service (--funnel for cloud agents such as Grok Bot, Muse and ChatGPT). Guide. A brain on another host: gbrain connect https://your-host/mcp --token gbrain_xxx --install (add --agent codex for Codex). Hosted brains use native OAuth or a private handoff; dashboard, clients and permissions live in MCP administration. Per-client guides: Claude Code · Codex · ChatGPT · Claude Desktop · Claude Cowork · Perplexity · Hermes · OpenClaw · opencode · Grok Build · Grok Bot · Muse · everything MCP. Two ways to query your brain Raw retrieval (what most personal-knowledge tools ship) and a synthesis layer that gives you an actual answer. They serve different jobs. # raw retrieval: top pages by hybrid score, no answer-generation call gbrain search "who's working on AI agents at portfolio companies?" # brain layer: synthesized answer with citations and gap analysis gbrain think "who's working on AI agents at portfolio companies?" gbrain search returns the top retrieved pages, ranked by hybrid scoring (vector + keyword + RRF + source-tier boost + reranker). Use it when you want raw material to skim: agent context windows, citation lookups, finding a specific quote. Configured embedding and reranking providers can still receive text and charge for retrieval. Keyless keyword search needs no model API; synthesis requires a configured chat capability. See memory boundaries. Search also tells you when its results are incomplete because projections are still rebuilding or a bounded vector scan ran short. Ask your agent "Check whether my search index is ready"; see search readiness and recovery before treating an empty result as proof that a page is missing. gbrain think runs the same retrieval, then composes a synthesized answer across the results with explicit citations to the source pages AND an honest note on what the brain doesn't know yet. The gap analysis is the differentiator: the answer tells you when a page is stale, when a claim is uncited, when two pages contradict each other, when there's a hole you should fill. Say to your agent: "What do we know about acme-example?" — "Tell me about alice-example before my meeting tomorrow" — "Search for who's working on AI agents." Your agent routes these to the brain automatically; you never type the commands yourself. Why it compounds. Pair the brain layer with find_trajectory and you get answers like "how have the company's metrics changed AND what does the team look like right now AND what did they promise / share AND when did we last meet AND what's the value-add I can offer here": well-scored, well-cited, in one shot. That's the strategic moat. That's why building a 150K-page brain is worth the effort. gbrain agent run "..." exposes the same surface to a sub-agent through the Minions queue, with crash-safe two-phase persistence. Same answers, durable. How to get data in Start with an explicit fact or a notes folder; opt into connectors, capture, and enrichment separately. Already have a company knowledge repository? Say to your agent: “Connect our existing company brain, preserve its files, and show me the import plan first.” Try gbrain sources demo company-brain without keys or private data, then inspect your committed Markdown with gbrain sources inspect <path> --profile company-brain. The company-brain ingestion guide covers explicit destination approval, typed relationships, and resumable verification. It does not enable embeddings, sharing, schedules, or curation automatically. Say to your agent: "Remember this with its source" — "What should I import first?" Data ingestion guide covers files, conversations, connectors, Google data, and capture commands. Your brain's shape (schema packs) Most personal-knowledge tools force one fixed layout: their idea of "notes" + "people" + "tags." Drop a Notion export or your own years-old Obsidian vault on top, and the agent doesn't know what a Projects/ folder means or whether Reading/ is people or sources. gbrain doesn't have a fixed layout. It ships with bundled schema packs and lets you author your own when none fit: gbrain-base-v2 (default) — 15-type DRY/MECE canonical taxonomy (14 canonical + note catch-all): person, company, media, tweet, social-digest, analysis, atom, concept, source, deal, email, slack, writing, project, note. Subtypes/format/origin pushed to frontmatter. gbrain-base (legacy) — the wider 24-type layout. Stays bundled for back-compat; brains on it can upgrade via gbrain onboard --check --explain → gbrain jobs submit unify-types --params '{"target_pack":"gbrain-base-v2","apply":true}' (omit "apply":true for a dry-run preview — that is the default). gbrain-recommended — extends gbrain-base with the 13 additional directories from docs/GBRAIN_RECOMMENDED_SCHEMA.md (source, place, trip, conversation, personal, civic, project, etc.). Activate with gbrain schema use gbrain-recommended. Your own pack — gbrain schema detect clusters your actual filesystem into proposed types, gbrain schema suggest runs an LLM pass over them, and gbrain schema review-candidates --apply promotes the ones you like. Three commands and the brain knows your shape. Authoring a successor pack (declares migration_from: so existing brains can opt in): see docs/architecture/pack-upgrade-mechanism.md. gbrain schema active # which pack is running, which tier set it gbrain schema list # bundled + installed packs gbrain schema detect # propose types matching your filesystem gbrain schema suggest # LLM-refined proposals on top of detect gbrain schema review-candidates # human gate: promote / rename / ignore gbrain schema use my-pack # activate Say to your agent: "My schema isn't matching my notes — propose new types from my corpus" — "Add a page type for lab results to my brain's schema." The schema-author skill runs the detect → suggest → review flow for you. The active pack threads through every read + write path: parseMarkdown infers page type from the pack's path prefixes; whoknows scopes expert routing to types declared expert_routing: true; extract_facts runs only on extractable: true types. The retained search-cache key includes the pack name + version, but semantic result reuse is temporarily disabled. Switch packs and the brain re-interprets itself; switch back and nothing's lost. Seven-tier resolution chain (per-call flag → env var → per-source DB key → brain-wide DB key → gbrain.yml → ~/.gbrain/config.json → gbrain-base default). Full reference + authoring guide: docs/architecture/schema-packs.md. Tutorials Step-by-step walkthroughs for getting the most out of GBrain. Each one takes you from zero to a working outcome, with concrete commands and real numbers. Set up your personal AI agent + brain from zero — the canonical full-stack install. Two GitHub repos, a Telegram bot, AlphaClaw on Render, OpenClaw + GBrain + Supabase. End-to-end in about 2 hours. Set up GBrain as your company brain — federated, multi-user, OAuth-scoped institutional memory for a 10-50 person team. About 90 minutes end-to-end. Auto-improve a skill with gbrain skillopt — treat a SKILL.md as a trainable parameter. Generate a starter benchmark straight from the skill with --bootstrap-from-skill (or write your own), strengthen the judges, then watch the optimizer propose edits and keep only the ones that measurably score higher. ~20 minutes, ~$1 in API calls. Flag + cost + safety reference: docs/guides/skillopt.md. More walkthroughs in progress: connecting an existing agent (Claude Code, Cursor, OpenClaw, Hermes) to a GBrain memory layer; setting up GBrain for VC dealflow with founder scorecards and meeting prep; migrating an existing Notion or Obsidian vault; indexing a codebase as a queryable code brain. Full tutorial index: docs/tutorials/. Want to see a tutorial that isn't here yet? Open an issue describing the workflow you want documented. What it does (the loop) signal → search → respond → write → auto-link → sync (every (brain-first (informed (page + (typed edges (cron message) retrieval) by context) timeline) + backlinks) keeps fresh) Signal detector, after you opt in, captures durable ideas and entity mentions from substantive messages. Explicit remembering works without automatic capture; paid enrichment is a separate choice. Brain-first lookup before any external API call. The cheapest, fastest, most personal information source you have. Auto-link extracts graph links for trusted local page writes. No LLM calls; pure pattern matching on page references such as [[people/alice-example]]. Unresolved extracted facts keep their provenance without inventing a backing page. Cron-driven enrichment runs while you sleep: dedup people pages, fix citations, score salience, find contradictions, prep tomorrow's tasks. The whole loop is described in docs/architecture/topologies.md with diagrams. Say to your agent: "Set up autopilot" (installs the cron that runs the loop) — "Run dream" — "Did the dream cycle run?" Capabilities GBrain combines keyword and semantic retrieval, typed graph traversal, optional cited synthesis, background jobs, and curated agent skills. Say to your agent: "What search mode am I running?" — "Who works at acme-example?" — "What does my brain know about this project?" Capability reference keeps the commands, benchmark scope, cost controls, and feature-specific guides. Integrations Data flowing into the brain. Each integration is a recipe — markdown + setup hints — that ships in recipes/ and is discoverable via gbrain integrations list. Say to your agent: "Set up voice calls into my brain" — "Wire my email and calendar into the brain" — your agent reads the recipe and walks the setup with you. Voice: Phone calls create brain pages via Twilio + OpenAI Realtime (or DIY STT+LLM+TTS). Setup recipe: recipes/twilio-voice-brain.md. Gmail + Calendar + Contacts (native): the google source kind syncs threads, events, and contacts through your own OAuth client and runs the open-loop engine on top (gbrain waiting). Setup: docs/guides/google-connect.md; recipes: recipes/email-to-brain.md, recipes/calendar-to-brain.md. Meeting notes + Slack channels (native): the meetings source kind (Fireflies first) writes one page per meeting and the slack source kind one page per channel per day, synced on a schedule, on brains with or without a Git repository. Setup: docs/guides/meeting-and-slack-sources.md. Email + calendar (webhooks): webhook handlers that route to brain signals. docs/integrations/meeting-webhooks.md. Embedding providers: Voyage (new-install default: voyage-4 @ 1024d), OpenAI, OpenRouter, Google Gemini, Azure OpenAI, MiniMax, Alibaba DashScope, Zhipu, Ollama (local), llama.cpp llama-server (local), LM Studio, Together, and LiteLLM proxy. Pricing matrix + decision tree in docs/integrations/embedding-providers.md. Existing vectors are never converted by changing the default; use the explicitly approved embedding migration. Rerankers: Voyage rerank-3-lite hosted (the default unless search.reranker.model is set; on in balanced and tokenmax, same VOYAGE_API_KEY as embeddings; gbrain config set search.reranker.model voyage:rerank-2.5 restores the previous default), plus the llama-server-reranker recipe for fully-local cross-encoder rerank via llama.cpp running Qwen3-Reranker against the same gateway.rerank() seam. Setup walkthrough in docs/ai-providers/llama-server-reranker.md. Credential vault + gateway: gbrain creds manages OAuth and API credentials in a local vault (recipes/credential-gateway.md); agent-side vault-aware secret distribution: docs/integrations/credential-gateway.md. MCP clients: every major MCP client is supported. docs/mcp/ per-client setup. Memorable (procedural memory): optional, off by default. Your brain remembers what happened; Memorable makes your agent remember how — finished sessions become replayable procedures stored on your machine (in a standalone local store, or inside your brain database if you opt in), recalled when a similar task comes back. See the section below, and docs/memorable-agents.md for the agent-facing detail. Memorable — remember how, not just what (optional) Memorable stores replayable procedures from coding sessions. Its relay is off by default and requires an explicit disclosure/consent step; it can send redacted traces and query text off-machine. Read the Memorable integration guide for installation, data flow, per-harness limitations, and removal. Say to your agent: "Explain Memorable's data sharing before enabling it." Architecture flowchart LR Repo[Markdown brain repos] --> Sync[Sync and parse] Sync --> Engine{Brain engine} Engine -->|default| PGLite[(PGLite)] Engine -->|shared or large| Postgres[(Postgres and pgvector)] Agent[AI agent or operator] --> Surface[CLI or MCP] Surface --> Ops[Contract-first operations] Ops --> Search[Hybrid retrieval] Ops --> Graph[Typed graph traversal] PGLite --> Search Postgres --> Search PGLite --> Graph Postgres --> Graph Search --> Synthesis[Synthesis and gap analysis] Graph --> Synthesis Synthesis --> Answer[Cited answer] Two engines, one contract. PGLite (Postgres 17 via WASM, zero-config, default) for personal brains up to ~50K pages. Postgres + pgvector (Supabase or self-hosted) for shared, large or multi-machine brains. Both implement one BrainEngine contract (src/core/engine.ts); CLI and MCP share one op registry. Canonical files preserve file-backed knowledge. Your brain repo holds the Markdown; the database is an index rebuildable from it, and git deletes become soft-deletes. DB-only pages, unresolved facts, history and operational state need a database backup: where your memory lives, system of record. Publish public subsets, share team mounts, or point a thin client at a colleague's brain. Topologies in docs/architecture/topologies.md. Two organizational axes (brain ⊥ source). A brain is a database (your personal brain, a team mount you joined). A source is a repo inside that brain. Routing uses .gbrain-source dotfiles and a 6-tier precedence chain. Diagrams in docs/architecture/brains-and-sources.md. Why the graph matters. Vector search finds similar text; graph retrieval follows stored relationships. Extracted edges are evidence to inspect, not proof that a relationship is true. Graph freshness depends on the write path and maintenance described in memory boundaries. Deep dive: retrieval architecture; entity recall. Troubleshooting Start with gbrain doctor. For database access failures, use gbrain engine status --probe and gbrain db-repair before changing configuration. Say to your agent: "Check my brain health and show me the repair plan before changing anything." Troubleshooting reference covers installation recovery, PGLite startup, embedding dimensions, locks, import failures, and sync. Docs docs/INSTALL.md — every install path, end to end docs/guides/bootstrap.md — the persistent-personal-agent bootstrap contract (interview, identity files, hooks, private repo, security posture, uninstall), plus local harness mode (gbrain bootstrap harness) for wiring framework-spawned Claude Code/Codex sessions to a running serve Anatomy of a page — frontmatter, timeline, facts; per-client facts docs/what-schemas-unlock.md — why schemas matter: 7 killer use cases, the structural argument for typed page kinds, the agent-co-curates pattern docs/schema-author-tutorial.md — 5-minute walkthrough: fork the bundled pack, add a custom type, backfill existing pages, prove the wiring via gbrain whoknows docs/architecture/ — system design, topologies, retrieval theory docs/guides/ — how-to runbooks (google connect, open loops, sub-agent routing, minion deployment, skill development, brain-first lookup, idea capture, diligence ingestion) docs/integrations/ — connecting external data sources (voice, email, calendar, embedding providers) MCP task guide — deployment and per-client setup (Claude Desktop, Code, Cursor, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Cowork) MCP administration — owner dashboard access, client registration, OAuth, permissions, and token recovery Evals and research — methods and results docs/ethos/ — philosophy (thin harness, fat skills, markdown as recipes, origin story) AGENTS.md — entry point for non-Claude agents CLAUDE.md — entry point for Claude Code (deep operating context) CONTRIBUTING.md — contributor guide, test discipline, eval-capture mode SECURITY.md — install-path trust model, self-update integrity, automated scanning, OAuth threat model, hardening defaults Contributing Run bun run test for the fast loop, bun run verify for the pre-push gate, bun run ci:local to run the full Docker-backed CI stack locally. Detailed test discipline in CONTRIBUTING.md. Community PRs are batched into release waves rather than merged one-by-one — see the community-PR-wave process in docs/RELEASING.md. Contributor attribution stays attached via Co-Authored-By: trailers. We credit every accepted contribution in CHANGELOG.md. If you find a bug or want a feature: open an issue first. Quick fixes (typo, doc bug, obvious regression) can go straight to a PR. Anything touching schema, retrieval ranking, MCP protocol, or the security boundary needs a design discussion in the issue first. License + credit MIT. I built GBrain to run my OpenClaw and Hermes deployments — the production brain behind my AI agents. Origin story: docs/ethos/ORIGIN.md. Community PR contributors are credited in CHANGELOG.md per release. Attribution for the retired provider's historical embedding and reranker integration remains in Git at 6040075c6cb95be5881cc2e1b76ef7d71f4e5d29. Voyage AI for the asymmetric-encoding recipe template. Ramp Labs for the search quality improvements lineage.
