See parameter reads, freshness, and examples. 🆚 ha-mcp vs. Home Assistant's built-in MCP Server Home Assistant ships its own MCP Server integration. It is built on the Assist pipeline, so a connected MCP client can read and control the entities you have exposed to Assist and run the intents Assist understands — handy for voice-style control of already-exposed devices. ha-mcp is a standalone server built for configuring, building, and debugging your smart home, not just controlling it. On top of device control, it adds capabilities the built-in integration does not have: Capability Built-in MCP Server ha-mcp Control exposed devices, query states Yes Yes Entity scope Only entities exposed to Assist Everything in Home Assistant Create / edit automations, scripts, scenes No Yes Build & edit dashboards No Yes Debug automations from traces, read history & logs No Yes Manage helpers, areas, zones, labels, groups No Yes Backups, apps, HACS, device & entity registry No Yes Rule of thumb: Use the built-in integration for voice-style control of devices you have already exposed; use ha-mcp when you want an AI assistant that can also build and maintain your Home Assistant setup. 🔌 Custom Component (ha_mcp_tools) — File & YAML Services The HA-MCP integration also powers a set of privileged tools that standard Home Assistant APIs can't provide: file system access and YAML config editing. (The same component runs the full server in-process — that's the recommended install in the Get Started section at the top.) Its File & YAML services entry (HA-MCP File & YAML Tools) enables the tools below. Tools that require the component: Tool Description ha_config_set_yaml (beta) Safely add, replace, or remove top-level YAML keys in configuration.yaml and package files (automatic backup, validation, and config check) ha_list_files (beta) List files in allowed directories ha_read_file (beta) Read files from allowed paths (config YAML, logs, and allowed directories) ha_write_file (beta) Write files to allowed directories ha_delete_file (beta) Delete files from allowed directories Template helper edit backups and restores also require the component, using either its Server entry or File & YAML Tools entry. These five tools return an error with installation instructions if the component is missing. These tools also require beta feature flags. See Beta Features for how to enable them — including the ENABLE_BETA_FEATURES master flag, which must be on before the filesystem/YAML sub-flags take effect. On Home Assistant 2026.8–2026.10: open HACS, search for HA-MCP, and Download. On 2026.11 or newer: open Marketplace, accept the first-run warning, search for HA-MCP, and Install. The main repository is in the default catalog for both. Or copy custom_components/ha_mcp_tools/ from this repository into your HA config/custom_components/ directory. After installing, restart Home Assistant, then open Settings > Devices & Services > Add Integration, search for HA-MCP, and add the HA-MCP File & YAML Tools entry. To run the full ha-mcp server in-process through this same component, see the Get Started section at the top and the full in-process server documentation →. 🧠 Better Results with Agent Skills This server gives your AI agent tools to control Home Assistant. For better configurations, pair it with Home Assistant Agent Skills — domain knowledge that teaches the agent Home Assistant best practices. An MCP server can create automations, helpers, and dashboards, but it has no opinion on how to structure them. Without domain knowledge, agents tend to over-rely on templates, pick the wrong helper type, or produce automations that are hard to maintain. The skills fill that gap: native constructs over Jinja2 workarounds, correct helper selection, safe refactoring workflows, and proper use of automation modes. Bundled Skills (built-in) Skills from homeassistant-ai/skills are bundled and served as MCP resources via skill:// URIs. Any MCP client that supports resources can discover them automatically — no manual installation needed. For tool-only clients (claude.ai, etc.), the best-practices skill is reachable through the ha_get_skill_guide tool: call it with no arguments to read SKILL.md, or with file set to a path SKILL.md links to read that reference file. Resources are not auto-injected into context — clients must explicitly request them, so idle context cost is just the metadata listing. ha_get_skill_guide is a mandatory tool: the catalog always exposes it (it can't be disabled) so tool-only clients never see a silently missing skill surface. Skills can still be installed manually for clients that prefer local skill files — see the skills repo for instructions. 🔍 Tool Discovery for AI Agents By default, the full tool catalog (~87 tools) is listed to the client through the standard MCP tools/list response. Clients with deferred / on-demand tool loading (claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Claude Code) handle that fine — tools are pulled into context only when needed, so idle context cost is near-zero. For setups without deferred tool support — models like Claude Haiku, Gemini, OpenAI-compatible local models and smaller open-weights models, or clients that inline all tool schemas regardless of model (e.g. GitHub Copilot CLI) — listing the full tool catalog up front adds a lot of idle context and can overwhelm smaller models. To address that, the server ships with a search-based discovery mode built on top of FastMCP's BM25 search transform. Smaller or local LLMs (Ollama, etc.) If your model can't see the tools or your Home Assistant, it may be getting handed the whole tool catalog at once and struggling with it. It's recommended to try the following to see if it helps: Enable tool search (ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true, or the app option below). Instead of listing every tool up front, the server defers the catalog behind a search interface so the model pulls in only the tools it needs, when it needs them. Raise the model's context window above the default. Local runtimes ship with small defaults (Ollama's num_ctx is one example) that can't hold a large tool set plus the conversation — increase it well beyond the default. Enable search-based discovery Set ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true (or toggle the option in the HA app). The full catalog is replaced in the tool list with four entry points plus a small set of always-visible "pinned" tools (ha_search, ha_get_overview, ha_report_issue, etc.). All tools remain callable directly by name once discovered: Tool Purpose ha_search_tools BM25 English-keyword search across all tools, pinned ones included. A hidden tool comes back compact: name, one-line description (the docstring's first paragraph), a one-line params list (types, enum values, required) and the proxy that executes it. ha_search_tools(tools=[...]) returns the full definition (description, input schema and annotations) of the named tools, the second hop before a call. A pinned tool returns a name-only stub (pinned: true) pointing back at the tool list, and does not use up a result slot. ha_call_read_tool Execute a readOnlyHint tool by name. Safe — clients can auto-approve. ha_call_write_tool Execute a write tool that creates or updates data. ha_call_delete_tool Execute a tool that removes / deletes data. The proxy split lets MCP clients apply different permission policies per category (e.g. auto-approve reads, prompt for writes, confirm deletes) without parsing tool docstrings. A ha_manage_* tool combines several operations, so it is reachable from more than one proxy: ha_call_write_tool and ha_call_delete_tool run the whole tool, while ha_call_read_tool runs only the read actions Read Only Mode approves (the same per-call verdict), so a manage tool with no approved read actions is not reachable there. Search results list each proxy the tool can be reached through. In Read Only Mode only ha_call_read_tool is listed; the other two still answer a client that holds them in a cached tool list, and any write they carry gets the Read Only Mode error rather than Unknown tool. Setting Default Description ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH false Replace full tool catalog with search-based discovery (tools deferred behind on-demand search). TOOL_SEARCH_MAX_RESULTS 5 Max hidden tools returned per ha_search_tools call (range 2–10); a pinned tool that ranks inside that top count is added as a name-only stub on top of it. PINNED_TOOLS empty Comma-separated tool names to keep always visible. The web settings UI is the primary way to manage this. When to enable Claude Haiku, OpenAI-compatible local models, Gemini, or any model without native deferred tool support — large idle-context savings. The same applies to clients that inline all tool schemas regardless of model (e.g. GitHub Copilot CLI, even when running Claude Sonnet/Opus). MCP clients that cap total tool count (some cap at 100) — surfaces a minimal set (~10 tools) instead of 87. Cost-sensitive deployments — fewer idle tokens per turn. Leave it off in clients with deferred tool loading (claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Claude Code); the full catalog has no idle cost there, direct calls skip the search step, and the client's built-in tool search is the better choice — there is no benefit to running ha-mcp's on top of it. Whether tools are deferred depends on the client and model combination: the same model can behave differently per client — GitHub Copilot CLI running Claude Sonnet/Opus inlines the full catalog and still benefits from tool search here. Some Codex models and ChatGPT include deferred tools too — check your client/model directly to confirm its features so you don't leave this enabled unnecessarily. 🔄 Refresh your client's tool list after changing this (or any) setting. Toggling ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH (or changing pinned/disabled tools, Read Only Mode, etc.) changes the tools the server exposes, but your AI client keeps serving its cached tool list until it re-fetches. Restarting the app or Home Assistant does not refresh the client — reconnect or refresh the MCP server in your client (e.g. in ChatGPT open Settings, then the plugin settings, select the connector and click Refresh tools; disconnect and reconnect a Claude Desktop custom connector; refresh the tools list of a claude.ai connector; or quit and reopen Claude Desktop for a server in claude_desktop_config.json), then start a new conversation. If you skip this, newly enabled tools won't appear in the client at all, and tools the server no longer exposes still show as available but fail when called (Unknown tool, or the Read Only Mode error for a write tool that mode hides). ChatGPT sometimes keeps serving the stale list even after the connector is removed and re-added under the same name — if tools are still missing after a refresh, delete the connector and create a new one with a different name. The FAQ has the full steps. For the HA app, the same option is documented in homeassistant-addon/DOCS.md along with the in-app settings UI for fine-grained tool enable/disable/pin. Per-URL tool catalog ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH defaults to off, and it sets the catalog of the main endpoint only. When several clients share one server, give each the URL for the catalog it needs: a client with built-in tool search keeps the full list, a small-context client gets the search tools. The suffixes are fixed overrides that ignore ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH: Main endpoint (follows ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH): https://example.com/private_your_secret Always the full catalog: https://example.com/private_your_secret/catalog/full Always the search tools: https://example.com/private_your_secret/catalog/search Read-only, search tools: https://example.com/private_your_secret/readonly/catalog/search Each URL keeps its catalog for the life of the connection, so a client picks its catalog only by the URL it is given. Reconnect the client after changing its URL so it refreshes its tool list. Home Assistant webhook URLs accept the same suffixes, alone or after /readonly: https://your-ha.example/api/webhook/<webhook-id>/catalog/search. This needs an embedded integration or Webhook Proxy app (add-on) release that serves them, with a matching MCP server; an older one returns 404 for a suffixed URL. Stdio runs one client per server process, so set ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH in that client's server environment instead. Read-only HTTP connections Append /readonly to the server's HTTP MCP endpoint to restrict that connection to the existing Read Only Mode while other clients keep normal access: Normal: https://example.com/private_your_secret Read-only: https://example.com/private_your_secret/readonly OAuth and OIDC connections use the same login/provider: for example, https://example.com/mcp/readonly. No additional secret or server is required. Read-only connections hide write tools and block write calls, including calls through cached tools or search proxies. The global Read Only Mode setting still restricts both endpoints when enabled. Reconnect the client after changing its URL so it refreshes its tool list. This is a connection mode for automated agents, not a separate permission on the credential: the same credentials still work at the normal endpoint. Home Assistant webhook URLs also accept the suffix: https://your-ha.example/api/webhook/<webhook-id>/readonly. This requires the updated embedded integration or Webhook Proxy dev app (add-on), together with the updated MCP server. 🧪 Dev Channel Want early access to new features and fixes? items.title: How Natera designed an agentic AI system for lab ops with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.summary: At Natera, a leader in cell-free DNA (cfDNA) testing, keeping lab instruments up and running is critical, because equipment downtime disrupts sample processing. Natera’s lab engineering team, led by Ariel Jirau worked with AWS to build SWARM (Systematic Workflow Analytics and Resolutions Manager), an agentic AI system for lab operations. This post walks through how the Natera team built an agentic AI system for lab operations using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that captures and deploys institutional knowledge at scale. It describes the full architecture, from knowledge base construction to automated system deployment and evaluation, so you can apply the same patterns to your own operational workflows. SWARM delivers about 130x faster first response time and 96.2 percent automated coverage across support tickets, giving engineers immediate access to institutional knowledge the moment a ticket arrives. The challenge: Knowledge continuity Natera’s lab operations rely on a wide range of precision instruments spanning multiple equipment families, each with its own failure modes, vendor documentation, and resolution patterns. The service engineering team responsible for maintaining this infrastructure is organized around deep individual expertise rather than standardized playbooks. When a senior technician who had spent years diagnosing a particular instrument family departed, the institutional knowledge they carried was effectively lost. No system existed to capture, organize, or deploy that expertise at scale. With over 65 tickets per day across three Jira queues and an average first response time of 17.4 hours, instrument downtime delayed lab samples and patient reporting. Hiring more engineers couldn’t keep pace. SWARM had to respond in minutes, deliver accurate diagnostics across a wide range of equipment types, and improve continuously through a structured evaluation loop. Why Natera chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore The Natera team chose to build SWARM on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a fully managed, extensible service by AWS designed to build, deploy, connect, secure, and operate AI agents at scale. Three core requirements drove the decision: Autonomous processing of high-volume support tickets without human intervention. Deep integration with existing operational tools such as Jira and Confluence. Built-in security and observability (encryption, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) integration, and distributed tracing) without requiring the team to build and maintain custom infrastructure. “We needed a managed runtime that would let us focus engineering effort on diagnostic accuracy rather than infrastructure plumbing—AgentCore gave us that, along with built-in identity management and the flexibility to swap models without rewriting agent logic,” Jirau said. AgentCore provides native integration with services including Amazon DynamoDB, a fully managed NoSQL database service, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), and AWS X-Ray, a capability of Amazon CloudWatch. How SWARM works: Two agents, one skill library SWARM uses two complementary runtimes sharing a single skill library. The swarm-agent autonomously generates structured diagnostic reports before an engineer opens a ticket, while engineers use swarm-hive to interact in real time, upload images, and explore alternative troubleshooting paths. “The system does not replace engineers—it gives them access to the full depth of institutional knowledge the moment a ticket arrives,” Jirau said. Four layers connect the architecture: The event layer routes Jira tickets through Amazon EventBridge and Amazon SQS. The agent layer hosts swarm-agent, swarm-hive, and the skill library, and delivers diagnostic reports back to engineers. The context layer draws on vendor manuals, historical tickets, and operational data. The observability and delivery layer captures traces, logs, and metrics. Figure 1: Architecture of Natera’s SWARM on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Security architecture The Natera team’s first architectural decision was where to run the agents. The team required a managed runtime that would handle container orchestration, scaling, and security without requiring them to maintain custom infrastructure. They chose AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, because it hosts both swarm-agent and swarm-hive in a secure, managed environment with built-in identity management and monitoring, avoiding the need to build and operate a custom agent execution layer. You can adopt this pattern regardless of the framework you choose. The team chose a keyless deployment model because SWARM runs in a clinical environment where credentials exposure is unacceptable. OpenID Connect (OIDC) and AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) generate temporary credentials scoped per deployment, with no long-lived keys in the pipeline. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) enforces least privilege at the component level. Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) with private subnets and VPC endpoints keeps traffic off the public internet. AWS Secrets Manager rotates the few credentials that exist on an automatic 30-day cycle. GitLab CI runners authenticate to AWS by presenting an OIDC token to an IAM identity provider configured in the account. AWS STS exchanges the token for short-lived credentials scoped to the deployment role (no long-lived access keys are stored in the pipeline). For setup details, see the IAM OIDC provider documentation. The following example illustrates the pattern: an IAM OIDC trust policy for GitLab CI follows this structure: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:oidc-provider/gitlab.com" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "gitlab.com:sub": "project_path:YOUR_PROJECT:ref_type:branch:ref:main" } } } ] } These infrastructure-level security controls work in concert with SWARM’s data governance policies. Together they form the full compliance posture required for operating an AI system in a regulated clinical environment. Compliance and data governance SWARM runs on HIPAA-eligible AWS services under a Business Associate Agreement (BAA), reflecting Natera’s obligations as a clinical laboratory operator. Every agent invocation is audit-logged (a searchable record that satisfies data access traceability requirements). No patient-identifiable information touches the vector index or the language model. Tickets contain only equipment and workflow metadata. Teams building under HIPAA or similar regulatory frameworks should confirm BAA coverage and data separation requirements before designing the knowledge base pipeline. Knowledge base and document pipeline construction Early prototypes using general-purpose retrieval without equipment-specific metadata produced inconsistent results, so the Natera team built a custom document processing pipeline tailored to technical equipment documentation. Amazon Titan Text Embeddings generates vector representations for semantic search, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), converting documents into embeddings stored in batches of 100, a size chosen to balance indexing throughput against API rate limits. For heavily structured source documents with tables and diagrams, investing in a custom parsing pipeline rather than relying on default chunking compounds accuracy gains across every diagnosis. Amazon Bedrock services, including Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore are available in multiple AWS Regions. For the latest information, see Amazon Bedrock supported Regions and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore supported Regions. The Natera team uses the tiktoken tokenizer with the cl100k_base encoding to measure chunk boundaries. The following example illustrates the pattern, the chunking configuration follows a standard structure: # Document chunking configuration chunk_size = 1000 # tokens chunk_overlap = 150 # tokens encoding = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base") batch_size = 100 # documents per embedding API call For more on batch ingestion patterns, see the Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases documentation. “Diagnostic accuracy is a data quality problem first,” Jirau said. “Adding missing vendor manuals for the lowest-scoring instrument family lifted accuracy from 71% to 75% with no model changes.” This shaped the Natera team’s improvement approach: when accuracy plateaus, the team checks data coverage before model tuning, because gaps in vendor documentation are the most common cause of missed diagnoses. The pipeline reprocesses new or updated documents and refreshes the vector index without disrupting active operations. Skill library architecture The Natera team faced a key architectural choice: embed logic directly in agent prompts, or build a separate, versioned skill library. Natera chose the library approach because it makes SWARM auditable and improvable. “When a diagnosis is wrong, we need to point to a specific skill rather than debug the whole system — that’s why we built a versioned skill library from the start,” Jirau said. The library contains 33 skills: 24 instrument-specific skills covering the full range of equipment families Natera supports, plus 9 cross-cutting workflow skills that apply broadly across ticket types. Each skill has a defined interface, is independently testable, and is evaluated against the same standards as the overall system, treated as production software, not embedded prompt logic. The skill architecture follows a clear split: Python handles deterministic tasks such as parsing Jira fields or formatting HTML reports, while large language model (LLM) skills handle language reasoning such as interpreting symptoms, matching vendor documentation, and generating diagnostic narratives. For teams building a multi-skill agent, this split between deterministic Python skills and LLM-powered reasoning skills is one of the highest-impact decisions to make. Agent runtime deployment Natera split diagnostic work into two distinct runtimes because autonomous background analysis and interactive engineering collaboration have fundamentally different latency and context requirements. The swarm-agent is built for throughput. It selects skills based on equipment type and symptoms, queries the knowledge base, and produces a structured HTML report with a lead cause hypothesis, ranked troubleshooting steps, and a confidence label. The report is delivered to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and linked to the Jira ticket within minutes. Swarm-hive is designed for depth: engineers can engage in interactive follow-up, upload images, and explore alternative paths, with AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, retaining per-engineer conversational context across sessions. Because swarm-hive accepts free-form engineer input, prompts are routed through Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for content filtering. Event-driven Jira integration SWARM integrates with Jira through Amazon EventBridge Scheduler and a polling AWS Lambda function, a serverless compute service that runs code in response to events, avoiding webhook configuration. Verified tickets enter an Amazon SQS queue for reliable delivery. DynamoDB handles deduplication using the ticket ID as a partition key with time-to-live (TTL) based expiry, and stores per-run metadata such as status, cost, and token usage to feed the evaluation loop. This EventBridge-to-SQS pattern decouples the agent runtime from the ticketing system’s availability. The following example illustrates the pattern. The deduplication table uses a minimal schema with TTL-based expiry: dynamodb.create_table( TableName='swarm-deduplication', KeySchema=[ {'AttributeName': 'ticket_id', 'KeyType': 'HASH'} ], AttributeDefinitions=[ {'AttributeName': 'ticket_id', 'AttributeType': 'S'} ], TimeToLiveSpecification={ 'Enabled': True, 'AttributeName': 'ttl' } ) Observability design Agentic systems with many interacting components are difficult to debug without per-invocation traces, so the Natera team built observability into SWARM before the first production deployment. If you’re running agents in production, per-invocation tracing is non-negotiable: without it, debugging a bad diagnosis means guessing which skill misbehaved. In a clinical lab environment, where instrument downtime directly impacts patient reporting, the ability to trace, alert on, and audit every agent action isn’t a “nice to have”. It’s a regulatory and operational requirement. SWARM’s observability stack uses Amazon CloudWatch to capture searchable logs for every run, providing a clear record of operational health. AWS X-Ray traces each run from ticket intake to diagnostic report, recording time and cost per tool call so the team can pinpoint the specific skill responsible when something is slow or expensive rather than guessing. Amazon Simple Notification Service delivers failure alerts by email, while a Slack tracker gives the entire team real-time visibility into agent activity. Continuous evaluation methodology SWARM uses a continuous evaluation loop rather than testing once at deployment, which is especially critical for systems handling changing documentation or evolving workflows. On every ticket processed, the agent provides a lead cause hypothesis, ranked troubleshooting steps, and a self-rated confidence label. Engineers record what they found and fixed, and an evaluator grades each response as Accurate, Partial, or Wrong, broken down by instrument family. Results are reviewed to identify where the agent is underperforming, the fix is applied (typically by updating the knowledge base), and the evaluation set is re-run to confirm improvement. SWARM’s self-rated confidence labels show a directional relationship with actual accuracy. Tickets labeled High confidence achieve 74 percent accuracy across 154 evaluated cases, while Moderate and Low confidence tickets both achieve 65 percent across 78 and 37 cases respectively. Note that Moderate and Low currently share the same accuracy rate. The Low confidence sample size of 37 cases is too small to draw statistically meaningful conclusions, and the Natera team expects the two tiers to diverge as the evaluation dataset expands. The separation between High and the remaining tiers gives engineers a useful signal for how much weight to place on each diagnosis at the point of reading a diagnostic report. SWARM performance The Natera team evaluated SWARM across 524 support tickets to establish a performance baseline. Of the 524 tickets in the evaluation set, 269 received a High, Moderate, or Low confidence label and had a corresponding engineer-verified resolution available for comparison. The remaining tickets were either labeled none or lacked a verified resolution at the time of analysis. Average first response time dropped from 17.4 hours to roughly 8 minutes (about 130x faster). These measurements were collected from Jira ticket metadata over a 90-day production evaluation period. Coverage matters just as much: 96.2 percent of tickets get an automated first response without an engineer having to initiate the diagnostic process. Coverage was measured as the percentage of incoming tickets that received a SWARM-generated diagnostic report before engineer review. Lessons from building agentic AI in production Several architectural decisions in SWARM translate directly to teams building similar systems. Treat chunk size and overlap as tunable parameters. The right values depend on how your source documents are structured. Build traceability into your skill library from the start. When a diagnosis is wrong, you want to point to a specific skill, not debug the whole system. If your workload mixes batch processing with interactive querying, separate them into distinct runtimes. Getting started Try these patterns yourself with the AgentCore samples repository, Building Agentic systems on AWS or the Getting Started with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore guide for deploying agents securely at scale. Healthcare and life sciences organizations facing similar challenges with institutional knowledge loss, high-volume operational workflows, or clinical compliance requirements will find that the architectural patterns Natera developed with SWARM provide a replicable, production-tested foundation for building agentic AI systems on AWS. About the authors Ariel Jirau Ariel is a Principal Software Engineer at Natera. He leads technical implementation and infrastructure decisions for enterprise readiness, overseeing the system architecture and production deployment of SWARM. Veronica Rule Veronica is a Senior Customer Solutions Manager at AWS with over 10 years of experience supporting healthcare and life science customers on their cloud journey. She specializes in guiding organizations through AI/ML adoption, agentic AI strategies, and cloud transformation initiatives. She is passionate about bridging the gap between advanced AI capabilities and real-world health care and life sciences outcomes. Tamara Gagliardi Tamara is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS with over 15 years of experience in the technology field, spanning across industries including financial services, retail and manufacturing. For the past several years, she has focused her expertise on the healthcare and life sciences sector, partnering closely with medical devices and bio-diagnostic customers to accelerate their cloud journeys. As a trusted technical advisor, Tamara helps organizations translate complex business challenges into scalable, secure technical solutions with a particular emphasis on generative AI, where she guides customers in identifying high-impact use cases and architecting intelligent workflows.

cookie 的 Secure 标记（true / false）；默认按 x-forwarded-proto 自动推导。反向代理终结了 TLS 但没传这个头时，cookie 不会带 Secure（不影响登录，但少了这层保护），设 true 可强制 60S_API_BASE 否 影视榜单推荐源（60s API）实例地址，默认 https://60s.crystelf.top；有限流，高频使用可自部署 DEFAULT_LIVE_SOURCES 否 预置直播源（M3U 订阅），JSON 数组：[{"name":"源名","url":"https://.../list.m3u","epg":"https://.../epg.xml.gz"}]，epg 为可选的 XMLTV 节目单地址 DEFAULT_SUBSCRIPTIONS 否 预置数据源订阅（LibreTV-SourceList JSON 链接，也接受 TVBOX 配置与接口目录地址），JSON 数组：["https://.../sources.json", {"url":"https://.../list.json","name":"名称","refreshDays":10}]。首次访问自动导入点播源与直播源，之后按 refreshDays（1-365，缺省 1 天）静默刷新；用户删除后不再自动加回。refreshDays 只是初始值，用户在源管理面板改过之后以面板设置为准 DEFAULT_RECOMMEND_SOURCE 否 首页推荐数据源的默认值（douban / bangumi / hot-list，出厂默认 hot-list）；仅对未在设置中主动选择过的用户生效，用户的选择始终优先 LIVE_ALLOW_PRIVATE 否 设为 1 时允许直播流代理访问内网/保留地址（自建 IPTV 场景），默认关闭以维持 SSRF 防护 使用说明 添加点播源：设置 → 源管理 → 点播源 → 添加 API，填入 Apple CMS 采集站地址（如 https://example.com/api.php/provide/vod），可选填详情页地址（部分源需要爬详情页提取播放地址）。 搜索：勾选点播源后输入片名；搜索通过服务端聚合，个别源失败不影响整体结果。 播放：详情弹窗选择剧集进入 /watch；支持快捷键（空格/←→/↑↓/F/Alt+←→）、移动端长按 3 倍速、自动连播、换源测速。观看/暂停时后续分片自动缓存到本地（设置可关），播放页可「下载本集」（TS/MP4）离线观看。播放页「跳过标记」可标记片头/中段/片尾区间（快捷键 Shift+I 片头结束、Shift+O 片尾开始、Shift+S·Shift+E 中段区间），之后同剧各集与同名资源自动跳过——片头/中段跳到片段末尾，片尾则直接结束本集（是否连播下一集由自动连播决定），三类片段共用「自动跳过片段」一个开关；跳过时提示条带「撤销」，「跳过标记」侧栏可逐剧关闭、微调边界、试跳起点/终点（记录与试跳都会先暂停），命中区间在进度条上着色。侧栏是非模态的：不遮画面、不挡播放器点击，可以一边看一边标。 进度与历史：自动保存在本设备 IndexedDB，仅定位信息入库，播放时自动同步最新剧集。 配置迁移：设置 → 数据 → 配置导入导出（兼容旧版 LibreTV-Settings JSON 的历史记录迁移）。 直播 / IPTV 添加直播源：设置 → 源管理 → 直播源 → 填入 M3U/M3U8 地址（可选填 XMLTV 节目单地址），添加后自动探活并显示频道数量；也可在「源管理 → 数据源订阅」中与点播源一起订阅导入；部署者还可用 DEFAULT_LIVE_SOURCES 环境变量预置。 观看：进入「直播」页，按分组标签筛选或搜索频道，点击即播；支持 HLS（m3u8）与 HTTP-FLV 两种直播流，直连失败自动走代理通道重试。 节目单：频道带 tvg-id 且订阅配置了 EPG 地址时，展示当前/接下来节目与播放进度。 收藏与导出：频道可收藏；订阅可一键导出为标准 M3U 文件，供 PotPlayer / VLC 等外部播放器使用。 完整说明见 直播 / IPTV 文档。 ⚠️ 项目不内置任何频道源，也不存储、不制作任何直播内容，仅提供第三方公开播放列表的解析与播放能力，内容的合法性由对应数据源负责。内网自建源默认被 SSRF 防护拦截，自部署者可显式设置 LIVE_ALLOW_PRIVATE=1 放行。 数据源订阅 / 分享 数据源（点播源 + 直播源）可以 导出为一份 JSON → 托管到公开 URL → 他人在「设置 → 源管理 → 数据源订阅」里填入该 URL 订阅。 托管地址没有特殊要求，可用 npoint.io 免费托管 JSON（粘贴内容即可得到一个公开 URL），Gist、对象存储、任意静态托管同样可用。 订阅格式（LibreTV-SourceList JSON） { "name": "我的源列表", "version": 2, "sources": [ { "name": "示例点播源", "url": "https://example.com/api.php/provide/vod", "detail": "https://example.com", "isAdult": false } ], "liveSources": [ { "name": "示例直播源", "url": "https://example.com/list.m3u", "epg": "https://example.com/epg.xml.gz" } ] } 字段说明： 字段 位置 类型 必填 说明 name 顶层 string 否 列表名称，订阅后显示在订阅条目上；缺省时显示订阅地址主机名 version 顶层 number 否 格式版本，当前为 2（新增 liveSources）；导入端目前忽略该字段 sources 顶层 array 否 点播源数组（Apple CMS 采集站），最多 100 个，超出部分截断 sources[].name 项 string 否 源显示名；缺省时使用 URL 主机名 sources[].url 项 string 是 Apple CMS 采集接口地址（公网 http/https），结尾 / 自动去除 sources[].detail 项 string 否 详情页根地址，用于列表接口拿不到播放地址、需要爬详情页提取 m3u8 的源 sources[].isAdult 项 boolean 否 成人内容标记，默认 false。标记为 true 的源名称旁显示 (18+) 徽章；设置中的「成人内容过滤」开启（默认开启）时该源不可勾选、不参与搜索，需先关闭过滤才能启用 liveSources 顶层 array 否 直播源数组（M3U 播放列表），最多 50 个，超出部分截断 liveSources[].name 项 string 否 源显示名；缺省时使用 URL 主机名 liveSources[].url 项 string 是 M3U 播放列表地址（http/https） liveSources[].epg 项 string 否 XMLTV 节目单地址（xml / xml.gz），用于 /live 页展示节目单；地址非法时只丢弃该字段、保留整条源 兼容与限制： 只写 sources 的老订阅照常可用（纯点播），只写 liveSources 则是纯直播订阅；两者都缺时提示「订阅内容格式不正确」；裸数组 [{ "name": "...", "url": "..." }] 视为点播源； 按 url 去重（先到先得）；非 http(s) 地址会被过滤；点播源另需为公网地址（内网/回环/保留地址会被静默过滤），直播源在部署者设置 LIVE_ALLOW_PRIVATE=1 时可使用内网自建源地址； 订阅由服务端拉取（拉取前经过 SSRF 校验），因此订阅地址无需配置 CORS，Gist、对象存储、任意静态托管均可。 兼容 TVBOX 配置 订阅地址也可以直接填 TVBOX 配置（形如 {"sites": [...], "lives": [...], "parses": [...]}）：服务端按内容结构自动识别格式，无需手动选择。 点播源：导入 sites 中 type: 1 的 JSON 接口（即 Apple CMS 采集站）；部分共享配置省略 type 或写成 0，但地址命中 api.php/provide/vod 时同样导入；站点自身标记 searchable: 0（不可搜索）时跳过； 直播源：导入 lives 中 type: 0（或省略）的 M3U 播放列表，epg 字段一并带上；txt 频道列表与单仓 JSON 不支持； Spider 类站点会跳过：type: 3 的 Spider（csp_* / .jar / .js / .py）需要 TVBOX 自身的 Spider 引擎才能运行，Node 侧无法执行；XML 接口、外链 JSON 同理。被跳过的条目不影响其余导入，导入结果会如实提示，如「已同步 8 个点播源、2 个直播源（TVBOX 配置）；跳过 96 个不可用条目（Spider 引擎 92、XML 接口 4）」； TVBOX 配置常含上百条站点且以 Spider 为主，只导入个位数到十几个属正常现象； 格式容错：配置里的 // 注释、尾随逗号、字符串内未转义的换行会自动修正后再解析（共享配置中很常见，TVBOX 客户端用的 fastjson 同样容忍这些写法）； 其他限制：订阅地址需直接返回 JSON（Base64 / 压缩包装的分享链接不支持）；TVBOX「多仓」配置（顶层为 urls 数组）不支持，请填单仓配置；地址公网校验、去重与数量上限与上方格式完全一致。 兼容接口目录（source-catalog） 订阅地址也可以填一份接口目录——裸数组，元素为 { "name": "...", "baseUrl": "..." }： [ { "name": "示例接口", "baseUrl": "https://example.com/api.php/provide/vod" }, { "name": "已停用的接口", "baseUrl": "https://old.example.com/api.php/provide/vod", "enabled": false } ] 只导入 baseUrl（点播接口），不含直播源；enabled 缺省视为启用，写 false 的条目跳过并在结果里计数； 顶层数组全部条目都带 baseUrl 才按接口目录解析；混用 baseUrl 与 url 两种条目会直接报格式错误，避免其中一批被静默丢弃； 地址归一化、去重与数量上限与 LibreTV 源列表一致（baseUrl 去尾部斜杠与空的 ? / #）。 订阅行为 订阅：设置 → 源管理 → 数据源订阅 → 填入订阅地址 → 「订阅」，导入的点播源自动勾选、直播源自动启用，均带「订阅」标识，条目上显示「点播 N · 直播 M」； 同步：订阅条目上的 ⟳ 手动强制同步，整体替换该订阅名下的点播源与直播源； 自动刷新：每个订阅可单独设置刷新周期（条目上的周期下拉：关闭 / 1 / 3 / 7 / 14 / 30 天，默认关闭即纯手动）。设为 N 天后，打开站点时检查是否到期，到期才在后台静默同步；单次最多刷新 5 个、并发 2 个，页面不可见或离线时跳过，不阻塞首屏。连续失败 3 次自动暂停该订阅（条目显示「已暂停」），手动同步成功或改周期后恢复计数。环境变量 DEFAULT_SUBSCRIPTIONS 里的 refreshDays 只作为初始值，用户在面板里改过之后以面板为准； 管理边界：订阅源以远端列表为准，单独编辑会在下次同步时被覆盖，单独移除会在重新同步时恢复；如需调整请改远端列表，或直接删除整个订阅。删除订阅时点播源全部移除；直播源为多归属共享——同一 M3U 可被多个订阅引用（名称/EPG 以首次导入为准），删除订阅或远端列表中移除该源后再同步，都只摘除本订阅的引用，仅当不再被任何订阅引用时才移除该源，手动添加的源不受同步影响，收藏的频道始终保留； 导出分享：设置 → 源管理 → 数据源订阅 → 「导出数据源」，把当前全部点播源与直播源（预置 + 手动 + 订阅，按 URL 去重）导出为上述 JSON；也可用「发布为链接」，把当前已勾选启用的源一键上传到公开粘贴板（paste.rs，失败自动降级 0x0.st），直接返回可填入订阅框的 URL，无需自备托管。注意：发布的内容公开可读，且每次发布生成新链接、不支持覆盖更新，需长期稳定请用导出 + 自行托管。 订阅由服务端拉取（经过 SSRF 校验），因此订阅地址无需配置 CORS。完整说明见 数据源文档。 开发 npm install PASSWORD=dev-password npm run dev # http://localhost:8080 npm test # 核心库单元测试（cms-parser / m3u8 / ssrf） npm run typecheck 测试范围、发布流程与文档结构见 开发文档。 发布新版本 版本号以 package.json 为单一来源，发布镜像由 GitHub Actions 自动完成： npm version patch # 或 minor / major；会更新 package.json 并打 git tag git push && git push --tags CI 校验通过后自动构建并推送 ghcr.io/librespark/libretv:<版本>（详见部署文档）。 安全说明 密码只保存在服务端环境变量中，前端不持有任何可重放凭证。 登录接口有 IP 速率限制（10 次 / 10 分钟）。 代理内置 SSRF 防护：拒绝内网/保留地址（含 DNS 解析后校验），仅放行 http(s)。 未登录会话仅允许代理图片类目标（豆瓣封面防盗链需要）。 衍生作品 项目 说明 OrionTV Apple TV / Android TV 客户端（React Native TVOS + Expo），配合 MoonTV 使用 LunaTV 影视聚合站（Next.js），支持 Redis / Upstash 等多存储后端 Selene-TV Android TV（Leanback）客户端，Kotlin + Compose，对接 MoonTV / Helios EchoTV Flutter 全平台客户端（已归档） WarHutTV Go + React 的自托管影视聚合站 DecoTV 聚合播放站（原 KatelyaTV） Joyflix macOS 原生影视聚合客户端（Objective-C） MoonCakeTV 影视聚合搜索站（Next.js），文件存储、一键脚本部署 OrangeTV 跨平台影视聚合播放器（Next.js），Kvrocks/Redis/Upstash 多存储与多端同步 MQTV 重构与优化 LibreTV NextTV 影视聚合站（Next.js + Zustand），支持弹幕 DpadTV Android TV 原生客户端（Kotlin + Media3/ExoPlayer），对接自建服务端，不依赖 WebView LibreTV-for-HarmonyOS HarmonyOS NEXT 原生客户端（ArkTS + ArkUI + AVPlayer） 旧版 LibreTV（静态 HTML + Express）完整代码见 backup-2025 分支。 免责声明 本项目不存储、不制作任何视频内容，仅提供第三方公开接口的聚合与播放能力，内容的合法性由对应数据源负责。 ☕ 觉得有用的话，可以到 AFDIAN 请我喝杯咖啡。

items.summary: An open source design system that's fully customizable and agent ready http://astryx.atmeta.com Astryx An open source design system that's fully customizable and built for how we build now: by people and the agents working alongside them. Currently in Beta · Built on React 19+ and StyleX Docs · Storybook · Sandbox · Contributing · Discord Overview Astryx is an open source design system that grew inside Meta over the last eight years, where it became the most-used and largest design system in the company — powering 13,000+ apps and shaped by the engineers, designers, and product teams who depend on it every day. It ships 150+ accessible components, brand-level theming, dark mode, ready-to-ship templates, and a CLI as one cohesive system. You import pre-built CSS and use typed React components — no build plugin, no styling library to adopt — and both people and AI assistants build with the same tooling. What makes Astryx different: Open internals. Components are built to be composed at any level, not locked behind a closed top-level API. The building blocks you'd reach for are exported directly, and when you need to go deeper, swizzle ejects a component's full source into your project to own. No styling lock-in. Astryx authors its styles with StyleX, but that's invisible to consumers. Override with className using Tailwind, CSS modules, or plain CSS — whatever your project already uses. Customize without wrapping. A theme is a set of CSS custom property overrides, so a designer can make Astryx unmistakably theirs without forking or wrapping component source. Built for people and agents. The API, docs, and CLI are designed together so a person and an AI assistant build the same way, from the same reference. Getting Started Astryx requires React 19 or later (react and react-dom are peer dependencies of @astryxdesign/core). Install Astryx, a theme, and its peer dependencies: # npm npm install @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/theme-neutral @stylexjs/stylex npm install -D @astryxdesign/cli # pnpm pnpm add @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/theme-neutral @stylexjs/stylex pnpm add -D @astryxdesign/cli # yarn yarn add @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/theme-neutral @stylexjs/stylex yarn add -D @astryxdesign/cli You can also install the CLI once for your computer, so astryx works in any folder and every coding agent knows Astryx; in a project, it still runs that project's own version: npm i -g @astryxdesign/cli Project install, global install, or both? astryx docs global/project-global-or-both compares them (both is recommended), and astryx docs global explains how global mode works. The simplest setup is a few CSS imports plus a theme provider — no build plugin, no PostCSS or Babel config. See the @astryxdesign/core README for the full guide (Next.js, Tailwind, Vite, and CDN). For reliable CLI access, add a script to your package.json: "scripts": { "astryx": "node node_modules/@astryxdesign/cli/clients/cli/bin/astryx.mjs" } Then use it as npm run astryx -- component --list. This avoids path errors when AI assistants or new developers invoke the CLI directly. Packages Package Description README @astryxdesign/core Components, theme system, and utilities README @astryxdesign/cli CLI tooling: component docs, templates, scaffolding, themes, and codemods README @astryxdesign/build Build plugins for StyleX source builds README @astryxdesign/theme-* Seven ready-made, fully customizable themes (neutral, butter, chocolate, matcha, stone, gothic, y2k) README @astryxdesign/lab (experimental components) is used internally for Storybook and the sandbox and is not published to npm. @astryxdesign/vega (Vega/Vega-Lite chart wrapper) and @astryxdesign/charts (chart components) are published to npm only under the @canary dist-tag — there is no stable release yet. Principles These are the promises Astryx makes to the people building on it. Guidance over enforcement. Components give you capability rather than guardrails that fight you. Design opinions live in docs and examples — if you pass a value, the component renders it. Strong, documented conventions. Every component follows the same naming, prop, and composition rules, and every one is thoroughly documented — so once you've learned a few, the rest feel familiar, and both people and AI can predict how an unfamiliar component behaves. One system for humans and AI. The API, conventions, docs, and CLI are designed together so people and AI assistants build the same way. Every change that made Astryx easier for AI made it easier for people too. Earned by measurement. We test conventions rather than assert them, hold the results loosely, and revisit them when a new situation proves them wrong. Architecture Foundations The building blocks for visually cohesive and accessible interfaces: typography, color, layout, and accessibility. Components A library of 150+ reusable UI building blocks with full TypeScript support. Patterns Battle-tested design solutions for common interactions and workflows: table pages, detail page layouts, form wizards, navigation patterns, data entry flows. Project Structure Directory Purpose apps/ Example apps, the docsite, and Storybook packages/ Published packages: core, cli, build, themes internal/ Internal tooling: test utilities, eslint plugin, vibe tests Contributing We welcome contributions! See CONTRIBUTING.md for the full guide. Questions, or want a hand with a PR? Come find us in Discord. Our conventions and review rubrics live in the Contributing wiki — including API Conventions, Design Conventions, the Component Lifecycle, the Contributing Templates, and the Blog Review Rubric. Read the relevant rubric before opening a PR. Quick start for contributors: this repo uses Node 22+ on an active LTS line and pnpm 11. Install pnpm directly, or enable Corepack once so the pinned pnpm version installs automatically: corepack enable pnpm install If corepack is missing, install pnpm directly or install Corepack manually; see the troubleshooting notes in CONTRIBUTING.md. The Theme Showcase DOM tests use the root ui project for shared DOM and StyleX test setup. Run pnpm exec vitest run --project ui apps/docsite/src/__tests__/theme-showcase/ from the repository root. License MIT

items.title: Migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base with your coding agent
items.summary: With a customer-managed knowledge base on Amazon Bedrock, you provision and scale the vector store, tune the embedding model and index settings, and plan capacity for each new data source. The migration guide in the Agent Toolkit for AWS helps you migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base. Managed Knowledge Base takes over that work and adds new retrieval capabilities, and your team keeps control of the content and the application that uses it. Moving a production knowledge base means your team maps its configuration, creates the replacement, ingests content, updates the application’s retrieval call, and validates retrieval before switching traffic. To help, we added a knowledge base migration guide to the amazon-bedrock skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS. The guide gives your coding agent the context to plan the migration with you, starting with read-only discovery and a plan you review line by line. On your approval, the agent creates the new knowledge base and its data sources alongside the original, or writes a migrated infrastructure as code (IaC) template for your pipeline. Ingestion and updating your application’s Retrieve calls stay with you, and your agent can walk you through both. In this post, we explain why we recommend the move and how the migration guide works, review the prerequisites, install the skill, plan a migration, update the application’s retrieval call, and validate retrieval before cutover. Why move to Managed Knowledge Base We recommend Managed Knowledge Base because it balances ease of use, retrieval accuracy, and cost. AWS runs the store With a Managed Knowledge Base, Amazon Bedrock handles ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval, and the store scales automatically as your content grows. Hybrid search, which combines keyword and semantic matching, is always on, with no index to configure. The knowledge base includes a managed embedding model, a managed reranker, and a built-in parser for multimodal file types. You can still bring your own Amazon Bedrock embedding model when you create the knowledge base. On each retrieval request, you choose the managed reranker, an Amazon Bedrock reranking model, or no reranking. The managed reranker requires the managed embedding model. Built-in capabilities Managed Knowledge Base includes capabilities you’d otherwise build yourself: Native connectors ingest content directly from sources such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Microsoft SharePoint, and Atlassian Confluence. For the current list, see supported connectors. After the first full sync, later syncs pick up only changes, on demand or on a schedule. The Managed Knowledge Base includes a deletion safeguard to help protect against accidental bulk removal of indexed content. Access control list (ACL) awareness ingests document permissions with the content, so retrieval returns only what the signed-in user can access. For connectors that support it, such as Microsoft SharePoint and Atlassian Confluence, a real-time check against the source also catches permission changes since the last sync. ACL awareness doesn’t authenticate users, so your application must verify and pass the user’s identity. Agentic retrieval answers questions that a single search can’t by handling multi-part questions and retrieving iteratively. It can search more than one knowledge base in a single request. Integration with AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, exposes your knowledge base as a target. Any client that supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP) can then query the knowledge base, and the gateway handles authentication. Resource-based policies let applications in other AWS accounts use one team’s knowledge base. Scope each policy to the specific roles that call the knowledge base, and grant only the actions they use, such as bedrock:Retrieve. Agentic retrieval, AgentCore Gateway integration, and resource-based policies are not available on customer-managed knowledge bases. For the AWS Regions where managed knowledge bases are available, and the features that AWS GovCloud (US-West) doesn’t support, see Supported AWS Regions. Higher quotas As of this writing, higher default quotas change how you can organize content. With 200 data sources per knowledge base, you can group related content in one knowledge base. With 10,000 knowledge bases per account, per Region, each team or product line can use a separate knowledge base. Default quota Customer-managed Managed Knowledge bases per account, per Region 100 10,000 Data sources per knowledge base 5 200 Concurrent ingestion jobs per knowledge base 1 50 Query input characters 1,000 10,000 For current values, see Amazon Bedrock endpoints and quotas and Service quotas for managed knowledge bases. Pay for what you store and retrieve Cost is one of three things teams weigh when they consider this move, alongside customizability and direct control of the vector store. On a customer-managed knowledge base, you choose, provision, scale, and update the vector and text stores, and pay separately for the infrastructure you select. On a Managed Knowledge Base, those stages are part of the service, and storage and retrieval are metered directly. The pricing models can differ too. With a customer-managed knowledge base, storage and retrieval charges depend on the vector store you choose. Some stores charge for provisioned or minimum capacity, and others, such as Amazon S3 Vectors, a capability of Amazon S3, charge only for what you use. A Managed Knowledge Base is priced on what you store and retrieve, so cost follows real usage. Usage-based pricing can fit enterprise question-answering, policy, and support knowledge bases that run at low utilization. For current rates, see Amazon Bedrock pricing. For the parsers available on a customer-managed knowledge base and how each is billed, see Parsing options for your data source. Cost driver Customer-managed knowledge base Managed Knowledge Base Vector storage Priced separately by your chosen store. A provisioned retrieval service can have a minimum idle cost even at low volume Included in the base storage rate of $5 per GB per month Multimodal document parsing Requires Amazon Bedrock Data Automation, billed by page or image, or a foundation model, billed by token. Text-only parsing is free. Included Embedding generation Billed separately at your embedding model’s rate Included with the default model. Charges apply only if you choose a custom model Ingestion, sync, and re-sync compute Re-embedding, orchestration code, and indexing compute spikes on each sync add recurring cost Included, with incremental sync that processes only new and changed content Connectors Building and running custom connectors can add compute cost Native connectors are included Standard retrieval No Amazon Bedrock charge per query. Your vector store can charge per query, as Amazon S3 Vectors does. $1 per 1,000 retrieval requests Reranking Amazon Rerank is charged at $1 per 1,000 queries. A custom reranking model is billed at its own rate Included in the $1 per 1,000 retrieval requests Agentic retrieval You build the agentic workflow on a Bedrock model, which can cost roughly $18 to $24 per 1,000 queries before development and maintenance. Because model usage is billed by token, the price per query varies. Agentic retrieval costs an additional $4 per 1,000 queries on top of the underlying retrieval calls, including multi-shot retrieval, reranking, and answer generation. Depending on the number of underlying retrieval calls, the total can range from roughly $6 to $9 per 1,000 queries. Rates are only part of the total cost of ownership. On a customer-managed knowledge base, your team provisions, scales, and operates each stage as a separate resource. A Managed Knowledge Base consolidates them into one resource, with a default embedding model, foundation model, and reranker, and with per-knowledge-base rate limits by default. You manage the content and the application that uses it, and Amazon Bedrock operates the managed storage, embedding model, foundation model, and reranker. Solution overview A customer-managed knowledge base uses the VECTOR type, with a vector store you configure. A Managed Knowledge Base uses the MANAGED type. The migration guide directs your agent to create a new MANAGED knowledge base alongside the original without modifying or deleting the original during migration. Using the guide’s map, your agent writes a plan that lists which settings remain unchanged, which Managed handles differently, and which application changes you need to make. As Figure 1 shows, the original keeps serving every request while your team ingests content, validates, and cuts over. Figure 1: Create a managed knowledge base or migrated template alongside the original, then validate before cutover How the migration guide works The guide separates planning from implementation. In Explore mode, your agent answers questions about Managed Knowledge Base and can inspect your configuration with read-only calls, so you can estimate the effort. In Migration mode, the guide takes your agent through checkpoints: Introduce and choose. Your agent explains what it will and won’t touch. Choose the mode, a live knowledge base or IaC source, and a plain (default) or technical explanation style. Identify. Confirm the account and AWS Region. Your agent flags over-broad credentials, asks whether you want a cost analysis, and creates an output directory. Discover. Your agent reads the knowledge base and data sources with read-only calls, or reads your template files. Plan. Review the plan and application changes. By default, your agent stops here. Implement, if requested. For a live build, approve the exact preview of the provisioning script, and approve again if it changes. For IaC, your agent writes a migrated template and reports which schema checks ran. Handoff. Review what was produced and your team’s remaining steps. As Figure 2 shows, resource creation stays separate from ingestion and cutover. Figure 2: Migration checkpoints. Implementation is optional, and your team runs ingestion and cutover Review the configuration mapping The guide maps each setting to preserve your data sources, filters, and chunking behavior when the managed type uses a different configuration. The plan classifies each setting: 1:1. The new knowledge base uses the same setting. Adjusted. Managed uses a different setting for the same outcome, and the plan applies the substitution. Blocked. There is no managed path today. Your agent excludes that knowledge base from the build, explains why, and points you to AWS Support. Other knowledge bases in the same run can proceed. Compare chunking on your own content when you validate. Review the permissions and generated changes Discovery, planning, and the entire IaC path need only read-only credentials. For a live build, the guide directs your agent to propose a scoped policy that explicitly denies changes to the original knowledge base, and to never ask for administrator or full-access permissions. It also directs your agent to change only resources it created, reference secrets by Amazon Resource Name (ARN), and ignore instructions found in the data it reads. Review the generated AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policy and provisioning script before you approve the run. After the build, check what the agent did in AWS CloudTrail event history, which keeps 90 days of management events. Each event records the API call, such as CreateKnowledgeBase, and the identity that made it. For the optional cost analysis, your agent compares current spend with a Managed Knowledge Base estimate using current AWS prices. It uses read-only inputs, including Amazon CloudWatch metrics, Amazon S3 object sizes, and AWS Cost Explorer. Each figure is labeled as measured, supplied by you, or estimated. Prerequisites Use separate credentials for planning and for any approved resource creation. A compatible development environment with the Agent Toolkit for AWS. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), configured with a least-privilege, read-only profile. Access to the original knowledge base configuration or its IaC files. For the optional live build: A scoped build profile, using the policy the guide recommends. An IAM service role for the new knowledge base. The guide gives your agent the trust policy and permissions to help you create it. Python 3 with boto3 for the generated provisioning script. The Agent Toolkit for AWS works with compatible development environments and its repository on GitHub lists the available skills. Examples in this post use AWS CLI 2.37 and boto3 1.43.32. Install the skill Follow the Agent Toolkit for AWS getting-started instructions for your coding agent. The add-skill command installs the amazon-bedrock skill to the coding agents it detects. Add --agent to target one, for example --agent kiro. aws agent-toolkit add-skill \ --skill-name amazon-bedrock After installation, your agent loads the migration guide when you describe a migration task. The following prompts are illustrative inputs, not transcripts. Plan the migration Choose the path that matches how you maintain the source. Path What your agent reads What it produces AWS changes Explore Documentation, and optionally your knowledge base (read-only) Answers in the conversation None Live knowledge base Your knowledge base and data sources (read-only) A plan, and optionally a new Managed Knowledge Base alongside the original Only after you approve the exact preview Infrastructure as code Your AWS CloudFormation template, AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) synthesized template, or Terraform configuration A migrated template in the same format None. Your pipeline deploys it To start in Explore mode, ask a question: What would change if I moved knowledge base <your-kb-name> in <your-region> to a Managed Knowledge Base? Use Explore mode. When you’re ready, choose the live or IaC path. Migrate a live knowledge base Ask for a plan before authorizing resource creation: Plan a migration of knowledge base <your-kb-name> in <your-region> to a Managed Knowledge Base. Stop after the plan. Confirm the account and Region, then review the plan’s mappings and application changes. By default, the new knowledge base takes the original’s name with a -managed suffix. To build it, confirm the service role exists, switch to the build profile, inspect the provisioning script and its preview, and approve. Your agent runs the script, which creates the knowledge base and data sources, and reports their status. Migrate infrastructure as code Point your agent at the source template or configuration: Review <path-to-source-template> and plan a migration to a Managed Knowledge Base. Your agent writes the migrated file to the output directory, deploys nothing, and shows you the diff. To keep the diff, ask your agent to save it. Run terraform init -backend=false and terraform validate before deployment. Your agent can walk you through both commands, but the guide leaves these checks to you because terraform init downloads the large AWS provider. Before you apply the deployment plan, check that it keeps the original resources you need for rollback. Example conversation The migration runs as a conversation. Before reading anything, your agent states its scope and asks how to proceed: It never changes or deletes <your-kb-id>, never starts ingestion, and never cuts your application over; every AWS change is shown to you and approved first. Nothing has run against your KB yet. 1. Mode: Explore (read-only Q&A about Managed KBs and your KB, no plan or build) or Migration (run the phases: identify, discover, plan, and optionally build)? 2. Target type, if Migration: migrate the live KB <your-kb-id> (kb path, which can build a new Managed KB on approval), or migrate the Terraform/CloudFormation that defines it (iac path, which only emits a migrated file and provisions nothing)? 3. Explanation style: plain or technical. I'll use plain unless you say otherwise. The plan summary shows each mapping, the caller changes, and the decisions you need to make: Phase 3, Plan: written (plan.md) - Mapping: - Vector store becomes auto-provisioned (adjusted, Yes). - SEMANTIC chunking is dropped for the managed default (adjusted, Partly). - Parsing becomes SMART_PARSING (adjusted, Yes). - The S3 prefix and metadata sidecars carry over 1:1. - Changes for callers: - New KB id. - managedSearchConfiguration replaces vectorSearchConfiguration. - overrideSearchType: SEMANTIC can't be sent; search is hybrid. Your input needed before this can go further. - D1 embeddingModelType: MANAGED (recommended): keeps the managed reranker. CUSTOM Titan v2 1024/FLOAT32: turns off the managed reranker. - D2 aclEnabled: recommend false, since the source has no ACLs. On S3 this can't be changed after create. - Next step: stop with this plan (the default), or opt into Phase 4? For a live build, your agent stops at a preview, and the approval command requires the plan’s hash: If you approve, the command to run is the following. It is MUTATING: AWS_PROFILE=build-profile AWS_REGION=<your-region> \ python3 provision_managed_kb.py --execute \ --expect-plan-sha256 <plan-sha256> --execute refuses to start unless it is given --expect-plan-sha256 and the hash matches. What the preview would create: - Knowledge base (CreateKnowledgeBase, MANAGED): support-docs-managed - Data source (CreateDataSource, managed connector, deletion protection ENABLED/15): support-docs-s3-managed The script never calls StartIngestionJob, Retrieve, Update*, Delete*, or a standalone TagResource. Example exchanges are lightly edited, with identifiers replaced. Update the application’s retrieval call Your application uses the same Retrieve operation for both types. The managed request targets the new knowledge base ID and replaces vectorSearchConfiguration with managedSearchConfiguration. Passing vectorSearchConfiguration to a managed knowledge base returns a validation error. Managed retrieval always uses hybrid search, so the managed request shape has no overrideSearchType field. Metadata filters keep the same syntax, except that managed knowledge bases don’t support the startsWith and stringContains operators. For the full syntax, see the Retrieve API reference. The example assumes both knowledge bases contain the locale metadata used by the filter. # Illustrative: the managed request shape was checked with boto3 1.43.32; adapt the IDs and filter to your knowledge base. import boto3 client = boto3.client("bedrock-agent-runtime") query = {"text": "How do I return an online order?"} locale_filter = {"equals": {"key": "locale", "value": "en-US"}} # Customer-managed (VECTOR) knowledge base. original_response = client.retrieve( knowledgeBaseId="<original-kb-id>", retrievalQuery=query, retrievalConfiguration={ "vectorSearchConfiguration": { "numberOfResults": 5, "overrideSearchType": "SEMANTIC", "filter": locale_filter, } }, ) # Managed target: different ID and search configuration. managed_response = client.retrieve( knowledgeBaseId="<managed-kb-id>", retrievalQuery=query, retrievalConfiguration={ "managedSearchConfiguration": { "numberOfResults": 5, "filter": locale_filter, } }, ) Validate retrieval and cut over Evaluate the new knowledge base while the application still uses the original. If using IaC, review and deploy the target configuration through your pipeline. Sync each data source and review any failures. See Sync your data. Grant your application’s runtime IAM role bedrock:Retrieve on the new knowledge base ARN, and keep its access to the original knowledge base so you can roll back. Run representative queries against both knowledge bases with Retrieve, using that role. The two types use different score scales. Managed scores also depend on rerankingModelType, which defaults to MANAGED with the managed embedding model and to NONE with a custom one. Tune thresholds per mode, and hold the mode constant while comparing. Test metadata filters and permission-aware retrieval where used, including content the signed-in user shouldn’t receive. On an ACL-enabled data source, requests without userContext.userId (the user’s email) return no results. After acceptance, deploy the new knowledge base ID and request shape. Keep the original knowledge base, with current content, and application configuration through your rollback period. For each query, check whether both return the same top document and how much results overlap. A short script can report pass or fail against criteria such as a matching top document on at least 90 percent of queries and no zero-result queries on the managed knowledge base. Tune that threshold for your workload. For other retrieval quality measures, such as context relevance and context coverage, see Use metrics to understand RAG system performance. Watch for these differences when you compare results: Normalize source locations before comparison. A customer-managed knowledge base can return s3://bucket/key in location.s3Location.uri, and a managed knowledge base can return an https:// URL. Compare by object key. Compare the top result instead of assuming equal result counts. The two knowledge base types can return different numbers of results, and numberOfResults sets a maximum rather than a guarantee. Compare the top document, and review each query where it changes. For details, see Configure and customize queries for managed knowledge bases. Map renamed system metadata keys. For example, replace x-amz-bedrock-kb-data-source-id with _data_source_id in comparison code. Your own metadata attributes keep their names. For details, see Configure and customize queries for managed knowledge bases. Clean up If you complete the migration, retire the original only after the rollback period and a dependency review. Keep the source documents and buckets the managed knowledge base ingests from, and storage that other workloads use. Clean up IaC-managed resources through their owning template. If you end the evaluation instead, keep the original and delete what you created in this order: Delete each managed data source and wait until it’s gone. Delete the managed knowledge base and wait until it’s gone. If you created the service role only for this evaluation, delete its inline policy, then the role. With a customer managed key, check aws kms list-grants for grants Amazon Bedrock created, which can remain after the knowledge base is deleted. Keep any S3 bucket that another knowledge base still reads. Deletion protection on a managed data source limits how much a sync can delete, not whether you can delete the data source. Deleting the original knowledge base doesn’t delete its vector store, which continues to incur charges until you remove it. See Delete an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. Conclusion With Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, your team no longer runs a vector store or manages the underlying retrieval infrastructure. With the migration guide in the amazon-bedrock skill, you ask your agent for a plan, review it, and approve only the resources you want built. To get started, set up the Agent Toolkit for AWS and ask your agent for a read-only assessment of your knowledge base. After migration, explore agentic retrieval for multi-part questions. To learn more, see Build enterprise search for agents with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base on the AWS Machine Learning Blog. About the authors Josh DeMuth Josh is a Generative AI Solutions Architect at AWS. Over 20 years in the tech industry, including several years in systems integration, he has focused on making disparate systems work together. He now helps customers build generative AI applications that work with the systems and data they already have. Siddhant Sahu Siddhant is a Senior Product Manager at AWS and the single-threaded owner of Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, the product leader accountable for its strategy, roadmap, and launch. He conceived and launched its agentic retrieval and application connectors, enabling AI agents to perform complex search queries across enterprise data in crucial business applications such as Microsoft SharePoint, Atlassian Confluence, and Amazon S3. Since its launch in June 2026, the service has been adopted by OpenAI, Syngenta, MRH Trowe, Sony, and other enterprises building AI agents on enterprise data. Arjun Tapde Arjun is a Software Engineer at Amazon Web Services (AWS), where he builds AI agent systems and enterprise retrieval infrastructure for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases and AWS Quick. He focuses on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and secure, scalable access to enterprise data, helping customers build reliable AI applications and agents grounded in their business knowledge. Ibhan Aggarwal Ibhan is a Software Development Engineer at AWS. He builds AI agent evaluation harnesses for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, focusing on testing agents against live AWS environments, and grading their behavior through LLM-as-a-judge workflows, tool-call trace analysis, and adversarial testing across frontier models. His work helps customers trust their agents to act accurately and safely. Aniket Panda Aniket is a Software Development Engineer at AWS who builds AI and enterprise retrieval systems for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and AWS Quick. He focuses on agentic workflows, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and giving agents secure, scalable access to enterprise data, so customers can build reliable AI applications grounded in their own business knowledge.

items.title: nab138/iloader
items.summary: User friendly sideloader https://iloader.app iloader Install SideStore (or other apps) and import your pairing file with ease This repository and iloader.app are the only official ways to download iloader. There is also an unofficial Homebrew cask, an unofficial AUR package, and an unofficial Fedora COPR repository maintained by the community. Do not download from any other sources or websites. How to use Install usbmuxd for your platform Windows: iTunes macOS: Included Linux: Potentially included, if not, install via your package manager Install the latest version for your platform from the releases NixOS: Install iloader from nixpkgs-unstable, or use the flake github:nab138/iloader Fedora: Use the .RPM or the unofficial Fedora COPR repository Arch: Use the unofficial AUR package, Plug in your iDevice to your computer Open the app Sign into your Apple ID Select your action (e.g. install SideStore) Features Install SideStore (or LiveContainer + SideStore), import certificate and place rppairing+lockdown pairing files automatically Import any IPA Intelligent error suggestions to help resolve common issues Manage pairing files in apps like StikDebug, SideStore, Protokolle, etc See and revoke development certificates & app ids Troubleshooting If you are unable to solve an issue on your own, copy the full error message and ask on the idevice Discord server or open an issue. You can view app logs with the "View Logs." If nothing is showing up, change the log level to "Debug." If those logs aren't helpful, logs with additional are stored in the following locations: Windows: %APPDATA%\me.nabdev.iloader\logs macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/me.nabdev.iloader/logs Linux: ~/.local/share/me.nabdev.iloader/logs/ Translating iloader needs localization! If you speak another language and notice iloader does not support it or has mistakes, please consider contributing. To update/edit an existing language, make a PR modifying src/locales/<lang>.json. To add a new language, add your language to src/i18next.ts, and in src/locales copy en.json to a new file titled <langcode>.json and update the strings. i18next.ts: const languages = [ ["en", "English"], ["es", "Español"], // Your language here... ] as const; You can also add your name to the translators section of the README. Thank you for translating! Building from source Install bun (or Node.js) and Rust Clone the repository and cd into it Run bun i (or npm i) For development with hot reload: bun tauri dev (or npm run tauri dev) Make a production build: bun tauri build (or npm run tauri build) Credits Icon made by Transistor UI improved by StephenDev0 idevice by jkcoxson for communicating with iOS devices isideload for installing apps idevice by jkcoxson crate is used to communicate with the device apple-codesign-quick by Dadoum for codesigning and entitlements Impactor by claration was used as a reference for cryptography operations (converting certs to p12, etc.). Sideloader by Dadoum was used as a reference for how apple private developer endpoints work idevice_pair was used as a reference for pairing file management App made with tauri Translators Thank you to everyone who has contributed translations! See the Translating section if you would like to contribute as well.
