items.title: openai/codex-security
items.summary: OpenAI's Codex Security CLI and TypeScript SDK for finding, validating, and fixing security vulnerabilities. npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@openai/codex-security https://developers.openai.com/codex/security Codex Security Codex Security helps you find, investigate, and fix vulnerabilities in your code. Use its security workflows in Codex, or automate them with the @openai/codex-security CLI and TypeScript SDK. In Codex: choose a security workflow. In a terminal: install the CLI and scan your repository. In automation: use the TypeScript SDK or GitHub Action. Features Scan repositories, selected paths, or Git changes. Deep scans repeat Standard scans and return their deduplicated findings. Validate candidate findings, generate patches, and verify existing fixes. Draft SECURITY.md policies and save threat models for later review. Browse saved scans and findings, identify duplicates, assess severity against your own rubric, and suggest owners from source and Git history. Preview third-party scanner findings, save them locally, or publish supported reports to Codex Security Cloud. Scanner import guides. Track findings in Linear, Jira, or GitHub, publish completed scans, or export SARIF, JSON, and CSV. Integration workflows. Automate scans across repositories or project components, including in CI and containers. Use in Codex Open your repository in a Codex session with the Codex Security plugin enabled, then ask: Run a Codex Security scan on this repository, focusing on authentication and authorization. Return the saved report, source evidence, and coverage limits. A completed scan saves a report and findings. Read the report for source evidence and exclusions, then request a patch or ask Codex to verify an existing fix. See the agent workflow guide for setup, task selection, and recovery. Quick start Requires Node.js 22.13.0+ within 22.x, or Node.js 24.x or 26.x, and Python 3.10+. Python 3.10 also requires tomli. Install the CLI globally and sign in: npm install --global @openai/codex-security cs login Run your first scan from the repository directory: cs scan . When the scan completes, open the Markdown file at the REPORT path in the terminal. Run cs scans show from the same repository to find its latest completed scan again. See scan scope and follow-up work for how to interpret exclusions in the report. cs and codex-security run the same CLI. If the short name conflicts with another command, use codex-security. To skip the global install, or if npm reports an EEXIST conflict, use npx @openai/codex-security in place of cs for both login and scanning. For CI, set OPENAI_API_KEY or CODEX_API_KEY in the scan process's environment. For a headless machine, see device or SSH login. Scan options Choose a scope and scan mode: # Scan selected paths. cs scan . --path src --path tests # Scan committed changes from a base revision to HEAD. cs scan . --diff origin/main # Run a deep scan of the repository. cs scan . --mode deep Use cs scan . --max-time 15 for an advisory 15-minute Standard investigation allowance. See investigation time for timing semantics and Deep Scan limits. Use cs --help to browse commands, or cs scan --help for scan options, cost limits, and patching after a scan. For an application spread across repositories, see review one system across repositories. Use bulk scans for independent repository reviews in one resumable campaign. Scans use existing root and component SECURITY.md guidance. To write or revise it, see Generate SECURITY.md. Some cybersecurity requests and protected findings require Trusted Access for Cyber. For accounts with Daybreak access, see Daybreak opt-in for the Codex toggle and Cyber access programs to select a program explicitly. TypeScript SDK Install the package locally in your TypeScript project: npm install @openai/codex-security Then import it: import { CodexSecurity } from "@openai/codex-security"; const security = new CodexSecurity(); try { const result = await security.run("/path/to/repository"); console.log(result.reportPath); } finally { await security.close(); } The SDK guide includes deep-scan configuration, validation, severity classification, owner suggestions, and result handling. Linked Git worktrees share scan history and saved findings when they use the same Codex Security state directory. Keep CODEX_SECURITY_STATE_DIR stable to retain that shared history and sign-in scope. See the scan history guide. Read existing Cloud findings When Codex Security Cloud is available to your account, the Security plugin's $cloud-findings skill can read findings, reports, recorded assignment and verification, and scan status in Codex desktop or the Codex CLI. Cloud is an optional connection; local scans work without it. See Cloud connection setup and CLI reads for authentication requirements and a read-only example. Generate SECURITY.md Use policy to draft a new SECURITY.md or update an existing one. Use --path to select a component: cs policy . cs policy . --path services/api --knowledge-base architecture.md The command saves its draft outside the repository and leaves existing files unchanged. Review the diff and notes, edit the draft, then copy only SECURITY.md to the displayed Policy target. Keep the saved architecture and threat-model documents outside the repository. Scans already use root and component SECURITY.md files. Keep your current policy if it needs no changes. When updating it, preserve its vulnerability-reporting instructions. If the command says the policy is already up to date, no copy is needed. Files at .github/SECURITY.md or docs/SECURITY.md often contain reporting instructions. Preserve them when drafting a policy; those locations do not automatically provide repository-wide scan guidance. See the policy guide for policy locations, unanswered questions, saved artifacts, and SDK usage. Save and export threat models Scans and policy generation save threat models with their results. Export a saved model without starting another analysis: cs export --scan SCAN_ID --artifact threat-model --output threatmodel.md Omit --scan to use the current repository's latest completed scan. The export guide also covers findings, SARIF output for CI, and the offline TypeScript API. For ServiceNow Application Vulnerability Response, see Export findings for ServiceNow. GitHub Actions To run a weekly repository scan on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu: Add an OpenAI API key as the repository secret CODEX_SECURITY_API_KEY. Copy the weekly workflow to .github/workflows/codex-security.yml. Replace REPLACE_WITH_REVIEWED_COMMIT with the reviewed distribution commit SHA from an Action release. To try the workflow before the next scheduled run, open Actions → Codex Security repository → Run workflow. The example uses an estimated $5 limit per scan and reports findings without failing the job. Requests in progress can exceed the limit. For a severity threshold, pull request checks, or runner requirements, see the Action guide. For eligible accounts, see Daybreak access. Containerized bulk scans Scan a list of repositories with the included Docker Compose configuration, which keeps results and authentication between runs. See the container quick start. The workflow runner runs individual CLI stages in containers and can connect to a separately deployed findings service. Findings storage and deduplication The findings guide covers local storage, deduplication, and compatibility with independently operated endpoints through publish scan --to custom and explicit --findings-url. The local serve command and browser dashboard have been removed; existing databases and scan artifacts remain available. Other providers Scans support OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock, OpenRouter, Fireworks AI, and Cheaper Inference. Bedrock uses AWS credentials and does not require a separate OpenAI login. See Bedrock setup for AWS profiles, regions, and model access. For OpenRouter, Fireworks AI, and Cheaper Inference, set the provider's API key and choose a supported model. See provider configuration for examples. items.title: OpenCTI-Platform/opencti
items.summary: Open Cyber Threat Intelligence Platform https://opencti.io Note: Building connectors, contributing to the platform, or running OpenCTI in production? Join us on the Community Slack to ask questions, talk through a PR before you open it, or compare notes on integrations. Introduction OpenCTI is an open source platform allowing organizations to manage their cyber threat intelligence knowledge and observables. It has been created in order to structure, store, organize and visualize technical and non-technical information about cyber threats. The structuration of the data is performed using a knowledge schema based on the STIX2 standards. It has been designed as a modern web application including a GraphQL API and a UX-oriented frontend. Also, OpenCTI can be integrated with other tools and applications such as MISP, TheHive, MITRE ATT&CK, etc. Objective The goal is to create a comprehensive tool allowing users to capitalize technical (such as TTPs and observables) and non-technical information (such as suggested attribution, victimology etc.) while linking each piece of information to its primary source (a report, a MISP event, etc.), with features such as links between each information, first and last seen dates, levels of confidence, etc. The tool is able to use the MITRE ATT&CK framework (through a dedicated connector) to help structure the data. The user can also choose to implement their own datasets. Once data has been capitalized and processed by the analysts within OpenCTI, new relations may be inferred from existing ones to facilitate the understanding and the representation of this information. This allows the user to extract and leverage meaningful knowledge from the raw data. OpenCTI not only allows imports but also exports of data under different formats (CSV, STIX2 bundles, etc.). Connectors are currently developed to accelerate interactions between the tool and other platforms. Editions of the platform OpenCTI platform has 2 different editions: Community (CE) and Enterprise (EE). The purpose of the Enterprise Edition is to provide additional and powerful features which require specific investments in research and development. You can enable the Enterprise Edition directly in the settings of the platform. OpenCTI Community Edition, licensed under the Apache 2, Version 2.0 license. OpenCTI Enterprise Edition, licensed under the Enterprise Edition license. To understand what OpenCTI Enterprise Edition brings in terms of features, just check the Enterprise Editions page on the Filigran website. You can also try this edition by enabling it in the settings of the platform. Documentation and demonstration If you want to know more on OpenCTI, you can read the documentation on the tool. If you wish to discover how the OpenCTI platform is working, a demonstration instance is available and open to everyone. This instance is reset every night and is based on reference data maintained by the OpenCTI developers. Releases download The releases are available on the Github releases page. You can also access the rolling release package generated from the master branch of the repository. Installation All you need to install the OpenCTI platform can be found in the official documentation. For installation, you can: Use Docker Install manually Use Terraform (community) Use Helm charts (community) Contributing Code of Conduct OpenCTI has adopted a Code of Conduct that we expect project participants to adhere to. Please read the full text so that you can understand what actions will and will not be tolerated. Contributing Guide Read our contributing guide to learn about our development process, how to propose bugfixes and improvements, and how to build and test your changes to OpenCTI. Beginner friendly issues To help you get familiar with our contribution process, we have a list of beginner friendly issues which are fairly easy to implement. This is a great place to get started. Development If you want to actively help OpenCTI, we created a dedicated documentation about the deployment of a development environment and how to start the source code modification. Community Status & bugs Currently OpenCTI is under heavy development, if you wish to report bugs or ask for new features, you can directly use the Github issues module. Discussion If you need support or you wish to engage a discussion about the OpenCTI platform, feel free to join us on our Slack channel. You can also send us an email to contact@filigran.io. About Authors OpenCTI is a product designed and developed by the company Filigran. Data Collection Usage telemetry To improve the features and the performances of OpenCTI, the platform collects anonymous statistical data related to its usage and health. You can find all the details on collected data and associated usage in the usage telemetry documentation.

items.title: opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox
items.summary: Secure, Fast, and Extensible Sandbox runtime for AI agents. https://open-sandbox.ai OpenSandbox An Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) Project Run AI agents in sandboxes on your own infrastructure. OpenSandbox gives AI applications isolated environments to execute code, run commands, manage files, and operate browsers or desktops. Start locally with Docker and deploy on Kubernetes through a unified sandbox API. Quick Start · Examples · Documentation · Fast Sandbox Features Feature What it enables Learn more Fast Sandbox runtime Fast, high-density sandboxes on Kubernetes. Firecracker creation: 64 ms P50 (serial) / 125.4 ms P99 (10 concurrent). Firecracker sandboxes support pause/resume with memory and disk state preserved. Integration · Performance · Pause/resume Agent working environments Execute commands, manage files, and run code with built-in APIs. Integration examples show how to run coding agents, browsers, and desktops inside sandboxes. Examples Network access control Route inbound traffic through a unified ingress gateway and control outbound access with per-sandbox egress policies. Ingress · Egress Credential Vault Let agents call external services without exposing real credentials to sandbox workloads. Credential Vault Local to cluster Start with Docker and deploy on Kubernetes through a unified lifecycle API. Resource pools and batch creation support agent evaluation and RL training workloads. Kubernetes runtime SDKs, CLI, and MCP Integrate with Python, Java/Kotlin, TypeScript/JavaScript, C#/.NET, or Go SDKs. Use osb from the terminal or connect agents through MCP. SDKs · CLI · MCP Extensible sandbox protocol Build custom runtime integrations against defined sandbox lifecycle and execution APIs. API specs Getting Started Requirements: Docker (required for local execution) Python 3.10+ (required for examples and local runtime) Install and Configure the Sandbox Server uvx opensandbox-server init-config ~/.sandbox.toml --example docker uvx opensandbox-server # Show help # uvx opensandbox-server -h Create a Sandbox and Execute Commands/Scripts Install the Sandbox SDK uv pip install opensandbox Create a sandbox from an alpine image and execute commands and scripts. import asyncio from opensandbox import Sandbox from opensandbox.models import WriteEntry async def main() -> None: # 1. Create a sandbox from the alpine image sandbox = await Sandbox.create("alpine") try: # 2. Execute a shell command execution = await sandbox.commands.run("echo 'Hello OpenSandbox!'") print(execution.logs.stdout[0].text) # 3. Write a script file await sandbox.files.write_files([ WriteEntry( path="/tmp/hello.sh", data="echo \"Hello $1\"\necho '2 + 2 =' $((2 + 2))", mode=755, ) ]) # 4. Read the file back content = await sandbox.files.read_file("/tmp/hello.sh") print(f"Content: {content}") # 5. Execute the script execution = await sandbox.commands.run("sh /tmp/hello.sh OpenSandbox") for log in execution.logs.stdout: print(log.text) finally: # 6. Cleanup the sandbox await sandbox.destroy() if __name__ == "__main__": asyncio.run(main()) Examples Explore examples by what you want your agent to do. Runnable source code lives in examples/. Use case What you can build Examples Coding agents Run coding agents in isolated environments to edit files, execute commands, and complete development tasks. Claude Code · Codex CLI · DeerFlow Code execution and data analysis Execute model-generated code and work with results through the Code Interpreter SDK. Code Interpreter Browser and desktop automation Automate web interactions and testing, or give agents access to a desktop environment. Playwright · Chrome · Desktop Agent evaluation Run evaluations with a separate sandbox for each trial. Harbor Evaluation See the full example catalog for more coding agents, framework integrations, remote development environments, Kubernetes deployment, and storage patterns. SDKs Pick your language: Python pip install opensandbox Java/Kotlin (Gradle Kotlin DSL) dependencies { implementation("com.alibaba.opensandbox:sandbox:{latest_version}") } Java/Kotlin (Maven) <dependency> <groupId>com.alibaba.opensandbox</groupId> <artifactId>sandbox</artifactId> <version>{latest_version}</version> </dependency> JavaScript/TypeScript npm install @alibaba-group/opensandbox C#/.NET dotnet add package Alibaba.OpenSandbox Go go get github.com/alibaba/OpenSandbox/sdks/sandbox/go CLI OpenSandbox also provides osb, a terminal CLI for the common sandbox workflow: create sandboxes, run commands, move files, inspect diagnostics, and manage runtime egress policy. Install: pip install opensandbox-cli # or uv tool install opensandbox-cli Quick start: osb config init osb config set connection.domain localhost:8080 osb config set connection.protocol http osb config set connection.api_key <your-api-key> osb sandbox create --image python:3.12 --timeout 30m -o json osb command run <sandbox-id> -o raw -- python -c "print(1 + 1)" See the CLI README for the full command reference. MCP The OpenSandbox MCP server exposes sandbox creation, command execution, and text file operations to MCP-capable clients such as Claude Code and Cursor. Install and run: pip install opensandbox-mcp opensandbox-mcp --domain localhost:8080 --protocol http Minimal stdio config: { "mcpServers": { "opensandbox": { "command": "opensandbox-mcp", "args": ["--domain", "localhost:8080", "--protocol", "http"] } } } See the MCP README for client-specific setup. Official Container Images OpenSandbox release images are published under the same component name in three official registries: Docker Hub: docker.io/opensandbox/<component> GitHub Container Registry: ghcr.io/opensandbox-group/opensandbox/<component> Alibaba Cloud Container Registry: sandbox-registry.cn-zhangjiakou.cr.aliyuncs.com/opensandbox/<component> Pin production images by digest and check the release verification guide for signing coverage before deployment. Legacy per-component releases support Cosign signatures and provenance attestations; current umbrella releases have a tracked signing and provenance gap and must not be assumed to provide the same verification evidence. Documentation Website — Project homepage and documentation site Architecture — System design and component responsibilities Deployment Guide — Kubernetes installation and operations Server Configuration — Runtime and server settings SDK Reference — Language guides and capability coverage CLI Guide — Installation and command reference MCP Integration — Setup for MCP-capable clients API Reference — Sandbox lifecycle and execution contracts Credential Vault — Outbound credential injection Release Verification — Image signing and artifact verification Enhancement Proposals — Design proposals and technical direction Roadmap — Project priorities and planning Contact and Discussion Issues: Submit bugs, feature requests, or design discussions through GitHub Issues Discord: Join the OpenSandbox Discord community DingTalk: Join the OpenSandbox technical discussion group About OpenSandbox is a project of the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF). Code is licensed under the Apache 2.0 License. See the contribution guide for documentation licensing and contribution terms.

items.title: OpenViking 3D理解模型上线轴测八视图及PMI解析
items.summary: 原创 OpenViking 2026-11-12 18:00 北京 OpenViking如何理解一个3D模型 OpenViking发布原生3D内容理解模型，支持三维.STEP文件的导入与解析，信息还原率做到 100%。 导入一个3D文件，不仅会提取常规的正交视图、几何信息，还会使用八轴侧视图来补充被遮挡的内部结构和几何特征，同时保留全部的尺寸、公差、装配、工艺（PMI）细节。看得见内部结构，也能读懂规格参数。 解析目录 正交六视图 轴侧八视图 信息摘要（含PMI） 模型明细 左右滑动查看更多精彩内容 二、轴侧视图如何用｜同一类零件，识别细节差异 以两款四方嵌件底座为例：外形完全相同，唯一的区别在内壁盲窝——型号 1 是圆形，型号 2 是六角形。 型号1 嵌件底座 型号2 嵌件底座 这个差异藏在壳体内部，正交六视图里看不到，两款零件的六视图完全一致。同样问 Agent：“帮我找一个内壁有六边形盲孔的四方嵌件底座，之前有设计过”，结果截然不同： _ 只有正交六视图 正交六视图 + 轴测八视图 检索结果 无法确认，只能给出型号 1、型号 2 两个候选 直接定位到型号 2 判断依据 六视图看不到内壁孔口和孔底 轴测图中能看到内壁的六边形凹孔和孔底 后续动作 需要你逐个打开模型确认 无需人工确认 只有正交六视图时，Agent 找到两款外形相符的候选，但无法判断哪一款带六边形盲孔： OpenViking + Codex 检索结果：无法确认 仅保留正交六视图 型号 1 / 2 的正交六视图一致 左右滑动查看更多精彩内容 加上轴测八视图后，Agent 从轴测图中识别出内壁的六边形凹孔，直接给出答案： OpenViking + Codex 检索结果：直接定位型号 2 正交六视图 + 轴测八视图 型号 1 型号 2 左右滑动查看更多精彩内容 再细节的差异也能被3D内容理解模型捕捉，Agent都能检索到。 三、PMI信息如何用｜提供零件规格，实现精准定位 PMI（Product and Manufacturing Information，产品制造信息）是 3D 模型中附带的尺寸、公差、材料、工艺等制造信息。以一个基础安装座为例： 安装底座模型 PMI&模型对应关系图 OpenViking的3D内容理解模型可以对3D结构的全部PMI信息进行理解，同时区分几何、尺寸、公差、装配、工艺五个部分，自动加工到Summary.md文件中，供Agent按需读取。 几何 尺寸 公差 装配 工艺 左右滑动查看更多精彩内容 当你需要找到一个精确尺寸的零件，可以问Agent：“找一个底板厚2cm，带4个直径6.6 mm安装孔的底座”，Agent 会定位到「基础安装座标品.step」，逐项对照你的要求列出零件参数——板厚 20 mm（±0.05 mm）、4 个贯通底板的安装孔、孔径 Ø6.6 mm（±0.1 mm），并标明信息来源。 OpenViking导入 OpenViking + Codex检索 最后 OpenViking 作为业内首个理解三维世界的 Agent 上下文数据库产品，能够完整准确理解3D模型的所有细节特征和规格参数，实现精准检索。看得见内部结构，也能读懂规格参数。现在接入，点击【阅读原文】即刻使用。 🚀 上手试用，前 50 文档免费： https://s.c1ns.cn/TwLos 🌟开源 OpenViking： 访问 GitHub 仓库（https://github.com/volcengine/OpenViking），为我们点亮一颗 Star！ ❓三分钟测出你是哪种 Agent 饲养员选择属于你的 OpenViking https://blog.openviking.ai/post/should-you-use-openviking/ 💬 加入飞书交流群&微信群！ 点击「阅读原文」立即体验 阅读原文 跳转微信打开

items.title: Optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock
items.summary: Part 1 of this series built the operating model that controls Amazon Bedrock spend: attribution with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal tags and Cost and Usage Report 2.0, observability with model invocation logging, enforcement at three tiers, and a review cadence. That layer answers who spent it, and you can stop them. It can’t tell you whether the spend was well spent. This post answers two questions that Part 1 deliberately left open. First: Why is this workflow expensive? The answer requires thinking in cost per task, not cost per token. Second: Is the agent better than the humans were? The answer requires baselines, controlled experiments, and a scorecard tied to decisions. In this post, you learn a framework for calculating true model cost (including four hidden cost drivers that the pricing page doesn’t show), techniques for reducing cost per task through caching, routing, and output constraints, and a discipline for measuring agent ROI with human baselines, holdout experiments, and a five-dimension scorecard. This post is written for two audiences: the application and platform engineers who own the optimization levers, and the product owners and FinOps partners who need to justify agent spend to leadership. Cost per task, not cost per token Price per token invites quick comparison, but it doesn’t reflect what you actually pay. The published rate reflects the cost of a single token. Your bill reflects the cost of completing a task. A task is one complete unit of work your application asks a model to do: resolve one support email, extract fields from one invoice, or answer one user question. A task runs from the request through to a usable result, however many model calls it takes. The lower-priced model might not be the cheaper one to run. A cheaper model might fragment your text into more tokens, pad responses with filler, misread your tool schema and loop through corrections, or burn thousands of reasoning tokens before answering. None of these costs appear on the Bedrock pricing page. The four hidden cost drivers Four model characteristics determine what that published rate actually costs you on your workload. Tokenizer efficiency A token isn’t a word, and it is not equal across models. Every model family uses a different tokenizer and vocabulary. The same text, code, or JSON payload splits into different token counts. If Model A’s list price is 15 percent lower but its tokenizer needs 40 percent more tokens for your data (common with structured schemas and numerical arrays), Model B is cheaper. The gap widens for non-English text: many tokenizers fragment non-Latin scripts into two to three times more tokens than the equivalent English. Output alignment and verbosity Output tokens commonly cost 3–5x more than input tokens (the ratio varies by family. Refer to the Bedrock pricing page). A model that ignores formatting constraints like “return only raw JSON” makes you pay that output premium for filler words. A model that follows formatting instructions closely saves money by generating fewer of these more expensive output tokens. Agentic loop efficiency Agentic workflows change the cost math entirely. Tool use (function calling) lets a model invoke external functions, requiring a multi-turn loop: analyze the prompt, decide to call a tool, wait for the observation, generate an answer. Each turn re-sends the full conversation history and tool results as input tokens. A model that takes four turns (each one re-sending a larger context payload) costs far more than one that finishes in a single pass. Reasoning overhead Many models support extended thinking, working through a chain of thought before the visible answer. Reasoning tokens bill as output tokens, so a model that thinks for 2,000 tokens before a 200-token answer bills you for 2,200. Some models redact the reasoning while still charging for it. Start with reasoning turned off and enable it only when benchmarks show a quality gap that justifies the cost. Cost per task: A worked example Figure 1: Comparing two models across five cost dimensions. List price is only one of five factors that determine actual cost Consider an agentic workflow that reads a 750-word customer email, extracts entities, calls an API to verify account status, and outputs strict JSON. The following comparison uses illustrative prices (always benchmark against your own data and current Bedrock pricing): Metric Model A (lower list price) Model B (higher list price) Input list price $0.50 / 1M tokens $1.00 / 1M tokens Output list price $1.50 / 1M tokens $3.00 / 1M tokens Tokenizer efficiency (turn 1 input) 1,500 tokens 1,000 tokens Output verbosity (final response) 450 tokens 150 tokens Agentic loops required 3 turns (error correction) 1 turn (zero-shot) Cumulative input tokens, all turns 6,150 1,000 Cumulative output tokens, all turns 750 150 Total task cost $0.0042 $0.00145 Model A: (6,150 x $0.50 + 750 x $1.50) / 1,000,000 = $0.0042 Model B: (1,000 x $1.00 + 150 x $3.00) / 1,000,000 = $0.00145 Figure 2: Why the higher-priced model costs 65% less. Each extra turn re-sends a growing context payload, compounding the bill Why the 2x-priced model costs 65 percent less: three compounding factors. Model A’s tokenizer fragments the email into 50 percent more tokens, inflating every input payload. It pads its JSON with filler, tripling output tokens. And it misaligns with the tool schema, needing two correction turns that each re-send a growing history. Cost per successful task The preceding example assumes both models eventually succeed. In production they won’t, and a failure is rarely free. The formulas: For retry-until-success workflows: cost per successful task = cost per attempt / success rate For escalate-on-failure workflows: cost per successful task = cost per attempt + (1 - success rate) x escalation cost Input further splits into three buckets when prompt caching is active: uncached input at base rate, cache reads below base rate, and cache writes above base rate. Measuring it on your own workload Which model is actually cheaper only shows up when you benchmark against your own data. Amazon Bedrock model evaluation is the managed feature for the quality half of that: define criteria, upload your prompt datasets, and get scored results with automatic metrics and optional human review, with no custom infrastructure required. Quality scores alone don’t produce a bill, though. Three more Bedrock features supply the token and turn counts you price against them: CountTokens returns the input token count a given model would charge for a given payload without running inference. It’s the cheapest way to compare tokenizer efficiency (driver #1) across candidates before you spend anything on generation. Model invocation response carries a usage block with inputTokens, outputTokens, cacheReadInputTokens, and cacheWriteInputTokens. Accumulating those across the turns of a single task gives you the four terms of the preceding cost-per-attempt formula. One gotcha: when caching is enabled, inputTokens counts only the uncached tokens, so your total input volume is inputTokens + cacheReadInputTokens + cacheWriteInputTokens. Sum them to know the footprint, but price them separately, since the three bill at different rates. Evaluate this multiple times throughout your journey and set the cache checkpoints based on what is the active current load. The drift in cache checkpoints happens as the application progresses and the tools become stale. This means that you will be writing more to the cache in 3 months from now when the drift has happened. Evaluating your data constantly for optimal cache usage becomes a primary lever to reduce cost. Model invocation logging writes per-invocation token counts to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch Logs, so you can measure turns-to-completion against real production traffic instead of a sample. Tag calls with request metadata to slice those logged token counts by team, feature, or experiment. However, these are log fields, not cost allocation tags, and never appear in AWS Cost Explorer or your Cost and Usage Report. Application inference profiles do reach both, at a grain of one usage type per day. That grain is right for chargeback but too coarse for cost per task. Multiplying logged token counts by the published rates gives you a near real-time estimate rather than an invoice. It won’t reflect commitments, batch pricing, or provisioned throughput unless you model them. Reconcile against your Cost and Usage Report before you treat it as the bill. Reducing cost per task: Four levers Each of the four drivers has a lever, and each is documented in depth. Prompt caching cuts the re-sent context that made Model A expensive, which makes it the largest win on agentic paths. Intelligent prompt routing sends the easy requests to a cheaper model in the same family. A tool schema plus a maxTokens cap holds verbosity down more reliably than prose instructions do, and extended thinking stays off until a benchmark shows it earns its cost back. Batch inference halves the rate on bulk single-turn work, though it rules out tool calling and multi-turn exchange. Proving agent ROI: Describe the human baseline Efficient isn’t the same as valuable. An agent can be perfectly optimized and still not be worth running. The question that decides budgets is: is the agent better than the humans were? Document the human process first The biggest mistake in agent ROI is trying to prove value without first describing the human workflow. Before building or scaling an agent, write down the current process in operational terms: what triggers the work, which human roles are involved, where the handoffs sit, how completion is defined. This sounds like bureaucracy. It’s actually measurement design. Every instrumentation decision downstream (what counts as a run, what counts as success, where human time is spent) falls out of this description. Measure the baseline before the agent ships With the process described, measure the human baseline over a meaningful window: time to completion, queue time, active effort, reopen rate, escalation rate, cost per task, and outcome quality. Baselines must be measured before the agent goes live, not reconstructed from memory after the fact. Retrospective baselines are systematically flattering to the agent: people remember the average case and forget the fast ones. Instrument the workflow as an experiment After the baseline exists, instrument the agent workflow as an experiment from day one. Every run gets a trace ID, and every meaningful step is observable. A workflow-run record aggregates everything above the model call into a single analyzable unit: { "runId": "run-8f3a2c", "workflow": "renewal-risk-summary", "agent": "renewal-agent", "principalArn": "arn:aws:sts::123456789012:assumed-role/BedrockRuntimeRole/gw-alex", "team": "sales-ai", "costCenter": "CC-2041", "experiment": { "variant": "treatment", "holdout": False, "promptVersion": "v14", "policyVersion": "2026-07" }, "ops": { "latencyMs": 41200, "retries": 1, "toolCalls": 6, "humanApprovals": 1, "humanMinutes": 35, "escalations": 0 }, "econ": { "inputTokens": 48210, "outputTokens": 3105, "cacheReadTokens": 31500, "estCostUsd": 0.87 }, "outcome": { "status": "success", "accepted": True, "reopened": False, "revenueEventId": "opp-44121" } } Three fields deserve emphasis: experiment block: Stamped at run creation and propagated into Bedrock request metadata, so model-level and workflow-level records join cleanly. humanMinutes: What most teams omit and most need. Without it, “the agent did the work” silently excludes the 35 minutes a human spent reviewing it. revenueEventId: The hook that makes revenue attribution possible later. It costs nothing to record and can’t be reconstructed afterward. The rule: If the workflow telemetry can’t answer the business question, the instrumentation is incomplete. Join cost to outcomes With invocation logs landing in Amazon S3 (Part 1) and workflow-run records in your analytics store, one join produces the metrics that matter. Amazon Bedrock logs record tokens, not dollars, so first build a view that prices each invocation from token counts and your model rate sheet, aggregated by run ID. Then query with Amazon Athena: SELECT w.workflow, w.variant, COUNT(*) AS runs, SUM(IF(w.outcome_status = 'success', 1, 0)) AS successes, ROUND(SUM(c.est_cost_usd) / NULLIF(SUM(IF(w.outcome_status = 'success', 1, 0)), 0), 2) AS cost_per_success, ROUND(SUM(w.retries) * 1.0 / NULLIF(SUM(IF(w.outcome_status = 'success', 1, 0)), 0), 2) AS retries_per_success, ROUND(SUM(w.human_minutes) / NULLIF(SUM(IF(w.outcome_status = 'success', 1, 0)), 0), 1) AS human_min_per_success FROM workflow_runs w JOIN invocation_costs_by_run c ON c.run_id = w.run_id GROUP BY w.workflow, w.variant ORDER BY cost_per_success DESC Note: Column names and join keys shown in the preceding query are illustrative. Verify against your invocation log schema and workflow telemetry store, which might vary by implementation. Cost per successful outcome, retries per success, and human minutes per success are the three numbers that survive contact with a skeptical CFO. Cost per call flatters agents that loop. Cost per success doesn’t. Note the variant grouping: the same query, split by experiment arm, is the ROI comparison. Compare agents and humans correctly The most credible evaluation is an A/B or holdout test. Controlled treatment and control groups compare the agent-assisted workflow against the human baseline without confusing the result with market, seasonal, or organizational changes. For customer-facing or revenue-linked workflows, randomize at the visitor, lead, account, or case level. For internal workflows (support operations, coding assistants), use matched cohorts: teams, repository groups, or pods. The comparison covers four dimensions: Efficiency: time to completion, hours recovered, queue-time reduction. Quality: error rate, approval rate, reopen rate, escalation rate. Cost: cost per task, cost per successful outcome, total cost to serve. Business value: conversion lift, retention lift, expansion rate, revenue per rep or per workflow. If the agent improves one dimension while meaningfully degrading another, the result is ambiguous and the deployment needs tuning. Revenue: The hardest metric Efficiency gains are the easiest part of the ROI story to prove. Revenue impact is harder, and it is the metric leadership funds against. In revenue-adjacent workflows, measure whether the agent improves conversion, time-to-response, deal progression, or revenue per rep. Holdout tests are the most reliable way to separate incremental revenue attributable to the agent from general business momentum. When revenue lift is real, the conversation changes. The organization stops asking whether the Bedrock bill went up and starts asking whether the additional spend is buying a meaningful increase in business output. The scorecard Based on what we have observed working with customers, a strong operating model doesn’t require fifty metrics. What works is a small scorecard tied to decisions, reviewed on a regular cadence for every production agent. The following thresholds are starting points, not prescriptions. Calibrate them against your own fleet data and organizational context. Dimension Metric Green Yellow Red Adoption Active users / intended users >70% 40-70% <40% Quality Tasks completed without rework >90% 75-90% <75% Efficiency Hours recovered per week >target 50-100% of target <50% of target Cost Cost per successful outcome ≤budget 1-1.5x budget >1.5x budget Business impact KPI lift compared to baseline Significant Marginal None or negative Green means scale: the agent beats baseline while meeting cost and quality thresholds. Yellow means tune: promising but needs work. Red means retire or redesign: the agent consumes cost without enough measurable value. The willingness to actually retire a red agent is what makes the rest of the scorecard credible. Conclusion In this post, you learned how to calculate the true cost of a model by accounting for four hidden cost drivers (tokenizer efficiency, output alignment, agentic loop efficiency, and reasoning overhead), how to reduce cost per task through prompt caching, model routing, output constraints, and batch inference, and how to prove agent ROI by measuring human baselines, instrumenting workflows as experiments, joining cost to outcomes, and running holdout comparisons. The cost optimization half answers “why is this expensive and how do I fix it.” The ROI half answers “is the agent better than the humans were.” Together with Part 1’s operating model (attribute, observe, enforce, optimize, operate), they form a complete framework: you can see who spent it, explain why, reduce the waste, and justify what remains. To get started, benchmark your top model candidates against your own prompts using Amazon Bedrock model evaluation, capture tokens and turns from the usage block or your invocation logs, price them against current Bedrock pricing, and divide by success rate. For ROI measurement, consult the Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens for agent cost governance best practices. If you have found other techniques for reducing cost per task or measuring agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock, let us know in the comments. About the authors Majd Arbash Majd Arbash is an Enterprise Solutions Architect at AWS based in Toronto, where he helps enterprise customers build secure, scalable cloud solutions and adopt generative AI. A member of the Serverless and Generative AI Technical Field Communities, Majd focuses on application modernization, security, and hands-on generative AI experimentation. Aswath Ram A Srinivasan Aswath is a Senior Specialist Solutions Architect for Bedrock focusing on Bedrock Core models, Features and cost optimization/attribution. He helps ISVs and strategic customers solve their challenges and he works with enterprise teams to design inference architectures that balance performance, cost, and operational simplicity, responsibly. In his free time he is a photographer and loves reviewing science journal papers on neurosymbolic AI and Responsible AI. Ajit Mahareddy Ajit is an experienced Product and Go-To-Market (GTM) leader with over 20 years of experience in product management, engineering, and go-to-market. Prior to his current role, Ajit led product management building AI/ML products at leading technology companies, including Uber, Turing, and eHealth. He is passionate about advancing generative AI technologies and driving real-world impact with generative AI.
