items.title: Run agents securely and efficiently with the next generation AgentCore runtime
items.summary: AI agents have moved past one-off prompts. They now run multi-step workloads for hours at a time. The length of task that frontier agents can complete on their own doubles about every four months (METR), and 40 percent of large enterprises are scaling AI agents, up from 27 percent a year ago (McKinsey). As agents run longer and with more autonomy, the focus shifts from what agents can do to how securely, reliably, and economically they can operate at scale. Agents do more than traditional software: they execute code, navigate browsers, access sensitive data, and act on behalf of users. These capabilities introduce new security and infrastructure demands, making strong isolation essential for production deployments. Every agent session needs a secure, isolated environment. But delivering that isolation at scale introduces a fundamental challenge: balancing performance, cost, and efficiency. Pre-provisioned environments consume resources even when idle, driving up costs. On-demand environments reduce wasted capacity but introduce cold-start latency, delaying agent execution. Neither approach scales efficiently without trade-offs. As organizations move from deploying a handful of agents to running thousands of concurrent sessions, building and managing custom sandboxes becomes increasingly complex, expensive, and unpredictable. The challenge is evident. Only 15 percent of organizations have scaled orchestrated, multi-agent systems, and 70 percent say they can’t yet trust and govern their agents (Deloitte). Scaling agents shouldn’t mean choosing between security, speed, and cost. The next generation of agent infrastructure must deliver strong isolation with fast startup times, elastic scaling, and usage-based economics. Because as AI agents move into production, secure execution shouldn’t be the bottleneck. It should be the foundation that makes scale possible. The fastest path to production should also be the safest one. The next generation AgentCore runtime We built Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to help developers build, connect, and optimize agents securely at scale. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is the managed compute layer. It gives developers a fully managed environment to deploy and run agents without building or maintaining infrastructure. Since launching, our customers have been pushing their agents into increasingly complex workloads. As those workloads grow, so do the demands on the execution environment: more compute, more flexible billing, and trust boundaries that extend to data, not only compute. Agents reach production at scale if the infrastructure underneath was built for both scale and speed. Today we’re announcing updates to AgentCore runtime that meet those demands. The core guarantee stands: every session runs in its own hardware-isolated Firecracker micro virtual machine (MicroVM), with its own identity, policy, and audit trail. These updates expand what’s possible within that guarantee. Sessions now start up to 15x faster, scale to 4x more compute, and run up to 68% more efficiently, with the isolation boundary fully intact. Here’s what’s new. Run bigger workloads without waiting longer to start Teams building increasingly advanced agents asked for more flexibility: the ability to scale memory and compute within the isolated session to match the demands of their workloads. From large codebase compilations to browser-driven workflows to local model inference, the execution environment needs to keep pace. Sessions now scale 4x compared to the previous version, up to 8 vCPUs and 32 GB, with support for container images up to 10 GB. Sessions start in under 2 seconds, independent of image size and concurrency. You no longer need warm pools and pre-provisioned clusters to manage cold starts. “AgentCore Runtime lets us run AI-driven development at scale. Each coding agent session runs in its own hardware-isolated environment, which we need when agents execute code, and the runtime scales elastically with demand and starts fast every time, so our engineers move quickly without managing any infrastructure.” — Siwei Shen, VP of Engineering, Coinbase “Mission is using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime to power a natural-language query agent that helps users retrieve property and sales insights without navigating complex data systems. In our initial comparison of both runtime versions, the same workload delivered 35% faster cold starts for inference requests and 77% faster starts for health checks, while reducing measured runtime cost per call by 17%. The new AgentCore runtime gives us a compelling combination of faster agent experiences and more efficient resource utilization as we bring enterprise agents into production.” — Dr. Ryan Ries, Chief AI & Data Scientist, Mission Cloud “Our approach is to run Zuora’s cloud with automation and AI agents wherever we can, and that only works if the runtime is efficient and reliable. The next generation AgentCore runtime cut our memory footprint per invocation by around 60% in many use cases while handling more traffic at steady latency. That gives us a stronger cost profile as we expand agentic workloads across our platform.” — Brad Ruppert, VP of Cloud and Security, Zuora “The Rescale platform helps R&D and engineering teams accelerate product development with agentic digital engineering. Our engineering-specific agents validate simulation inputs, troubleshoot jobs, select hardware, and generate reports, while engineers stay in control. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime allows us to deploy and scale those agents in production without building or operating the underlying agent infrastructure, so we can deliver new agents to customers faster.” — Mark Whitney, VP Engineering, Rescale Stop paying for idle agents As teams move agents closer to production, they asked for billing that reflects how agents actually work. Agents spend much of their time waiting on a model response, a tool call, or a human decision. Agents should be billed for the work they do, not the time they spend waiting. The runtime now reclaims memory within minutes of the agent releasing it, and an idle agent scales to zero. For multi-turn agents with natural pauses between interactions, this means up to 68 percent less memory consumed per session. For always-on agents, committed baseline pricing sets a memory baseline per session, billed as a minimum, with room to burst up to four times that baseline on demand. This gives steady workloads a predictable rate at AWS Lambda MicroVM rates. The runtime uses compute more efficiently, so you pay less for the same work. That makes the finance conversation that often gates production rollouts easier to close. “The next generation Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime helps us deliver more responsive AI experiences by starting agents faster and using memory more efficiently. Aligning consumption with actual usage gives our clients great confidence to scale agentic solutions while keeping costs connected to real demand.” — Ashwin Patil, Principal, AI and Data Leader, Deloitte Consulting LLP “AgentCore runtime gives us a managed foundation for building agentic products and platforms around our customers’ data, tools, and business processes. The next generation Agentcore runtime makes that foundation more responsive and resource-efficient by restoring initialized environments and reclaiming unused memory. We’re beginning to build on the latest version because the cost and latency reductions make a significant difference in how our customers’ businesses operate.” — Randall Hunt, CTO, Caylent Isolation now extends to your data Many enterprises face a persistent gap in their agent security model. The agent runs inside an isolated session, but the data it requires resides outside that boundary. Long-running agents pick up context as they go: files, credentials, tool outputs, and more. Teams end up building their own rules for how data moves in and out, adding complexity and risk with every new agent. Isolation that stops at compute is only half a boundary. The next generation AgentCore runtime closes that gap. Each session still runs in its own hardware-isolated environment with its own identity, access policy, and audit trail. Agents can now dynamically mount and save their work to a filesystem, such as an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket with FUSE support. Your data stays inside the trust boundary for the entire job, governed by a single set of controls you define once. “At Okta, the combination of AgentCore runtime and Lambda MicroVMs provide the isolated execution environment and contextual memory our agents need to inspect code, run test suites, and open pull requests within ephemeral sandboxes. Paired with our identity-governed policy controls, AgentCore Runtime and Lambda MicroVMs demonstrate how we can safely scale autonomous engineering agents without risking workspace leakage or privilege escalation.” — Monica Bajaj, SVP Engineering, Okta “From helping car shoppers value a trade-in to helping dealers book service appointments and structure deals, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore powers dozens of agentic solutions across Cox Automotive’s brands. Having a single, governed agent platform lets our teams across our business move from pilot to production with confidence.” — Chris Dillon, VP, Product and Engineering, Cox Automotive “With the next generation of CoCounsel Legal, we set out to build an agentic system that does more than answer questions: it works through a matter end to end, from research to trusted work product. Getting that into customers’ hands quickly meant spending our time on legal reasoning and quality, rather than on running agent infrastructure. With AgentCore Runtime handling the hosting and scaling, we moved from prototype to production fast and kept complete control over how our agents operate and integrate with our existing systems. Our developers build on their preferred frameworks, and Runtime gives us the enterprise-grade reliability and isolation we need to run CoCounsel’s agentic legal workflows at scale for legal professionals around the world.” — Danilo Tommasina, Distinguished Engineer – Thomson Reuters Our commitment The agents that reach production are the ones you trust to act on your behalf, with real data, real stakes, and real accountability. Trust isn’t a feature you add later. It’s the runtime you build on. This release is a step toward that future: bigger sessions, efficient resource use, and storage inside the trust boundary, without loosening the isolation that makes the work trustworthy. By re:Invent, per-session scoping will bind each session to its own storage folder through session-labeled credentials, and we will keep building from there. Get started The next generation AgentCore runtime is available today in AWS Regions across North America, South America, Europe, and Asia Pacific. Visit Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to build on it or open the Amazon Bedrock console to start exploring. About the author Madhu Parthasarathy Madhu is the GM of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, where he leads the team building the platform that companies use to build, connect, and optimize production AI agents. He brings more than 20 years of experience building large-scale distributed infrastructure, including over 16 years at Amazon, where he has led major initiatives across Amazon Retail, Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS), and now AgentCore. Before returning to Amazon, Madhu held senior leadership roles at LinkedIn, where he led the enterprise platform powering all of LinkedIn’s enterprise lines of business, and at a neo-cloud startup, where he led AI infrastructure and set the vision for security and developer experience. He is based in Santa Clara, California.

items.title: saleor/saleor
items.summary: Saleor Core: the high performance, composable, headless commerce API. https://saleor.io Commerce that works with your language and stack GraphQL native, API-only platform for scalable composable commerce. Get to know Saleor: Talk to a human | Talk to the API Join our community: Website | Twitter | Discord Blog | Subscribe to newsletter Table of Contents What makes Saleor special? Why API-only Architecture? Features Installation Documentation Saleor Platform Storefront Dashboard Contributing License What makes Saleor special? Technology-agnostic - no monolithic plugin architecture or technology lock-in. GraphQL only - Not afterthought API design or fragmentation across different styles of API. Headless and API only - APIs are the only way to interact, configure, or extend the backend. Open source - a single version of Saleor without feature fragmentation or commercial limitations. Cloud native - battle tested on global brands. Native-multichannel - Per channel control of pricing, currencies, stock, product, and more. Why API-only Architecture? Saleor's API-first extensibility provides powerful tools for developers to extend backend using webhooks, attributes, metadata, apps, subscription queries, API extensions, dashboard iframes. Compared to traditional plugin architectures (monoliths) it provides the following benefits: There is less downtime as apps are deployed independently. Reliability and performance - custom logic is separated from the core. Simplified upgrade paths - eliminates incompatibility conflicts between extensions. Technology-agnostic - works with any technology, stack, or language. Parallel development - easier to collaborate than with a monolithic core. Simplified debugging - easier to narrow down bugs in independent services. Scalability - extensions and apps can be scaled independently. What are the tradeoffs? If you are a single developer working with a small business that doesn't have high traffic or a critical need for 24/7 availability, using a service-oriented approach might feel more complex compared to the traditional WordPress or Magento approach that provides a language-specific framework, runtime, database schema, aspect-oriented programming, and other tools to a quick start. However, if you deploy on a daily basis, reliability and uptime is critical, you need to collaborate with other developers, or you have non-trivial requirements you might be in the right place. Features Enterprise ready: Secure, scalable, and stable. Battle-tested by big brands Dashboard: User-friendly, fast, and productive. (Decoupled project repo ) Global by design Multi-currency, multi-language, multi-warehouse, tutti multi! CMS: Manage product or marketing content. Product management: A rich content model for large and complex catalogs. Orders: Flexible order model, split payments, multi-warehouse, returns, and more. Customers: Order history and preferences. Promotion engine: Sales, vouchers, cart rules, giftcards. Payment orchestration: multi-gateway, extensible payment API, flexible flows. Cart: Advanced payment and tax options, with full control over discounts and promotions. Payments: Flexible API architecture allows integration of any payment method. Translations: Fully translatable catalog. SEO: Unlimited SEO freedom with headless architecture. Apps: Extend dashboard via iframe with any web stack. Installation See the Saleor docs for step-by-step installation and deployment instructions. For local development without Docker, follow our Contributing Guide. Note: The main branch is the development version of Saleor and it may be unstable. To use the latest stable version, download it from the Releases page or switch to a release tag. The current production-ready version is 3.x and you should use this version for all three components: Saleor: https://github.com/saleor/saleor/releases/ Dashboard: https://github.com/saleor/saleor-dashboard/releases/ Storefront: https://github.com/saleor/react-storefront/releases/ Saleor Cloud The fastest way to develop with Saleor is by using developer accounts in Saleor Cloud. Register here or install our CLI tool: npm i -g @saleor/cli and run the following command: saleor register Bootstrap your first storefront with: saleor storefront create --url {your-saleor-graphql-endpoint} Documentation Saleor documentation is available here: docs.saleor.io To contribute, please see the saleor/saleor-docs repository. Saleor Platform The easiest way to run all components of Saleor (API, storefront, and dashboard) together on your local machine is to use the saleor-platform project. Go to that repository for instructions on how to use it. View saleor-platform Storefront An open-source storefront example built with Next.js App Router, React.js, TypeScript, GraphQL, and Tailwind CSS. React Storefront Repository View Storefront Example Dashboard For the dashboard, go to the saleor-dashboard repository. Contributing We love your contributions and do our best to provide you with mentorship and support. If you are looking for an issue to tackle, take a look at issues labeled Good first issue and Help wanted. If nothing grabs your attention, check our roadmap or start a Discord discussion about a feature you'd like to see. Make sure to read our Contribution Guidelines before opening a PR or issue. Get more details (e.g., how to run Saleor on your local machine) in our Contributing Guide. License Disclaimer: Everything you see here is open and free to use as long as you comply with the license. There are no hidden charges. We promise to do our best to fix bugs and improve the code. Crafted with ❤️ by Saleor Commerce hello@saleor.io

items.summary: High Performance Serving Runtime For Interactive Super Intelligence System https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/ Blog | Documentation | Quick Start | Cookbook | SGLang | Join Slack ⭐ Star SGLang-Omni to help more builders discover open infrastructure for multimodal and speech serving! News [2026/11] 🎙️ Voxt 2.0 redefines open-source voice interaction on Mac: voice input, any-to-any translation, and a local AI assistant, with a 92% shorter wait after long dictation than 1.x. [Download] [Changelog] [2026/11] 🔁 OpenRSI × SGLang-Omni: recursive self-improvement (RSI) scaled to production AI infrastructure, with 14 merged PRs across 8 speech and omni models and +7.6% to +326.5% throughput on H100. [Blog] [2026/10] 🗺️ A unified runtime for interactive intelligence: native full-duplex models, turn-based multimodal models, and cascaded systems, coordinated through composable graphs and persistent sessions. [Blog] [2026/10] 🚀 SGLang-Omni v0.2.0 is on PyPI. Install with uv pip install --prerelease=allow "sglang-omni==0.2.0". [Installation] [2026/10] 🐟 Day-0 support for Fish Audio Drama 3: multi-speaker text-to-speech with voice cloning and natural-language control, streamed on /v1/audio/speech. [Blog] [Cookbook] [Technical Report] [2026/10] 🎙️ Introducing Voxt, an open-source voice input tool for Mac, now integrating SGLang-Omni for faster local speech recognition on Apple Silicon. Combine ASR with LLM-based text refinement and personal system prompts for accurate technical terminology and personalized voice input, with fully local or remote inference options. [Download][Demo] Earlier news [2026/09] 🐧 Day-0 support for AuK and AuK-Flash: text + voice instructions → 24 kHz speech on /v1/audio/speech, audio + editing instructions → edited speech on /generate. [Cookbook] [2026/08] 🎵 Day-0 support for MiniMax Music 3: lyrics + caption → 32 kHz stereo song on /v1/audio/speech. [Cookbook] [2026/08] 🚀 TTS architecture refactor: shared pipeline state, engine construction, reference encoding, capability metadata, and vocoder scheduling. [Roadmap] [Blog] [2026/06] 🔥 MOSS-TTS Local Transformer v1.5 on SGLang-Omni with native-streaming 48 kHz speech. [Blog] [Cookbook] [2026/06] 🔥 Higgs Audio v3 TTS for real-time, controllable speech. [Blog] [Cookbook] About SGLang-Omni is a multi-stage serving runtime for omni, speech, and TTS models. Its design target is multi-stage decoding: generation split across heterogeneous stages with different compute patterns, dependency structures, and resource needs. SGLang-Omni owns the pipeline topology, stage lifecycle, inter-stage transport, model-family integration layer, and OpenAI-compatible serving surface, while composing with SGLang for high-performance autoregressive scheduling and model execution where applicable. Multi-stage runtime: SGLang-Omni models generation as coordinated stages: preprocessing, encoders, autoregressive engines, talkers, decoders, vocoders, and aggregators. Stage-specialized scheduling: Each stage runs behind a scheduler matched to its workload, from SGLang-backed autoregressive scheduling to lightweight preprocessing and streaming vocoder loops. Transport-aware execution: A control plane coordinates requests while the relay data plane moves tensor payloads across shared-memory, NCCL, NIXL, and Mooncake backends. API surface: OpenAI-compatible endpoints expose multimodal chat, speech generation, batch speech, streaming speech, uploaded voices, and transcription. What SGLang-Omni Serves Omni chat and speech: Qwen3-Omni, MiniCPM-o 4.5, Ming-Omni, Ming-3.0-audio-flash — multimodal understanding and text/audio replies. Native full-duplex conversation: MiniCPM-o 4.5, PersonaPlex, NemotronLabs VoiceChat — live listening and speaking over /v1/realtime, including camera input with MiniCPM-o. Full-duplex guide. Cascaded voice assistants: Compose ASR → LLM → TTS services into streaming, turn-based conversations with voice activity detection, conversation history, turn taking, and interruption. Streaming cascade guide. Image and video generation: LLaDA2.0-Uni for text/image understanding, image generation, and editing; Cosmos3 Nano for interleaved understanding and generation, with native image, video, and action routes. Music generation: MiniMax Music 3 — lyrics + caption → 32 kHz stereo song. Speech generation: Higgs Audio v3, MOSS-TTS, MOSS-TTS Local, Fish Audio Drama 3, Fish Speech S2-Pro, Qwen3-TTS, Fun-CosyVoice3, Voxtral TTS, Ming-Omni-TTS, Ming-3.0-TTS, dots.tts, ZONOS2 — /v1/audio/speech, with batch, streaming, and voice features varying by model. Instruction-driven speech generation and editing: AuK and AuK-Flash — text and voice instructions → speech; audio and editing instructions → edited speech. Audio transcription: Qwen3-ASR, Fun-ASR, ARK-ASR, Nemotron 3.5 ASR, Nemotron Transcribe, Ming-3.0-ASR, experimental Whisper, and MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize via /v1/audio/transcriptions. MOSS-TD also returns speaker labels and timestamps (response_format=verbose_json). Speaker diarization: Nemotron 3 Diarization — speaker intervals for uploaded recordings and live audio, including overlapping speech. Speech translation: Hy-SimulMT — Chinese speech → English text and English speech → Chinese text, with file and realtime translation. See the audio translation guide for endpoint and model support. Hardware Support Backend Status Notes NVIDIA CUDA Supported Default backend with full model coverage. Apple Silicon Experimental Qwen3-ASR runs through Torch MPS on macOS arm64. Install with install.sh and follow the Qwen3-ASR guide. Intel GPU (XPU) Supported Intel Arc GPUs via PyTorch XPU. Qwen3-ASR, Whisper ASR, Fun-ASR-Nano, Nemotron 3.5 ASR, MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize, Qwen3-TTS, Fun-CosyVoice3, ZONOS2, Audar-TTS, Qwen3-Omni, MiniMax Music 3, MiniCPM-o, Ming-Omni, Ming-Omni-TTS, Nemotron VoiceChat, PersonaPlex, AuK/AuK-Flash and dots.tts serve end-to-end. The Intel XPU guide has the install steps, each model's launch command and how many cards it needs; the backend is auto-detected. Additional model guides, including experimental and research-oriented paths, are available in the Cookbook. Quick Start Installation TTS usage ASR cookbook Community & Support SGLang-Omni welcomes contributors working on inference systems, kernels, scheduling, inter-stage communication, model runners and cache efficiency, model integration, benchmarking, production deployment. Join the SGLang Slack or read the developer reference. Organizations interested in supporting SGLang-Omni, TTS, or omni model serving can contact Chenyang Zhao at zhaochenyang@lmsys.org. Citation If you use SGLang-Omni for your research, please cite our technical blogs on the unified interactive runtime and the Stage--Process--GPU topology: @misc{sglangomniinteractive2026, title={Unified Runtime for Full-Duplex Interactive Intelligence with {SGLang Omni}}, author={{SGLang-Omni Team}}, howpublished={\url{https://www.sglang.io/blog/omni-interactive-runtime}}, year={2026}, month={oct} } @misc{sglangomni2026, title={Fish Audio Drama 3 Meets {SGLang-Omni}: Day-0 Support and the Stage--Process--GPU Topology}, author={{SGLang-Omni Team}}, howpublished={\url{https://www.sglang.io/blog/spg-topology}}, year={2026}, month={oct} } Acknowledgments SGLang-Omni builds on the SGLang ecosystem and on open model work from the TTS, speech, and omni-model communities. We thank the model teams, systems contributors, and partner organizations helping make open multimodal serving faster, more reliable, and easier to extend.

items.title: shadcn/improve
items.summary: Use your most capable model to audit your codebase and write plans for cheaper models to execute. improve An agent skill that audits any codebase and writes implementation plans for other agents to execute. The idea: use your most capable model for the part where intelligence compounds — understanding the codebase, judging what's worth doing, writing the spec — and hand execution to cheaper models. The skill never implements anything itself. The plan is the product. you → /improve (expensive model, advises) plans/ → 001-fix-n-plus-one.md (self-contained specs) other agent → implements, tests, ships (cheap model, executes) Install npx skills add shadcn/improve Works in any agent that supports Agent Skills format. The plans it writes are plain markdown, so any agent (or human) can pick them up. Usage /improve full audit → prioritized findings → plans /improve quick cheap pass: hotspots, top findings only /improve deep exhaustive: every package, every category /improve security focused audit (also: perf, tests, bugs, ...) /improve branch audit only what the current branch changes /improve next feature suggestions — where to take the project /improve plan <description> skip the audit, spec one thing /improve review-plan <file> critique and tighten an existing plan /improve execute <plan> dispatch a cheaper executor, review its work /improve reconcile refresh the backlog: verify, unblock, retire /improve ... --issues also publish plans as GitHub issues How to use A typical first run, start to finish: Open your agent in the repo and run /improve (or /improve quick to keep it cheap). It maps the repo, audits it, and comes back with a findings table. Reply with the ones you want planned — "plan 1, 3 and 5". Plans land in plans/ — one file each, plus an index with the recommended order. Read them; they're meant to be reviewed. Hand a plan to any agent ("implement plans/001-*.md"), or let the skill run it: /improve execute 001. It dispatches a cheaper model in an isolated worktree, reviews the diff against the plan, and reports back with a verdict. Merging stays up to you. Next session, run /improve reconcile to clean up the backlog: verify what landed, refresh what drifted, unblock what got stuck. Before a PR, /improve branch does the same thing scoped to just what your branch changes. Example A run against shadcn/ui came back with findings like: | # | Finding | Category | Effort | Confidence | |---|------------------------------------------------|-----------|--------|------------| | 1 | shadow-config duplicated in search.ts/view.ts, | tech-debt | M | HIGH | | | copies already drifted (TODO at search.ts:31) | | | | | 2 | O(n²) icon migration (migrate-icons.ts:168) | perf | S | HIGH | …and rejected a few, with reasons recorded so they don't come back next run: - [SEC-01] https_proxy env var "SSRF": by-design — standard proxy convention, every CLI honors it. Not a finding. Picking #1 produced this plan — current code excerpted, exact steps, the repo's own test/lint commands as verification gates, and STOP conditions for when reality doesn't match. How it works Recon. Maps the repo: stack, conventions, and the exact build/test/lint commands — these become verification gates in every plan. It also ingests intent and design docs when present — ADRs (docs/adr/), PRDs, CONTEXT.md, DESIGN.md, PRODUCT.md — so decided tradeoffs aren't re-flagged as findings, direction suggestions stay grounded in stated product intent, and plans speak the repo's own vocabulary. Composes with any repo that already maintains these docs. Audit. Fans out parallel subagents across nine categories: correctness, security, performance, test coverage, tech debt, dependencies & migrations, DX, docs, and direction (feature suggestions — every one must cite evidence from the repo itself, no generic idea-slop). Every finding carries file:line evidence, impact, effort, and confidence. Vet. Subagents over-report, so the advisor re-reads every cited location itself before showing you anything — false positives get dropped, wrong attributions get corrected, rejections get recorded. Prioritize. Findings land in a table ordered by leverage (impact ÷ effort, weighted by confidence). You pick what becomes plans. Plan. One file per selected finding, written into plans/ with an index, priority order, and dependency graph. What makes the plans executable Plans are written for the weakest plausible executor — a model that has never seen the advisor session and may be much smaller. Three properties carry that: Self-contained. All context is inlined: exact file paths, current-state code excerpts, repo conventions with an exemplar file, verified commands. No "as discussed above." Verification gates. Every step ends with a command and its expected output. Done criteria are machine-checkable. The executor never has to judge whether it succeeded. Hard boundaries. Explicit out-of-scope lists, and STOP conditions — "if X, stop and report" — instead of letting a small model improvise when reality doesn't match the plan. Each plan also stamps the git commit it was written against, so executors run a mechanical drift check before touching anything. Closing the loop Plans aren't fire-and-forget: execute <plan> spawns a cheaper executor subagent in an isolated git worktree, hands it the plan, then reviews the result like a tech lead — re-runs every done criterion, checks scope compliance, reads the diff against intent. Verdict: approve (merging stays your call), send back for revision (max 2 rounds), or block and refine the plan. reconcile processes what happened since: verifies DONE plans still hold, investigates BLOCKED ones and rewrites around the obstacle, refreshes drifted plans, retires findings that got fixed independently. --issues publishes plans as GitHub issues — same self-contained body, so any agent or human can pick them up where work already lives. Hard rules Never modifies source code itself. The only writes go to plans/; executors edit only in disposable worktrees, and merging is always yours. Never runs commands that mutate your working tree — read, search, and read-only analysis only. Never reproduces secret values. Locations and credential types only, rotation always recommended. Asked to implement? It declines and points at the plan (or offers execute). License MIT © shadcn

items.title: sherlock-project/sherlock
items.summary: Hunt down social media accounts by username across social networks https://sherlockproject.xyz Hunt down social media accounts by username across 400+ social networks Installation • Usage • Contributing Installation Warning Packages for ParrotOS and Ubuntu 24.04, maintained by a third party, appear to be broken. Users of these systems should defer to uv/pipx/pip or Docker. Method Notes pipx install sherlock-project pip or uv may be used in place of pipx docker run -it --rm sherlock/sherlock dnf install sherlock-project Community-maintained packages are available for Debian (>= 13), Ubuntu (>= 22.10), Homebrew, Kali, and BlackArch. These packages are not directly supported or maintained by the Sherlock Project. See all alternative installation methods here. General usage To search for only one user: sherlock user123 To search for more than one user: sherlock user1 user2 user3 Accounts found will be stored in an individual text file with the corresponding username (e.g user123.txt). $ sherlock --help usage: sherlock [-h] [--version] [--verbose] [--folderoutput FOLDEROUTPUT] [--output OUTPUT] [--csv] [--xlsx] [--site SITE_NAME] [--proxy PROXY_URL] [--dump-response] [--json JSON_FILE] [--timeout TIMEOUT] [--print-all] [--print-found] [--no-color] [--browse] [--local] [--nsfw] [--txt] [--ignore-exclusions] USERNAMES [USERNAMES ...] Sherlock: Find Usernames Across Social Networks (Version 0.16.0) positional arguments: USERNAMES One or more usernames to check with social networks. Check similar usernames using {?} (replace to '_', '-', '.'). options: -h, --help show this help message and exit --version Display version information and dependencies. --verbose, -v, -d, --debug Display extra debugging information and metrics. --folderoutput FOLDEROUTPUT, -fo FOLDEROUTPUT If using multiple usernames, the output of the results will be saved to this folder. --output OUTPUT, -o OUTPUT If using single username, the output of the result will be saved to this file. --csv Create Comma-Separated Values (CSV) File. --xlsx Create the standard file for the modern Microsoft Excel spreadsheet (xlsx). --site SITE_NAME Limit analysis to just the listed sites. Add multiple options to specify more than one site. --proxy PROXY_URL, -p PROXY_URL Make requests over a proxy. e.g. socks5://127.0.0.1:1080 --dump-response Dump the HTTP response to stdout for targeted debugging. --json JSON_FILE, -j JSON_FILE Load data from a JSON file or an online, valid, JSON file. Upstream PR numbers also accepted. --timeout TIMEOUT Time (in seconds) to wait for response to requests (Default: 60) --print-all Output sites where the username was not found. --print-found Output sites where the username was found (also if exported as file). --no-color Don't color terminal output --browse, -b Browse to all results on default browser. --local, -l Force the use of the local data.json file. --nsfw Include checking of NSFW sites from default list. --txt Enable creation of a txt file --ignore-exclusions Ignore upstream exclusions (may return more false positives) Credits Thank you to everyone who has contributed to Sherlock! ❤️ Star History License MIT © Sherlock Project Creator - Siddharth Dushantha

后端启动后会在内存里保留一份完整的 enriched 历史宽表(指标 + 扩展数据列),供策略扫描、监控和回测直接复用,这是主要的内存来源。实测(243 个交易日、约 108 万行、105 列): 场景 常驻内存 启动预热峰值 默认配置(按 CPU 核数并行) ~1.3 GB ~1.5–1.8 GB POLARS_MAX_THREADS=2 ~0.8 GB ~1.2 GB 给出的是 macOS arm64 实测值。Windows 的内存工作集通常比 macOS 的 RSS 更"实",同一数据量下数值接近或略高;Polars 释放的页不会立即归还系统,所以监控里看到的是历史高水位而不是实时占用。 2 GB 内存的服务器/小主机建议: # .env POLARS_MAX_THREADS=2 # 主要收益项: 用约 40% 的构建耗时换 500MB 内存 # docker-compose.yml 的 app 服务 mem_limit: 1500m memswap_limit: 3g # 留 swap 缓冲, 避免偶发峰值直接触发 OOM kill 不要在 2 GB 机器上跑回测/稳健优化/因子挖掘:这类任务会另起独立 worker 进程并重新加载整套后端,单个约 800 MB,与主进程叠加必然超出。 items.title: soxoj/maigret
items.summary: 🕵️‍♂️ Collect a dossier on a person by username from 6K websites https://maigret.app/gh Maigret English · 简体中文 · Français 📖 Documentation Maigret collects a dossier on a person by username only, checking for accounts on a huge number of sites and gathering all the available information from web pages. No API keys required. AI profiling (demo). Sponsors Go beyond account enumeration. WebVetted turns an email or username into a complete identity investigation with deep OSINT enrichment, breach intel, AI analysis, and an interactive identity graph. Start an Investigation → RapidProxy provides high-performance residential proxies for Twitter scraping, Selenium automation, and web data extraction. 90M+ IPs • Smart rotation • Anti-block • Non-expiring traffic. Special Offer: Try it free — Plans from $0.65/GB. Use code RAPID10 for 10% off. ThorData provides residential proxies and web data APIs for OSINT research, username lookup, and search reconnaissance. Access 100M+ residential IPs across 190+ countries to reduce failed requests, 403 errors, and location-based restrictions. Use SERP API for structured search results or Web Scraper API to collect public web data. Special Offer: Get a free 3-day trial and 10% OFF with code SOXOJ10. Contents In one minute Main features Demo Installation Usage Contributing Commercial Use About In one minute Ensure you have Python 3.10 or higher. pip install maigret maigret YOUR_USERNAME No install? Try the community Telegram bot or a Cloud Shell. Want a web UI? See how to launch it. See also: Quick start. Main features Supports 5,900 sites (see full list). A default run checks the 500 highest-ranked sites by traffic; pass -a to scan everything, or --tags to narrow by category/country. Embeddable in Python projects — import maigret and run searches programmatically (see library usage). Extracts all available information about the account owner from profile pages and site APIs, including links to other accounts. Performs recursive search using discovered usernames and other IDs. Allows filtering by tags (site categories, countries). Detects and partially bypasses blocks, censorship, and CAPTCHA. Fetches an auto-updated site database from GitHub each run (once per 24 hours), and falls back to the built-in database if offline. Works with Tor and I2P websites; able to check domains. Ships with a web interface for browsing results as a graph and downloading reports in every format from a single page. Optional AI analysis mode (--ai) that turns raw findings into a short investigation summary using an OpenAI-compatible API. For the complete feature list, see the features documentation. Used by Professional OSINT and social-media analysis tools built on Maigret: Demo Video Reports PDF report, HTML report Full console output Installation Already ran the In one minute steps? You're set. Below are alternative methods. Don't want to install anything? Use the community Telegram bot. Windows Download maigret_standalone.exe from Releases. You can launch it two ways: Double-click it — Maigret will ask for a username, run a default search, and wait at the end so the report links stay visible. Run it from a terminal — open Command Prompt (press Win+R, type cmd, hit Enter) or PowerShell to pass extra options: cd %USERPROFILE%\Downloads maigret_standalone.exe USERNAME maigret_standalone.exe USERNAME --html :: also save an HTML report maigret_standalone.exe --help :: list all options Video guide: https://youtu.be/qIgwTZOmMmM. Cloud Shells Run Maigret in the browser via cloud shells or Jupyter notebooks: Snap (Linux) sudo snap install maigret # usage maigret username Available for amd64 and arm64, no Python required. The snap is strictly confined and can write inside your home directory, so run it from there. For USB drives, connect the interface once with sudo snap connect maigret:removable-media. Local installation (pip) # install from pypi pip3 install maigret # usage maigret username From source # or clone and install manually git clone https://github.com/soxoj/maigret && cd maigret # build and install pip3 install . # usage maigret username Docker Two image variants are published: soxoj/maigret:latest — CLI mode (default) soxoj/maigret:web — auto-launches the web interface # official image (CLI) docker pull soxoj/maigret # CLI usage docker run -v /mydir:/app/reports soxoj/maigret:latest username --html # Web UI (open http://localhost:5000) docker run -p 5000:5000 soxoj/maigret:web # Web UI on a custom port docker run -e PORT=8080 -p 8080:8080 soxoj/maigret:web # manual build docker build -t maigret . # CLI image (default target) docker build --target web -t maigret-web . # Web UI image Troubleshooting Build errors? See the troubleshooting guide. PDF reports (--pdf) are an optional extra — install with pip install 'maigret[pdf]'. They need system-level graphics libraries on Linux/macOS; see the PDF reports section for per-OS install steps. Usage Examples # make HTML, PDF, and XMind reports maigret user --html maigret user --pdf maigret user --xmind # legacy XML with a manifest for XMind 2022+ readers # machine-readable exports maigret user --json ndjson # newline-delimited JSON (also: --json simple) maigret user --csv maigret user --txt maigret user --graph # interactive D3 graph (HTML) maigret user --neo4j # Neo4j Cypher script (graph database) # search on sites marked with tags photo & dating maigret user --tags photo,dating # search on sites marked with tag us maigret user --tags us # highlight sites whose page also mentions specific keywords maigret user --keywords python rust # keyword-matched sites are shown with "[++]" in bright green # search for three usernames on all available sites maigret user1 user2 user3 -a # AI-assisted investigation summary (needs OPENAI_API_KEY) maigret user --ai --neo4j writes a *_neo4j.cypher script of the results graph; import it with cypher-shell -u neo4j -p <password> < report_user_neo4j.cypher or paste it into the Neo4j Browser. Re-imports are idempotent. See the Neo4j export docs. Run maigret --help for all options. Docs: CLI options, more examples. Running into 403s or timeouts? See TROUBLESHOOTING.md. Web interface Maigret has a built-in web UI with a results graph and downloadable reports. Don't want to run it yourself? Deploy the published soxoj/maigret:web Docker image as a hosted app in one click: Runs on Render's free tier (spins down after 15 min idle, spins back up on the next request). No login is set up on the instance, so anyone with the URL can use it. Web Interface Screenshots maigret --web 5000 Open http://127.0.0.1:5000, enter a username, and view results. Python library Maigret can be embedded in your own Python projects. The CLI is a thin wrapper around an async function you can call directly — build custom pipelines, feed results into your own tooling, or run it inside a larger OSINT workflow. See the full library usage guide for a working example, async patterns, and how to filter sites by tag. Useful CLI flags --parse URL — parse a profile page, extract IDs/usernames, and use them to kick off a recursive search. --permute — generate likely username variants from two or more inputs (e.g. john doe → johndoe, j.doe, …) and search for all of them. --self-check [--auto-disable] — verify usernameClaimed / usernameUnclaimed pairs against live sites for maintainers auditing the database. --ai / --ai-model — run the AI analysis over the search results and stream a short investigation summary to the terminal. AI analysis --ai collects the search results, builds an internal Markdown report, and sends it to an OpenAI-compatible chat completion endpoint to produce a short, neutral investigation summary (likely real name, location, occupation, interests, languages, confidence, follow-up leads). Per-site progress is suppressed and the model's output is streamed to stdout. export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... maigret user --ai # pick a different model maigret user --ai --ai-model gpt-4o-mini The key can also be set as openai_api_key in settings.json. The endpoint defaults to https://api.openai.com/v1, but openai_api_base_url in settings.json can point to any OpenAI-compatible API (Azure OpenAI, OpenRouter, a local server, …). See the settings docs for the full list of options. Tor / I2P / proxies Maigret can route checks through a proxy, Tor, or I2P — useful for .onion / .i2p sites and for bypassing WAFs that block datacenter IPs. # any HTTP/SOCKS proxy maigret user --proxy socks5://127.0.0.1:1080 # Tor (default gateway socks5://127.0.0.1:9050) maigret user --tor-proxy socks5://127.0.0.1:9050 # I2P (default gateway http://127.0.0.1:4444) maigret user --i2p-proxy http://127.0.0.1:4444 Start your Tor / I2P daemon before running the command — Maigret does not manage these gateways. Cloudflare bypass Experimental. The Cloudflare webgate is under active development; the configuration schema, CLI behaviour, and the set of routed sites may change without backwards-compatibility guarantees. A subset of sites in the database require a real browser to solve a JavaScript challenge. Maigret can offload these checks to a local FlareSolverr instance: docker run -d -p 8191:8191 --name flaresolverr ghcr.io/flaresolverr/flaresolverr:latest maigret --cloudflare-bypass <username> The bypass is opt-in (--cloudflare-bypass or cloudflare_bypass.enabled in settings.json) and only fires for sites whose protection field matches. See the feature docs for backend options and configuration. Contributing Add or fix new sites surgically in data.json (no json.load/json.dump), then run ./utils/update_site_data.py to regenerate sites.md and the database metadata, and open a pull request. For more details, see the CONTRIBUTING guide and development docs. Release history: CHANGELOG.md. Commercial Use The open-source Maigret is MIT-licensed and free for commercial use without restriction — but site checks break over time and need active maintenance. For serious commercial use — with a daily-updated site database or a username-check API — reach out: 📧 maigret@soxoj.com Private site database — 5 000+ sites, updated daily (separate from the public open-source database) Username check API — integrate Maigret into your product About Disclaimer For educational and lawful purposes only. You are responsible for complying with all applicable laws (GDPR, CCPA, etc.) in your jurisdiction. The authors bear no responsibility for misuse. Feedback Open an issue · GitHub Discussions · Telegram SOWEL classification OSINT techniques used: SOTL-2.2. Search For Accounts On Other Platforms SOTL-6.1. Check Logins Reuse To Find Another Account SOTL-6.2. Check Nicknames Reuse To Find Another Account License MIT © Maigret

items.title: Tokenomics at scale: Track and cap Amazon Bedrock spend per IAM principal with CUR 2.0 and AWS Budgets
items.summary: Generative AI spend is hard to attribute. Before an organization expands AI access, CFOs and CTOs usually want three answers: what do we spend per person or per team, can we cap it, and how much work does it take to get there. In our previous post, Tokenomics at Scale: How Jamf Built Real-Time Spend Enforcement for Amazon Bedrock, we explained a custom enforcement loop built on AWS IAM Identity Center, Amazon Athena over Amazon Bedrock model invocation logs, and AWS Lambda. This approach gives near-real-time control, but it requires code you then own and operate. This post shows how to get per-identity Amazon Bedrock cost visibility and enforceable spend limits using only AWS-native features, with no application code to write for the common case. The approach relies on three things: IAM principal attribution, which Amazon Bedrock records automatically; AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR) 2.0 or AWS Cost Explorer for reporting; and AWS Budgets with budget actions for enforcement. By the end, you will have per-identity cost reporting and an automatic guardrail that restricts Amazon Bedrock access when a threshold is crossed. Solution overview The solution has three parts: attribute, report, and enforce. Attribute. Amazon Bedrock captures the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal identity, the IAM user or role, for every inference request. This happens automatically, with no change to your Amazon Bedrock model inference calls. If several people share one role, you add per-user detail with session tags passed at role assumption time. If each person or application has its own role, principal tags on the role are enough. Report. Activate those tags as cost allocation tags, then read the data either in Cost Explorer for a console-only view, or in a CUR 2.0 data export for detailed line-item analysis and SQL queries. Enforce. Create an AWS Budget scoped to Amazon Bedrock and filtered to one identity or tag value, then attach a budget action that applies a Deny IAM policy when the threshold is crossed. The following sections show each part in more detail, alongside the implementation steps. Prerequisites To deploy this solution, you need: An AWS account with Amazon Bedrock model access enabled. Permissions to tag IAM principal, activate cost allocation tags, create data exports, and create budgets and budget actions. Amazon Bedrock accessed through IAM roles or IAM users. AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) configured with appropriate credentials. A CUR 2.0 data export and an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket to receive it. (optional, for detailed line-item analysis). Amazon Athena. (optional, for querying the export). AWS Billing Console access is managed separately from most IAM permissions. Confirm you have it before starting. Walkthrough Before configuring anything, check what you already have. Amazon Bedrock records caller identity for every inference request automatically. Open Cost Explorer, filter Service to Amazon Bedrock, and group by the available identity or tag dimension. For accounts where each application or person already uses a distinct IAM role, this may be all the visibility you need. To configure additional visibility: Step 1 gives you identity-level visibility. Steps 2 through 4 add tag dimensions and detailed reporting. Step 5 adds enforcement. Step 1: Decide how identity maps to your users How you tag depends on how your IAM principals are organized. One role per person or per application. Attach principal tags directly to each IAM role or user. These are static and apply to every request from that principal. Use the IAM console, or the AWS CLI: aws iam tag-role \ --role-name BedrockDeveloperRole-alice \ --tags Key=user,Value=alice@example.com Key=team,Value=platform Key=CostCenter,Value=CC-1001 A shared role used by several people, or a gateway. Principal tags cannot distinguish users on a shared role, because every session carries the same tags. Use session tags instead, passed when the role is assumed. Session tags are dynamic and can vary per session. If a session tag and a principal tag share a key, the session tag wins for that session. The role’s trust policy must allow sts:TagSession. Session tags can be passed three ways: sts:AssumeRole with --tags, for a gateway assuming a role per user or tenant. AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, with tags in the https://aws.amazon.com/tags claim of the OpenID Connect (OIDC) ID token (this is a claim name, not a URL you browse to). AssumeRoleWithSAML, by mapping PrincipalTag:* attributes in the identity provider’s Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) assertion. If your organization already captures a claim like saml:sub for other purposes, that alone does not make it available here. Your identity provider must separately map that attribute to a PrincipalTag:* SAML attribute statement, and the role’s trust policy must allow sts:TagSession, before it flows through as a session tag. The two integrations draw from the same SAML assertion but are configured independently. Common tag keys are user, team, Department, CostCenter, and Environment. You can apply up to 50 principal or session tags per IAM user or role. Figure 1: Attribution with principal tags compared to session tags Step 2: Activate cost allocation tags Tags do not appear in billing data until you activate them. Open the AWS Billing and Cost Management Console. Choose Cost allocation tags. Filter by type IAM principal. Select your tag keys and choose Activate. In an AWS Organization, activate IAM principal cost allocation tags in the management account (payer). Member accounts cannot activate them independently. Two things to expect: A tag key only appears in this list after the principal has made at least one Amazon Bedrock call, so make a test call first if the list looks empty. It might take up to 24 hours for a newly applied tag key to appear for activation, then up to another 24 hours after you activate it before it begins populating billing data. Activation does not apply retroactively by default, so activate tags before you need the data. Step 3: Create a CUR 2.0 data export that includes caller identity Skip this step if Cost Explorer is enough for your reporting. In the Billing and Cost Management console, choose Data Exports. Choose Create and create a CUR 2.0 (Standard) export. Under Additional export content, select Include caller identity (IAM principal) allocation data. Under Time granularity, select Hourly. Under Report data integration, select Amazon Athena. This sets the file format to Parquet and, importantly, delivers a setup script to your S3 bucket alongside the export data. Choose the destination Amazon S3 bucket. Run the delivered setup script (or the Glue crawler/DDL it defines) once. This is what actually creates the Glue Data Catalog table you’ll query in Step 4. The preceding console flow does not create it for you automatically. If you already have a CUR 2.0 export created before enabling identity attribution, it will not include identity data retroactively. Create a new export with the caller identity option selected. In the export, principal and session tags appear as columns prefixed iamPrincipal/, and resource tags as resourceTags/. For example, a tag key team appears as iamPrincipal/team. AWS publishes a ready-made query set for this exact pattern in aws-samples/sample-cur-iam-principal-bedrock-tracking. Step 4: Read the data The following diagram compares the two ways to read the data: a console-only path through Cost Explorer, and a SQL path over the CUR 2.0 export with Amazon Athena. Figure 2: Reporting with Cost Explorer compared to CUR 2.0 and Amazon Athena Console path, no custom code. Cost Explorer, filtered to Amazon Bedrock and grouped by your tag key, gives per-team or per-user spend as a chart and table. This covers most recurring reporting needs and requires no query authoring. SQL path, low code. Point Amazon Athena at the CUR 2.0 export to group spend by iamPrincipal/team and usage type: SELECT tags['iamPrincipal/team'] AS team, line_item_usage_type, SUM(line_item_unblended_cost) AS cost FROM cur2_view WHERE product_servicecode IN ('AmazonBedrock', 'AmazonBedrockService') AND billing_period = '2026-09' GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 3 DESC Things to note: Service code: Amazon Bedrock spend can be recorded under more than one product_servicecode value, for example, AmazonBedrock and AmazonBedrockService. Table name: The table name (cur2_view) is whatever the setup script from Step 3 named it when it created the Glue table. Check the script or your Glue catalog if it differs. Column names match the CUR 2.0 Parquet schema regardless of table name. Billing-period column. Confirm how your export exposes the period. Some exports use billing_period (YYYY-MM). Others partition on a start-date or year/month column. Two notes worth carrying into any query you write. Count all token types: Amazon Bedrock bills four token types, each at a different rate: input, output, cache read, and cache write. Each is a separate line item with its own usage type and unit price, so summing only input and output undercounts. The gap is largest for workloads that use prompt caching heavily. Refer to the AWS document Understanding Amazon Bedrock pricing in CUR for the latest information. Match the rate to the line item, not the model: Amazon Bedrock pricing in CUR is determined by three things: the token type, the service tier, and whether the request was routed through cross-Region inference. In-Region and cross-Region requests are priced differently, and service tier is reflected in the usage type as well. The usage type carries a suffix indicating cross-Region routing and service tier, so if your workloads mix these, match the rate to each line item rather than applying one rate per model. Refer to the CUR usage type examples for examples. Step 5: Add enforcement with AWS Budgets and budget actions AWS Budgets performs the attach, so there is no custom code for this workflow. Budget actions attach to a specific IAM user, group, or role. This isolates one person’s access only if that person already has their own role. If your Amazon Bedrock traffic runs through a role that many people share, a Deny action attached to that role blocks everyone on it, not only the person who crossed the threshold. The following diagram explains the enforcement workflow. Figure 3: Enforcement with AWS Budgets and budget actions AWS Budgets can run an action when a threshold is crossed. Available actions include applying a custom IAM policy, applying a service control policy (SCP), and targeting Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) or Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) instances. For this use case, the IAM policy action is the relevant one. First, create the Deny policy the action will attach. This example denies the higher-cost models while leaving a lower-cost model available, so the user can keep working: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Deny", "Action": [ "bedrock:InvokeModel", "bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream" ], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:bedrock:*::foundation-model/[HIGHER-COST-MODEL-ID]" ] } ] } Replace [HIGHER-COST-MODEL-ID] with the model ID you want to deny in your environment. Then set up permissions and the budget itself. There are two distinct roles here, and the AWS managed policy only covers one of them: Your own user or role (the one configuring the budget) needs the AWS managed policy AWSBudgetsActionsWithAWSResourceControlAccess. It grants budgets permissions plus the conditioned iam:PassRole needed to hand your budget action role to AWS Budgets. The IAM role AWS Budgets assumes to perform the action is not covered by a single named managed policy for this use case. Create it with a trust policy that allows the principal budgets.amazonaws.com to assume it (scoped with aws:SourceArn and aws:SourceAccount conditions), and a permissions policy granting iam:AttachRolePolicy and iam:DetachRolePolicy (and organizations:AttachPolicy and organizations:DetachPolicy if you are also using SCPs). Refer to Setting up a role for AWS Budgets to run budget actions for the grantable permissions. Create the budget action role described earlier. Create a cost budget scoped to Amazon Bedrock, filtered to the identity or tag value you want to cap. In Configure alerts, add an alert threshold. Choose Actual for realized spend or Forecasted to act before the spend lands. Under Attach actions, choose Add Action, select the budget actions role, and choose the IAM policy action. Select the Deny policy and the IAM user, group, or role to attach it to. For automatic enforcement, choose Yes to run the action automatically. Choose No to require a human to approve each action from the Alert details page. Configure at least one notification so the affected user is told why access changed. You can attach multiple actions to a single threshold, and multiple thresholds to one budget. That is how you build tiers: for example, deny the premium model at 80 percent and the mid-tier model at 100 percent, while never denying the low-cost model. Only the management account can apply SCPs, and from the management account you can apply an SCP to another account. Considerations AWS Budgets is not near-real-time: Budget data refreshes up to three times a day, so spend can overshoot a threshold before the action runs. Cost allocation tags are not retroactive: Expect up to 24 hours for a newly applied tag key to appear, then up to another 24 hours after you activate it before it begins populating billing data. CUR does not contain per-request line items: Both classic CUR and CUR 2.0 aggregate Amazon Bedrock cost by usage type, operation, and pricing/resource attributes over an hour or a day. IAM principal fields require CUR 2.0: The legacy CUR format does not include them. Per-token cost breakdowns are available in both formats. Session tags are bound at AssumeRole time, not per request. Their values are constant for every call made with that session’s credentials, and they surface only as aggregated billing data. Session tags are not written to model invocation logs. Logs capture the caller’s identity.arn. To distinguish users on a shared session at the request level, use a per-user RoleSessionName, or set the user in request metadata on each call. Budget actions attach to IAM users, groups, and roles. If your users are federated and have no standing IAM identity, the action needs a role to target. This is why the pattern works best when each person or application has its own role. If your users share a role or are federated without their own role, see our previous post for a per-user enforcement approach. A shared gateway role collapses attribution by default. With a large language model (LLM) gateway, the identity captured is the gateway’s execution role. New models need attention. Usage types are model-specific. When you enable a new model, confirm it appears in your queries and budget filters as expected rather than assuming it is covered. Decision framework Requirement Recommended path Quick reporting Cost Explorer grouped by identity Per-team reporting Cost Explorer with activated tags (Steps 1, 2, and 4) Detailed line-item analysis CUR 2.0 export (Steps 1 through 4) Enforcement AWS Budgets with budget actions (Steps 1 and 5) Cleanup To avoid ongoing charges, delete all the resources you created. Conclusion In this post, you learned how to get per-identity Amazon Bedrock cost visibility and enforceable spend limits using only AWS-native features, with no application code to write for the common case. As generative AI adoption scales, the organizations that win will be the ones that can answer the tokenomics question with confidence: what do we spend per person or per team, can we cap it, and how much work does it take to get there. Now, it’s your turn to start exploring. We are here to help, and if you need further assistance, reach out to AWS Support and your AWS account team. About the author Arun Chandapillai Arun is a Senior Cloud Architect passionate about helping customers accelerate IT modernization through business-first cloud adoption strategies. He specializes in building and deploying AI and Generative AI solutions, from agentic workflows to production-ready applications, on AWS. Arun is an automotive enthusiast and avid speaker who is passionate about giving back and believes ‘you get back what you give.’ Cami Persson Cami is a Principal Account Manager at AWS, partnering with Independent Software Vendors to drive value creation through cloud adoption and AI integration. She focuses on accelerating partners’ revenue growth and platform modernization at scale. Based in Minneapolis, Cami resides with her husband. Aditya Mettu Aditya is a Technical Account Manager at AWS, supporting Independent Software Vendor (ISV) customers. He helps engineering teams run generative AI on AWS reliably and cost-effectively, with a focus on AI FinOps: cost visibility, governance, and optimization for services such as Amazon Bedrock. He enjoys turning cloud spend data into practical guardrails that let teams scale AI adoption without runaway costs. Andre Bernardo Andre is a builder at the intersection of Cloud Infrastructure, FinOps, and AI design, specializing in systems that scale cleanly and stay out of the engineer’s way. He builds the cloud automation and generative AI platform that lets Jamf adopt AI safely, without slowing teams down. He combines a background in finance, economics, and data science with cloud engineering expertise to help teams understand, control, and optimize the cost of AWS and Generative AI workloads. items.title: vercel-labs/agent-browser
items.summary: Browser automation CLI for AI agents https://agent-browser.dev agent-browser Browser automation for AI agents: open pages, read them as an accessibility tree, and act on elements from the shell. agent-browser is a native Rust CLI that gives an AI agent a browser it can drive one command at a time. snapshot returns the page as compact text with a ref such as @e1 for each element. The agent acts on a ref, reads the page again to check the result, and repeats. The browser stays open between commands, so each step is one short shell call. Install npm install -g agent-browser agent-browser install # download Chrome for Testing (first time only) Homebrew: brew install agent-browser, then agent-browser install. Linux: agent-browser install --with-deps also installs the browser's system libraries. No install: npx agent-browser open example.com. Project installs, building from source, upgrade, and doctor are covered in Installation. Quick start agent-browser open example.com agent-browser snapshot -i # interactive elements, each with a ref agent-browser click @e1 # act on a ref from that snapshot agent-browser get url # check the result agent-browser close The snapshot for example.com: - link "Learn more" [ref=e1] Refs describe the page at the time of the snapshot. After navigation or a DOM change, take a new snapshot before using refs again. CSS selectors, text, XPath, and semantic locators also work, for example agent-browser find role button click --name "Submit". See Selectors. A click fails, instead of reporting success, when the target is hidden, disabled, outside the viewport, or covered by another element such as a consent banner. Dismiss the covering element, take a new snapshot, and retry. The full walkthrough is in the quick start. How it works The CLI sends each command to a background daemon that starts on the first command and controls the browser over the Chrome DevTools Protocol. Each --session gets its own daemon and browser. By default, the daemon closes a headless browser and exits after one hour without commands, saving state first when session persistence is configured. Chrome for Testing is the default browser. You can also attach to a running Chrome with --cdp or --auto-connect (CDP mode), select the Lightpanda or Obscura engine with --engine, drive Mobile Safari in the iOS Simulator, or use a cloud browser provider such as Browserbase, Browserless, Browser Use, Kernel, or AgentCore. For AI agents The CLI ships skills that match its version: agent-browser skills get core # the core loop, refs, waiting, and common workflows agent-browser skills get core --ref commands # one reference, such as the full command list agent-browser skills get core --full # adds the full command reference and templates agent-browser skills list # specialized skills: electron, slack, dogfood, and more Install the discovery skill into an agent harness from skills.sh: npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-browser The installed skill is a thin stub that tells the agent to load agent-browser skills get core, so its instructions always match the installed CLI. Or add this to your AGENTS.md: Use `agent-browser` for browser automation. Before the first use, run `agent-browser skills get core` and follow it. For MCP clients, agent-browser mcp starts an MCP server over stdio. See MCP server. Commands Run agent-browser --help for the full list, or agent-browser <command> --help for one command. Group Commands Docs Navigate and read open, back, forward, reload, read, snapshot, get, is Core, Snapshots Interact click, dblclick, fill, type, press, keyboard, hover, focus, select, check, uncheck, scroll, drag, upload, mouse, find Core, Find elements Wait wait Wait Capture screenshot, pdf, record, download, diff Recording, Diffing, Files Page and network state cookies, storage, network, set, clipboard, eval, pushstate Network, Settings Tabs, frames, and dialogs tab, frame, dialog Tabs and frames Debug and performance console, errors, highlight, inspect, trace, profiler, vitals, react, a11y Debugging, Profiler, React Sessions and auth session, state, auth, profiles, confirm, deny Sessions, Security Agents and integrations skills, mcp, webmcp, flow, chat, batch, plugin Skills, WebMCP, Plugins Observe stream, dashboard Streaming, Dashboard Setup install, upgrade, doctor, connect, close Installation Flags, environment variables, and agent-browser.json are documented in Configuration. Platforms Native binaries ship for macOS (ARM64, x64), Linux (ARM64, x64, glibc and musl), and Windows (x64). The npm package picks the right binary for the host. Development Building from source requires Node.js 24 or later, pnpm 11 or later, and Rust: pnpm install pnpm build:source # builds the dashboard and the native CLI pnpm link --global agent-browser install Run the Rust checks from cli/: cargo fmt -- --check cargo clippy cargo test cargo test e2e -- --ignored --test-threads=1 # launches real headless Chrome AGENTS.md lists the files to update with each change, the docs checks, and the release process. Documentation agent-browser.dev: introduction, guides, and reference Commands and Configuration Security: the auth vault, domain allowlists, action policies, and content boundaries Next.js and Vercel and eve: running agent-browser in Vercel Sandbox and eve agents Changelog License Apache-2.0

items.title: we-promise/sure
items.summary: The personal finance app for everyone (by everyone) https://sure.am Deutsch | Español | Français | 日本語 | 한국어 | Português | Русский | 中文 Sure: The personal finance app for everyone Get involved: Discord • Website • Issues Important This repository is a community fork of the now-abandoned Maybe Finance project. Learn more in their final release doc. Backstory The Maybe Finance (archived/abandoned repo) team spent most of 2021–2022 building a full-featured personal finance and wealth management app. It even included an “Ask an Advisor” feature that connected users with a real CFP/CFA — all included with your subscription. The business end of things didn't work out, and so they stopped developing the app in mid-2023. After spending nearly $1 million on development (employees, contractors, data providers, infra, etc.), the team open-sourced the app. Their goal was to let users self-host it for free — and eventually launch a hosted version for a small fee. They actually did launch that hosted version … briefly. That also didn’t work out — at least not as a sustainable B2C business — so now here we are: hosting a community-maintained fork to keep the codebase alive and see where this can go next. Join us! Hosting Sure Sure is a fully working personal finance app that can be self hosted with Docker. Sure can be accessed from a browser, the macOS desktop app, the mobile app, API clients, and LLM agents. See Sure Clients for an overview. Forking and Attribution This repo is a community fork of the archived Maybe Finance repo. You’re free to fork it under the AGPLv3 license — but we’d love it if you stuck around and contributed here instead. To stay compliant and avoid trademark issues: Be sure to include the original AGPLv3 license and clearly state in your README that your fork is based on Maybe Finance but is not affiliated with or endorsed by Maybe Finance Inc. "Maybe" is a trademark of Maybe Finance Inc. and therefore, use of it is NOT allowed in forked repositories (or the logo) Performance Issues With data-heavy apps, inevitably, there are performance issues. We've set up a public dashboard showing the problematic requests seen on the demo site, along with the stacktraces to help debug them. https://www.skylight.io/app/applications/s6PEZSKwcklL/recent/6h/endpoints Any contributions that help improve performance are very much welcome. Local Development Setup If you are trying to self-host the app, read this guide to get started. The instructions below are for developers to get started with contributing to the app. Requirements See .ruby-version file for required Ruby version PostgreSQL >9.3 (latest stable version recommended) Redis > 5.4 (latest stable version recommended) Getting Started cd sure cp .env.local.example .env.local bin/setup bin/dev # Optionally, load demo data rake demo_data:default Visit http://localhost:3000 to view the app. If you loaded the optional demo data, log in with these credentials: Email: user@example.com Password: Password1! For further instructions, see guides below. Setup Guides Mac dev setup Linux dev setup Windows dev setup Dev containers - visit this guide One-click Install Render expects each button target branch to have a render.yaml at the repository root. The branch-ready Blueprint files live in branches/<branch-name>/render.yaml in a separate repo and can be copied to each corresponding branch root. Option What it deploys latest stable Sure - No AI Sure web, Sidekiq worker, Render Postgres, and Render Key Value. AI tokens are intentionally blank. Sure - Simple AI Sure with OpenAI-backed AI settings, pgvector-ready Postgres, Sidekiq, and Render Key Value. Render prompts for the OpenAI token. Sure - External AI Sure with external assistant settings plus AlphaClaw, which manages the OpenClaw gateway on Render. License and Trademarks Maybe and Sure are both distributed under an AGPLv3 license. "Maybe" is a trademark of Maybe Finance, Inc. "Sure" is not, and refers to this community fork.

items.title: WhiteTowerAI/ohmygame
items.summary: The open-source studio for making games with AI. Your own one-person game studio. Everything you need to make games with AI, in one app. Game canvas. Bring your own key. https://ohmygame.ai/ The open-source studio for making games with AI. English | 简体中文 | 日本語 Website · Docs · Community games · Changelog Describe a game, and the agent designs it, makes the art, writes the code, plays it to check it works, and publishes it to a link anyone can open. Design docs, images, video, 3D, and audio live on one canvas next to the code, instead of across five different apps. Note OhMyGame is in beta. Expect rough edges, and tell us what breaks. Download Platform Download macOS (Apple silicon) OhMyGame for Mac Windows (x64) OhMyGame for Windows Older builds and release notes are on Releases. The Windows build isn't code-signed yet, so SmartScreen may warn on first install. Intel Mac and Linux are on the roadmap. OhMyGame ships without a model. On first launch, connect a provider or a coding agent you already use: first run. Features Let the agent build the game. The agent drafts the design doc, writes the code, runs the game in a live preview, then plays it and tries a fix when something breaks. One canvas for every asset. Generate images, video, 3D models, animation, voices, sound effects, and music with AI, and keep them organized on one canvas, ready to use in your game. Publish to a link. Anyone can play it in the browser, and it shows up in the Community. A multiplayer game's rooms, and its players' sign-in, saves, and leaderboards, come with it. Extend it with plugins. A plugin can teach the agent new skills, give it new tools, and add panels and project types to the app. Bundled plugins cover Godot, Unity, Unreal Engine, Blender, Aseprite, Tiled, and platforms like WeChat and Douyin Mini Games. Or make your own. Bring your own agent. Run OhMyGame on Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode, or on any of 40+ model providers with your own keys. No per-run credits. It works the other way too: use the canvas, media generation, and playtesting from your agent over MCP. Models · External agents What you can make Three games our team made with OhMyGame: Interactive film Island builder Deckbuilding roguelike Web games (Phaser, Three.js, React Three Fiber) are the best place to start. Interactive stories cover visual novels, interactive films, and story games. General games work with any engine or stack. Web games can be multiplayer, from board and card games to realtime arenas, played online with friends with no server of your own. See Multiplayer. Play what others made. Documentation Guides for using OhMyGame are at ohmygame.ai/docs: install, first run, models, and plugins. Technical references live in this repo under docs/, such as the runtime, coding agents, custom models, and the plugin contract. Build from source Requires Bun 1.4.2+ and Node.js 22.19+. git clone https://github.com/WhiteTowerAI/ohmygame.git cd ohmygame bun install --frozen-lockfile bun run dev # web renderer + local daemon bun run dev:desktop # or the Electron app Builds from source send no telemetry. For branches, checks, and optional cloud setup, see CONTRIBUTING.md. Privacy Your projects and API keys stay on your machine, and prompts go straight to the providers you choose. You only need an account to publish. Release builds send usage data and crash reports, which you can turn off in Settings → About. See logs and diagnostics. Contributing Issues and pull requests are welcome. Branch from dev and open PRs against dev; main holds releases. Read CONTRIBUTING.md, pick up a help wanted issue, and report security problems privately through SECURITY.md. Community Discord · QQ group 460706923 · Issues Star History License Apache-2.0.
