items.title: HCRS@WWW 2027 征稿｜当推荐系统遇上 AI Agent，如何坚持「以人为本」？
items.summary: 原创 快手技术 2026-11-11 19:51 北京 第三届以人为本推荐系统 Workshop（HCRS@WWW 2027）正式征稿！ 从看到一条视频、学习新知识，到做出一次消费决策，推荐系统正在影响人们获取信息与做出选择的方式。随着生成式 AI 与智能体（AI Agent）的发展，推荐系统也在发生变化：Agent 可以理解用户目标、保留交互记忆、调用工具，并通过多步行动协助完成任务；智能体工作流则开始参与推荐模型的修改、评估与部署。 当推荐从一次排序走向持续协作，“以人为本”也有了新的研究命题：Agent 究竟在为谁的目标服务？用户能否理解、检查和纠正它的行为？系统在持续演进的过程中，能否真正创造长期价值？ 围绕这些问题，第三届以人为本推荐系统 Workshop（HCRS@WWW 2027）正式征稿，诚邀推荐系统、信息检索、人机交互、负责任 AI、社会计算等领域的研究者与技术实践者参与，共同探索 Agent 时代人本推荐的新方法、评估体系与保障机制。 继 WWW 2025、WWW 2026 两届研讨会之后，以人为本推荐系统 Workshop 将迎来第三届，持续汇聚相关领域的研究者与技术实践者，推动跨学科交流与长期合作。本届 HCRS@WWW 2027 由来自快手、中国人民大学、中国科学院计算技术研究所、复旦大学、莱顿大学、香港浸会大学、中国科学院大学的研究者共同组织。Workshop 将于 The Web Conference 2027 大会期间（2027 年 5 月 10—11 日），在爱尔兰都柏林线下举办，具体日期待后续公布。 从工业实践出发，快手在短视频、搜索、电商等多个场景相继研发并部署高性能生成式推荐大模型和 Agentic 解决方案，近年来形成了 OneRec 系列、GoalRank、AgentX、PlatformBid 等代表性研究与实践成果。这些工业实践也带来了新的研究命题：当推荐系统更加智能、具备更强的自主行动能力时，如何保障用户的控制权、持续对齐人的意图，并创造长期价值？带着这些来自真实业务场景的问题，快手消费策略算法部连续三届参与组织 HCRS@WWW，并积极支持相关方向的高校合作研究与学术社区建设，推动工业实践与学术研究相互启发，共同探索“以人为本”推荐系统的设计与评估方法。 本届 Workshop 围绕「Agent 时代如何让推荐系统更好地服务于人」这一核心问题，聚焦主体性、对齐与长期价值三大主题，进一步推动推荐系统、人机交互与 AI 安全等领域的交流，探索如何将技术进展转化为对用户、创作者和社区的实际价值。活动将设置主题报告（Keynote）、论文口头报告、海报（Poster）交流与最佳论文颁奖环节，为学界与工业界搭建分享研究成果、交流实践经验与探索合作的平台。 主题报告嘉宾（Keynote Speakers）： Maarten de Rijke（意向确认）：阿姆斯特丹大学人工智能与信息检索杰出教授，ACM Fellow、荷兰皇家艺术与科学院院士。 Yupeng Hou（已确认）：Google DeepMind 研究科学家，主要研究方向为生成式推荐与大语言模型（LLM），研究成果发表于 ICML、KDD、WWW 等国际学术会议。 *嘉宾出席情况及报告安排以研讨会官网最终公布的信息为准。 「投稿征集」 我们欢迎围绕以下三大主题、立足具体推荐场景提交研究成果，包括实证研究、理论研究、观点论文，以及系统演示、数据集和用户研究等贡献。录用论文将以口头报告或海报形式在 Workshop 展示，并参与 Best Paper Award（最佳论文奖）评选。 1. Agency（主体性） 人如何掌控目标与授权。面向发现与决策支持的个人 Agent；目标表达与修正；混合主动交互；用户对记忆、工具、数据、权限的控制；同意与纠正机制；平台准入与用户选择。 2. Alignment（对齐） 系统如何对齐人的意图与价值。模糊、冲突、漂移下的偏好获取；人类与 Agent 反馈；奖励模型；推荐系统开发部署中的可验证 Agent 机制；用户与 Agent 记忆的溯源与污染；Reward Hacking 与能力漂移；可复现性；公平性审计和可信推荐。 3. Long-term Value（长期价值） 超越单步相关性与短期参与。长时程用户建模；满意度、学习、福祉、自主性；延迟反馈；对用户、创作者、社区的长期影响；仿真与纵向评估；操纵与依赖；信息茧房与伤害。 「重要日期」 *相关截止时间均采用 AoE（UTC−12）；线下活动时间以最终议程为准。 投稿截止：2027 年 1 月 4 日 录用通知：2027 年 2 月 1 日 终稿提交（Camera-ready）：2027 年 2 月 16 日 Workshop 举办：2027 年 5 月 10—11 日期间，具体日期待公布 「投稿与参与方式」 HCRS@WWW 2027：https://hcrs2027.github.io 征稿详情：https://hcrs2027.github.io/cfp.html 论文投稿：https://openreview.net/group?id=ACM.org/TheWebConf/2027/Workshop/HCRS 评审委员申请：https://forms.gle/R6ki6u9gVDY7yGQE7 在 Agent 加速融入推荐系统的背景下，如何保障用户的自主性、让系统持续对齐人的意图，并创造可衡量的长期价值，值得学界与工业界共同探索。我们期待通过 HCRS，让更多研究问题得到深入讨论，让前沿方法与真实场景相互启发。 欢迎投稿、参与交流，期待在都柏林与你相聚，共同推动推荐技术更好地服务于人！若你对快手在相关领域的工作和团队感兴趣，也欢迎加入我们！ 团队介绍 消费策略算法部是负责快手短视频推荐的核心算法团队，致力于用强化学习、因果推断、增益模型、跨域学习、元学习、图模型、运筹优化、博弈机制、端上智能等前沿技术持续优化用户的内容消费体验，提升用户对平台粘性和大盘 DAU，不断改进冷启动和大盘流量分配机制，促进社区生态的长期繁荣与多种营收指标共同提升。 团队负责场景覆盖快手单列、双列、关注、同城等核心页面。技术成果在KDD/SIGIR/WWW/NeurIPS/ICLR/WSDM/CIKM 等顶会上发表，并获得 CIKM Best Paper 和SIGIR Best Paper Award Honorable Mention。 成员多来自国内外顶尖高校硕博毕业，很多有国内外头部大厂核心团队经历，不乏头顶快Star/阿里星/天才少年/ACM 金牌等光环者，同时团队积累了业内领先的人才和充足的算力，期待加入一起探索AI时代的新推荐系统。 岗位介绍 职位名称 大模型Agent算法工程师-短视频推荐方向 推荐算法工程师-【主APP】 推荐算法工程师-【极速版单列推荐】 推荐算法工程师-【内容生态算法】 推荐算法工程师-【多业务混排】 推荐算法工程师-【创新孵化&评论生态】 推荐算法工程师 -【日常实习】 职位描述 负责短视频推荐场景算法迭代与大模型Agent能力建设，优化推荐召回、排序、重排全链路，探索生成式推荐、模型Scaling、用户长序列建模等技术，落地LLM智能推荐新范式； 打造具备自主规划（Planning）、工具调用（Tool Use）、长短期记忆（Memory）、多 Agent 协同（Multi-Agent）等能力的智能推荐 Agent； 结合大语言模型、多模态模型与传统推荐算法，完成用户理解、内容理解、个性化策略生成，提升推荐精准度、用户体验与内容生态质量； 探索Agent在推荐场景的落地应用，覆盖内容消费、策略优化、实验迭代、算法辅助研发等场景，推动传统模型推荐向Agent智能推荐升级； 基于用户行为与多模态数据，研究大模型与推荐模型的融合方案，包括表征学习、奖励建模、强化学习优化，持续提升时长、留存、互动、VV等核心指标； 跟进Agent、大模型、强化学习、世界模型等前沿技术，结合短视频业务完成技术验证、方案迭代与线上落地。 加入我们，你将获得 探索推荐系统的下一代技术范式：从传统推荐模型迈向 Agent 驱动的智能推荐，参与行业前沿技术创新； 拥有丰富的真实业务场景： 面向亿级用户、千万级创作者及海量内容，在真实推荐场景中验证和迭代 Agent 能力； 充足的数据与算力资源：依托大规模推荐系统和大模型基础设施，探索 LLM、Agent 与推荐融合的最佳实践； 技术成长空间广阔：深度参与大模型、推荐系统、强化学习、多模态、Agent 等多个热点方向，推动科研成果快速转化为业务价值。 投递方式 扫描下方二维码投递，或投递简历至邮箱：chenyuxi09@kuaishou.com 👇 点击【阅读原文】，即可投稿！ 阅读原文 跳转微信打开

items.title: How DXC Technology built a multi-model AI substrate on Amazon Bedrock
items.summary: This post is co-written with Nick Tamburro of DXC Technology. When an AI agent can act on a production server at a bank or a hospital, access to a capable foundation model is only the starting point. Recent public incidents, in which autonomous agents took destructive actions their operators never intended, show that the real risk is rarely the model alone. It’s an agent holding more authority than its task requires, with nothing in the architecture to stop it. Avoiding that starts with a substrate that governs model access at the infrastructure level. Amazon Bedrock provides that substrate. Through a single managed interface, it gives DXC OASIS access to multiple foundation models: Anthropic Claude, Amazon Nova, Meta Llama, and open-weight families. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails enforce content filtering, personally identifiable information (PII) redaction, and denied-topic policies uniformly across every model. AWS PrivateLink keeps inference traffic within the customer’s virtual private cloud (VPC), and serverless scaling avoids self-managed GPU infrastructure as a failure point. Because these are system-level controls rather than bolt-ons, they gave DXC Technology a governed foundation for what no model layer can deliver on its own: a trusted harness that orchestrates, governs, and audits AI agents across enterprise IT operations at scale. Model availability varies by AWS Region. See Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock. DXC Technology runs managed IT services for some of the world’s most regulated organizations: banks, hospitals, and government agencies. With more than 115,000 employees across 70 countries, DXC operates mission-critical systems where resilience and governance are non-negotiable. When DXC set out to build DXC OASIS, the harness for mission-critical IT operations, the team separated the problem into two layers. The first is a governed model substrate built on Amazon Bedrock. The second is the trusted harness built on top: DXC’s own orchestration, governance, and assurance layer. In this post, we explore how DXC built the resilient, flexible model substrate beneath DXC OASIS on Amazon Bedrock. We also show where DXC drew the line between what the substrate provides and what the harness must provide. Since general availability in March 2026, DXC OASIS has reduced resolution time by 95% on average across 56 measured use cases. Across every model, customer data stays within the AWS data boundary: prompts and completions are not shared with third-party model providers and are not used to train the underlying foundation models. “Our customers operate complex, business-critical environments and need both choice and resilience in how they adopt AI. Amazon Bedrock provides access to a broad ecosystem of models with the governance, security, and operational controls required at enterprise scale. That flexibility allows us to use the right model for the right task, adapt as technology evolves, and stay focused on delivering measurable business outcomes for our customers.” — Dan Gray, President, GIS, DXC Technology Solution overview DXC OASIS separates the question of which model from the question of how work gets done. Amazon Bedrock is the substrate: a governed gateway to foundation models (FMs), reachable through one consistent API, with security and networking controls that keep traffic inside the AWS perimeter. The harness is everything DXC builds on top: orchestration across tools and systems, operational context drawn from 60 years of runbooks and escalation logic, policy enforcement, human-oversight gates, and full auditability of every agent action. The design goals were: Resilience: No single point of failure at the model layer. Flexibility: Route each task to the most appropriate model on cost, latency, and capability. Regulatory sovereignty: Meet the data-handling expectations of regulated tenants. Safety by design: Bound what every agent can do, so that no action with operational impact runs without policy checks and, where required, human approval. The main risk DXC designed against was coupling the system to any single provider, framework, or deployment target. The following diagram shows the key AWS services in the DXC DXC OASIS architecture. Engineers and operators reach the system through Amazon Route 53 and an Application Load Balancer inside the customer’s Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC). The DXC OASIS agent runtime runs on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) in a private subnet. There, a supervisor agent delegates to capability agents that draw on a knowledge base, AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon EventBridge, and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). Every model call leaves the subnet through a VPC interface endpoint and AWS PrivateLink to reach Amazon Bedrock, so inference traffic doesn’t traverse the public internet. AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM), AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS), TLS 1.2, Amazon CloudWatch, VPC Flow Logs, AWS CloudTrail, and OpenTelemetry provide security and observability across every layer. Figure 1: The DXC OASIS architecture on AWS Building the DXC OASIS substrate DXC began building DXC OASIS as a prototype in early 2025. A cross-functional team reached general availability in March 2026, scaling toward 130 customer environments on Amazon EKS with per-tenant namespaces and GitOps rollout. Building the substrate involved the following tasks: Establish governed, multi-model access through Amazon Bedrock. Engineer resilience into every layer of the architecture. Route each workload to the most appropriate model. Draw the line between the substrate and the harness. Establish governed, multi-model access through Amazon Bedrock Every model DXC OASIS uses (Anthropic Claude, Amazon Nova, Meta Llama, and open-weight families) is reached through Amazon Bedrock model inference. A provider outage or deprecation therefore becomes a routing decision, not a system rebuild. Uniform access isn’t the same as uniform behavior, however: models differ in capability, response style, and failure modes. Substituting one model for another is an assurance activity as much as a routing change. Before a model enters production routing, the harness (not the API) evaluates it against DXC OASIS task suites. For more information, see Getting started with Amazon Bedrock. Engineer resilience into every layer Resilience in DXC OASIS isn’t one control but the compounding of several. The following table summarizes the resilience controls and what each does for DXC OASIS. Resilience control What it does for DXC OASIS No single-provider dependency Every model is reached through Amazon Bedrock model inference. A provider outage or deprecation is a routing decision rather than a system rebuild, with the harness assuring behavioral differences between models before a switch goes live. Serverless model layer Amazon Bedrock is serverless and the Amazon EKS control plane is AWS managed, removing single points of failure. Scope-of-impact containment Amazon Bedrock Guardrails apply content filters, denied topics, PII filters, and contextual controls consistently regardless of model, containing the scope of any single failure. Private, encrypted paths Amazon VPC and AWS PrivateLink keep model traffic off the public internet. TLS 1.2 in transit and AWS KMS at rest protect data. Elastic capacity Amazon EKS autoscaling with per-tenant namespaces makes onboarding a new tenant a capacity-planning exercise. Beyond resilience, DXC OASIS also addresses data residency and sovereignty. Regional inference controls and AWS PrivateLink keep inference within approved AWS Regions and off the public internet, meeting the data-handling expectations of regulated tenants. Route each workload to the most appropriate model The strategic reason DXC built on Amazon Bedrock is optionality. Because every model sits behind the same API, the team routes each task to the most appropriate model on cost, latency, and capability, and adopts new frontier models as they arrive without re-plumbing the system. Model choice as a workload decision Each task’s capability, latency, and cost requirements determine which model it uses, not system constraints. Intelligent prompt routing – A single serverless endpoint predicts response quality and routes requests between models in the same family. It sends simpler prompts to lower-cost models and complex reasoning to more capable ones. Prompt caching further cuts latency and cost. For more information, see Intelligent prompt routing in the Amazon Bedrock documentation. Custom model import – With Custom Model Import, the same governance and tooling extend to models that DXC or its clients bring themselves. Open and closed models together Amazon Bedrock supports open-weight models alongside proprietary ones, so DXC pairs frontier reasoning with open-weight models a client can adapt and deploy under one set of guardrails. Draw the line between the substrate and the harness Every enterprise agent needs six capabilities. Some are substrate capabilities Amazon Bedrock provides directly. Others are things only the harness can provide because they depend on DXC’s operational context and accountability model. This boundary is also where agent safety is won or lost. Guardrails on model inputs and outputs are necessary, but only the harness can limit what an agent is allowed to do. The following table draws that line. Capability What Bedrock provides What the harness adds Orchestration A foundational service layer the harness calls, wraps, or extends. Supervisor and capability-agent delegation across tools, systems, and multi-step workflows, built on the open source LangGraph runtime. Context Knowledge-base infrastructure and prompt caching for retrieval. 60 years of runbooks, escalation logic, and live IT service management (ITSM) data. Governance AWS IAM, regional inference controls, and tenant-isolated model access. Per-request policy enforcement, persona-based authorization, and field-level constraints. Guardrails Amazon Bedrock Guardrails: content filters, denied topics, PII filters. Operational-policy enforcement above the substrate filters: tiered knowledge hierarchy, scoped and auditable agent roles, and customer-specific rules on what an agent can act on. Human oversight Not a substrate function. Four authority tiers (observe, propose, act with approval, act within scope), with every persona starting read-only, plus approval gates and escalation paths. Assurance Encryption, auditable infrastructure, and VPC Flow Logs. OpenTelemetry traces for every action, each with a unique execution ID, giving end-to-end traceability from intent to action. How a workload flows through DXC OASIS To make the architecture concrete, the following use cases come from the DXC OASIS demo environment. The environment is built around AnyCompany Airlines, a fictional mid-sized airline running a hybrid on-premises and AWS estate. Incident resolution: Diagnose and fix an at-risk production server, from alert to resolution in under 10 minutes. Problem management: The ITSM agent ranks the top five incident categories and suggests how to reduce each, work that takes 2–3 hours by hand. Cloud cost analysis: For the AWS cloud engineer, the Metrics agent breaks down a 90-day cost trend by service and region, then investigates spending peaks on request. The incident-resolution workflow shows how the substrate and the harness work together: Alert in business terms – A runbook fails to clear disk space on the FlightOps server. The CIO sees the alert as a business risk: Flight Operations scheduling might be affected within 4 hours. At the same moment, the Linux engineer sees the same alert with the technical detail needed to act. Plan and delegate – The engineer opens AI Assist from the dashboard widget, and the metric carries into the chat as context. A supervisor agent breaks the request into a plan and delegates to capability agents (DXC OASIS Metrics, Linux System, and ITSM), with every model call made through Amazon Bedrock. Grounded diagnosis – The DXC OASIS Metrics agent confirms the server is 99% full and cites the knowledge base articles behind its answer. The Linux System agent traces the problem to a single 5 GB temporary file. Human approval – The agent presents its full execution plan, and nothing runs until the engineer confirms it. In this workflow, the agent operates at the act-with-approval tier: it can diagnose freely, but it can’t change the production server without an explicit, recorded approval. Governed execution – The fix runs, and DXC OASIS records what ran, on which server, who approved it, and when. The audit trail comes from the harness, not from the agent’s own account of what it did. Learn and observe – The engineer can turn the conversation into a draft knowledge article. The Query Metrics view shows the agent timeline, delegation flow, and token usage behind the answer. Results Since reaching general availability in March 2026, DXC OASIS agents now serve 12 operational personas, spanning Linux, Windows, SAP, virtualization, backup and patching, AWS, Azure, and network operations. Across 56 measured use cases, DXC OASIS has reduced resolution time by 95 percent on average. The following table shows representative measurements. Task Before After Time saved Filesystem incident 53–90 mins 3–6 mins ~89–97% Database performance incident 2–3 hours 5–12 mins ~90–97% Cloud policy validation 4–8 hours 15–30 mins ~88–97% Patching validation 45–90 mins 5–10 mins ~85–90% Complex problem management 2–6 days 8–10 mins ~99% Diagnostic accuracy is 92% or better, validated against senior engineer judgment. Lessons learned and what comes next Four architectural decisions proved most valuable: Separate model choice from orchestration By keeping model selection, orchestration framework, and deployment target as independent decisions, DXC avoids re-platforming when a layer evolves. Compound resilience controls No single control makes the system resilient. The combination of serverless infrastructure, guardrails at the model layer, private networking, and human-oversight gates creates defense in depth. Draw the substrate-harness line explicitly Clarity about what the cloud provides versus what you must build avoids both under-engineering (trusting the model to govern itself) and over-engineering (rebuilding capabilities the substrate already offers). Bound autonomy before you scale it. Every DXC OASIS persona starts read-only, and broader authority is granted deliberately, one tier at a time. Treating autonomy as something granted per task, rather than a default, is what lets DXC put agents in front of production systems with confidence. Bound autonomy before you scale it Every DXC OASIS persona starts read-only and broader authority is granted deliberately, one tier at a time. Treating autonomy as something granted per task, rather than a default, is what lets DXC put agents in front of production systems with confidence. Looking ahead, DXC is evaluating Amazon Bedrock AgentCore alongside the current orchestration layer, and expanding the system to support additional regulated workloads as new frontier models become available through Amazon Bedrock. Conclusion In this post, we showed how DXC Technology built DXC OASIS, the harness for mission-critical IT operations, on a governed, multi-model substrate in Amazon Bedrock. Keeping model reasoning separate from operational orchestration builds resilience, flexibility, and regulatory compliance into the architecture from the start. The payoff is measurable: resolution time is down 95 percent on average across 56 measured use cases. For teams building their own agentic systems, the lesson is to treat the substrate (what Amazon Bedrock provides) and the harness (what you build on top) as separate layers. Decide early which capabilities belong in each. As scrutiny of autonomous AI grows, that clear line, together with bounded, auditable agent authority, is what lets a system earn trust at scale. To get started with multi-model architectures on Amazon Bedrock, see the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. To learn more about how DXC OASIS applies this architecture to enterprise IT operations, contact DXC Technology. Related resources Amazon Bedrock User Guide Amazon Bedrock Guardrails documentation AWS PrivateLink documentation DXC OASIS About the authors Nick Tamburro Nick is the DXC OASIS Chief Architect at DXC Technology, where he leads architecture and engineering for the DXC OASIS platform. He focuses on bringing governed, multi-model AI to mission-critical IT operations for regulated enterprises. Asif Fouzi Asif is a Principal Solutions Architect at AWS who helps Global System Integrators (GSIs) such as DXC evolve their businesses using the latest advances in technology. When he isn’t innovating on behalf of customers, he likes to play guitar, travel and spend time with his family.

items.title: ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in October 2026
items.summary: At AWS, we believe AI builders should be able to choose the right model for every task, trust their agents in production, and see clearly what their AI workloads cost. That belief guides how we invest across our portfolio. Amazon Bedrock gives you access to leading models and the tools to build and scale AI applications securely. We extend this foundation with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which provides the platform to build, connect, and optimize agents using any model and any framework. That includes Strands, our open source agent development toolkit. Together, they take you from first prototype to production. As agents move into core business workflows, the bar rises. You need the flexibility to use different models as tasks, budgets, and latency targets change. When a primary model is throttled or unreachable, your agents must keep working. They also must act within limits you set and return output other software can use as is. Their answers must stay grounded in sources you allow, and their cost must hold up at high volume. What we shipped in October addresses each of these needs. New models help you match each task to the right price and speed, from high-volume subagents to real-time voice. Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore updates keep agents available, hold them to the processes you define, and help you trust what they return. New pricing and cost reporting make spend more predictable. Strands adds new ways to build, contain, and test agents. Match the model to the task on Amazon Bedrock Run fast, low-cost subagents. Claude Haiku 5.5 is built for subagents and high-volume, cost-sensitive work. According to Anthropic, it is the most capable Haiku yet and costs around 75 percent less than Claude Haiku 4.5 for most tasks. It is also the first Haiku with effort controls, so you can tune cost against intelligence for each task. In a multi-agent setup, a model such as Claude Opus 5.5 can plan the work and hand well-defined coding, tool use, and browser automation tasks to Haiku. This keeps running many agents in parallel affordable. Get near-flagship results at a lower price. OpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock. On OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam evaluation, it performed on par with GPT-6 Astra and completed tasks more than three times faster than GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. Its input and output token prices are at least 50 percent lower than those of GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra. It accepts text and images with up to 1 million input tokens, which suits drafting proposals, interpreting technical drawings, and building agents that work across business systems. For latency-sensitive work such as real-time coding assistants, GPT-6.1 Sol now also offers Ultrafast mode. Build voice agents that reason in real time. Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic, our latest speech-to-speech model, improves reasoning, instruction following, and tool-calling accuracy, with lower latency at the same price as Amazon Nova 2 Sonic. A customer service agent can now look up an order, check return eligibility, and start a return in a single conversation. Pick specialized models for coding and video. GLM 5.3 by Z.ai is an open-weight model for agentic coding and long-horizon software engineering, with a 1-million-token context window and prompt caching, available to eligible enterprise customers. TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 turns entire videos into structured, time-coded metadata. It reads visuals, audio, and on-screen text in a single pass, with no separate ingestion pipeline. Use more models in AWS GovCloud (US). Claude Haiku 5.5 and OpenAI GPT-5.6 models with cross-Region inference are now available in AWS GovCloud (US). Daybreak Red from OpenAI, a model for authorized security work, is available to eligible customers in AWS GovCloud (US-East). Regulated teams get more models while maintaining US data sovereignty. Build and run agents you can rely on Build and operate agents from your terminal. AgentCore CLI, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is now generally available in version 1.0. We rebuilt it with faster startup, a consistent command structure, and support for more AgentCore resources. You can work with harnesses, runtimes, memory, identity, gateways, and payments directly or through a project. Existing projects move to version 1 with one command. The result is one tool from local development to day-to-day operations. Keep agents available when a model is throttled. AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, now supports the Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel APIs and model fallback. Your existing Amazon Bedrock SDK code can point at the gateway without per-provider code changes. When the primary model is throttled or unreachable, the gateway routes the request to the next model or provider in a chain you define. A circuit breaker skips destinations that are failing. The gateway can also reach private targets in your virtual private cloud (VPC) using certificates from your own private certificate authority. Your agents stay available without retry logic in every client. Turn your business workflows into agent tools. You can now use AWS Step Functions workflows, including your existing Standard and Express workflows, as tools through AgentCore Gateway. Your business logic stays in a workflow you already run and trust, so you don’t rebuild it inside the agent or rely on a prompt to follow it. The agent decides when to run a workflow, and Step Functions runs each step exactly as you defined it. For example, a support agent can start your refund workflow, and every refund still goes through the same eligibility check, approval, and credit steps. Get JSON your systems can use as is. Structured outputs are now available for all Claude models on Amazon Bedrock. You receive schema-compliant JSON without custom parsing or retries. You can extract every required field from an earnings report, or route support tickets with entities that always match your data model. Keep answers grounded in sources you trust. Web Search on Amazon Bedrock now supports domain filtering and user location for requests made with the OpenAI Responses API. You can allow up to 100 domains, block up to 100 domains, and return results relevant to a geography. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails then checks that answers stay true to their sources. Its new Standard tier for contextual grounding checks costs the same as the Classic tier, covers conversational and reasoning responses, and supports more languages. With both, you can control where answers come from and catch hallucinations in more of your applications. Predict and lower the cost of running agents Pay for agent memory based on what you use. AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, now prices short-term memory by the data your agents ingest, retrieve, and store, instead of a flat rate per event. Most workloads see lower costs, and small-payload use cases see the largest reductions. You can also set a time-to-live on long-term memory records to meet retention requirements and control storage costs. See what drives your Amazon Bedrock spend. AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, and AWS Cost Management Dashboards now break down Amazon Bedrock cost by model, model provider, inference type, and feature, at no additional charge. Finance and platform teams can find their most expensive models or set a budget alert for a single model, in the billing tools they already use. To lower input costs, Advanced Prompt Optimization can now also shorten your prompts, returning a shorter version only when it scores at least as high on your evaluation. Build voice, local, and well-tested agents with Strands Ship voice agents in a few lines of code. Strands Bidi Agents, for building two-way, speech-to-speech voice agents, are now generally available, with direct support for Amazon Nova Sonic, OpenAI, and Gemini models. Bidi Agents reconnect to the model in the background, so long calls keep going past a provider’s session limit. A voice agent can also hand longer work, such as research, to another agent and explain the results aloud. Let local agents work within your limits. Strands Box, now in developer preview, is an open source local sandbox for AI agents. It combines operating-system isolation with semantic policy. You set policy for each tool, and Box enforces it deterministically, whether the agent calls tools directly, through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), or by generating code. Box works with any model and any agent framework, so an agent can operate in your project without reaching files and services you didn’t allow. Find where your agent breaks before customers do. Red teaming in Strands Evals runs adversarial conversations, such as prompt injections and jailbreak attempts, against your agent and shows the messages and tool calls where it failed. Strands Evals can now also score structured output field by field, giving partial credit when an agent gets most fields right. Use them to fix weak spots before an agent reaches production. To get started, see the Strands Evals documentation. Cut the cost of routine agent decisions. Strands Decider, the small, open source decision model we featured in last month’s recap, now comes in four sizes built on Gemma 4. Instead of generating text, it picks between options you define, such as which tool to call or where to route a request. When an Amazon team switched ticket classification in one of its largest internal ticketing systems to Decider, estimated cost per ticket dropped by about 98 percent. Average response time dropped by 78 percent. Get started Explore Amazon Bedrock, deploy agents with the AgentCore CLI, or build your first agent with the Strands Harness SDK. Interested in learning how Amazon Bedrock can support your team? Connect with us to start the conversation. About the author Tymofii Kryvtsun Tymofii Kryvtsun is a Technical Product Marketing Manager for the AI portfolio at Amazon Web Services (AWS), where he helps developers and enterprises worldwide build production-ready AI agents.

items.title: Introducing the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.summary: AI agents and applications that answer questions about recent events, product releases, prices, or regulations need information newer than their model’s training data. Until now, Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore delivered that information to agents through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. That means creating a gateway and a web search target and calling the tool from an MCP client. The setup fits platform teams that share one search policy across many agents, but it’s more than you need when your own code only requires search results. Today, we’re announcing the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. With it, your own code can search the web with a single API call. It returns ranked results from a web index that Amazon operates, each with a text extract and, when available, the page title, URL, and publication time. You call it from the AWS SDKs or the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), signed with the same AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) credentials you use for your other AWS services. There are no resources to create first. Authenticate, call, and get results. Use it in an application, an agent loop you write yourself, or a data pipeline. Why a standalone API? The AgentCore Gateway is the recommended path for most agentic workloads. It gives agents one secure Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint that combines web search with your other tools. It also handles inbound and outbound authentication, semantic tool selection, and optional MCP sessions. But developers told us they also need a lower-level integration point for scenarios where the gateway is not the right fit: Custom orchestration frameworks – Developers building their own agent loops, or using frameworks like LangChain or LlamaIndex, want to call web search directly as a tool within their orchestration logic rather than routing through a gateway. Non-agent use cases – Not every application that needs web grounding is an agent. Search-powered dashboards, fact-checking pipelines, content enrichment workflows, and monitoring systems all benefit from real-time web results without requiring agent infrastructure. Tighter control over the request lifecycle – Some developers want to manage retries, caching, and error handling themselves rather than delegating to the gateway. Simpler integration for existing applications – Applications that already have their own API layer can call the Web Search API directly, adding web grounding without adopting the full AgentCore Gateway stack. The Web Search API complements the gateway. It runs on the same search infrastructure that powers Alexa+, Kiro, Quick, and other Amazon products, with the same quality and compliance posture, exposed as a direct API operation. How it works The Web Search API is the InvokeWebSearch operation on the bedrock-agentcore data plane, the same endpoint that other AgentCore tools such as AgentCore Browser, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, use. Requests are signed with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) from your standard AWS credentials, so there’s no API key or secret to manage. Figure 1: How a Web Search API request flows The numbered steps are: Your application calls InvokeWebSearch with the AWS SDKs or the AWS CLI, which sign the request with SigV4 using its AWS credentials. From a virtual private cloud (VPC), the call can go through an interface VPC endpoint. The API checks with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) that the caller has bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch on the AWS managed web search tool. The API applies the filters in the request: the domains to include or exclude and the publication time range. The API searches a web index that Amazon operates. Queries are served inside AWS and aren’t sent to a third-party search engine. The API returns up to maxResults ranked results, each with a text extract and, when available, the page title, URL, and publication time. The calling identity needs one IAM permission on an AWS managed resource. It’s the same action and resource that a gateway’s service role uses for web search, so one policy covers both routes. For details, see Grant permission to call the API. { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "InvokeWebSearch", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch", "Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:aws:tool/web-search.v1" } ] } A first search request The following example searches two trusted domains for pages published in 2026, in the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2), with the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3): import boto3 client = boto3.client("bedrock-agentcore", region_name="us-west-2") response = client.invoke_web_search( webSearchId="web-search.v1", searchQuery="multi-region EKS cluster deployment best practices", maxResults=10, filters={ "domainFilter": {"include": ["aws.amazon.com", "kubernetes.io"]}, "publishedDateFilter": {"publishedAfter": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"}, }, ) for result in response["results"]: print(result.get("publishedAt"), result.get("title"), result.get("url")) Every result has a text extract. The title, URL, and publication date come back when the index has them, so read them with get. One result from a live call, shortened: { "title": "One Amazon EKS, many edges: How to choose your edge container strategy on AWS", "url": "https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/containers/one-amazon-eks-many-edges-how-to-choose-your-edge-container-strategy-on-aws/", "text": "Separate the standard from the deployment model Choosing the wrong platform isn't really the issue. ...", "publishedAt": "2026-09-25T15:52:00Z" } That’s the full integration. If your code runs on AWS Lambda, Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), the execution role provides credentials automatically. Add the permission to that role, and the same code runs unchanged. Key API features Domain filtering – Include or exclude specific domains to scope search results to trusted sources (for example, only aws.amazon.com and kubernetes.io for an assistant focused on AWS). Each list holds up to 100 domain names, and a root domain also matches its subdomains. Date filtering – Restrict results to a publication time range with publishedAfter and publishedBefore, given as RFC 3339 date-times in UTC such as 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z. Both bounds are inclusive. Configurable result count – Request between 1 and 25 results per query. If you don’t set maxResults, the API returns up to 25. The search text, searchQuery, can be up to 200 characters. Results with text extracts – Each result includes a text extract and, when available, the page title, URL, and publication time, ready to feed into your model’s context window. Getting started in under 5 minutes Here are two ways to get a first result: Option 1: AWS CloudShell (no local setup) Open AWS CloudShell in your browser. It uses the credentials of your console session. Your role will have the bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch permission, from the preceding policy or from the broader AWS managed policy BedrockAgentCoreFullAccess. Run: aws bedrock-agentcore invoke-web-search \ --web-search-id web-search.v1 \ --search-query "latest EKS features" \ --max-results 5 Option 2: Local development Install the AWS CLI, or the AWS SDK for your language. For Python, use Boto3 1.43.127 or later. Create an IAM role with the preceding policy. Get credentials for that role: assume it from your application or an AWS CLI profile, or sign in with it through your identity provider. Run the preceding Python example, or call the API from any AWS SDK. There’s no resource to create and no API key to manage. Authenticate, call, and get results. Using the Web Search API with agent frameworks The Web Search API fits naturally into popular agent frameworks. LangChain agents get it through the AgentCore web search tool in langchain-aws 1.9.3 and later: from langchain.agents import create_agent from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model from langchain_aws.tools import create_web_search_toolkit toolkit, tools = create_web_search_toolkit(region="us-west-2") model = init_chat_model("bedrock_converse:us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5", region_name="us-west-2") agent = create_agent(model, tools=tools, system_prompt="Cite the URL of every fact you use.") The tool can also hold rules that the model can’t change, such as domains to exclude, a date floor, and a search budget. It returns its results as data that your code can check. For a complete example, see the daily dependency watch sample. It researches three package ecosystems in parallel with LangGraph, and checks every finding against its sources before it reports anything. If you prefer to wrap the call yourself, a plain LangChain tool works too: from langchain.tools import tool import boto3 import json client = boto3.client("bedrock-agentcore", region_name="us-west-2") @tool def web_search(query: str) -> str: """Search the web for current information.""" response = client.invoke_web_search( webSearchId="web-search.v1", searchQuery=query, maxResults=5, ) return json.dumps(response["results"], indent=2, default=str) # Pass web_search to an agent, for example create_agent(model, tools=[web_search]) Without a framework, the WebSearchClient in the AgentCore Python SDK wraps the same call and returns results with parsed dates. langchain-aws 1.9.3 and the AgentCore Python SDK 1.26.0 add Web Search API support, so install those versions or later. Enterprise controls, built in Because the Web Search API uses standard IAM authentication, you get enterprise controls from the first call: IAM policies. Grant or deny bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch per user, group, or role. Use service control policies (SCPs) to enforce guardrails across accounts. AWS CloudTrail logging. CloudTrail records InvokeWebSearch requests as data events. Data events aren’t logged by default, so add an event selector for the AWS::BedrockAgentCore::WebSearch resource type to a trail or event data store. Events record the web search tool and maxResults, not the search text or filters. For details, see Log AgentCore Web Search API calls with AWS CloudTrail. VPC support. Use AWS PrivateLink to route API calls over your private network rather than the public internet. For setup and endpoint policies, see Private connectivity with AWS PrivateLink later in this post. Compliance. For a list of compliance programs that cover AgentCore, see Compliance validation for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Searches stay in AWS. Queries are served from a web index that Amazon operates and aren’t sent to a third-party search engine. Acceptable use. For details, see the Web Search API Acceptable Use documentation. Quotas apply per account. For the defaults and how to request an increase, see Quotas for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. By default, each account can send up to 10 requests per second in each Region, and you can request an increase. For details, see AgentCore Web Search Service Quotas. Private connectivity with AWS PrivateLink Agents and pipelines that handle sensitive data often run in private subnets with no route to the internet. With AWS PrivateLink, that code can call the Web Search API through an interface VPC endpoint in your VPC. Traffic between your VPC and the API stays on the AWS network, and you don’t need an internet gateway, a NAT gateway, or a proxy to reach it. Figure 2: Calling the Web Search API through AWS PrivateLink The numbered steps are: Your application calls InvokeWebSearch at the API’s standard Regional name. With private DNS, that name resolves to the interface endpoint in your subnet. The endpoint policy applies, and the request reaches the API over the AWS network. The API checks with IAM that the caller has bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch, including any aws:SourceVpce condition. The API applies the request’s filters and searches the Amazon-operated web index. The results return through the endpoint to your application. To set it up, create an interface endpoint for the AgentCore data plane service, com.amazonaws.<Region>.bedrock-agentcore, in each VPC and Region that calls the API, and turn on private DNS: aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint \ --region us-west-2 \ --vpc-id vpc-0123456789abcdef0 \ --vpc-endpoint-type Interface \ --service-name com.amazonaws.us-west-2.bedrock-agentcore \ --subnet-ids subnet-0123456789abcdef0 subnet-0fedcba9876543210 \ --security-group-ids sg-0123456789abcdef0 \ --private-dns-enabled With private DNS turned on, the API’s standard Regional name, bedrock-agentcore.us-west-2.amazonaws.com, resolves to the endpoint’s private IP addresses inside your VPC. The Boto3 and AWS CLI examples in this post run unchanged, with no endpoint URL to set. The endpoint’s security group must allow inbound HTTPS (port 443) from the resources that call the API. PrivateLink also gives you controls on top of IAM: Endpoint policies – A VPC endpoint policy applies to InvokeWebSearch requests in addition to your IAM policies, so you decide which principals can search through the endpoint. The same endpoint also carries the other AgentCore data plane APIs, such as AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Memory, Identity, Browser, and Code Interpreter. If workloads in the VPC call them too, add statements that allow those calls. The following policy lets only one role call the API through the endpoint: { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/WebSearchAppRole" }, "Action": "bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch", "Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:aws:tool/web-search.v1" } Require the private path – Add an aws:SourceVpce condition to the IAM policy that grants the permission. The role can then search only through your endpoint, and the same call from outside the VPC is denied: { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch", "Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:aws:tool/web-search.v1", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:SourceVpce": "vpce-0123456789abcdef0" } } } Network-level control – Security groups and subnet placement decide which instances, containers, and functions can reach the endpoint at all. PrivateLink works the same way in every Region where the Web Search API is available. Interface endpoints are billed at standard AWS PrivateLink pricing. For details, see Call AgentCore Web Search through AWS PrivateLink. Try it in the console You can try the Web Search API in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console before you write any code. In the navigation pane, under Connections, choose Web Search. Figure 3: Web Search in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console Configure. In the Configure panel, set: Max results: how many results each query returns, from 1–25. The console starts at 10. Published date: a date range in YYYY/MM/DD format. Only results published inside it come back. Leave it empty to include results from any date. Domain filtering: up to 100 domains to include and up to 100 to exclude. Choose View and manage domains to edit the lists. Test. Enter a query of up to 200 characters in the Test Web Search API panel. Each query calls the Web Search API with your settings. The panel shows how many results came back and how long the call took. For each result it shows the title, a text snippet, the publication date and the source URL. Figure 4 shows a search for “How do I set up Amazon S3 lifecycle rules?” with results limited to aws.amazon.com and docs.aws.amazon.com. Figure 4: A test search with included domains Integrate. When the results look right, you have two options: Generate code snippet: get code that calls the API with the same settings, ready to paste into your agent or application. Create gateway target: add Web Search as a tool on an AgentCore Gateway, so agents can call it through MCP. The console signs each call with your own IAM identity, so your role needs the bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch permission. When to use the API compared to the gateway Scenario Recommended path Building agents with MCP-compatible tools AgentCore Gateway Several tools behind one MCP endpoint, with optional MCP sessions AgentCore Gateway One administrator source policy for many agents and teams AgentCore Gateway MCP clients that need search, such as Claude with the AWS Web Search connector AgentCore Gateway Custom orchestration Web Search API Non-agent use cases (dashboards, pipelines) Web Search API Want direct control over retries and caching Web Search API Adding web search to an existing application Web Search API Both paths search the same index. They differ in a few ways. A gateway can also authorize callers with a JSON Web Token (JWT), while the API authorizes with IAM only. On a gateway, an administrator can set domain lists on the target that apply to every request without the calling agent seeing them. With the API, each request carries its own filters. The field names differ too: the API takes searchQuery, publishedAfter, and publishedBefore, and the gateway’s MCP tool takes query, from, and to. For more guidance, see Choose between the API and the Gateway connector. Pricing The Web Search API meters to the same usage type as the gateway connector, so it’s billed at the Web Search rate of $7 per 1,000 queries. Because no gateway is involved, there are no gateway charges. For details, see Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing. Availability The Web Search API is available in the US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Ireland), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Asia Pacific (Sydney) Regions. For the current list, see Supported AWS Regions. Get started Use the following resources to help you get started. Web Search API documentation Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore InvokeWebSearch API reference About the authors Shubham Divekar Shubham is a Sr Software Development Engineer at Amazon Web Services (AWS), working in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. He focuses on developing scalable systems on the cloud that enable AI applications frameworks and orchestrations. Shubham also has a background in building distributed, scalable, high-volume-high-throughput systems in IoT architectures. Outside of work, he spends time playing ping pong, badminton and hiking through the great PNW mountains. Sundar Raghavan Sundar is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS on the Agentic AI Foundations team. He leads the developer experience for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, owning the SDK and CLI, and drives the framework and ecosystem integrations strategy. He focuses on how developers build, deploy, and scale production AI agents on AWS. He is also bringing the same agent developer experience to Physical AI through Strands Robots. Uday PB Uday is a Software Development Engineer at Amazon AGI, working on large-scale distributed systems, information retrieval, grounding, and agentic AI infrastructure. His work focuses on building scalable services that connect foundation models and AI agents with real-time information and external tools, enabling reliable information retrieval, complex reasoning, and research capabilities across AI applications. Kalyan Garimella Kalyan is a Principal Product Manager at Amazon AGI, where he leads the development and launch of web search capabilities for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. His work focuses on solving a core limitation of modern AI agents; their inability to access real-time, factual information; by enabling agents to ground their reasoning in live web data. Kalyan lives in the Bay Area with his family. items.title: OpenAI Codex on Amazon Bedrock
items.summary: Developers increasingly use Codex with Amazon Bedrock to explore unfamiliar code, make changes, and handle repetitive engineering work. For platform teams, the challenge is to make those tools available without creating a second model-access, identity, and operations stack. Codex can use Amazon Bedrock for inference with supported OpenAI models. In this post, we show how to fit that path into the AWS identity, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), Regional, and observability practices your organization already uses. Codex still runs on the developer workstation. The main design choice is how its model requests reach Amazon Bedrock and where your organization applies policy and operational controls. We begin with a small, least-privilege pilot and work through the checks that matter before access expands. The examples use GPT-5.6 Sol. Before starting the pilot, review Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock to confirm that Sol, Terra, or Luna is available in the AWS Region and inference path you plan to use. Recommended default: Start with Native AWS Access for a small, least-privilege pilot. Choose AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, when you want AWS managed gateway infrastructure for routing or Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Choose an LLM Gateway when a platform team wants to enforce controls in the request path. A custom integration is the advanced version of the LLM Gateway pattern, not a quick start. The examples come from the open source Guidance for Codex on AWS repository. It includes quick starts for Native AWS Access, AgentCore Gateway, LiteLLM on ECS, Portkey, the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT), and the Amazon CloudWatch setup used later in the post. Choose the quick start that matches your architecture, use it for the pilot, and adapt it to your environment. Choose your rollout path Authentication is only one part of an enterprise rollout. Decide who can use the service and which models and Regions are approved. Also define where configuration lives, what telemetry to collect, how usage is allocated, and which skills or Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers are allowed. The following table maps those needs to an access path and an owning team. Choose the access path that provides the controls you need now. The most straightforward path that meets the requirement usually has the lowest operational overhead. Decision rules Native AWS Access is the usual starting point when AWS identity and IAM controls are enough for the pilot. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Within the platform, AgentCore Gateway fits teams that want AWS managed gateway infrastructure for routing, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, or related controls. A large language model (LLM) Gateway fits organizations that already operate a gateway or want to enforce controls in the request path. Building a custom gateway is the advanced version of this option. The following diagram compares where identity, routing, policy, telemetry, and operational ownership sit across the three rollout paths. Figure 1: Codex runs on the developer workstation in each scenario. Native AWS Access uses AWS IAM Identity Center, a configured AgentCore Gateway can apply managed routing and Guardrails, and a configured LLM Gateway can apply request-path controls Native AWS Access If Native AWS Access fits the pilot, the repository’s Native AWS Access quick start provides the complete procedure and supporting files. The following abbreviated walkthrough focuses on the sequence and the checks that matter most. Use your workforce identity provider for sign-in Employees continue to sign in through the identity provider they already use. In this example, Okta handles authentication through Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) and provisions users and groups into IAM Identity Center through System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM). IAM Identity Center then issues the temporary AWS credentials used by Codex. The identity provider is not configured in Codex. Prerequisites Add each pilot user to a dedicated group in the workforce identity system and provision that group to IAM Identity Center. Keep the assignment limited to the pilot. Choose an Amazon Bedrock Region and an OpenAI model available to the pilot identity, plus an inference profile if the selected API requires one. Check Sol, Terra, and Luna separately for the chosen account, Region, and inference path. Grant only the Amazon Bedrock model inference permissions used by Codex, any direct validation commands, and the selected observability destination. Prepare a non-production repository and name a rollback owner. Configure The pilot has three checks. First, sign in using the IAM Identity Center profile configured for the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and call Amazon Bedrock Runtime directly. Next, point Codex to the approved model. Finally, run a safe Codex task. The direct call isolates AWS access problems. The final step confirms the Codex configuration. Step 1: Sign in and validate Amazon Bedrock Runtime access. aws sso login --profile codex-bedrock export AWS_PROFILE=codex-bedrock aws bedrock-runtime converse --model-id us.openai.gpt-5.6-sol --messages '[{"role":"user","content":[{"text":"Reply with OK"}]}]' --region us-east-2 This command creates a short-lived AWS session and checks whether the profile can invoke the chosen model in the chosen Region. If it fails, resolve the profile, Region, model or inference-profile access, or IAM permissions before configuring Codex. Step 2: Configure the Codex provider. # ~/.codex/config.toml (or managed user configuration) model_provider = "amazon-bedrock" model = "openai.gpt-5.6-sol" [model_providers.amazon-bedrock.aws] profile = "codex-bedrock" region = "us-east-2" The model value is the Codex model ID. The profile selects the AWS IAM Identity Center session, and region tells Codex which AWS Region to use. Keep these settings in user-level or managed configuration so a repository cannot change the provider. Verify the pilot and confirm rollback Before adding users, make sure the pilot reaches the approved model, produces the expected records, and can be disabled cleanly. Identity: aws sts get-caller-identity returns the expected IAM Identity Center assumed-role session. Model access: The pilot profile invokes the approved model through the API and Region selected for the test. Codex access: The user completes a safe, read-only task in a non-production repository, and the expected request-path evidence is available. Evidence and rollback: The identity, invocation, audit, and optional telemetry records are present. Remove the configuration or IAM Identity Center assignment, handle any active session according to your procedure or wait for it to expire, and verify that a new invocation is denied. Watch the Native AWS Access walkthrough The walkthrough shows the complete pilot sequence: workforce sign-in, direct Amazon Bedrock Runtime validation, Codex provider configuration, and a safe test task. Figure 2: Native AWS Access walkthrough covering workforce sign-in, Amazon Bedrock Runtime validation, Codex provider configuration, and a safe pilot task Use the video to verify the order of the checks and the evidence to collect before adding more pilot users. Run a two-user identity-isolation check Two users are required to test identity isolation. A single user shows that sign-in works. A second user tests whether attribution remains distinct. Have two pilot users sign in separately and run the same harmless task. Their assumed-role sessions and audit records, and telemetry records if configured, should remain distinct. The following diagram shows how separate pilot identities should produce separate AWS sessions, request evidence, and optional telemetry while using the same approved Codex and Amazon Bedrock path. Figure 3: Use trusted identity enrollment for attribution. A local collector can add approved identity context only when it is deployed and configured as part of a managed enrollment process Gateway paths for request-path controls AgentCore Gateway is an option when you want AWS managed gateway infrastructure for centralized routing or Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. If your organization already runs an LLM Gateway or wants to enforce controls in the request path, use that gateway instead. Validate the selected gateway before exposing it to pilot users. LLM Gateway: Validate before a pilot Check that the gateway accepts the Codex request format. Use the sign-in or token flow defined by the gateway team. Before inviting pilot users, test model routing, monitoring, failure handling, and rollback. Custom enterprise integration A custom enterprise integration is the most involved form of the LLM Gateway pattern. Consider it only when Native AWS Access, AgentCore Gateway, and an existing gateway cannot meet a specific requirement. The result is another service to design, secure, test, support, and operate, so platform engineering and security need to own it from the start. Observe, govern, and allocate cost Codex OpenTelemetry, Amazon Bedrock service records, AWS identity records, and billing data answer different questions. Codex OpenTelemetry describes client activity. Amazon Bedrock service metrics and model invocation logs show service-side activity when enabled. AWS identity records and the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) provide identity and billed-usage evidence. Correlate them for the path you deploy, and do not present token volume as a cost report. Define what code, prompts, files, and tool output Codex might send through the selected model path. Exclude secrets and restricted data unless the organization has approved that data flow. Require developers to review and test generated changes before merge. Telemetry does not establish correctness or safety. OpenTelemetry metrics from Codex For observability, this post uses the ADOT collector configuration and CloudWatch dashboard from the repository’s monitoring and operations guidance. Deploy that configuration to each managed pilot device, then run a safe Codex task. The repository provides the configuration files. Follow its deployment instructions to install the approved ADOT collector and configure its AWS authentication. # ~/.codex/config.toml or managed user configuration [otel] environment = "pilot" log_user_prompt = false metrics_exporter = { "otlp-http" = { endpoint = "http://127.0.0.1:4318/v1/metrics", protocol = "binary" } } Validate the repository path: run a safe Codex task and confirm that the expected operational metrics appear on the managed CloudWatch dashboard. Telemetry plane Examples Attribution boundary Codex OpenTelemetry metrics Token usage, turns, API requests, request duration, tool calls, session source. Per-user and team dashboard grouping only after the local collector adds validated identity attributes. Amazon Bedrock service metrics Invocations, latency, input tokens, output tokens, client errors, server errors. Use the documented namespace, metric names, and dimensions for the selected Runtime, Mantle, or AgentCore path. AWS identity evidence, model invocation logs, and CUR Assumed-role single sign-on (SSO) principal plus billed Bedrock line items. For Native IAM Identity Center access, CUR 2.0 with caller-identity allocation can expose the SSO principal. Gateway paths require gateway telemetry and spend records for end-user allocation. Amazon CloudWatch dashboard and evidence The Amazon CloudWatch Coding Agent Insights managed dashboard in the Guidance for Codex on AWS repository shows Codex operational metrics collected through ADOT. Use it to understand client activity, and use AWS identity, audit, and billing records separately when you need attribution or cost evidence. Question Decision Evidence to keep Who invoked the model? Use the AWS identity/audit source for the path you selected. Pilot identity record and request correlation, where available. What did it cost? Use billing data for actual charge and label any inferred allocation clearly. CUR source, allocation method, and known uncertainty. Can we stop unsafe or expensive behavior? Use alarms for detection. Use IAM and managed client controls for their respective access and action boundaries. Use gateway policy when request-path enforcement, such as hard budgets or rate limits, is required. Control test results and rollback procedure. Watch the Codex OTel and CloudWatch walkthrough The walkthrough shows how to query Codex OpenTelemetry metrics and confirm that the expected token and request data appears in Amazon CloudWatch. Figure 4: Codex OpenTelemetry metrics shown in an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard The example validates the aliased metric result in Amazon CloudWatch Query Studio and shows how the dashboard represents Codex client activity. Standardize team behavior After the infrastructure path is working, turn to the developer experience. Repository guidance, managed plugins, hooks, and approved MCP servers can make the rollout consistent without asking each team to assemble its own setup. Plugins Organization-owned plugins are a practical way to distribute shared skills, hooks, and approved MCP integrations. Give each plugin an owner and version, review changes before release, and publish it only through approved sources. Test updates with a pilot group and keep a documented removal path. A plugin might include an MCP server configuration, but that does not make every bundled tool approved. Allow only the servers and tools the organization has reviewed, with user confirmation where it is needed. Hooks Hooks can be declared in hooks.json or directly in configuration. Keep the documented event casing, and deploy organization-owned policy commands through approved endpoint tooling. [[hooks.PreToolUse]] matcher = "^Bash$" [[hooks.PreToolUse.hooks]] type = "command" command = "/usr/local/bin/company-pre-tool-policy" timeout = 30 Use PreToolUse, PostToolUse, or SessionStart where they solve a specific need. Before wider deployment, test allow, deny, timeout, and disconnected-endpoint behavior. MCP An MCP server connects Codex to another system, so each server creates a separate trust boundary. Limit access to the users and tools that need it, manage credentials through an approved OAuth or secrets process, and require confirmation for tools that change external systems. Keep MCP credentials out of the model-provider configuration. Roll out in phases The following diagram defines the scope and evidence required to advance from preparation through pilot, expansion, and organization-wide standardization. Figure 5: Start with a controlled pilot, expand after validating the access path and operational evidence, and standardize the rollout after the operating model is proven Administrator launch checklist Record the selected path, owning team, Region, and model in the change record. Limit the pilot identity to the required permissions, and document how issued credentials or tokens are handled. Run a non-production test that covers sign-in, model availability, and one safe Codex task. Check telemetry and audit output from the deployed version rather than assuming the example applies unchanged. Separate billed amounts from estimates in cost reporting. Exercise recovery: remove the configuration or assignment, handle any active session through the approved procedure or wait for it to expire, and verify that a new invocation is denied. Clean up When the pilot ends or access must be disabled, remove the rollout resources that are no longer required. Remove the Codex model-provider and telemetry configuration from managed devices. Remove the IAM Identity Center pilot assignment or gateway access, revoke pilot tokens and secrets, and handle active sessions according to the approved procedure. Uninstall or disable the ADOT collector, and delete the pilot CloudWatch dashboard and alarms if they are not shared with another workload. Verify cleanup by confirming that a new model invocation is denied and that retired telemetry resources receive no new data. Configuration boundaries Keep model-provider, credential, and organization telemetry settings in user-level or managed configuration. Project-local .codex/config.toml is repository-scoped configuration: Review it as code, but do not treat it as an enterprise enforcement boundary. AGENTS.md is useful for durable repository guidance, such as test commands and coding conventions, but it is not an enforcement boundary either. Setting type Recommended location Reason Model provider, credentials, Region User-level or managed configuration These are endpoint and enterprise choices, not repository defaults. OpenTelemetry exporter User-level or managed configuration Telemetry destination and data handling are organization controls. Repository instructions AGENTS.md Carries durable guidance but is not an enforcement boundary. Permission requirements Organization-managed requirements.toml Constrains supported security-sensitive client choices. Conclusions and next steps Codex can use Amazon Bedrock for inference with supported OpenAI models. Start with the least-complex access path that meets the requirement, prove the identity and model path with a small pilot, and add gateway or client controls only when they solve a specific need. AgentCore Gateway provides an AWS managed gateway option for routing or Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Choose an LLM Gateway when a platform team wants to enforce controls in the request path. Build a custom integration only when the available paths cannot meet a documented requirement. Expand in stages and use evidence from each stage to decide what comes next. The Guidance for Codex on AWS repository contains the maintained configurations and validation procedures used in this post. About the authors Shivi Bhatia Shivi Bhatia is a Senior Solutions Architect for Amazon Bedrock in the AWS Worldwide Specialist Organization. He works with enterprise customers on generative AI, agentic systems, production inference, and AI/ML architecture. His professional interests include multi-agent orchestration, inference optimization, model evaluation, observability, and secure enterprise AI adoption. Sebastien Couturier Sebastien Couturier Senior GenAI Specialist Solutions Architect at AWS, working closely with enterprise customers and partners on GenAI, agentic AI and developer tools. Sriharsha M S Sriharsha M S is a Principal Gen AI specialist solution architect in the Strategic Specialist team at Amazon Web Services. He works with strategic AWS customers who are taking advantage of AI/ML to solve complex business problems. He provides technical guidance and design advice to foundational model science and agentic AI applications at scale. His expertise spans application hardware accelerators, architecture, big data, analytics and machine learning.
