items.title: Semantic diffing of formal policies with anti-unification
items.summary: When reviewing code, you start with a diff. You wouldn’t compare two 3,000-line files by eye and hope to spot every change. Formal policies can be even harder to compare because a textual diff often highlights syntactic changes that don’t affect meaning. Reorder two conjuncts, swap the arguments of an equality, or use an equivalent predicate, and much of the file might appear changed. A real change in behavior, such as an Or where the requirement says and, can get lost in that noise. A semantic diff shows what two policies have in common and where they disagree. The open source engine used in this post computes this diff using anti-unification, which finds a most specific common pattern for two expressions. Plotkin’s 1970 paper gives the classical formulation. The engine works over an e-graph, which keeps track of expressions known to be equal. We supply the algebraic laws and domain rules that justify those equalities, such as equating an external destination with one that isn’t internal. The result shows the shared parts once and keeps both versions of each differing part for review. If no differences remain, the policies are equivalent under those laws and rules. When the rules or the search are incomplete, a remaining difference might reflect an equivalence the engine has not found. One use case is autoformalization. Autoformalization translates natural language into a formal language. Suppose you want to turn requirements into SMT-LIB, the standard input language for satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solvers such as Z3 and cvc5, or into Cedar or Dogwood to control authorization in your software system. A large language model (LLM) generates the formal artifact from the prose. The model writes the artifact. It plays no part in computing the diff. Run the model twice, and it might produce two different formalizations, with no ground truth to identify the correct one. A semantic diff shows where they agree and where they differ. Generate more candidates by varying the model, prompt, or sampling temperature. Comparing them shows which parts stay the same and which vary. Review the varying parts first. Requirements can also become OpenShell sandbox policies or Common Expression Language (CEL) expressions. OpenShell uses YAML to describe an agent’s filesystem and network access. CEL is embedded in applications to evaluate expressions, including policy conditions. These languages and formats differ in what they express, but translations into any of them can disagree about a condition, a scope, or an event. The following table gives illustrative disagreements: Language or format Policy focus Example disagreement Cedar Who can perform an action on a resource, under which conditions. One translation requires ownership and approval. Another accepts either. Dogwood Authorization involving the current request and recent event history. One translation checks a successful prior response. Another checks a request event. OpenShell policies An agent’s filesystem and network access, including rules for particular binaries. One translation permits repository-scoped GET. Another permits organization-scoped POST. CEL Conditions evaluated over inputs supplied by a host application. One translation requires production for both allowed ports. Another requires it for only one. In each worked example, we compare translations of the same requirement within one policy context. We encode the relevant syntax as terms and declare the equalities used in the comparison. The engine reads these encodings. It doesn’t import native policies from the four formats. The idea is a formal-methods analogue of semantic entropy, described by Farquhar et al. in Nature (2024). That approach samples several natural-language answers, clusters those that entail one another, and reports a single number. For formal outputs, anti-unification preserves more information. It identifies the shared structure and each divergence instead of returning only a score. Counterexamples help explain the consequences of a disagreement. An SMT solver can find a concrete assignment that satisfies one formula and violates the other. A reviewer can then trace that assignment through the formulas to understand the conflicting decisions. The anti-unifier gives a different view: it organizes the shared structure and the fragments that differ, without issuing an SMT query. A solver or policy validator can help resolve those fragments. We assume you can read S-expression syntax, as in SMT-LIB, and know what an authorization policy is. E-graphs and anti-unification are explained as they come up. When several translations agree on part of a requirement, the diff shows that part once. Where they disagree, it keeps the alternatives visible for review. How semantic diffing represents disagreement Say a policy-generation pipeline hands you two candidate rules for this requirement: sensitive data sent to an external destination must be encrypted. Rule A Rule B sensitive(data) ∧ external(dst) → encrypted ¬internal(dst) ∧ sensitive(data) → audited Whether these are the same rule isn’t obvious. The conditions are reordered, external is expressed indirectly as not internal, and the conclusions do not match. The engine computes a most specific anti-unifier for these terms. In its input language, the two rules are S-expressions. The complete program first declares the vocabulary: (sort Formula) (sort Data) (sort Dest) (function Lit (bool) Formula) (function And (Formula) Formula :assoc-comm-idem :identity (Lit true)) (function Implies (Formula Formula) Formula) (function Not (Formula) Formula) It then adds one function line for each predicate (sensitive, external, internal) and constant (data, dst, encrypted, audited). Here, And is declared associative, commutative, and idempotent, as the next section explains: (let ruleA (Implies (And (sensitive (data)) (external (dst))) (encrypted))) (let ruleB (Implies (And (Not (internal (dst))) (sensitive (data))) (audited))) (antiunify ruleA ruleB :algorithm exact) The engine answers with a single term: (anti-unify :size 11 :cr 0.5000 :completion exact (Implies (And (sensitive data) (Variants (external dst) (Not (internal dst)))) (Variants encrypted audited))) The reordering doesn’t appear in the result because And is declared associative, commutative, and idempotent. Two Variants nodes remain, each marking a place where the inputs disagree, and only one of them is a difference in meaning. The difference between (external dst) and (Not (internal dst)) is a difference in vocabulary. Both express the same domain fact. The engine can’t infer that from syntax alone. State the domain fact as a rewrite, run it to saturation (until no rule adds a new equality), and diff again: (rewrite (external d) (Not (internal d))) (run 2) (antiunify ruleA ruleB :algorithm exact) After saturation, the engine answers: (anti-unify :size 8 :cr 0.1429 :completion exact (Implies (And (sensitive data) (external dst)) (Variants encrypted audited))) One Variants node remains: Rule B audits where the requirement demands encryption. A textbook presentation would put a fresh variable at that spot. The engine instead writes (Variants encrypted audited): a node that holds both readings. Select the first child of every Variants node and you reconstruct rule A, up to the declared algebra and rewrites. Select the second child and you get rule B. The anti-unifier is a lossless merge of both terms: Shared structure appears once, and every genuine disagreement is a localized, reviewable node. Three fields describe the result: :size, :cr, and :completion. The :size field counts the concrete nodes (a Variants marker itself isn’t counted, but both of its children are, so structure can’t hide inside one). The :cr field reports the compression ratio (s - a) / b, where s is the result size and a and b are the smaller and larger input sizes. For each input, we use its smallest known equivalent form in the current e-graph. A score of 0 means full agreement under the declared equalities. After the preceding rewrite, both inputs have seven nodes and the result has eight, giving (8 - 7) / 7, or approximately 0.1429. Keeping both complete policies in a single Variants node would use fourteen nodes, giving (14 - 7) / 7 = 1. This is the reference value for no sharing. A score of 1 is a reference value, not an upper bound. The search might use larger equivalent forms than the smallest known inputs. A result larger than their combined sizes therefore scores above 1. For example, if both smallest input forms have ten nodes and a result has twenty-three, the ratio is (23 - 10) / 10 = 1.3. The :completion field reports exact when the search space was exhausted and budget when the default anytime search (a Monte Carlo search, described in the implementation section) reached its playout limit before exhausting the search space. A low :cr means the inputs share more structure under the declared equalities. It doesn’t establish correctness: two candidates can share the same mistake. An entropy score summarizes variation in one number. The full semantic diff also identifies where the candidates disagree and retains both alternatives in Variants nodes. A semantic diff ignores only the differences covered by the declared equalities. A plain syntactic anti-unifier would also have reported the reordering in this example. The next three sections show how to declare the algebra and add domain identities. The anti-unifier stores shared structure once and marks each disagreement with a Variants node. Selecting one side of every node reconstructs the corresponding input, modulo the declared equalities. Run a semantic diff in 5 minutes The engine requires only a pinned Rust toolchain to build from source. Its formal-verification annotations, covered in the implementation section, compile away under plain rustc. These commands pin the revision used for the worked examples: git clone https://github.com/yaspar-org/semi-persistent.git cd semi-persistent git fetch origin 5a7969ae4ea88117a64faac4f42af5c358e213e2 git checkout --detach FETCH_HEAD cargo build --release ./target/release/semi-persistent doc/book/examples/12-first-au.egg It prints a single (anti-unify ...) term. The command-line interpreter reads one S-expression file (.egg by convention). You declare sorts and operators, define two terms with let, optionally add rewrite rules and run them to saturation, and issue antiunify. Two mechanisms tell the engine which syntactic changes do not affect meaning: annotations that assign algebraic properties such as associativity, commutativity, and idempotence to operators, and explicit rewrite rules for everything else. Here is the algebraic part of the signature used in the worked example: (function Lit (bool) Formula) (function And (Formula) Formula :assoc-comm-idem :identity (Lit true)) (function Or (Formula) Formula :assoc-comm-idem :identity (Lit false)) (function Eq (Account Account) Formula :comm) And and Or are variadic, associative, commutative, and idempotent, and each has a Boolean neutral element. Eq is commutative. Every reordering, regrouping, and duplication of conjuncts therefore counts as the same term. Nothing else is assumed: Only the stated laws hold, and any further identities must be written as explicit rewrites. The :identity element is what lets the diff align a conjunct that one input has and the other lacks: The missing conjunct is paired with (Lit true) rather than causing the entire And expression to fail to align. Both case studies rely on this identity alignment. :assoc-comm-idem makes reordered, regrouped, and duplicate operands equivalent. :identity lets the diff align a missing operand with the operator’s neutral element. Worked example with two policy bugs The running example ships with the repository as egraph/examples/au_policy_divergence.egg. Consider one policy sentence: A cross-Region replication request is permitted only if the source bucket has versioning enabled and the destination bucket lies in an approved Region. If the object is tagged confidential, the destination and source accounts must be the same and server-side encryption with a customer managed key must be in effect. Objects up to the multipart threshold are copied directly. Larger objects require a multipart copy. Two people, or two independent runs of the same model, produced formalizations of it (formulaA and formulaB in the file): Encoding A (Implies (permit) (And (versioningOn (src)) (approvedRegion (regionOf (dst))) (Implies (taggedConfidential (obj)) (And (Eq (accountOf (dst)) (accountOf (src))) (sseCmk))) (Ite (Lte (sizeOf (obj)) (multipartThreshold)) (directCopy) (multipartCopy)))) Encoding B (Implies (permit) (And (Ite (Lt (sizeOf (obj)) (multipartThreshold)) (directCopy) (multipartCopy)) (Implies (taggedConfidential (obj)) (Or (Eq (accountOf (src)) (accountOf (dst))) (sseCmk))) (Or (usEast1 (regionOf (dst))) (euWest1 (regionOf (dst)))) (versioningOn (src)))) Five things differ textually. Three are presentational: The conjuncts are reordered, the Eq arguments are swapped, and approvedRegion is explicitly expanded into two AWS Regions (us-east-1 and eu-west-1). Two involve different operators: An And became an Or in the confidential clause, and Lte became Lt at the size threshold. A unified diff of the two encodings marks 18 of their 28 lines as changed (Figure 1, textual-diff pane) and gives no indication of which of the five differences change meaning. The exact anti-unifier of the two encodings follows: (anti-unify :size 42 :cr 0.5862 :completion exact (Implies permit (And (Implies (taggedConfidential obj) (And (Or (Eq (accountOf dst) (accountOf src)) (Variants (Lit false) sseCmk)) (Variants sseCmk (Lit true)))) (Ite (Variants (Lte (sizeOf obj) multipartThreshold) (Lt (sizeOf obj) multipartThreshold)) directCopy multipartCopy) (versioningOn src) (Variants (approvedRegion (regionOf dst)) (Or (usEast1 (regionOf dst)) (euWest1 (regionOf dst))))))) Two of the five differences disappear. The conjunct reordering is absorbed because And is declared associative, commutative, and idempotent (ACI). The swapped Eq arguments have the same printed order in both readings because :comm canonized them. Neither changes meaning, so neither is reported. The confidential clause uses Or where the requirement says and. Encoding A requires both the same-account check and server-side encryption with a customer managed key. Encoding B accepts either. The engine aligns A’s conjunction with B’s disjunction through their neutral elements, so the disagreement surfaces as two adjacent Variants nodes. Choose the first child at each node to reconstruct A: The Or collapses onto the plain equality, and sseCmk remains a mandatory conjunct. Choose the second child at each node to reconstruct B: The mandatory sseCmk weakens to (Lit true) and survives only as an alternative inside the Or. Together, the two Variants nodes show that encoding B accepts server-side encryption alone and therefore admits cross-account replication of confidential objects. You might have expected sseCmk to be shared rather than repeated. However, a first-order anti-unifier can’t generalize the connective itself, so And versus Or forces the split into two alignments. Identity alignment still shares the five-node equality once. The exact solver’s exhaustive search finds no smaller form, and the printed result is one node smaller than holding both clauses whole in a single Variants. Add the domain rewrite and run the diff again. The Variants node for the Region is not a bug. It reflects missing domain knowledge: In this deployment, the approved Regions are exactly those two. State that as a rewrite, saturate, and diff again: (rewrite (approvedRegion r) (Or (usEast1 r) (euWest1 r))) (run 3) (antiunify formulaA formulaB :algorithm exact) The Region difference moves into the shared backbone, and :cr drops from 0.5862 to 0.4000. The full result is the semantic-diff pane of Figure 1. Exactly two disagreements remain: the weakened confidential clause and the threshold. B’s Lt is strict, so an object exactly at multipartThreshold is copied directly under A and takes the multipart path under B. The divergence is confined to the Ite condition. Both branches sit in the shared backbone. Both surviving differences are genuine bugs that an authorization reviewer must resolve. The algebra and one domain rewrite account for the other differences. The same file also runs the anytime search, (antiunify formulaA formulaB :algorithm uct :playouts 3000), which returns the identical size-35 term. The whole program completes in well under 100 ms on an Apple M3 Pro laptop (50–60 ms after the binary is warm). That covers parsing, declarations, saturation, five anti-unification queries with their regression checks, and process startup. We measured the wall-clock time of ./target/release/semi-persistent egraph/examples/au_policy_divergence.egg using a release build at Rust 1.97.1 and the shell’s time command over five warm runs. The Get started section shows the same command. textual diff: 18 of 28 lines flagged (Implies (permit) (And - (versioningOn (src)) - (approvedRegion (regionOf (dst))) + (Ite + (Lt (sizeOf (obj)) (multipartThreshold)) + (directCopy) + (multipartCopy)) (Implies (taggedConfidential (obj)) - (And - (Eq (accountOf (dst)) (accountOf (src))) + (Or + (Eq (accountOf (src)) (accountOf (dst))) (sseCmk))) - (Ite - (Lte (sizeOf (obj)) (multipartThreshold)) - (directCopy) - (multipartCopy)))) + (Or + (usEast1 (regionOf (dst))) + (euWest1 (regionOf (dst)))) + (versioningOn (src)))) semantic diff: two disagreements, localized (anti-unify :size 35 :cr 0.4000 :completion exact (Implies permit (And (Implies (taggedConfidential obj) (And (Or (Eq (accountOf dst) (accountOf src)) (Variants (Lit false) sseCmk)) (Variants sseCmk (Lit true)))) (Ite (Variants (Lte (sizeOf obj) multipartThreshold) (Lt (sizeOf obj) multipartThreshold)) directCopy multipartCopy) (versioningOn src) (approvedRegion (regionOf dst))))) Figure 1: The same pair of encodings under diff and anti-unification. On the left, the textual diff flags 18 of 28 lines (removed, added). On the right, one domain rewrite moves the shared structure into the gray backbone, and the highlighted Variants confine the remaining differences to the weakened confidential clause and the strict threshold. The semantic-diff pane wraps one long line to fit After applying the declared algebra and one domain rewrite, the five textual differences reduce to two semantic disagreements: the weakened confidential clause and the strict size threshold. Semantic diffing for Cedar and Dogwood policies In an authorization policy, a dropped guard widens what is permitted and can cause the policy to fail open. Cedar is the open source authorization policy language behind Amazon Verified Permissions. Dogwood extends Cedar authorization policies with temporal conditions for runtime verification of AI agents. Its temporal sublanguage uses recorded event history to guard an action. The engine doesn’t evaluate Dogwood policies. It diffs their abstract syntax modulo a declared algebra. Validation (schema checking) and replay (evaluating a policy against a recorded event history) remain Dogwood’s job. The engine’s user guide has a worked chapter that diffs two independently produced Dogwood candidates for one requirement: The agent may POST to /deploy, but only if a health check has already come back 200 in the last 15 minutes. Candidate A keeps both request guards (method and path) but reads the status code from a request event, an event kind that carries no such field. Candidate B uses the correct response event but drops the /deploy path guard. After any matching health check, B also permits a POST to /admin/purge-all. The candidates differ in six additional presentational ways, all of which the declared algebra or a three-rule comparison theory absorbs: Presentational difference Absorbed by Cedar condition order eAnd :assoc-comm-idem temporal conjunction order tAnd :assoc-comm-idem predicate field order args :assoc-comm-idem method == "POST" versus "POST" == method eEq :comm 15m versus 900s unit rewrite + constant fold count >= 1 versus 1 <= count (birewrite (tLte a b) (tGte b a)) The comparison theory consists of three visible rewrites, not a hidden normalization pass: (rewrite (mins x) (secsTimes x 60)) (rewrite (secsTimes x y) (secs (IBig::* x y))) (birewrite (tLte a b) (tGte b a)) (run 4) The anti-unifier of the two candidates (doc/book/examples/20-dogwood-simple.egg in the repository) has size 61, :cr 0.1864, and exactly two disagreements in an otherwise shared policy backbone: (anti-unify :size 61 :cr 0.1864 :completion exact (rule permit (head anyPrincipal (actionEq aHttpRequest) anyResource) (eAnd (eEq (eCtx (fld fInput (fld fMethod fnil))) (eStr vPOST)) (temporal ... (pred aHttpRequest (Variants request response) ... (Variants (eEq (eCtx (fld fInput (fld fPath fnil))) (eStr vDeploy)) eTrue)))) Use the simplest available check for each disagreement. Two binary disagreements give four candidate completions. Dogwood validation resolves the first without human review by rejecting both request completions (“predicate … mentions field output.status_code, which is not declared on that event”). The second disagreement is an identity alignment: Candidate A’s path guard pairs against eTrue, showing that candidate B omitted the guard. The requirement resolves it (keep the guard), and a replay covering two decision points shows the consequence: After a health check, candidate B allows the off-target POST, whereas the repaired policy denies it. Combining B’s event kind with A’s guard produces a policy that neither candidate wrote. Choosing between the candidates would have kept one of the two bugs. Commutativity has a side condition, and the engine doesn’t check it. Cedar’s && short-circuits, so commuting it is sound only when neither operand can raise an error. The comparison therefore relies on validation to rule out order-dependent errors, such as an attribute access that is safe only behind a has guard. The engine doesn’t re-check that condition. A canonical printer can remove the presentational differences, but it can’t recover a dropped guard. A canonizing printer plus textual diff can absorb most, arguably all, of the six differences in the table more cheaply. No normalizer can align a two-conjunct condition against a three-conjunct one inside an otherwise matched term. Matching modulo the identity element aligns them by pairing the dropped conjunct with eTrue. In a permit condition, that dropped conjunct exposes the widening that makes the policy fail open. For the Dogwood candidates, the algebra and three rewrites remove six presentational differences. The remaining disagreements expose a schema error and a dropped guard. Combining the correct choices produces a policy that neither candidate supplied. Comparing policy translations: OpenShell and CEL The next two examples adapt predicates from the OpenShell and CEL articles. For each, we construct candidate translations of the same requirement. These are illustrative encodings, not recorded LLM samples. OpenShell: Method and path scope. The OpenShell example models network permissions as predicates over a binary, host, port, layer, method, and path. We adapt the article’s reduced SMT-LIB model, whose path condition is a prefix test. We use that vocabulary for this requirement: Allow inspected REST requests made by /usr/bin/gh to api.github.com on port 443 when the method is GET and the path begins with /repos/NVIDIA/OpenShell/issues/. Deny all other requests. Candidate A requires GET and the repository’s issues prefix. Candidate B uses POST and the broader /repos/NVIDIA/ prefix. The other checks appear in a different order. In the encoding, gh, github, and https name the binary, host, and port shown earlier. The names issuePrefix and orgPrefix identify the two prefixes. The exact solver returns: (anti-unify :size 21 :cr 0.1053 :completion exact (And (EqText binary gh) (EqText host github) (EqText layer rest) (EqText method (Variants GET POST)) (EqNumber port https) (Prefix (Variants issuePrefix orgPrefix) path))) The binary, host, port, and layer checks are shared. Their ordering disappears because And is declared associative, commutative, and idempotent. Two Variants nodes identify the conflicting readings: the permitted operation and the path scope. The requirement settles both choices here. For an ambiguous requirement, the same nodes would give its owner two specific alternatives to resolve. CEL: The scope of a shared condition. The CEL example exposes a production check lost during refactoring. We reuse the expressions as candidate translations of this requirement: Allow a request exactly when it is in production and its port is either 80 or 443. // Candidate A (is_prod && port == 80) || (is_prod && port == 443) // Candidate B is_prod && port == 80 || port == 443 CEL’s && binds more tightly than ||, so candidate B applies the production check only to port 80. We encode the expressions with supplied Boolean and integer inputs, using isProd, port80, and port443 for the corresponding input and literals: (anti-unify :size 13 :cr 0.3636 :completion exact (Or (And (Eq port port443) (Variants isProd (Lit true))) (And isProd (Eq port port80)))) The port-80 branch is shared. In the port-443 branch, (Variants isProd (Lit true)) shows the missing production condition. At is_prod = false and port = 443, A denies the request and B allows it. The diff directs the review to one part of the sentence: whether “in production” applies to both alternatives. This example assumes that is_prod is supplied as a Boolean and port as an integer. Under these assumptions, neither expression raises an error. The encoding doesn’t model CEL errors or unknown values, and the engine doesn’t check these input assumptions. CEL-Java’s verification framework can check equivalence and policy invariants with Z3. Such checks can provide evidence when resolving a disagreement. The anti-unifier itself doesn’t decide which translation matches the requirement, and a mistake shared by both candidates would remain shared. Implementation and performance The algorithm runs over an e-graph, a data structure that stores a term together with everything it is known to equal. E-graphs (equivalence graphs) come from congruence-closure procedures in theorem provers and were popularized for compiler optimization by equality saturation, as described by Willsey et al. in “egg: Fast and Extensible Equality Saturation” (POPL 2021). This engine’s e-graph adds native canonization for associative and commutative operators. Anti-unification over e-graphs is also used for abstraction learning and program compression in babble (Cao et al., POPL 2023). Earlier implementations didn’t scale beyond small examples. Our saturation-based prototype also stalled there. Native AC canonization, AC-aware matching over distinct children, and direct search made subsecond queries practical. Semi-persistence reduced the cost of repeated queries. Native AC canonization. Associativity, commutativity, and idempotence are not rewrite rules in this engine. They are properties of the data structure. Associative-commutative (AC) operators store their children as canonical sorted multisets (ACI operators as canonical sorted sets) at insertion time. One e-node therefore represents all reassociations and permutations of a term and, for idempotent operators, treats duplicate children as one. Equality modulo the declared laws is structural equality. The rewrite-based alternative floods the e-graph with an exponential family of equivalent copies before real work starts. AC-aware matching over distinct children. Pattern matching against multiset nodes uses maximum-partition semantics: It branches over the distinct children of a node rather than enumerating multiplicity splits, so heavily repeated arguments do not cause a combinatorial blowup. Direct search instead of rewriting. Anti-unification itself isn’t encoded as rewrite rules either. An exact dynamic programming solver (:algorithm exact) solves the joint-decomposition problem optimally. Optimal here is relative to its size-first objective, the current e-graph, and the configured cycle policy. An anytime Monte Carlo graph search (:algorithm uct, the default) returns its best answer for any playout budget. On the worked example’s pair, 3,000 playouts reproduce the exact optimum. Both optimize first for result size and then, among equal-size answers, prefer those that retain more structure in the shared backbone. Semi-persistence. The e-graph supports (push) and (pop) snapshots recorded as sparse diffs rather than deep copies. Restoring a state therefore costs work proportional to what changed because the snapshot, plus the cost of repairing derived indexes. Proportional-cost restore lets the engine compare many candidates over one shared graph. A backtracking search can restore an earlier state without copying the full graph. A verified core and its scope. The e-graph’s underlying container layer is verified in Verus, a verifier for Rust. The verified property is that restore reproduces the state at the matching (push) (1,703 verified conditions, 0 errors). The anti-unification crate proves its objective-order and lower-bound lemmas, but the full solver doesn’t yet have an end-to-end refinement proof. The engine can log a justification for every equivalence it derives (--proofs). As the repository notes, these records aren’t yet independently replay-checked certificates. All of these claims, with evidence tiers and retractions, are in the repository’s claims inventory (doc/claims.md). Native canonization avoids materializing equivalent AC terms. Distinct-child matching controls multiplicity, direct solvers avoid encoding anti-unification as rewrites, and semi-persistence reduces the cost of repeated queries. Using semantic diffing in a pipeline The same method extends from two candidates to a larger sample. Generate N candidate formalizations of the requirement. Load them into one shared e-graph, saturate under your domain rules, and cluster them using pairwise equality checks. In the user guide’s larger Dogwood study, five samples collapse into three clusters. Candidates that differ only in presentation join the same equivalence classes during construction. Anti-unify the cluster representatives pairwise. Then, in a layer built on top of the engine’s output, group recurring Variants nodes by their position in the shared backbone. In the study, three pairwise diffs reduce to exactly two review items. Use the simplest available check for each item: schema validation, replay, example I/O pairs, or human review. With (push) and (pop) snapshots, you can test a proposed resolution without rebuilding the graph. Temporarily assert one branch of a Variants node as a domain fact, run the diff again, and roll back. A tool built on top of the engine could select and repair a full candidate against hard and soft constraints, for example with a MaxSMT solver over the variant space. MaxSMT (maximum satisfiability modulo theories) seeks a solution that satisfies all hard constraints while satisfying as many soft constraints as possible, or maximizing their total weight. Section 8 of Programming Z3 describes this form of optimization. That capability is not part of the current engine. Figure 2 summarizes the pipeline. Figure 2: A pipeline for clustering candidate formalizations, locating recurring disagreements, and routing each disagreement to an appropriate check. Cluster sizes and review-item counts are from the user guide’s larger Dogwood study Use a semantic-diff budget in continuous integration (CI). The command (checkau A B :max_size N :algorithm exact) prints nothing on success and causes the program to fail when the anti-unifier exceeds the budget. Every printed result in the user guide is pinned this way, so the guide and the engine can’t drift apart. The same command can serve as a regression gate. Set a maximum result size for a reference formalization and a regenerated one, and fail the pipeline when the anti-unifier exceeds it. The binary follows standard shell conventions: Results go to stdout, diagnostics (ok --- N nodes) go to stderr, and the process exits non-zero if any check fails. The diff can also guide a follow-up prompt or a question to the requirement owner. Mean pairwise :cr across samples gives a disagreement score for each requirement. A Variants node already contains the alternatives needed for a specific clarification, such as “did you mean strictly less than the threshold, or at most?” With several candidates, cluster equivalent outputs, compare the cluster representatives, and resolve recurring disagreements with validation, replay, examples, or human review. Get started Build the engine at the revision used for this post, then run the policy examples. These commands select the revision containing the OpenShell and CEL examples from pull request 103: git clone https://github.com/yaspar-org/semi-persistent.git cd semi-persistent git fetch origin 5a7969ae4ea88117a64faac4f42af5c358e213e2 git checkout --detach FETCH_HEAD cargo build --release # toolchain auto-pinned; Verus not required # The worked example from this post: ./target/release/semi-persistent egraph/examples/au_policy_divergence.egg # The Dogwood policy-diff example: ./target/release/semi-persistent doc/book/examples/20-dogwood-simple.egg # The constructed OpenShell and CEL translation examples: ./target/release/semi-persistent egraph/examples/au_openshell_policy.egg ./target/release/semi-persistent egraph/examples/au_cel_policy.egg # Your own formulas: declare a signature, two terms, and antiunify: ./target/release/semi-persistent MY_PROGRAM.egg The engine is Apache-2.0 on GitHub. The user guide progresses from basic terms to the policy case studies, and the test suite runs every program in it directly from the repository. Annex B documents the antiunify and checkau commands. If your artifact language has an abstract syntax tree (AST) and an equational theory, you can diff it: Declare the algebra, state the domain identities as rewrites, and ask for the most specific anti-unifier. If your policies are Cedar, whether handwritten or generated for Amazon Verified Permissions, the same recipe applies to them. The OpenShell and CEL examples show how to encode other policy constructs and compare candidate readings of a requirement. About the authors Ferhat Erata Ferhat is an Applied Scientist at AWS AI Labs. He combines large language models with formal reasoning to improve the safety and security of generative and agentic AI. His work includes autoformalization, verified code generation, and training reasoning models with verifier feedback. His offensive security research includes reverse engineering quantum circuits from power traces and detecting side-channel vulnerabilities in post-quantum cryptographic code. Over more than a decade in industry before his doctoral studies, he co-founded UNIT Research & Development, led the development of ModelWriter, a platform connecting text documents with formal models, and coordinated national consortia for EUREKA/ITEA industrial research projects. Ferhat holds a PhD in computer science from Yale University. His website is ferhat.ai. Rémi Delmas Rémi is a Principal Applied Scientist in the AWS Automated Reasoning Group, based in Boston. His work includes formal verification tools such as CBMC and Kani as well as neuro-symbolic autoformalization and reasoning systems. Before joining AWS, he worked at the Uber Advanced Technology Center in Paris on Urban Aerial Mobility. Before that, he spent a decade at ONERA, the French aerospace research lab, developing and applying formal methods for the design and verification of critical embedded systems. Earlier in his career, he worked at Prover Technology, building verification tools for railway control systems. He holds a PhD in computer science from ISAE-SUPAERO in Toulouse. His interests include automated reasoning, neuro-symbolic reasoning systems, software safety, and optimization.

items.title: The attendee’s guide to the AWS re:Invent 2026 AI/ML track
items.summary: From November 30th to December 4th, Amazon Web Services (AWS) will hold its annual premier learning event: re:Invent. At this event, attendees will become stronger and more proficient in various areas of AWS technology through a variety of experiences: keynotes given by AWS leaders, interactive working sessions led by AWS experts, and fun, immersive activities such as live entertainment and games at re:Play. There are over 2,000 learning sessions that focus on specific topics at various skill levels, and the AI/ML (AIM) track has more than 140 unique sessions for you to choose from. We’re here to help you identify the sessions that best fit your needs. Even if you can’t join in person, you can catch up with many of the sessions on demand and even watch the keynotes live. The basics: Session types If you can join us, then remember that we offer several types of sessions that can help maximize your learning in a variety of AWS topics. re:Invent attendees can choose to attend breakouts, chalk talks, builder sessions, workshops, and code talks. The breakout sessions are recorded and uploaded a few days after to the AWS Events YouTube channel, while the rest are live non-recorded interactive sessions. Here are the details for each session type: Breakout sessions: Attendees are in a lecture-style 60-minute informative session presented by AWS experts, customers, and partners. Chalk-talk sessions: Attendees interact with presenters, asking questions, and using a whiteboard in session. Builder sessions: Attendees participate in a one-hour session and build something. Workshop sessions: Attendees join a two-hour interactive session where you work in a small team to solve a real problem using AWS services. Code talk sessions: Attendees participate in engaging code-focused sessions where an expert leads a live coding session. Lightning talk sessions: Attendees watch a 20-minute demo dedicated to either a specific service or customer story (located in the Venetian Expo Hall or Wynn/Encore Upper Convention Promenade). With so many sessions to pick from, it helps to know how the pieces fit together. Here is how AWS thinks about its AI offerings, so you can decide where to begin and where to focus. The AWS AI stack overview and tie-in to re:Invent sessions AWS offers a comprehensive AI portfolio in the cloud. It covers everything from the physical infrastructure and AI chips that power AI workloads up through ready-to-use agentic solutions that teams can adopt today. Understanding how these services work together helps you navigate re:Invent and focus on the sessions most relevant to what you’re building. Figure 1: The AWS AI stack Global Infrastructure – It all starts with data centers designed and optimized for AI workloads. These facilities are built to handle the power, cooling, and networking demands that large AI training and inference jobs require. AI Chips – Running inside those data centers are two compute options: AWS Trainium, purpose-built for high-performance AI training and inference, and NVIDIA GPUs for teams that need GPU-based acceleration. Customers choose based on their workload, performance requirements, and cost targets. Data Foundation – AI is only as good as the data behind it. AWS Context connects your data across storage, databases, analytics, and search services, giving models and agents access to the right information at the right time. Models, Training, and Inferencing – This is where models get built, trained, fine-tuned, and served. Amazon Bedrock gives you managed access to hundreds of leading models from multiple providers through a unified API. Amazon SageMaker AI gives you full control to train, fine-tune, and deploy custom models on dedicated infrastructure. Many customers use both depending on the workload. Agent Development and Management – Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is where you build, deploy, and manage AI agents. It supports any model or provider mix, including models from both Amazon Bedrock and SageMaker AI, so teams can design agents that pick the right model for each task without being locked into a single provider. Agentic Solutions – At the top of the stack sit purpose-built agents that are ready to use. Kiro helps developers ship correctly the first time with spec-driven development. AWS Quick connects your applications, tools, and data into a personal knowledge graph that learns how you work. Amazon Connect delivers agents for customer experience, hiring, supply chain, and healthcare. AWS Marketplace gives you access to partner-built AI solutions. Security, Governance, and Cost Optimization run across every layer of the AI stack. They are built into the foundation, with hardware-level isolation at the chip layer and controls that enforce what agents can access and do. The AI-focused sessions at re:Invent span the full stack. Whether you’re evaluating AI chips, serving models in production, building custom models, deploying agents, or adopting ready-to-use solutions, this guide helps you find the sessions that matter most. Use it to build a smarter re:Invent schedule. The artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) track primarily focuses on three core layers of this stack: AI chips, models, training, and inference, and agent development and management, with security, governance, and cost optimization woven throughout. The following sections start at the chip layer and move up through models and agents. Then come sessions that tie the stack together. The guide ends with other relevant topics, such as sustainability and infrastructure where you run your AI workloads. Within each section, sessions for newcomers come first and technical deep dives come last. Want to skip ahead? Jump straight to the topic you care about: AWS AI platform sessions AI chips: NVIDIA GPUs and AWS Trainium Amazon SageMaker AI sessions Build and run AI applications and agents with Amazon Bedrock Build AI that works with documents, voice, and images Building trust in AI agents Other topics Plan your re:Invent AWS AI platform sessions These sessions cover the core AWS AI services together: Amazon Bedrock, Amazon SageMaker AI, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and the AI chips that they run on. They help you make architecture choices that still work as your usage grows. New to AI on AWS? Start with AIM204. It walks through the whole stack. You will see Trainium and Graviton chips, model inference on Amazon Bedrock and SageMaker AI, and production agents on AgentCore. If you’re already building, try AIM364. It helps you choose between Amazon Bedrock and SageMaker AI, and shows when to use both. The example is a real agentic coding app that runs on AgentCore. Other sessions dig into specific production problems. If you own data strategy, attend AIM363. This chalk talk shows how governed data products feed customization, inference, and agents. It also explains why cost levers like prompt caching, distillation, and batch inference work better on clean data. Need to prove the value of AI? AIM319 looks past cost to business impact. A live demo across the AI stack shows how to measure return on investment (ROI) and compare cost per outcome. Experienced builders should look at AIM443. In this 400-level chalk talk, you build a training pipeline on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod. You bring in company data and keep governance in place. Then you deploy the same model to Amazon Bedrock for inference or to AgentCore for agents. AI chips: NVIDIA GPUs and AWS Trainium AWS gives you two main choices of AI chips for training and inference: NVIDIA GPUs and AWS Trainium. Start with the one you use today, then explore the other. NVIDIA GPU sessions AWS offers a wide range of Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instances with NVIDIA GPUs. These sessions show how to run AI training and inference on them securely and reliably. Start with AIM2210 for the latest on GPU instances. In AIM3301, a customer shares how it gets the most from its GPU capacity by optimizing GPU scheduling. AIM392 explains when EC2 G7e and G7 instances are a good fit in place of P-series instances. Want to tune AI infrastructure with self-managed agents? Join AIM346. If you prefer hands-on learning, try AIM345 on disaggregated inference serving. In AIM344, you find the cause of real GPU cluster failures and how to recover from them. In the AIM347 workshop, you can practice GPU performance engineering. For data processing, see AIM3312. It shows how Amazon EMR with the NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark runs jobs up to 3.7x faster on EC2 G7 instances than on comparable CPU instances without code change. The session also covers DuckDB on GPUs. AWS Trainium sessions AWS Trainium is a family of AI chips purpose-built for next-generation deep learning training and inference. It delivers high performance at lower cost. Trainium runs on AWS Neuron, the software stack that connects Trainium to familiar frameworks like PyTorch, so teams build without rewrites. Customers who adopt Trainium-based Amazon EC2 instances may see better price performance than comparable instances. If you’re new to Trainium, AIM211 is the place to start. It traces the full stack, beginning with the silicon and working up to the application. For the latest system, AIM310 shows how Trainium3 and the Trn3 UltraServer keep large mixture-of-experts models performant. If you’re still evaluating transitioning to Trainium3, the AIM2213 panel gathers four AI leaders who have already shipped real products on Trainium. Several sessions are built around specific roles. Scientists and researchers who live in PyTorch should bring their questions to AIM339, a nanochat code talk, before getting hands-on in the AIM334 distributed-training workshop. ML engineers and developers can architect a production AI assistant with Hugging Face models in AIM349, and get hands-on with inference scaling in the AIM326 workshop. Performance engineers chasing peak throughput will want AIM329 on agentic optimization loops, followed by INV511, a 500-level look inside the Neuron Kernel Interface for serious kernel designers. If you want to run Trainium on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), AIM311 whiteboards a resiliency stack that holds up across deployments as large as twenty thousand accelerators. If you deploy through SageMaker AI instead, see the SageMaker AI section. For those who want to go further, world models are an emerging class that power simulation in gaming, robotics, and autonomous driving. AIM323 is a good starting point and covers serving world models with native PyTorch. From there, pick a hands-on path. In AIM304 you will deploy and optimize a real-time video world model using agentic Neuron workflows, while in AIM305 you will train vision-language-action models for physical AI. Both are builders’ sessions. Amazon SageMaker AI sessions Amazon SageMaker AI is the AWS service for customizing and deploying your own models. It handles the whole model lifecycle in one place. You can prepare data and customize a model on serverless compute. When you need more power, you can grow training jobs to thousands of accelerators. After your model is ready, deploy it on SageMaker inference endpoints or SageMaker HyperPod. You keep the model weights, and you decide where your models run. New to SageMaker AI? Start with AIM342. It shows how to build, customize, and deploy models with one service. Between sessions, stop by the Builder’s Hub and test your skills in one of three contests. Fine tune an agent, field a team in the Agentic Football Cup, or teach a robot a new task. For the latest on robotics, world models, and physical AI, hear a panel of builders in AIM2215. Still picking a model or learning to write evaluations? AIM2205 shows how to build evaluations on your own data. It also shows how to turn business knowledge into models that cost less to run. Customization starts with data. The AIM434 workshop shows how to prepare datasets for custom models. Next, AIM362 helps you pick the right compute for customization. Then fine-tune and deploy a large language model (LLM) in a few hours in AIM402. Customers will share their lessons too. In AIM393, Salesforce explains how it built and served its Koa models with open weights. Intuit tells its story in AIM361. If you build agents, AIM325 shows how to fine-tune agents that reason, using multi-turn reinforcement learning. The AIM456 workshop links evaluation, fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning into one pipeline. It spans SageMaker AI and Amazon Bedrock. And if you’re building domain-specific AI, you should join AIM2205. Learn how to test models on your own data and weigh quality against cost. The session also covers when customizing a model is worth it. In AIM398, watch the team behind Forge whiteboard a fast path to building tailored AI solutions, drawing on their end-to-end customer engagements. They will cover everything from setting the right evaluations and optimizing prompts, context, and inference serving to choosing a customization approach that modifies model weights during pre- or post-training. When you’re ready to grow training and inference, SageMaker HyperPod helps you get more from every GPU hour. Teams use it for specialized work like biology foundation models (FMs), physical AI, world models, and sovereign AI. Start with customers who push the limits. In AIM343, Tencent Games explains how it scaled to 1,000 GPUs. In AIM433, HUMAIN shows how it keeps GPU use high for both training and inference. For hands-on practice, build foundation model pipelines with Amazon EKS in AIM406, or tune AI pipelines with Ray in the AIM403 builders’ session. The AIM435 code talk teaches policy distillation, which trains a small model from a larger one. Physical AI teams can join the AIM318 workshop. It shows how to keep vision-language model training running when nodes fail. Robotics and autonomous vehicle teams can build a physical AI model factory on SageMaker HyperPod in AIM413. When it’s time to serve your models, two 200-level talks show inference in production. In AIM213, CrowdStrike explains how it runs LLM inference for threat detection with less operational work. In AIM214, Vanguard shares how it trains and serves custom LLMs on SageMaker HyperPod. To build agents on open-weight models with fast inference, try AIM405. To create fast, resilient inference endpoints, join the AIM404 workshop. Platform teams can practice governed ModelOps in the AIM348 builders’ session. They can also add observability with managed MLflow in the AIM408 workshop. Build and run AI applications and agents with Amazon Bedrock The model and inference approach you choose shapes what your AI app can do for users. Amazon Bedrock gives you a wide choice of models and helps you pick the right one for each task. It gives you the performance, security, and cost control to run AI apps in production. Some apps need to use tools and data, remember context, and act for you. For those, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore helps you build, connect, and improve agents. New to Amazon Bedrock? Start with AIM220. It covers what’s new in models, inference, security, and cost management. Then build and deploy your first Amazon Bedrock app in the hands-on AIM317 workshop. Next, think about the kind of workload you need to serve. A customer support app may need fast answers. A large document processing job may care more about cost and can wait for results. AIM448 helps you pick the Amazon Bedrock inference option that fits your needs. It weighs performance, capacity, cost, and data residency. If your app must reason across your company’s information, attend AIM308. In this session, you’ll build a knowledge assistant that finds answers across documents, images, structured data, and the links between them. Your inference plan also needs to stay affordable as usage grows. AIM437 helps you decide when to cache repeated context, route requests between models, or move work to batch inference. Model choice matters too. The newest model isn’t always the right one, and switching can change quality, speed, cost, and behavior. AIM438 shows how to test candidate models on your own use cases so you can switch with confidence. After your app is live, AIM374 covers the metrics, alarms, and operating habits to bring into production. Systems specialists can go deeper in INV517. This 500-level session looks at the scheduling and parallelism methods behind efficient large-model inference. If you want to build an agent, start with the full production picture rather than building infrastructure one piece at a time. AIM212 introduces the complete AgentCore lifecycle. Nasdaq also shares how it runs agents in a regulated industry. For a hands-on path, try AIM439. You start with a basic customer support agent. Then you add memory, tool access, identity, policies, observability, and evaluation until it’s ready for production. Ready to design a multi-agent system? AIM407 uses Strands Agents to coordinate specialized agents. You share state, handle failures, and deploy the result to AgentCore. After your agent is running, look at what happens under the hood. Each planning step, retrieval, tool call, and retry can add another model call. That changes cost, speed, and reliability. AIM429 connects agent design to inference behavior. It helps you think through context, harnesses, goals, and when an agent should stop. Developers who want to see these tradeoffs in code should follow it with AIM454. That session builds function calling, multi-step reasoning, and retrieval live. The stakes rise as agents serve more users and reach more systems. Bring your scaling questions to AIM436, where you work through traffic spikes, tool failures, model timeouts, and multi-tenancy. Platform teams that manage agents across a company should attend AIM303. It covers how to find agents, control tool access, manage identity, and see your whole fleet. If your priority is securing every step between a user request and an agent action, pair it with AIM370. Then use AIM440 to turn production traces and evaluations into a steady way to improve agent quality. Finally, pick a session that looks like the work you want an agent to do. AIM340 follows PepsiCo’s conversational ordering agent. It shows how memory, company APIs, and controls work together in a customer-facing workflow. AIM369 focuses on agents that respond to business events and run processes to the end, with human approval where needed. Software teams can get hands-on in AIM416. There, coding agents move off the laptop and run long-lived, parallel workflows on AgentCore. Build AI that works with documents, voice, and images AI apps often need to handle more than text. These sessions show how to build those skills on AWS. They add grounding, evaluation, and verification so your app holds up in real use. For document processing, start with AIM216 on Amazon Textract. Then, in AIM442, build a pipeline that turns documents into structured data you can check. Building voice apps? AIM217 introduces Amazon Polly and Amazon Transcribe, and AIM218 explores conversational AI with Amazon Nova Sonic. Go deeper with the AIM356 code talk, or build and deploy a voice agent in AIM352. Build cross-modal search in AIM357. To improve quality, add web grounding in AIM350 and automated evaluation in AIM351. You can also explore identity verification with Amazon Rekognition in AIM355. Building trust in AI agents AI agents now do real work, like approving claims, issuing refunds, and acting on customer data. Teams need a way to trust what those agents do and prove it to others. That starts with responsible AI, which helps organizations make careful choices about how AI systems are designed, built, and run. AWS builds on that with Trust in Depth. It’s an approach for giving agents more freedom without losing control. If you’re new to AI trust, start with the AIM2216 panel. It covers how to build confidence at each stage of an agent’s life. Topics include keeping an agent limited to its job and seeing exactly what it did. To see responsible AI governance in practice, attend AIM391. It shows how John Deere used AI Risk Intelligence to replace periodic manual reviews with continuous, automated governance. The change cut assessment time by more than 30 percent. Several sessions are built for specific roles. Developers can join the AIM336 workshop to audit a multi-agent claims system for responsible AI gaps. Then they fix what they find and write a report backed by evidence. Risk, compliance, and data science teams can join AIM332. This chalk talk covers testing whether agents treat people fairly when they approve loans or issue refunds. You learn how to choose fairness metrics and catch bias in outcomes that affect people’s lives. Do your agents decide things like insurance eligibility? The AIM335 workshop shows how to turn the rules behind those decisions into Automated Reasoning checks in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Each decision can then be proven correct and audited. For a deeper look at the science, several expert sessions cover automated reasoning. INV508 shows how subject matter experts can turn legal and regulatory policies into rules a machine can check. No coding is needed, and those rules then serve as AI guardrails. INV526 looks at what can be proven about agent behavior today, and where the limits are. The AIM451 chalk talk shows how to enforce rules that agents can’t get around. It also shows how to keep people involved in decisions machines shouldn’t make alone. Other topics A few more tracks round out your re:Invent planning, from sustainability to where you run your workloads. AWS Sustainability AWS is continuously innovating across its data centers, chips, and AI services to be more efficient and sustainable. AWS also gives you the data and tools to measure, track, and reduce the environmental impact of your own cloud and AI workloads running on AWS. These sessions discuss how we’re making our infrastructure more efficient and show how to act on sustainability data while still meeting your business goals. For the latest on the AWS Sustainability service, attend AIM201. This lightning talk covers new impact areas beyond carbon, more detailed data, and API access. In AIM205, learn how AWS makes AI infrastructure more sustainable. It uses hardware with low embodied carbon, energy-efficient custom chips, and data centers tuned by machine learning (ML). Want to understand the method behind your carbon data? Join the AIM321 chalk talk. It shows how to use that data to build AI workloads with a smaller footprint, which often cost less too. If you prefer hands-on learning, try AIM320. You build a generative AI pipeline with Amazon Bedrock that turns messy company data into sustainability insights. The session is based on how AWS handles life cycle assessment across its data centers. To go deeper, join AIM412. It uses Amazon Neptune and an Amazon Bedrock agent to map how stakeholders depend on each other. You then test ways to cut carbon on a knowledge graph. Local Zones and AWS AI Factories As teams move AI into production, where a workload runs matters as much as how it’s built. Large training jobs, fine-tuning, and real-time inference each need different things from infrastructure. AWS gives you several places to run them: AWS Regions, AWS Local Zones, AWS Dedicated Local Zones, AWS AI Factories, and AWS Outposts. Start with HMC303. It compares these options on the four factors that drive the choice: latency, data sovereignty, compute density, and scale. Databricks shares how it uses GPU capacity in select Local Zones. T-Mobile covers latency-sensitive distributed inference. In HMC307, see how Netflix supports its visual effects and animation teams from the Los Angeles Local Zone. Netflix starts Amazon EC2 G7e instances with NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs just in time. That way, artists get ComfyUI environments when they need them. Two hands-on workshops take different paths to building agents at the edge. HMC402 takes the managed route. You connect Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agents in an AWS Region to tools and agents in hybrid and edge locations. You use Model Context Protocol (MCP) and agent-to-agent (A2A) communication. HMC403 takes the self-managed path. You design, set up, and tune your own agents across Local Zones and Outposts. Then learn how to orchestrate fractional GPUs across the edge with NVIDIA Run:ai in the HMC401 code talk. Some organizations can’t move AI workloads to the public cloud at all. Data sovereignty, data gravity, or latency can stand in the way. AIM206 shows how AWS AI Factories bring AWS and NVIDIA AI infrastructure into your own data center. AWS runs and updates it for you. See how organizations run leading foundation models on premises for training and inference, while keeping full control of their data. Plan your re:Invent Use this guide to build your schedule. Then reserve your seats in the event catalog early, since popular sessions fill up fast. Pro tip: if sessions are showing as full in the online session catalog, we recommend favoriting the session and trying your luck by walking up to the session to see if any extra room has become available. There are other activities where you can learn about AWS AI/ML offerings. Visit the AI kiosks Between sessions, stop by the AI kiosks at the AWS Village in the Venetian’s Expo Hall. Each kiosk is run by AWS experts who focus on the topics covered, including product managers and solutions architects. They answer your questions, help you think through your use case, and run demos all day. When visiting the AWS Village, come visit these kiosks: Amazon Bedrock. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Amazon Foundation Models. Speech AI. Accelerated Computing. Strands Agents. AI League. Amazon SageMaker AI. Global Infrastructure & Sustainability. Hybrid Cloud & Edge Computing. Try the activations You can also get hands-on at four interactive experiences, also in the AWS Village in the Venetian’s Expo Hall: AWS Quick: See how work changes when AI agents join everyday operations. Watch solutions architects show Quick live at one of three live demo stations, or go through a demo on your own at one of three self-guided stations. You can also use the touchscreen knowledge graph to explore re:Invent content and sessions. Galactic Agents: Sit down at one of four builder stations to build a five-officer AI crew, then launch your starship. Your crew keeps exploring a shared galaxy on its own all week, even while you’re in sessions. Each officer maps to a real agent pattern that companies use. A giant live galaxy map and a look under the hood show how to run agents you can watch and trust on AWS. Curious how the game was built? Talk to the expert at the SME desk. Security at Machine Speed: Play a touchscreen tabletop game at one of two tables. You protect your cloud and earn points for each AWS security service you deploy. When you finish, visit the nearby security kiosks for deeper conversations. AWS Cloud Infrastructure: Don’t miss the infrastructure experience at the AWS Village. See the hardware behind the AWS Cloud, built on more than 20 years of cloud infrastructure innovation. A chip wall shows every generation of AWS Graviton, AWS Trainium, AWS Inferentia, and AWS Nitro Cards. Touchscreens explain how these chips work with partner chips for agentic AI, training, and inference. Get up close to Trainium and Graviton server trays and racks, and learn how they scale out with Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) and Amazon EC2 UltraClusters. Then explore a 3D model of AWS AI Factories to see how AWS brings its infrastructure into your own data center. It’s a good stop after the AI chips, AWS AI Factories, and Local Zones sessions. Can’t make it to Las Vegas? Watch the keynotes live and catch the breakout sessions later on the AWS Events YouTube channel. We hope to see you at re:Invent 2026. About the author Markus Adhiwiyogo Markus is a Senior Product Marketing Manager for AWS Trainium. He previously led product marketing for AWS Graviton, Amazon EC2 Spot Instances, and x86-based Amazon EC2 instances. Earlier, he worked as a cloud gaming product manager at Intel and in product & engineering roles at Lattice Semiconductor and Xilinx. He earned his BS and MS in Electrical and Computer Engineering at Carnegie Mellon University and his MBA at Duke’s Fuqua School of Business.
